formulas: Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b) for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD
Δn = gaseous product coefficients − gaseous reactant coefficients
keyPoints: Equilibrium is dynamic; forward and reverse rates are equal, not zero.
Use equilibrium concentrations; omit pure solids and liquids from K expressions.
K is temperature-dependent; catalysts do not change K.
Pressure favors fewer gas moles only when the sides have different gas counts.
Increasing temperature favors the endothermic direction.
notes: Equilibrium occurs when opposing processes have equal rates, so macroscopic properties remain constant. Chemical equilibrium is dynamic: forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates. A closed system at constant conditions is needed for stable equilibrium composition.

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c[D]^d/([A]^a[B]^b), using equilibrium concentrations and omitting pure solids and liquids. A large K means products are favored at equilibrium; a small K means reactants are favored. K describes position, not speed. At fixed temperature, changing concentration or pressure may shift composition but does not change K; temperature changes K.
For gaseous equilibria Kp uses partial pressures. Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is gaseous product coefficients minus gaseous reactant coefficients. Omit solids and liquids from Δn; if Δn = 0, Kp = Kc.

Le Chatelier's principle: a system shifts to partially oppose a disturbance. Adding reactant or removing product generally favors products; adding product or removing reactant favors reactants. Increasing pressure by decreasing volume favors the side with fewer gas moles; equal gas counts give no pressure shift. Raising temperature favors the endothermic direction and changes K; lowering temperature favors the exothermic direction. A catalyst speeds both directions and reaches equilibrium sooner but changes neither K nor equilibrium composition. Numerical calculations are not required in this unit.

Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat has four gas moles on the left and two on the right. Higher pressure shifts toward NH₃. Higher temperature shifts toward N₂ and H₂ because the forward reaction is exothermic. A catalyst changes rate, not position.
practiceQuestions: Write Kc for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g).
For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), predict the effect of increased pressure and explain.
For an exothermic forward reaction, predict effects of higher temperature and a catalyst.
For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), determine Δn and relate Kp to Kc.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/chemical.summary: Equilibrium constants describe composition at dynamic equilibrium. Use stoichiometric powers, count only gaseous species in Δn and apply Le Chatelier by identifying which disturbance the system partially opposes.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/chemical.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Chemical Equilibrium Study Guide

keyPoints: Select extraction methods according to ore composition and metal reactivity.
Calcination uses limited/no air; roasting is usually in excess air, especially for sulfides.
Flux plus gangue forms slag; roasting sulfides may release SO₂.
Downs process electrolyzes molten NaCl, not aqueous brine.
Group 2 hydroxide solubility generally rises down the group while sulfate solubility falls.
Memorize formulae and waters of crystallization for named industrial compounds.
notes: Metallurgy is extracting metals from ores and refining them. Hydrometallurgy uses aqueous solutions, pyrometallurgy uses high temperature, and electrometallurgy uses electrical energy. Gangue or matrix is unwanted ore material; flux reacts with gangue to form slag. An alloy is a metallic mixture; an amalgam contains mercury.

A typical extraction route includes concentration, conversion to a suitable compound, reduction and refining. Calcination heats an ore with limited/no air, often decomposing carbonates or hydroxides. Roasting usually heats sulfide ores in excess air, often forming oxides and SO₂. Smelting uses heat, reductant and flux to form molten metal and slag. Carbon reduction suits some oxides; thermite uses a more reactive metal such as aluminium; electrochemical reduction is used for highly reactive metals.

Poling uses reducing gases from green wood to remove oxide impurities from suitable molten metals. Electrorefining uses an impure anode, pure-metal cathode and electrolyte containing metal ions: target metal dissolves at the anode and deposits at the cathode; less reactive impurities may form anode mud.

Group 1 alkali metals have one valence electron, commonly form +1 ions, and become more reactive down the group. Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten NaCl in a Downs cell; CaCl₂ lowers the melting point. Sodium reacts vigorously with water to form NaOH and H₂. NaOH neutralizes acids and precipitates many metal hydroxides. Na₂CO₃ is an alkaline salt that releases CO₂ with acids.

Group 2 alkaline-earth metals commonly form +2 ions. Hydroxide solubility generally increases down the group, while sulfate solubility generally decreases; qualitative trends reflect lattice and hydration effects. Carbonate and nitrate thermal stability generally increases down the group as larger cations polarize the anion less. Common compounds: quicklime CaO; bleaching powder conventionally CaOCl₂; magnesia MgO; plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O; Epsom salt MgSO₄·7H₂O.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish calcination from roasting and state which is used commonly for sulfide ores.
Explain the roles of flux and slag during smelting.
Describe Downs-cell products and why molten salt is used instead of aqueous NaCl.
Write formulae of plaster of Paris and Epsom salt, including waters of crystallization.
State general Group 2 down-group solubility trends for hydroxides and sulfates.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/chemistr.summary: Extraction choices follow ore type and metal reactivity. Know the metallurgical sequence and vocabulary, then connect periodic trends to sodium chemistry and common industrial salts.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/chemistr.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Metals and Metallurgy Study Guide

formulas: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl (simplified aqueous equilibrium)
keyPoints: Reaction products and oxidizing behavior depend on conditions, including concentration and temperature.
Halogen oxidizing strength generally decreases down the group; hydrogen-halide reducing strength generally increases.
Ozone depletion involves catalytic radical chemistry in the stratosphere.
CO, NH₃, PH₃ and H₂S present serious inhalation hazards; H₂SO₄ is corrosive.
Learn each named substance's preparation, properties, tests and uses within the prescribed syllabus.
notes: Hydrogen isotopes are protium (¹H), deuterium (²H) and tritium (³H); heavy water is D₂O. Nascent hydrogen is a traditional term for freshly generated reactive hydrogen, not a distinct stable allotrope. Hydrogen peroxide decomposes as 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ and may act as oxidant or reductant depending on its partner. Oxides may be acidic, basic, amphoteric, neutral, peroxide or mixed; classify by behavior.

Ozone is bent O₃ formed from oxygen under energetic conditions. It is a strong oxidant and absorbs UV in the stratosphere. Ozone depletion is driven especially by catalytic chlorine/bromine radicals released from long-lived compounds; reducing ozone-depleting emissions supports recovery. Ozone depletion is not the same phenomenon as climate change.

N₂ is relatively inert because its N≡N bond is strong. Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal and a weak base: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. It forms ammonium salts with acids and reacts with oxygen under suitable conditions. Concentrated ammonia is hazardous. Nitric acid is a strong acid and oxidizer; products from metals depend on concentration and conditions. Nitrate can be tested by the brown-ring test using Fe²⁺ in acid.

Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂ are diatomic oxidizing non-metals; oxidizing strength generally decreases down the group. Reactions with water, alkalis and ammonia depend on conditions. Chlorine bleaches moist material through oxidation. Hydrogen-halide acidity in water generally increases down the group (HF is weak because of strong H–F bonding), while reducing strength rises down the group.

Carbon allotropes include diamond, graphite, fullerenes and amorphous forms. CO is a colourless, highly toxic reducing gas. PH₃ (phosphine) is toxic, weakly basic and reducing. H₂S is a toxic weak acid and reducing analytical reagent. SO₂ is an acidic oxide that can act as oxidant or reductant and as a bleaching agent. H₂SO₄ is acidic and, when concentrated, oxidizing and strongly dehydrating. Sodium thiosulfate is Na₂S₂O₃ and is used in photography and iodometric titration.

Never prepare or smell toxic gases as a home experiment. For each compound organize answers as preparation, observation, chemical explanation, balanced equation and use; state conditions. Concentrated acids and reagents require trained laboratory controls.
practiceQuestions: Classify acidic, basic, amphoteric and neutral oxides and give one example of each.
Explain nitrogen's relative inertness and one cause of ozone depletion.
Compare chlorine, bromine and iodine in oxidizing strength and describe a distinguishing test observation.
State two contrasting chemical roles of SO₂ and explain why CO is hazardous.
Describe the brown-ring test for nitrate and name the reagent responsible for the coloured complex.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/chemistr.summary: Organize non-metal chemistry by group and compound: preparation, condition-dependent reactions, characteristic tests and uses, with appropriate safety and environmental context.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/chemistr.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Chemistry of Non-metals Study Guide

keyPoints: Modern periodic position follows atomic number, not atomic mass.
Across a period, increasing effective nuclear charge usually contracts atomic radius.
Down a group, added shells usually increase size and metallic character.
For isoelectronic ions, greater proton count means smaller radius.
Ionization energy and electron affinity have exceptions; explain trends with shielding and shell structure.
notes: Modern periodic law states that properties of elements are periodic functions of atomic number. The table is arranged by increasing atomic number into periods and groups; blocks s, p, d and f indicate the subshell being filled. IUPAC groups are numbered 1–18.

Nuclear charge is +Ze. Inner electrons shield outer electrons; effective nuclear charge is often approximated as Z_eff ≈ Z − S, where S represents shielding. Across a period Z increases while shielding changes less, so valence electrons usually feel stronger attraction. Down a group, added shells and shielding change the attraction and increase the size of the valence shell.

Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases as effective nuclear charge rises; down a group it generally increases because a new shell is added. Cations are smaller than their parent atoms and anions larger. In an isoelectronic series, radius decreases as proton count rises. First ionization energy generally rises across and falls down, with subshell and pairing exceptions. Electronegativity generally rises across and falls down; it is a relative bonding scale. Metallic character generally decreases across and increases down.

Electron affinity is the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron. Trends are irregular and sign conventions vary: some sources use negative values for energy released, others quote energy released as a positive electron-gain enthalpy magnitude. State the convention if using numerical signs. Explain trends using effective nuclear charge, shielding and shell number rather than memorized arrows alone.
Example: O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ each have 10 electrons. Proton count increases from 8 to 12, pulling the shared electron cloud more strongly; radius decreases in the order O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺.
practiceQuestions: Explain why atomic radius generally decreases from Na to Cl but increases down Group 1.
Arrange N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻ and Na⁺ in increasing ionic radius and justify the order.
Distinguish nuclear charge from effective nuclear charge and describe shielding.
Describe general trends in first ionization energy, electronegativity and metallic character across a period.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/classifi.summary: Periodic properties recur with atomic number. Trends reflect the balance of nuclear attraction, shielding and shell number; use these to justify comparisons instead of memorizing directions alone.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/classifi.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Periodic Classification Study Guide
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/classifi.topicTitle: Classification of Elements and Periodic Table

formulas: % by mass of X = (mass of X in one formula unit ÷ Mᵣ) × 100%
Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass
keyPoints: Relative masses are ratios without units; molar mass is expressed in g mol⁻¹.
Empirical formula is the simplest ratio; molecular formula gives actual atom counts.
Use ion charges to form neutral ionic formulae and reduce subscripts to the simplest ratio.
Check percentage totals and state units in numerical answers.
notes: Chemistry explains the composition, structure, properties and transformations of matter, connecting microscopic atoms, ions and molecules with measurable properties. Physical chemistry studies principles and measurements; inorganic, organic and applied chemistry organize substances and practical uses.

An atom retains the chemical identity of an element. A molecule is a discrete bonded group; ionic compounds are described by formula units. Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) and relative molecular/formula mass (Mᵣ) are ratios to one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom and are dimensionless. Molar mass has units g mol⁻¹ and is numerically equal to the corresponding relative mass.

One atomic mass unit, u (or amu), is one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom. In school-level formulae, a radical is an atom or group of atoms that behaves as a unit and carries charge, such as NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻ or NO₃⁻. Write cations first, balance total charge, and use parentheses when a polyatomic ion occurs more than once.

A molecular formula gives actual atom counts (C₆H₁₂O₆); an empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio (CH₂O). Reduce subscripts by their greatest common divisor. If molar mass is known, multiply the empirical formula by n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass.

Mass percent of element X = (mass of X in one formula unit ÷ Mᵣ of compound) × 100%. For C₆H₁₂O₆, Mᵣ = 180 and carbon contributes 72/180 × 100 = 40.0%. Percentages should total approximately 100%; small differences can result from rounding.

Worked empirical-formula method: assume 100 g when percentages are given, convert each element's mass to moles, divide by the smallest amount, and scale to whole numbers. For 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O, the mole ratio is approximately 3.33:6.7:3.33 = 1:2:1, giving CH₂O.
Exam checks: distinguish dimensionless relative mass from molar mass in g mol⁻¹; verify ionic neutrality and simplest ratios; keep units in calculations and round only at the end.
practiceQuestions: Explain why relative molecular mass is dimensionless while molar mass has units.
Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in CaCO₃ using Ca = 40, C = 12 and O = 16.
Write the formulae of aluminium sulfate and ammonium phosphate from their ion charges.
A compound has empirical formula CH₂ and molar mass 56 g mol⁻¹. Determine its molecular formula.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/foundati.summary: Read formula subscripts, calculate relative masses, use ion charges to write neutral formulae, and distinguish empirical from molecular formulae.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/foundati.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Foundation and Fundamentals Study Guide

keyPoints: Select parent chain and numbering by IUPAC priority, then verify the complete structure.
Lassaigne's test detects selected elements after conversion into ions; it requires safe lab controls.
Cis/trans alkene isomerism needs restricted rotation and different groups on both alkene carbons.
d/l optical rotation is distinct from R/S configuration and D/L notation.
Homolysis produces radicals; heterolysis produces ions.
Inductive effects transmit through sigma bonds; resonance requires conjugation and delocalized electrons.
notes: Choose the longest parent chain containing the principal functional group and maximum multiple bonds. Number to give the senior functional group the lowest locant, then unsaturation and substituents by priority. Name substituents with locants, use di-/tri- for repeats, alphabetize substituent names ignoring multiplicative prefixes, then combine parent, unsaturation and suffix. Check that the name describes one unambiguous structure.

Lassaigne's sodium fusion converts covalently bonded nitrogen, sulfur and halogens into water-soluble ionic salts. Appropriate tests can detect nitrogen (Prussian blue after iron salts and acid), sulfur and halides (silver halide precipitates after acidification with nitric acid). Incomplete fusion and interfering ions can give false results. Sodium and reagents make this a supervised laboratory procedure, never a home experiment.

Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity or spatial arrangement. Structural isomerism includes chain, position, functional-group, metameric and tautomeric forms. Geometrical isomerism requires restricted rotation and, for an alkene, two different substituents on each double-bond carbon. Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of chiral molecules. d/l indicates optical rotation direction, not R/S configuration or D/L biochemical notation.

Homolytic fission divides a bond pair equally and makes radicals. Heterolytic fission gives both bonding electrons to one atom and makes ions. An electrophile accepts an electron pair; a nucleophile donates an electron pair; a free radical has an unpaired electron. Use full-headed curved arrows for electron pairs and fish-hook arrows for single electrons.

The inductive effect is sigma-bond polarization transmitted through a chain and weakens with distance. Groups may show +I electron release or −I withdrawal. Resonance describes electron delocalization through conjugation; +R groups donate electron density and −R groups withdraw it. Resonance contributors are bookkeeping structures for a hybrid: do not move atoms, and preserve total charge and electron count.
practiceQuestions: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, CH₃CH=CHCH₃ and CH₃CH₂CHO by IUPAC rules.
Draw structural isomers of C₄H₁₀ and classify their isomerism.
Explain why 2-butene can show geometrical isomerism.
Distinguish heterolytic from homolytic cleavage of a C–Br bond.
Compare inductive and resonance effects, including how each is transmitted.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/fundamen.summary: Solve organic problems by naming structures correctly, classifying isomerism and tracking electron movement. Keep connectivity, stereochemistry, bond fission and electronic effects distinct.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/fundamen.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Fundamental Principles of Organic Chemistry Study Guide

keyPoints: Product development includes research, pilot testing, scale-up, regulatory review and controlled commercialization.
Revenue, profit and cash flow differ; cash timing can affect viability.
Plant design integrates process performance, quality, worker safety and environmental controls.
Batch and continuous processes trade flexibility against throughput and operating stability.
Pollution prevention and life-cycle assessment should be considered from process design onward.
notes: The chemical industry converts raw materials into useful products such as fertilizers, medicines, fuels and polymers. Product development proceeds from need identification and research/formulation through laboratory testing, pilot trials, process and safety design, regulatory/environmental review, scale-up, quality assurance and improvement. Scale-up must consider heat/mass transfer, hazards, supply chains and reproducibility; a laboratory recipe cannot simply be multiplied without engineering review.

Production economics considers costs, revenue, capacity, quality and risk. Fixed costs include facilities/equipment; variable costs include feedstock, energy and packaging. Cash flow tracks when money enters and leaves; apparent profitability does not guarantee funds are available when operating costs are due. Consider break-even, working capital, yield, waste treatment, maintenance and demand. Distinguish revenue, profit and cash flow.

Plant design selects process route, equipment, compatible materials, operating conditions, control systems, utilities, waste treatment and emergency protections. A process flow diagram shows major equipment and stream directions; flow sheets support mass/energy accounting. Safe operation requires trained staff, monitoring, quality control, maintenance, hazard analysis and emergency procedures. Pressure, temperature, toxicity, flammability and corrosion inform design; industrial operation requires professional engineering and regulatory oversight.

Batch processing charges a defined quantity, completes a sequence, then empties and cleans equipment; it is flexible for varied or lower-volume production but can have downtime and batch variation. Continuous processing feeds and withdraws material during steady operation; it can provide high throughput and consistency but requires reliable demand, control and specialized equipment. Hybrid systems are common. Compare throughput, flexibility, capital, cleaning, quality and safety.

Environmental impacts can include emissions, wastewater, solid waste, greenhouse gases, resource depletion and spills. Prevention prioritizes avoiding/reducing hazardous inputs and waste at source, improving atom/resource efficiency, safe reuse/recycling, treating residual emissions and monitoring compliance. Life-cycle thinking considers raw-material extraction through manufacture, use and end-of-life. Environmental performance is a design requirement, not an afterthought.
practiceQuestions: Outline stages from laboratory formulation to commercial manufacture of a chemical product.
Distinguish fixed and variable costs and explain why positive profit may coexist with a cash shortage.
Compare batch and continuous processing for a frequently changing small product range.
Identify four environmental impacts of chemical manufacture and propose a prevention/control measure for each.
Explain why process scale-up requires engineering reassessment rather than multiplying laboratory quantities.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/fundamen.summary: Applied chemistry connects chemical principles with products and production systems. Strong answers trace product/process choices while integrating economic viability, safe plant operation and environmental protection.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/fundamen.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry Study Guide

formulas: RCOONa + NaOH (soda lime, heat) → RH + Na₂CO₃ (balance for the specific R group)
keyPoints: Addition occurs at π bonds; substitution replaces an alkane hydrogen.
The peroxide effect is a special HBr radical case, not a general HX rule.
Only terminal alkynes give characteristic ammoniacal Ag⁺/Cu⁺ precipitate tests.
Bromine-water and Baeyer's tests indicate unsaturation but do not identify one specific compound.
Show reagents and conditions above arrows and balance full reactions.
notes: Acyclic alkanes have formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and C–C single bonds; monoalkenes have CₙH₂ₙ; monoalkynes have CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. Rings or additional unsaturation change these formulae. Alkanes are relatively unreactive; π bonds make alkenes and alkynes undergo addition.

Alkane preparations include haloalkane reduction, Wurtz coupling (two alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether), decarboxylation of sodium carboxylates with soda lime, and catalytic hydrogenation. Alkanes undergo substitution: halogenation under light/heat uses a radical chain; nitration and sulphonation require suitable conditions. Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O; oxygen shortage may produce CO or carbon. Balance equations and state conditions.

Alkenes can be prepared by alcohol dehydration, haloalkane dehydrohalogenation or catalytic hydrogenation of alkynes. Electrophilic addition breaks the π bond. In usual Markovnikov addition of HX, H attaches to the carbon already bearing more H atoms. The peroxide effect is chiefly observed for HBr and gives anti-Markovnikov orientation by a radical pathway; do not generalize it to HCl or HI. Acid-catalyzed hydration produces alcohols; ozonolysis cleaves the double bond to carbonyl products after work-up.

Ethynes can be prepared from calcium carbide and water or by double dehydrohalogenation of suitable dihalides. Alkynes add H₂, HX and water, with selectivity depending on conditions. Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic because H is attached to an sp carbon; they form salts with suitable bases and precipitates with ammoniacal AgNO₃ or cuprous chloride. Internal alkynes lack this terminal H and do not give these tests.

Bromine water and alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's test) are decolorized/reduced by many unsaturated compounds, but these are qualitative indications, not unique structural proof. Similar-size hydrocarbons tend to have higher boiling points as size/surface area rises; branching tends to lower boiling point. Kolbe electrolysis couples carboxylate-derived radicals at the anode; follow the exact conditions and expected product.
practiceQuestions: Write equations for methane chlorination under light and complete ethane combustion.
Predict the major product of propene + HBr with and without peroxide, explaining the distinction.
Describe a test to distinguish 1-butyne from 2-butyne and explain why it works.
Show one syllabus preparation each for an alkane, alkene and alkyne.
Explain why terminal alkynes are weakly acidic and undergo addition.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/hydrocar.summary: Classify the hydrocarbon first, then select reaction patterns appropriate to its bonds. State conditions and remember the limited HBr peroxide effect and terminal-alkyne tests.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/hydrocar.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Hydrocarbons Study Guide

keyPoints: Haber and Contact operating conditions balance equilibrium, rate, safety and cost.
A catalyst speeds equilibrium attainment but does not change equilibrium constant.
Ostwald proceeds through NO and NO₂ before nitric-acid absorption.
The diaphragm cell separates chlorine from hydrogen/alkali products.
Solvay precipitates NaHCO₃ first; heating produces Na₂CO₃ and process materials are recycled.
Urea synthesis proceeds through ammonium carbamate.
notes: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic and reduces gas moles from four to two. Purified gases react under elevated pressure and a moderate temperature with an iron-based catalyst; ammonia is condensed and unreacted gases recycled. Pressure favors ammonia, while a very low temperature slows reaction, so conditions balance yield, rate, cost and safety. A catalyst changes rate, not equilibrium position.

Ostwald process: ammonia is catalytically oxidized to nitric oxide, NO is oxidized to NO₂, and NO₂ is absorbed in water with oxygen to form nitric acid while NO is recycled. Representative equations: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O; 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃. Control catalyst condition, absorption and NOₓ emissions.

Contact process: sulfur or sulfide ore is burned to SO₂, which is purified and oxidized: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃. Lower temperature and higher pressure favor the exothermic product side, but industry uses a practical compromise and vanadium(V) oxide catalyst. SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated sulfuric acid to form oleum, then carefully diluted; direct hydration can form acid mist. Heat recovery and emissions controls matter.

Diaphragm-cell brine electrolysis: anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻; overall 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂. A diaphragm limits mixing of chlorine with alkali and hydrogen. Brine purification and safe separation are critical.

Solvay process: brine saturated with ammonia and CO₂ precipitates NaHCO₃: NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl. Heating gives Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O from 2NaHCO₃. Limestone decomposition supplies CO₂ (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂); lime slaking helps recover ammonia. Identify recycled materials and distinguish the NaHCO₃ intermediate from final sodium carbonate.

Urea manufacture proceeds via ammonium carbamate: 2NH₃ + CO₂ ⇌ NH₂COONH₄, then NH₂COONH₄ ⇌ NH₂CONH₂ + H₂O. Unconverted reactants are recovered and recycled; product is concentrated and granulated/prilled. Urea supplies nitrogen, but agronomic efficiency depends on soil, water and application conditions.
practiceQuestions: Draw a Haber flow sequence and explain ammonia removal and gas recycle.
Write the Ostwald stages and balance the oxidation/absorption equations.
Explain the Contact-process equilibrium compromise and why SO₃ is absorbed in acid rather than directly in water.
Write diaphragm-cell electrode half-reactions and the overall NaOH manufacture equation.
Trace recycled materials through the Solvay process and identify its precipitated intermediate.
Write the two urea synthesis stages and identify ammonium carbamate.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/modern-c.summary: Industrial-process answers follow feed preparation, reaction conditions, intermediate separation, recycle and product finishing. Balance equations and explain how equilibrium, kinetics, safety and environmental controls shape manufacture.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/modern-c.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Modern Chemical Manufactures Study Guide

keyPoints: Oxidation/reduction and the oxidizing/reducing agents are named from their electron changes.
Oxidation-number sums equal the total charge of the species.
Oxidation is at the anode and reduction at the cathode in every cell.
An electrolytic-cell anode is positive and cathode negative.
Faraday calculations use balanced half-reaction electron number z and charge in coulombs.
notes: Oxidation is loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number, or classically addition of oxygen/removal of hydrogen. Reduction is electron gain, decrease in oxidation number, or removal of oxygen/addition of hydrogen. Both occur together. The reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidized; the oxidizing agent accepts electrons and is reduced.

An element in free form has oxidation number 0; a monatomic ion's number equals its charge. Fluorine is −1 in compounds. Oxygen is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides; positive in OF₂). Hydrogen is usually +1 with nonmetals and −1 in metal hydrides. Group 1 metals are +1 and Group 2 are +2. The sum of oxidation numbers equals total species charge. These are bookkeeping values, not necessarily actual charges in covalent compounds.

Oxidation-number method: identify atoms whose oxidation numbers change, calculate total increase and decrease, and choose coefficients to equalize electron loss and gain; balance remaining atoms and check charge. Half-reaction method in acid: balance non-H/O atoms, O with H₂O, H with H⁺, and charge with e⁻. In base, add OH⁻ to both sides to neutralize H⁺, form water and cancel excess water.

Electrolysis uses an external power source for a non-spontaneous redox reaction. Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode in all electrochemical cells. In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive and the cathode negative; cations move toward the cathode, anions toward the anode. Products depend on discharge tendencies, concentration, electrode material and whether the electrolyte is aqueous or molten.

Faraday calculations: Q = It; one mole of electrons carries F ≈ 96485 C mol⁻¹. If a product requires z electrons per particle, n = Q/(zF), and mass m = MIt/(zF). Determine z from the balanced electrode half-reaction, use current in amperes and time in seconds, and check the answer's units.
Worked check: 2.00 A for 30.0 min gives Q = 2.00 × 1800 = 3600 C. For Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, n(Cu)=3600/(2×96485)=0.0187 mol, or about 1.19 g with M=63.55 g mol⁻¹.
practiceQuestions: Find sulfur's oxidation number in H₂SO₄ and SO₄²⁻.
Balance MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ in acidic solution by half-reactions.
Calculate the silver mass deposited from Ag⁺ by 9650 C. Use Ag = 107.9 g mol⁻¹.
Explain why molten NaCl and aqueous NaCl can produce different electrolysis products.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/oxidatio.summary: Track electron transfer with oxidation numbers, balance redox equations with equal electron loss and gain, and use Q = It plus the electrode half-reaction for electrolysis quantities.
notes/guides/class-11/chemistry/oxidatio.title: Class 11 Chemistry — Oxidation, Reduction and Electrolysis Study Guide

formulas: At fixed P,n: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (T in K)
keyPoints: Use kelvin for gas-law calculations.
Dalton partial pressure equals mole fraction times total pressure for ideal mixtures.
Graham's rate ratio uses the square root of the inverse molar-mass ratio.
Real-gas deviations are greatest at high pressure and low temperature.
At boiling, vapour pressure equals external pressure; distinguish moisture behavior of solids.
notes: The ideal-gas kinetic model treats particles as widely separated, moving randomly with negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions. Boyle's law: P ∝ 1/V at fixed T,n. Charles's law: V ∝ T at fixed P,n. Avogadro's law: V ∝ n at fixed T,P. Combine them as PV = nRT. Convert temperature to kelvin and keep units consistent with R.

Dalton's law states total pressure equals the sum of component partial pressures; for an ideal mixture pᵢ = xᵢP. Graham's law gives r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁) for diffusion/effusion under the same conditions: lighter gases move faster. Do not reverse the molar-mass ratio.

Real gases have finite molecular volume and attractions. Deviations are strongest at high pressure and low temperature, especially near liquefaction. The van der Waals equation (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT corrects for attractions (a) and molecular volume (b); constants are gas-specific. Ideal behavior is approached at low pressure and high temperature.

Evaporation occurs at a liquid surface below its boiling point; condensation returns vapour to liquid. Vapour pressure is the pressure of vapour in equilibrium with the liquid. Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals external pressure, so boiling point depends on pressure. Surface tension generally falls as temperature rises. Liquid viscosity generally decreases with temperature; gas viscosity generally increases. Liquid crystals have partial order and properties between ordinary liquids and crystalline solids.

Crystalline solids have long-range order and a characteristic melting point; amorphous solids lack long-range order and soften over a range. Deliquescent solids absorb moisture until they dissolve; efflorescent hydrates lose water of crystallization; hygroscopic substances absorb moisture without necessarily dissolving. A crystal lattice repeats in three dimensions; a unit cell is its smallest repeating volume. Crystallization and crystal growth depend on controlled supersaturation and conditions.
Example: a 2.00 L sample at 300 K and 1.00 atm is heated to 450 K at constant pressure. Charles's law gives V₂ = 2.00 × 450/300 = 3.00 L. Use kelvin; Celsius ratios are invalid.

formulas: Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ; n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass
keyPoints: Balanced-equation coefficients give mole ratios, not mass ratios.
Use the smallest n/ν value to identify the limiting reactant.
Avogadro volume ratios require equal temperature and pressure.
Mass and atoms are conserved in balanced chemical reactions.
notes: Dalton proposed that matter consists of atoms, compounds form from atoms in fixed whole-number ratios, and chemical reactions rearrange atoms. Modern evidence refines that atoms contain subatomic particles and isotopes differ in mass. Conservation of mass requires the same number of every atom on each side of a balanced equation. The laws of definite and multiple proportions describe fixed composition and simple mass ratios in compounds.

Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Thus V ∝ n at fixed T and P. For ideal gases use PV = nRT; only use a stated molar gas volume when its reference conditions are specified. Vapour density relative to hydrogen is Mᵣ/2 for gases measured comparably.

One mole contains Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ specified entities. Identify whether the entities are atoms, molecules, ions or formula units. Convert mass using n = m/M, particle count using N = nNₐ, and ideal gas quantities using PV = nRT.

Balance the chemical equation by changing coefficients only, never formula subscripts. Coefficients provide mole ratios. Convert given quantities to moles, apply the equation ratio, then convert to the requested mass, volume or particle count.

For each reactant compute nᵢ/νᵢ, where nᵢ is its available amount and νᵢ its balanced-equation coefficient. The smallest ratio identifies the limiting reactant and controls the theoretical product amount; other reactants are in excess. Subtract the consumed amount to find excess remaining.

Theoretical yield is the maximum product predicted from the limiting reactant. Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%. For empirical formula from mass percentages, assume 100 g, convert to moles, divide by the smallest mole amount and scale to whole numbers. Molecular formula = empirical formula multiplied by n = molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass.
Worked limiting-reactant example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. With 4 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂, the ratios are 4/2 = 2 and 1/1 = 1, so O₂ limits. It forms 2 mol H₂O, consumes 2 mol H₂ and leaves 2 mol H₂.

Common checks: never choose the limiting reactant by comparing grams alone; convert to moles and divide by coefficients. Use a balanced equation, retain units and sensible significant figures, and check atom conservation. A measured yield above 100% usually signals impure/wet product or error rather than a physically possible pure-product yield.

notes: What is a Short Story?

A short story is a brief work of prose fiction that can normally be read in one sitting. It focuses on a single incident, character, or idea, and develops it with economy of language. Unlike a novel, a short story usually has a limited number of characters, one central conflict, and one main effect.
Key Elements of a Short Story

Plot: the sequence of events in the story — exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Character: the people (or animals, or forces) in the story; they can be round (well developed, changing) or flat (simple, unchanging). Setting: the time and place of the action, which influences mood and conflict. Theme: the central idea or message of the story — what the story means beyond its events. Point of view: the perspective from which the story is told — first person (I), second person (you), or third person (he/she/they; limited or omniscient). Conflict: the struggle at the heart of the story — internal (man vs self) or external (man vs man, man vs nature, man vs society).
How a Short Story is Built

A good short story starts with a hook that creates curiosity, moves through rising tension to a climax (the turning point), and ends with a resolution — which may be closed (everything is settled) or open (leaving the reader to decide). Writers often use foreshadowing (hints of what will come) and symbolism (objects or actions standing for larger ideas) to deepen meaning.
Short Stories in the NEB English Syllabus

In the NEB (Nepal Education Board) English curriculum, short stories are studied to develop skills of comprehension, analysis and interpretation. Students are expected to identify the elements above, explain the theme in their own words, relate the story to real life, and answer questions about character, setting, plot and moral values.

confusion: Students often confuse "the limit exists" with "the function is continuous". A limit can exist at a point where the function is not continuous (e.g., a removable discontinuity).
Do not treat limits as just algebra exercises — they have deep geometric and physical meaning that makes the rest of calculus meaningful.
notes: **What is calculus?** Calculus is the mathematics of change and motion. It has two main branches: differential calculus (rates of change) and integral calculus (accumulation and area). Both branches rest on the concept of a limit.

**Why limits matter:** Limits formalize the idea of "approaching" a value. Without limits, we cannot rigorously define the derivative (instantaneous rate of change) or the integral (area under a curve).

**Limits → Derivatives → Integration:** The derivative $f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$ uses a limit to define instantaneous rate of change. The definite integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is defined as a limit of Riemann sums.

**Continuity bridges limits and differentiation:** A function must be continuous (no breaks, holes, or jumps) at a point before it can be differentiated there. Continuity is necessary but not sufficient for differentiability.

**Key strategy for evaluating limits:** (1) Try direct substitution. (2) If it gives a number, that is the limit. (3) If it gives $0/0$ or another indeterminate form, use algebraic simplification, rationalisation, factoring, or standard limits.
**Standard limits to memorise:** $\lim_{x \to 0}(\sin x)/x = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 0}(e^x - 1)/x = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 0}\ln(1+x)/x = 1$, $e = \lim_{n \to \infty}(1+1/n)^n$.
**Types of discontinuity:** Removable (hole), jump (step), infinite (vertical asymptote), essential (oscillatory). Understanding these helps in sketching graphs and later in integration.
**Connection to real-world:** Limits model instantaneous velocity, marginal cost in economics, population growth rates, and any quantity that changes continuously over time.

notes: कविता साहित्यको त्यस्तो विधा हो जसमा भावना, अनुभव र कल्पनालाई लय, ताल, प्रतीक र अलङ्कारका माध्यमबाट कलात्मक रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरिन्छ। कविता भनेको शब्दहरूबाट बनेको चित्र हो जसले पाठकको मनमा भावना जगाउँछ।
कविताका तत्वहरू

भावना (Emotion): कविताको प्राण भावना नै हो — प्रेम, वेदना, देशभक्ति, प्रकृतिप्रतिको आकर्षण आदि। कल्पना (Imagination): कविले कल्पनाको सहाराले वस्तु र घटनालाई नयाँ रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्छ। लय (Rhythm): शब्दहरूको आवृत्तिबाट सिर्जना हुने संगीतात्मक प्रवाह। प्रतीक (Symbol): वस्तु वा घटनाले अर्को गहिरो अर्थलाई संकेत गर्छ। अलङ्कार (Figure of speech): उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा आदिको प्रयोगले कवितालाई सुन्दर बनाउँछ।
कविताका प्रकारहरू

कविता मुख्यतया दुई प्रकारकी हुन्छन्: गद्य कविता (Free verse) जसमा नियमित लय वा तुक नहुन सक्छ, र छन्दोबद्ध कविता (Metrical poetry) जसमा निश्चित छन्द, गति र तुक हुन्छ। विषयवस्तुका आधारमा कवितालाई प्रकृति कविता, देशभक्ति कविता, प्रेम कविता, आधुनिक कविता आदिमा वर्गीकरण गर्न सकिन्छ।
NEB पाठ्यक्रममा कविता

NEB (राष्ट्रिय परीक्षा बोर्ड) को नेपाली पाठ्यक्रममा कविता अध्ययनको उद्देश्य विद्यार्थीहरूमा भावनात्मक संवेदना, भाषिक सौन्दर्यबोध र आलोचनात्मक चेतना विकास गर्नु हो। कविता पढ्दा भाव, भाषा, शिल्प र सन्देश — यी चार पक्षमा ध्यान दिनुपर्छ।

notes: - **Newton's first law:** inertia — no net force ⇒ no change in velocity.

notes: - **Kinematics** studies motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without asking about forces.
- **Instantaneous velocity** v = dx/dt; **instantaneous acceleration** a = dv/dt.
- **Equations of motion (uniform a):** v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.
- **Relative velocity:** v_AB = v_A − v_B (same line: add when approaching, subtract when chasing).
- **Free fall:** v = gt; h = ½gt²; v² = 2gh; time to reach top for upward throw t = u/g; max height u²/2g.
- **Projectile:** T = 2u sinθ/g; H = u² sin²θ/2g; R = u² sin2θ/g; range maximum u²/g at 45°.
- **Graphs:** slope of x–t → velocity; slope of v–t → acceleration; area under v–t → displacement.
- **Remember:** at the top of a projectile or a vertical throw, velocity = 0 but acceleration = g — never zero.
- **Mechanics = statics + kinematics + dynamics** (forces → Newton's laws, covered in the Dynamics unit).
notes/guides/class-11/physics/kinematics.title: Quick Revision — Kinematics (Mechanics)

notes: - **Physical quantity** = magnitude × unit; measurable property of matter/energy.
- **Seven SI base units:** m (length), kg (mass), s (time), K (temperature), A (current), mol (amount), cd (luminous intensity).
- **Derived quantities** are formed from base quantities (area, velocity, force, pressure, power).
- **Dimension symbols:** length [L], mass [M], time [T], temperature [K], current [A].
- **Dimensional formulas:** velocity [L T⁻¹], force [M L T⁻²], work [M L² T⁻²], pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²], power [M L² T⁻³], G [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²].
- **Uses of dimensional analysis:** check correctness of equations, derive relations (up to a constant), convert units n₁u₁ = n₂u₂.
- **Homogeneity rule:** only quantities of same dimensions may be added/equated.
- **Limitations:** cannot determine dimensionless constants, functions (trig/log/exp), or distinguish same-dimension quantities (work vs torque).
- **Significant figures:** non-zero digits + zeros between them are significant; leading zeros are not.
- **Errors:** absolute error = |value − mean|; relative = Δa/a; percentage = Δa/a × 100%.
- **Scientific notation** a × 10ⁿ (1 ≤ a < 10); **order of magnitude** is the nearest power of ten.
notes/guides/class-11/physics/physical-q.title: Quick Revision — Physical Quantities & Dimensions

notes: - **Scalar:** magnitude only (mass, speed, work). **Vector:** magnitude + direction (velocity, force, displacement).
- **Resultant (parallelogram law):** $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$; direction $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$.
- **Triangle & polygon laws:** resultant closes the vector polygon — head-to-tail addition.
- **Resolution:** a vector $\vec{A}$ at angle $\theta$ to the x-axis has components $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$; $A = \sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$.
- **Unit vector:** $\hat{A} = \dfrac{\vec{A}}{A}$ (dimensionless, magnitude 1); $\vec{A} = A\hat{A}$.
- **Scalar (dot) product:** $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x+A_yB_y+A_zB_z$ (commutative, result is scalar).
- **Vector (cross) product:** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = AB\sin\theta \,\hat{n}$ (direction by right-hand rule; result is vector).
- **Component form:** $\vec{A}\times\vec{B} = (A_yB_z-A_zB_y)\hat{i}+(A_zB_x-A_xB_z)\hat{j}+(A_xB_y-A_yB_x)\hat{k}$.
- **Perpendicular** iff $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=0$; **parallel** iff $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=0$.
- **Applications:** finding force components, displacement in planes, work $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{s}$, torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r}\times\vec{F}$.
notes/guides/class-11/physics/vectors/01.title: Quick Revision — Vectors

notes: **Cell theory:** all living organisms are composed of cells; the cell is the structural and functional unit of life; all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow).
**Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells:** prokaryotes lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (bacteria); eukaryotes have a nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, ER, Golgi bodies.
**Mitochondrion:** powerhouse of the cell — site of aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis; has its own circular DNA (semi-autonomous organelle).

**Biomolecules:** carbohydrates (energy source; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆), proteins (made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds), lipids (fats/oils; concentrated energy store), nucleic acids (DNA/RNA carry hereditary information).
**Enzymes** are globular protein catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy; they are substrate-specific and work best at optimum temperature and pH.
notes/theory/class-11/biology/cell-biomo.title: Cell Biology & Biomolecules

notes: **Porifera (sponges):** pore-bearing aquatic animals with canal system; skeleton of spicules.
**Arthropoda:** largest phylum — jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton, open circulatory system (insects, crabs).
**Chordata characters:** notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits and post-anal tail at some stage of life.

**Oparin–Haldane theory:** life originated from non-living organic molecules in the primitive reducing atmosphere ('primordial soup'); Miller–Urey experiment (1953) supported it by producing amino acids from CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O with electric discharge.
**Darwinism:** natural selection — survival of the fittest; variations that help survival are inherited.

**Ecology levels:** organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome. Food chain shows energy flow; ~10% energy transfers to each trophic level. **Conservation:** in-situ (national parks) and ex-situ (zoos, seed banks).
notes/theory/class-11/biology/faunal-evo.title: Faunal Diversity, Evolution & Environment

notes: **Binomial nomenclature** was introduced by Carolus Linnaeus — every organism gets two names: generic name + specific epithet (e.g. Mangifera indica).
**Five kingdom classification (Whittaker):** Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell structure, body organisation and nutrition.

**Algae:** chlorophyll-bearing, aquatic thalloid organisms; green algae (Spirogyra) have ribbon-shaped spiral chloroplasts; brown algae (Laminaria) have fucoxanthin; red algae (Polysiphonia) contain r-phycoerythrin.
**Bryophytes:** amphibians of the plant kingdom; need water for fertilisation; e.g. mosses and liverworts.
**Bacteria:** prokaryotic, reproduce by binary fission; useful forms fix nitrogen (Rhizobium) and ferment milk into curd (Lactobacillus).
**Virus:** acellular obligate parasite with DNA or RNA core and protein coat (capsid); e.g. TMV, HIV.
**Fungi:** heterotrophic, cell wall of chitin; yeast is unicellular and used in fermentation; Penicillium gives the antibiotic penicillin.
notes/theory/class-11/biology/floral-div.title: Floral Diversity & Microbiology

notes: **Dalton's atomic theory:** matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; compounds form by combination of atoms in fixed ratios.

**Sub-atomic particles:** electron (e⁻, discovered by J.J. Thomson, charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass ≈ 1/1837 u); proton (p⁺, Goldstein/Rutherford, +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 u); neutron (n, Chadwick, neutral, 1 u).

**Bohr's model:** electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits (stationary states) with quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy is emitted/absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits: ΔE = hν. Radius rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å; energy E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV.

**Defects of Bohr's model:** cannot explain spectra of multi-electron atoms, fine structure (splitting of spectral lines), Zeeman and Stark effects, and the dual nature/wave character of the electron (de Broglie) or Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

**Quantum numbers:** principal (n), azimuthal (l = 0 … n−1: s, p, d, f), magnetic (m_l = −l … +l) and spin (m_s = ±½). **Pauli exclusion:** no two electrons in an atom have identical sets of four quantum numbers. **Hund's rule** and Aufbau principle govern filling order.
notes/theory/class-11/chemistry/atomic-s.title: Atomic Structure

notes: **Ionic bond:** electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by transfer of electrons (e.g. NaCl). High melting point, conducts electricity in molten/solution state.
**Covalent bond:** mutual sharing of electron pairs (e.g. H₂, CH₄). Directional; low melting/boiling point compared with ionic solids.
**Coordinate (dative) bond:** shared pair donated by one atom only (e.g. NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).

**VSEPR theory:** electron pairs around the central atom repel each other and arrange to be as far apart as possible. Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

Shapes: AX₂ linear (BeCl₂), AX₃ trigonal planar (BF₃), AX₄ tetrahedral (CH₄), AX₃E pyramidal (NH₃, 107°), AX₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°), AX₅ trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅), AX₆ octahedral (SF₆).

**Hybridisation:** intermixing of orbitals of comparable energy to form equivalent hybrid orbitals — sp (linear, 180°), sp² (trigonal planar, 120°), sp³ (tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal), sp³d² (octahedral).
notes/theory/class-11/chemistry/chemical.title: Chemical Bonding & Shapes of Molecules (VSEPR)

notes: **Chemical equilibrium:** the stage at which rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction; concentrations remain constant. Dynamic in nature.
**Le Chatelier's principle:** if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by changing concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change.
**Equilibrium constant K_c** = [products]^coeff / [reactants]^coeff. For gas reactions K_p = K_c(RT)^Δn.
**Acids & bases (Bronsted-Lowry):** acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. pH = −log[H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14.

**Organic chemistry basics:** catenation, tetravalency of carbon, homologous series, functional groups, isomerism (chain, position, functional), IUPAC nomenclature rules for alkanes/alkenes/alkynes and simple derivatives.
notes/theory/class-11/chemistry/equilibr.title: Chemical Equilibrium & Organic Fundamentals

notes: **Oxidation:** loss of electrons / gain of oxygen / increase in oxidation number. **Reduction:** gain of electrons / loss of oxygen / decrease in oxidation number.
**Oxidising agent** accepts electrons (is reduced); **reducing agent** donates electrons (is oxidised).

**Oxidation number rules:** free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge; O is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H is +1 with non-metals and −1 with metals; the sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule is 0.
**Balancing redox equations** — ion-electron (half-reaction) method or oxidation-number method; in acidic medium balance O with H₂O and H with H⁺.
**Applications:** electrochemical cells, electrolysis, corrosion, bleaching and titrations (redox titrations of KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₇).
notes/theory/class-11/chemistry/oxidatio.title: Oxidation, Reduction & Redox Reactions

notes: **Modern periodic law:** properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. The long form of the periodic table has 7 periods and 18 groups.

**Periodic trends:**
- **Atomic radius** decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge) and increases down a group (new shells added).
- **Ionisation energy** increases across a period, decreases down a group.
- **Electronegativity** increases across a period, decreases down a group.
- **Electron affinity** generally increases across a period.
- **Metallic character** decreases across a period and increases down a group.
**Anomalies:** Be > B and N > O in ionisation energy due to extra stability of fully/half-filled sub-shells (1s², 2s², 2p³).
**Diagonal relationship:** elements of period 2 (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) resemble the diagonal element of period 3 in properties.
notes/theory/class-11/chemistry/periodic.title: Periodic Table & Periodicity

notes: **Boyle's law:** at constant T, V ∝ 1/P. **Charles' law:** at constant P, V ∝ T. **Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules at same T and P.
**Ideal gas equation:** PV = nRT, R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

**Kinetic theory of gases:** molecules are in continuous random motion; collisions are perfectly elastic; volume of molecules is negligible compared with the container; no intermolecular attraction; average KE ∝ absolute temperature.
**Graham's law of diffusion:** rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√(molar mass).
**Real gases** deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature; van der Waals equation corrects for molecular volume and attraction.

notes: **Mole:** the amount of substance containing as many particles (atoms, molecules, ions) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. One mole = **6.022 × 10²³** particles (Avogadro's number, N_A).
**Molar mass:** mass of one mole of a substance in grams; numerically equal to its molecular/atomic weight. n = given mass / molar mass.
**Laws of chemical combination:** law of conservation of mass, law of definite (constant) proportions, law of multiple proportions and Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes.
**Empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; **molecular formula** = n × empirical formula where n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass.
**Limiting reagent:** the reactant that is completely consumed first and therefore limits the amount of product formed.
**Percentage yield:** (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100.

notes: **Tenses:** 12 forms built from present/past/future × simple/continuous/perfect/perfect-continuous. Watch time markers: *since/for* with perfect, *yesterday/tomorrow* fixing the frame.
**Articles:** 'a/an' before singular countable nouns (an + vowel *sound*); 'the' for specific or previously mentioned nouns and superlatives.
**Active & passive voice:** object of active becomes subject in passive; verb changes to be + past participle. E.g. 'She writes a letter' → 'A letter is written by her'.
**Direct & indirect speech:** reporting statements shifts tense back one step; questions use if/whether or wh-word order; imperatives use infinitive with told/requested/ordered.

**Paragraph writing:** one controlling idea per paragraph — topic sentence, supporting details (examples, facts), concluding sentence. **Essay structure:** introduction → body paragraphs → conclusion.
**Comprehension strategy:** skim for gist first, scan for keywords from the question, then read the relevant lines closely; answer in your own words.

notes: **Subject-Verb Agreement** is one of the most tested grammar topics in NEB English. The basic rule is: singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs. However, many nouns break this rule — they look plural but take singular verbs, or look singular but take plural verbs.
## 🔹 Looks Plural, Takes a Singular Verb
These nouns end in **-s** but are actually singular and take **is/was**:
### 📘 School Subjects / Science
- **Physics** is my favorite subject.
- **Mathematics** is not difficult if you practice.
- **Economics** is a popular choice for commerce students.
- **Genetics** is a branch of biology.
- **Robotics** is an emerging field.
### 🩺 Diseases
- **Measles** is a contagious childhood disease.
- **Mumps** is caused by a virus.
- **Diabetes** is a chronic condition.
- **Rabies** is fatal if not treated.
### 🎲 Games / Sports
- **Darts** is a popular pub game.
- **Billiards** is played on a large table.
- **Dominoes** is a game of tiles.
- **Gymnastics** requires great flexibility.
### 🌍 Countries / Places
- **The United States** is a large country.
- **The Netherlands** is known for tulips.
- **The Philippines** is an archipelago.
- **Headquarters** is located in the city center.
### 💰 Measurement Units (Time / Money / Distance)
- **Ten dollars** is too much for a coffee.
- **Five miles** is a long distance to run.
- **Three hours** is a long flight.
### 📰 Other Words
- **News** is broadcast at 6 PM.
- **Series** is my favorite TV genre.
- **Species** is a biological classification.
- **Crossroads** is a busy intersection.
> **Rule:** Words ending in **-s** that are names of academic subjects, diseases, games, countries, measurements, or abstract concepts often take **singular verbs**.
## 🔹 Looks Singular, Takes a Plural Verb
These nouns have no **-s** but are actually plural and take **are/were**:
### 👥 Groups of People
- **Police** are investigating the crime.
- **People** are waiting outside.
- **Clergy** were present at the ceremony.
- **Gentry** are known for their generosity.
- **Folk** are traditional and colorful.
### 🐄 Animals / Livestock
- **Cattle** are grazing in the field.
- **Poultry** are kept for eggs and meat.
- **Vermin** are pests that destroy crops.
### 💼 Work Groups (when focusing on members)
- The **staff** are having a meeting.
- The **crew** are working hard.
> **Rule:** Collective nouns that refer to groups of individuals often take **plural verbs** when emphasizing the members.
## 🔹 Compound Subjects Joined by 'And'
### 🍽️ One Single Meal / Dish → Singular Verb
These foods are served and eaten together as one dish:
- **Bread and butter** is my daily breakfast.
- **Rice and curry** is a popular meal in Asia.
- **Fish and chips** is a famous British dish.
- **Bacon and eggs** is a heavy breakfast.
- **Macaroni and cheese** is comfort food.
- **Strawberries and cream** is served at tennis matches.
### 🛒 Separate Food Items / Groceries → Plural Verb
Same-sounding pairs, but here they're two separate items:
- Bread and butter **are** both on the shopping list.
- Milk and cookies **are** in the kitchen.
- Apples and oranges **grow** on trees.
### 🤝 One Concept or Idiom → Singular Verb
- **Law and order** is important for a safe city.
- **Peace and quiet** is all I need.
- **Trial and error** is a great way to learn.
- **Slow and steady** wins the race.
- **All work and no play** makes Jack a dull boy.
### 👫 Distinct People or Roles → Plural Verb
- My mom and dad **are** coming.
- The teacher and the student **were** talking.
- Fire and water **do not** mix.
### 🏹 Two Objects Working as One Unit → Singular Verb
- A horse and carriage **was** outside.
- A needle and thread **is** needed.
- A bow and arrow **was** used.
### 🎒 Different Objects / Tools → Plural Verb
- A pen and a pencil **are** on the desk.
- The hammer and the wrench **are** in the box.
- Shoes and socks **are** in the closet.
### 🔍 How to Tell the Difference Quickly
Look at the little word **"the"** or **"a"** in the sentence — it's a major clue:
- **One article = Singular idea:** "The chef and owner is here." (one person, two jobs)
- **Two articles = Plural people:** "The chef and the owner are here." (two different people)
> **Example:** _Rice and curry is my favorite dish._ (one meal) vs. _Rice and curry are both sold at the market._ (two items)
## 🔹 Plural-Only Nouns: Clothing & Tools
These items have no singular form — they are always plural:
### 👖 Clothing and Underwear
- **Pants** — The pants **are** on the bed.
- **Jeans** — Blue jeans **look** great.
- **Shorts** — Running shorts **are** comfortable.
- **Trousers** — Black trousers **match** any shirt.
- **Pajamas** — My pajamas **feel** soft.
- **Leggings** — Yoga leggings **stretch** a lot.
- **Tights** — Warm tights **keep** you cozy.
- **Briefs / Boxers / Underpants** — These boxers **are** new.
- **Overalls** — Denim overalls **are** trendy.
- **Slacks** — Dress slacks **are** required for work.
- **Suspenders** — Clip-on suspenders **hold** up pants.
### ✂️ Tools and Instruments
- **Scissors** — Large scissors **cut** thick paper.
- **Pliers** — Needle-nose pliers **grip** wires tightly.
- **Tweezers** — Metal tweezers **pick** up small items.
- **Tongs** — Ice tongs **are** in the bucket.
- **Shears** — Hedge shears **trim** the bushes.
- **Clippers** — Nail clippers **are** sharp.
- **Forceps** — Medical forceps **hold** the bandages.
- **Handcuffs** — Steel handcuffs **lock** tight.
- **Nutcrackers** — Wooden nutcrackers **crack** walnuts easily.
- **Bellows** — Fireplace bellows **blow** air onto logs.
### 🕶️ Gear for Eyes and Ears
- **Glasses / Spectacles** — Reading glasses **help** you see.
- **Sunglasses** — Dark sunglasses **block** the sun.
- **Goggles** — Safety goggles **protect** your eyes.
- **Binoculars** — Heavy binoculars **make** birds look close.
- **Headphones / Earphones** — Wireless headphones **play** music clearly.
> **Rule:** Two-part items that are always plural — no singular form exists. Use **are/were**, never **is/was**.
## 📝 Quick Reference Table
| Category | Examples | Verb | Example Sentence |
| Ends in -s but singular | Physics, Math, Economics | **is** | Physics **is** easy. |
| Diseases ending in -s | Measles, Mumps, Diabetes | **is** | Measles **is** contagious. |
| Games ending in -s | Darts, Billiards, Gymnastics | **is** | Darts **is** fun. |
| Countries with 'The' | The United States, The Philippines | **is** | The Philippines **is** an island nation. |
| Measurements | Ten dollars, Five miles | **is** | Ten dollars **is** enough. |
| Group nouns (plural) | Police, Cattle, People | **are** | The police **are** coming. |
| Compound (one idea) | Bread and butter, Law and order | **is** | Bread and butter **is** delicious. |
| Compound (two things) | A pen and a pencil, Mom and dad | **are** | Mom and dad **are** here. |
| Always plural | Scissors, Pants, Glasses | **are** | Scissors **are** sharp. |
## ✅ Practice Questions
1. Physics _____ my favorite subject. (is/are)
2. The police _____ investigating the case. (is/are)
3. Bread and butter _____ my breakfast. (is/are)
4. My scissors _____ missing. (is/are)
5. The United States _____ a large country. (is/are)
6. Measles _____ a viral disease. (is/are)
7. The staff _____ having a meeting. (is/are)
8. Law and order _____ everyone's responsibility. (is/are)
9. Five miles _____ a long distance. (is/are)
10. The glasses _____ on the table. (is/are)
**Answers:** 1. is, 2. are, 3. is, 4. are, 5. is, 6. is, 7. are, 8. is, 9. is, 10. are

notes: **Arithmetic progression (AP):** aₙ = a + (n−1)d; Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n−1)d].
**Geometric progression (GP):** aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹; Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); S∞ = a/(1 − r) for |r| < 1. AM ≥ GM.

**Matrices:** order m × n, addition, scalar multiplication, matrix multiplication (row × column). Determinant of 2×2 and 3×3; singular if det = 0; inverse A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A| for solving simultaneous equations (Cramer's rule).
**Complex numbers:** i² = −1; z = x + iy with modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) and conjugate z̄. Multiplication/division in polar form uses r(cos θ + i sin θ).

notes: **Limit:** lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) → L as x approaches a. Standard limits: lim sin x/x = 1 (x in radians), lim (1 + 1/n)ⁿ = e.
**Derivative:** dy/dx = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h. Rules: power rule d(xⁿ)/dx = nxⁿ⁻¹; product rule; quotient rule; chain rule. Derivatives of sin x = cos x, cos x = −sin x, eˣ = eˣ, ln x = 1/x.
**Applications:** rate of change, increasing/decreasing functions, maxima and minima (dy/dx = 0 with second-derivative test), tangents and normals.
**Integration:** antiderivative; ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C (n ≠ −1); definite integral ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) — area under the curve.

notes: **Straight line:** slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); point-slope form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁); two-point, intercept and normal forms; general form ax + by + c = 0.
**Angle between lines:** tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1; parallel ⇒ m₁ = m₂. Distance of point from line = |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²).
**Pair of straight lines** through origin: ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0.
**Circle:** (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²; general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 with centre (−g, −f), radius √(g² + f² − c).
**Vectors:** position vector, magnitude |a|, unit vector â = a/|a|. Dot product a·b = ab cos θ (perpendicular if zero); cross product a × b = ab sin θ n̂ (parallel if zero).

notes: **Set:** a well-defined collection of objects. Representation: roster/listing form or set-builder form.
**Operations:** union A ∪ B, intersection A ∩ B, difference A − B, complement A′, symmetric difference A Δ B.
**De Morgan's laws:** (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
**Number of elements:** n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B); for three sets subtract all pairwise intersections and add back the triple intersection.
**Real numbers:** natural ⊂ whole ⊂ integer ⊂ rational ⊂ real. Irrational numbers cannot be written as p/q. Properties of order, intervals, absolute value |x|.

notes: **Fundamental identities:** sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.
**Compound angles:** sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B; cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B; tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B).

**Multiple angles:** sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A; tan 2A = 2tan A/(1 − tan²A).

**Half angle:** sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2, cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2.
**Transformation formulas:** product ↔ sum — 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A−B), etc. Conditional identities when A + B + C = π: sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C.
**Solutions of trigonometric equations:** general solutions of sin x = a, cos x = a and tan x = a.

notes: **सन्धी:** दुई वर्ण मिल्दा हुने वर्णविकार। प्रकारहरू — स्वरसन्धी (दीर्घ, गुण, यण्, अयादि), व्यञ्जनसन्धी र विसर्गसन्धी। उदाहरण — हिम + आलय = हिमालय (दीर्घसन्धी); तत् + पुरुष = तपस्वी।

**समास:** दुई वा बढी शब्द मिलेर एउटा नयाँ शब्द बन्ने व्याकरणिक प्रक्रिया। भेद — द्वन्द्व (मामा–चेला = मामाचेला), तत्पुरुष (गाईको दूध → गोदुध? सही रूप: नेपालको भाषा = नेपालभाषा जस्तै विभक्ति-लोप), कर्मधारय (ठूलो मान्छे → ठुलोमान्छे/महापुरुष), द्विगु (तीन लोक = त्रैलोक), बहुब्रीह (नील कमल = नीलकमल अर्थात् कमलजस्तो आँखा)।
**कारक र विभक्ति:** कर्ता (ले), कर्म (लाई), करण (ले/द्वारा), सम्प्रदान (लाई/निम्ति), सम्बन्ध (को/का/की), अधिकरण (मा/बाट), सम्बोधन (हे!) — जम्मा सात कारक।

notes: **Newton's first law:** a body at rest stays at rest and a body in motion stays in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. Inertia = the tendency to resist change in state of motion; mass is a measure of inertia.
**Newton's second law:** F = ma — the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force.
**Newton's third law:** for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces always act in pairs on different bodies.
**Impulse** = F·Δt = change in momentum. **Momentum** p = mv.
**Friction:** static, kinetic (sliding) and rolling. F_max = μN where μ is the coefficient of friction, N the normal reaction.

notes: **Temperature** is the degree of hotness measured on Celsius, Fahrenheit or Kelvin scale. T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15.
**Heat** is the energy transferred due to temperature difference. Specific heat capacity c: Q = mcΔt. Latent heat L: Q = mL.
**Newton's law of cooling:** rate of cooling ∝ temperature excess above surroundings (small excess).
**Thermal expansion:** linear ΔL = L₀αΔT, areal ΔA = A₀βΔT, volumetric ΔV = V₀γΔT with α:β:γ = 1:2:3.

notes: **Equations of motion** (uniform acceleration a, initial velocity u, time t): v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.
**Relative velocity** of A with respect to B: v_AB = v_A − v_B.
**Free fall:** acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² toward the Earth's centre, independent of mass (Galileo).
**Projectile motion:** u at angle θ — T = 2u sin θ / g, H = u² sin² θ / (2g), R = u² sin 2θ / g, max range at θ = 45°. Path is a parabola.

notes: **Physical quantity:** any property that can be measured — length, mass, time, force, energy. Every physical quantity has a *magnitude* and a *unit*.

**Fundamental quantities:** length (L), mass (M), time (T), temperature (Θ), electric current (A), amount of substance (mol), luminous intensity (cd). Derived quantities are expressed in terms of these (e.g. velocity = m s⁻¹, force = kg m s⁻²).

**SI base units** in NEB syllabus: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd). Prefixes: kilo (10³), centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), nano (10⁻⁹), pico (10⁻¹²).

**Dimensions:** the powers to which fundamental quantities are raised. Homogeneity principle — every term of a physically correct equation has identical dimensions. Use: checking correctness of equations, deriving relations, converting units.

**Error analysis:** absolute error, relative error, percentage error. Accuracy = closeness to true value; precision = reproducibility of measurement. Significant figures — rules for counting and arithmetic.

notes: **First law of thermodynamics:** ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW — heat supplied to a gas partly increases internal energy and partly does external work.
**Work in isothermal expansion:** W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁). In an isothermal process (constant T), ΔU = 0. In an adiabatic process (no heat exchange), ΔQ = 0.
**Second law / entropy:** entropy of the universe always increases in a spontaneous process; ΔS = ΔQ/T.
**Carnot engine:** efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁. Ideal efficiency depends only on the temperatures of source and sink.
notes/theory/class-11/physics/thermodyna.title: Thermodynamics

notes: **Scalar:** magnitude only (mass, speed, work, temperature). **Vector:** magnitude + direction (displacement, velocity, force, momentum).
**Triangle law / Parallelogram law:** resultant R of two vectors P and Q inclined at angle θ: R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ, tan α = Q sin θ / (P + Q cos θ).
**Resolution:** a vector can be split into components along chosen axes: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ.
**Scalar (dot) product:** A·B = AB cos θ = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z. Work is a dot product. Vectors perpendicular ⇒ dot product = 0.
**Vector (cross) product:** A×B = AB sin θ (direction by right-hand rule). Torque and angular momentum are cross products. Parallel vectors ⇒ cross product = 0.
notes/theory/class-11/physics/vectors.js.title: Vectors

notes: **Work** W = F·s = F s cos θ. Work done by a variable force = area under the F–s graph.
**Kinetic energy** KE = ½mv². **Work–energy theorem:** net work done = change in kinetic energy.
**Potential energy:** gravitational PE = mgh; elastic PE = ½kx². For conservative forces, total mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved.
**Power** P = W/t = F·v, SI unit watt (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). Energy units: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

questions.question: A 104°F fever endangers you, yet the pathogens die too. If heat harms both sides equally, why does raising body temperature ever HELP fight infection?
questions.solution: Asymmetric vulnerability: many pathogens (and their enzymes) are tuned to exactly 37°C with narrow tolerance, while your cells tolerate a few degrees more — fever pushes invaders off their optimum while your immune cells (which work FASTER warm: higher kinetic rates) accelerate. It is thermal warfare exploiting different denaturation curves. But past ~105°F your own proteins start failing — the weapon turns on its wielder, which is why extreme fever is an emergency.

questions.concept: Why no mammals in deep sea vents
questions.question: Tube worms thrive at scalding, crushing deep-sea vents with no sunlight. Why can't a mammal simply evolve the same trick and colonise the vents?
questions.solution: Energy economics: mammals burn enormous energy staying warm and active (endothermy), demanding rich, constant food — vent oases are tiny and patchy. Tube worms cheat by outsourcing: symbiotic bacteria chemosynthesise vent chemicals, feeding the worm passively at near-zero metabolic cost. A mammal's furnace can't run on a vent's trickle. Body plan sets the energy bill; only low-budget lifestyles fit extreme, food-poor addresses.

questions.question: Keeping 100 tigers in zoos costs crores yearly; protecting one reserve shelters 100 wild tigers plus thousands of other species. Why is in-situ conservation overwhelmingly cheaper PER SPECIES saved?
questions.solution: Shared infrastructure: a reserve's forests, guards and water serve EVERY resident species simultaneously — the cost per species divides by thousands. A zoo replicates habitat per species at full price (custom diets, vets, enclosures) and preserves no ecological interactions (pollinators, prey webs). Ex-situ is an intensive-care unit: vital for the nearly extinct, absurd as a general strategy. Habitat protects relationships; cages protect individuals.

questions.question: An acre supports millions of grass blades, thousands of rabbits, but at most one fox. Why does body size so strictly cap population — and what breaks if you add ten foxes?
questions.solution: The 10% law compounds: each level keeps ~10% of the level below, so energy reaching foxes is ~0.1% of grass energy — enough for few large bodies. Bigger bodies also burn more per individual. Add ten foxes: rabbits crash, grass explodes then overgrazes, and foxes starve — the classic overshoot. Pyramid shape is thermodynamics, not preference: size concentrates energy demand while supply thins upward. Top predators are rare by arithmetic.

questions.question: Penicillin worked universally in 1945; resistant strains appeared within years. Human evolution takes millennia. What TWO bacterial traits compress evolution into months?
questions.solution: (1) Generation time ~20 minutes: a year holds 26,000 bacterial generations vs less than one human generation — selection iterates furiously. (2) Horizontal gene transfer: bacteria swap resistance plasmids directly, spreading a winning mutation through a population sideways in days, not waiting for inheritance. Antibiotics then provide brutal selection, killing 99.9% and crowning the survivors. Fast generations plus shared genes turn hospitals into evolution accelerators — finish every prescription course.

questions.question: Insects outnumber all other animal species combined by millions. What THREE design features make the insect body plan evolution's most successful experiment?
questions.solution: Flight (first animals airborne — escape predators, colonise everywhere, find mates/morales efficiently), exoskeleton (armour + waterproofing + muscle-attachment in one cuticle, enabling tiny sizes), and metamorphosis (larva and adult occupy DIFFERENT niches — caterpillar eats leaves, butterfly sips nectar — so young never compete with parents). Small size + flight + life-stage division = multiply niches per species. Diversity follows design that avoids competing with itself.

questions.question: Nectar costs the plant precious sugar — given away free to insects. Why is this apparent waste actually cheaper than the wind-pollination alternative?
questions.solution: Precision beats volume: wind pollination wastes 99.99% of pollen (broadcast billions, hit one stigma by luck — hence hay fever). A nectar bribe hires a guided courier that flies flower-to-flower of the SAME species, delivering most pollen on target. The sugar salary is tiny beside the saved pollen mountain. Flowers outsourced delivery; grasses pay the broadcast tax. Coevolution turned waste into wages.

questions.question: Viruses reproduce and evolve but don't eat, breathe or maintain themselves. If you must vote ALIVE or NOT — what single criterion decides your vote, and why do textbooks quarrel?
questions.solution: Vote hinges on METABOLISM vs REPLICATION: the alive-camp demands independent metabolism (viruses: none — inert crystals outside hosts); the other camp accepts replication-with-evolution (viruses: yes). Textbooks quarrel because 'life' is a human category, not a natural joint — viruses sit exactly on the definitional seam. The productive answer: viruses are obligate molecular parasites, evolving replicators without cells. The label matters less than the mechanism.

questions.question: Soap-and-water beats alcohol sanitiser against stomach bugs (norovirus) though sanitiser kills more germs on contact. What does soap REMOVE that sanitiser leaves behind?
questions.solution: The MICROBES THEMSELVES: soap molecules pry grease and debris off skin and water RINSES everything down the drain — physical removal, including non-enveloped viruses alcohol can't dissolve (norovirus lacks the lipid coat alcohol attacks). Sanitiser kills in place but leaves corpses, spores and chemicals on your hands — and fails on dirty/greasy hands where germs hide under grime. Removal beats murder when the enemy has armour.

questions.question: Mountains have a sharp TREELINE: lush forest below, zero trees above — though alpine flowers thrive higher. Same cold, same wind. What resource runs out for trees but not herbs?
