questions.knowledgeNote: Period number equals the principal quantum number of the outermost electron, while group is decided by the valence electrons.
questions.question: Identify the elements with atomic numbers 19, 20, 31, 36 and 55, and state the period and group in which each one is placed in the long form of the periodic table.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Number of electrons and period.**

The period number equals the number of electron shells (principal quantum number) occupied, i.e. the $n$ value of the outermost electron.

**Step 2 — Group number.**

For elements of $s$- and $p$-blocks, group number $= (number of valence electrons) + 10$.

| $Z$ | Element | Electronic configuration (outer part) | Period | Group |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 19 | Potassium (K) | $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^1$ | 4 | 1 |
| 20 | Calcium (Ca) | $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2$ | 4 | 2 |
| 31 | Gallium (Ga) | $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^24p^1$ | 4 | 13 |
| 36 | Krypton (Kr) | $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^24p^6$ | 4 | 18 |
| 55 | Caesium (Cs) | $[\text{Xe}]\,6s^1$ | 6 | 1 |

Notice that four of the five elements lie in period 4, whereas caesium (Z = 55) lies in period 6, showing that period length is not fixed.

questions.knowledgeNote: A filled s subshell is extra stable, so Mg resists ionisation more than the higher 3p electron of aluminium.
questions.question: Explain the following periodic irregularities: (a) the first ionisation enthalpy of Mg is greater than that of Al although Mg is to the left of Al. (b) The atomic radius of Na is greater than that of Cl.
questions.solution:
**(a) $I_1(\text{Mg}) > I_1(\text{Al})$**

$$\text{Mg}: [\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 \qquad \text{Al}: [\text{Ne}]\,3s^24p^1$$

The first electron removed from Mg comes from a completely filled $3s$ subshell, which is a particularly stable arrangement. In Al the first electron is the $3p$ electron, which is higher in energy, is shielded by the $3s$ pair and is repelled less. Since Mg's valence electron is more tightly held, $I_1(\text{Mg}) = 596$ kJ mol⁻¹ and $I_1(\text{Al}) = 578$ kJ mol⁻¹.

**(b) $r(\text{Na}) > r(\text{Cl})$**

Na and Cl are in the same period, so the number of shells is the same (n = 3). Across a period the nuclear charge increases from Na (Z = 11) to Cl (Z = 17) while the added electrons go into the same shell, so effective nuclear charge per electron rises. The stronger pull draws the cloud closer, so the radius falls.

$$r(\text{Na}) = 186 \ \text{pm} > r(\text{Cl}) = 99 \ \text{pm}$$

questions.knowledgeNote: The Modern Periodic Law makes atomic number, not atomic mass, the basis of periodicity, giving 18 groups and regular periods.
questions.question: How does the Modern Periodic Law differ from Mendeleev's Periodic Law? State any three points of difference.
questions.solution:
| Mendeleev's Periodic Law | Modern Periodic Law |
| --- | --- |
| Properties are a periodic function of **atomic mass**. | Properties are a periodic function of **atomic number** ($Z$). |
| Periodic table had **8 groups** (or 8 + 8 + ... columns) and periods of **irregular** length, ranging from 2 to 8 elements. | Table has **18 groups** and periods of regular length, the number of elements increasing from 2 to 32 as $Z$ increases. |
| Positions of several elements could not be correctly predicted, and there were no **isotopes** concept. | Correctly accommodates **isotopes** (they have the same $Z$) and correctly predicts the positions of elements **discovered after Mendeleev**. |

Mendeleev successfully predicted the existence of eka-aluminium (gallium) and eka-silicon (germanium), but he could not explain the positions of the noble gases or the lanthanides.

Thus the modern law corrected the mass basis, gave the group/period structure, and removed all the anomalies left in the periodic table.

questions.question: What are s-, p-, d-, and f-blocks? Give one element belonging to each.
questions.solution:
Blocks named by the subshell receiving the last electron: **s-block** — Na; **p-block** — Cl; **d-block** (transition metals) — Fe; **f-block** (inner transition) — U.

questions.knowledgeNote: Half-filled/full subshells (N, P, Be, Mg, noble gases) always spike above the trend — the standard 'anomaly' question.
questions.question: Define ionisation energy. Explain why nitrogen has a higher first ionisation energy than oxygen.
questions.solution:
**Ionisation energy** is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom.

N (1s² 2s² 2p³) has a **half-filled p subshell** — extra stable. Removing its electron breaks that stability, costing more energy than removing one from O (2p⁴), where repulsion between paired electrons actually helps ejection.

questions.question: Define electronegativity. How does it vary across a period and down a group? Which element is the most electronegative?
questions.solution:
**Electronegativity** is an atom's pull on shared bond electrons.

It **increases left→right** (rising nuclear charge) and **decreases top→bottom** (larger, shielded atoms). **Fluorine (4.0)** is the maximum.

questions.knowledgeNote: Cations < parent atom < anions — size order within one element's ions.
questions.question: How does atomic radius vary across a period and down a group? Explain the trend in each case.
questions.solution:
**Across a period it shrinks:** added protons pull the same shell tighter.

**Down a group it grows:** each new principal shell outweighs the extra nuclear charge.

Diagonally adjacent elements (e.g. **Li and Mg**) resemble each other more than their own group members.

Cause: similar charge density (charge/radius) — moving right shrinks size while moving down grows it, roughly cancelling along the diagonal. Both form nitrides, sparingly soluble carbonates, and similar organometallics.

questions.knowledgeNote: In a product, significant figures equal the least number of significant figures among the factors, which here is three from 45.6.
questions.question: The density of a liquid is 0.8792 g cm⁻³. Calculate the mass of 45.6 cm³ of the liquid, and express your answer to three significant figures.
questions.solution:
Mass is obtained from density and volume:

$$m = \rho \times V$$

Substituting the values:

$$m = 0.8792 \ \text{g cm}^{-3} \times 45.6 \ \text{cm}^3$$

$$m = 40.09152 \ \text{g}$$

In a product the number of significant figures equals the least number of significant figures present in the factors. The figures are 4 (for 0.8792) and 3 (for 45.6), so the answer is reported to **3 significant figures**, i.e. the last digit (9) is rounded up because the next digit is 1.

$$m = 40.1 \ \text{g}$$

questions.knowledgeNote: The mole (mol) is one of the seven SI base units, measuring the amount of substance containing as many entities as atoms in 12 g of carbon-12.
questions.question: Which of the following is the SI base unit of amount of substance? (a) gram (b) mole (c) millimole (d) kilogram
questions.solution:
The International System of Units recognises exactly seven base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (electric current), kelvin (thermodynamic temperature), mole (amount of substance) and candela (luminous intensity).

Since the mole appears in this list it is by definition an SI base unit and not a derived unit. Gram and kilogram are units of mass, and the millimole is merely a submultiple of the mole.

**Answer: (b) mole**

questions.knowledgeNote: The mean is the most probable value, while the absolute error is half the spread between the maximum and minimum readings.
questions.question: Two readings for the length of a metallic wire are 10.4 cm and 10.6 cm. Calculate the mean value and the absolute error of the measurements, and comment on the precision of the data.
questions.solution:
**Mean value**

$$\bar{x} = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2} = \frac{10.4 + 10.6}{2} = \frac{21.0}{2} = 10.5 \ \text{cm}$$

**Absolute error**

$$\Delta x = \frac{x_{max} - x_{min}}{2} = \frac{10.6 - 10.4}{2} = 0.1 \ \text{cm}$$

**Relative (percentage) error**

$$\text{Percentage error} = \frac{0.1}{10.5} \times 100 \approx 0.95\%$$

The result is best written as **10.5 ± 0.1 cm**. Since the two readings differ by only 0.2 cm (less than 2%), the measurements are reasonably precise.

When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a small whole-number ratio.

questions.knowledgeNote: Reductive ozonolysis cleaves C=C so that each carbon bearing a hydrogen yields an aldehyde; a carbon without hydrogen yields a ketone.
questions.question: What happens when but-2-ene is treated with ozone followed by zinc and water? Give the equations involved and identify the products.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Ozonide formation (at 195 K).** Ozone adds across the C=C double bond to give a cyclic ozonide:

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH} = \text{CHCH}_3 + \text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH–OO–CHCH}_3 \quad (\text{ozonide})$$

**Step 2 — Reductive work-up with Zn dust and water.** The ozonide is cleaved and the Zn removes the excess oxygen as zinc oxide:

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH–OO–CHCH}_3 + \text{Zn} \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{ZnO}$$

**Products:** two molecules of **ethanal**.

**Why it works.** In reductive work-up each carbon of the original double bond picks up an oxygen and a hydrogen; a carbon carrying an H gives an aldehyde, while a carbon carrying no H gives a ketone. Here both double-bond carbons bear one H each, so both fragments are aldehydes. Had the reaction been carried out with hydrogen peroxide (oxidative work-up), the aldehydes would have been further oxidised to ethanoic acid.

questions.knowledgeNote: Chlorination of methane is a chain radical reaction with initiation, propagation and termination steps, giving a statistical mixture of products.
questions.question: Explain the mechanism of the free-radical chlorination of methane in the presence of ultraviolet light, and account for the mixture of products formed.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Initiation (homolytic fission by UV light).**

$$\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$

**Step 2 — Propagation.**

$$\text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{CH}_4 \rightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{CH}_3^\bullet$$

$$\text{CH}_3^\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$

The chlorine radical is regenerated, so the chain continues.

**Step 3 — Termination.**

$$\text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 \qquad \text{CH}_3^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} \qquad \text{CH}_3^\bullet + \text{CH}_3^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$$

**Why a mixture forms.** The reaction is not selective: chlorine can attack any of the four equivalent C–H bonds of methane, and the process is highly random. A mixture of chloromethane, dichloromethane, chloroform and tetrachloromethane is obtained. Excess chlorine pushes the substitution further:

$$\text{CH}_4 + 4\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{CCl}_4 + 4\text{HCl}$$

questions.question: What happens when ethene undergoes ozonolysis? Write the products.
questions.solution:
O₃ adds across the double bond (ozonide), and reductive work-up (Zn/H₂O) cleaves it:

CH₂=CH₂ → **2HCHO (formaldehyde)**.

Ozonolysis locates double bonds — each =CH₂ fragment reports as formaldehyde.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Acidity: acetylene > ethylene > ethane — s-character order (50% > 33% > 25%).
questions.question: Acetylene is acidic in nature. Explain with a chemical test.
questions.solution:
The sp-hybridised C–H bond (50% s-character) holds electrons tightly, so HC≡CH loses H⁺ relatively easily.

**Test:** with ammoniacal AgNO₃ it gives a **white precipitate of silver acetylide** (AgC≡CAg); with ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ a red copper acetylide — terminal alkynes only.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Decolourisation = unsaturation (C=C or C≡C) — the fastest functional-group screen in qualitative analysis.
questions.question: How will you distinguish ethane, ethene, and ethyne using bromine water?
questions.solution: **Ethane:** no change (alkane, substitution needs UV). **Ethene:** brown Br₂ water decolourised (addition). **Ethyne:** also decolourised — then apply ammoniacal AgNO₃, which precipitates only with the terminal alkyne.

questions.knowledgeNote: Ammonia is a precursor for fertilizers (NH₄NO₃, (NH₄)₂SO₄), explosives, and plastics.
questions.question: Describe the Haber process for ammonia manufacture. Why is high pressure used?
questions.solution:
**Haber process:** N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat

**Conditions:**
- Temperature: 450-500°C (compromise)
- Pressure: 200 atm (high pressure favors NH₃)
- Catalyst: Fe with Mo promoter
- Unreacted gases recycled

**Why high pressure?**
Reactants: 4 moles gas → Products: 2 moles gas.
Le Chatelier: increased pressure shifts equilibrium to fewer moles (right → NH₃).
Also increases reaction rate.

questions.knowledgeNote: Washing soda softens hard water by precipitating dissolved Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ as insoluble carbonates, leaving soluble sodium salts.
questions.question: What is hard water? Describe how temporary and permanent hardness are removed using washing soda, giving the reactions involved.
questions.solution:
**Hard water** contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts, chiefly the bicarbonates and sulphates. Soap does not form a lather with it; instead a sticky scum of calcium/magnesium soap is precipitated.

**Temporary hardness** (due to bicarbonates) is removed by boiling, but washing soda also removes it by precipitating the carbonate:

$$\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3\downarrow + 2\text{NaHCO}_3$$

$$\text{Mg(HCO}_3)_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MgCO}_3\downarrow + 2\text{NaHCO}_3$$

**Permanent hardness** (due to chlorides and sulphates) is removed by washing soda, $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\cdot10\text{H}_2\text{O}$:

$$\text{CaSO}_4 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3\downarrow + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$$

$$\text{MgCl}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MgCO}_3\downarrow + 2\text{NaCl}$$

Both cases follow the same pattern: the carbonate ion precipitates the metal as an insoluble carbonate, leaving soluble sodium salts behind.

questions.knowledgeNote: Sulfuric acid is the most important industrial chemical — used in fertilizers, batteries, petroleum refining.
questions.question: What is the Contact process? Write the key reactions and conditions.
questions.solution:
**Contact process:** Manufacturing sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄).

**Reactions:**
1. S + O₂ → SO₂
2. 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, 450°C, 1-2 atm)
3. SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum)
4. H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄

**Conditions:**
- V₂O₅ catalyst, 450°C, excess O₂
- SO₃ absorbed in H₂SO₄ (not directly in water — creates mist)
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: In the Solvay process brine is saturated with NH₃ and CO₂, and the precipitated NaHCO₃ is calcined to Na₂CO₃.
questions.question: Describe the Solvay process for the manufacture of sodium carbonate, giving balanced equations for each step.
questions.solution:
**Stage 1 — Saturation of brine with ammonia and carbon dioxide.**

A concentrated solution of sodium chloride is saturated first with ammonia and then with carbon dioxide. Sodium hydrogencarbonate has a low solubility and precipitates out, while ammonium chloride stays in solution:

$$\text{NaCl} + \text{NH}_3 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{NaHCO}_3\downarrow + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$

**Stage 2 — Decomposition (calcination) of the bicarbonate.**

The precipitated $NaHCO_3$ is filtered off and heated at about 500 °C to give anhydrous sodium carbonate:

$$2\text{NaHCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$$

**Recovery of ammonia.** The $NH_4Cl$ from stage 1 is treated with lime, Ca(OH)₂, to release ammonia which is recycled:

$$2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{NH}_3\uparrow + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Since ammonia is recovered and reused, the net cost is low and the products are cheap.

questions.question: Define mole. Calculate the number of moles in 44 g of CO₂.
questions.solution:
A **mole** is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of C-12 (6.022 × 10²³ particles).

Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 32 = 44 g mol⁻¹.

n = mass/molar mass = 44/44 = **1 mole**.

questions.question: State Avogadro's law. What volume does 0.25 mole of a gas occupy at STP?
questions.solution:
**Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

At STP, 1 mole occupies 22.4 L ⇒ 0.25 mole occupies 0.25 × 22.4 = **5.6 L**.

questions.question: An organic compound contains 40% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen and 53.33% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16).
questions.solution:
Divide each % by atomic mass: C = 40/12 = 3.33; H = 6.67/1 = 6.67; O = 53.33/16 = 3.33.

Divide by the smallest (3.33): C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1.

**Empirical formula = CH₂O**.

questions.question: Distinguish between empirical and molecular formula with an example.
questions.solution:
The **empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound; the **molecular formula** gives the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

Example — benzene: molecular formula C₆H₆, empirical formula CH.

questions.question: State Dalton's atomic theory. What are its main drawbacks?
questions.solution:
**Dalton's postulates:** matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties; atoms of different elements differ; compounds form by combination of atoms in simple whole-number ratios.

**Drawbacks:** atom is divisible (electrons, protons, neutrons exist); isotopes of an element have different masses; it cannot explain complex ratios, isotopy or the nature of bonding.

questions.question: Write the electronic configuration of Fe (Z = 26) and Cr (Z = 24) and explain any anomaly.
questions.solution:
**Fe:** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶.

**Cr:** 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹ 3d⁵.

**Anomaly:** chromium takes one electron from 4s into 3d to give a half-filled 3d⁵ configuration, which has extra stability due to symmetrical distribution and maximum exchange energy.

questions.question: Why is ionisation energy of nitrogen greater than that of oxygen?
questions.solution: Nitrogen has a half-filled stable 2p³ configuration, which requires more energy to remove an electron. In oxygen, removing one electron gives a more stable half-filled 2p³ arrangement, so less energy is needed — hence IE(N) > IE(O).

questions.question: Define hybridisation. What is the shape and bond angle of NH₃?
questions.solution:
**Hybridisation** is the intermixing of atomic orbitals of nearly equal energy to form an equal number of identical hybrid orbitals.

In NH₃ nitrogen is sp³ hybridised: one lone pair + three N–H bonds ⇒ **pyramidal shape**, bond angle **107°** (compressed from 109.5° by the lone pair).

questions.question: What is a limiting reagent? 2 g of hydrogen reacts with 32 g of oxygen to form water. Identify the limiting reagent and the mass of water formed.
questions.solution:
A **limiting reagent** is the reactant completely consumed in the reaction and which therefore limits the amount of product.

Reaction: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (4 g H₂ reacts with 32 g O₂).

Here only 2 g H₂ is available ⇒ H₂ is the **limiting reagent**.

4 g H₂ → 36 g H₂O, so 2 g H₂ → **18 g of water**.

questions.question: State Boyle's law and Charles' law. Write the ideal gas equation.
questions.solution:
**Boyle's law:** at constant temperature the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure (V ∝ 1/P).

**Charles' law:** at constant pressure the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V ∝ T).

Combining with Avogadro's law gives the **ideal gas equation: PV = nRT**.

questions.question: Define oxidation number. Find the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄.
questions.solution:
**Oxidation number** is the charge an atom would have if electrons were transferred completely to the more electronegative atom.

In H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 ⇒ S = +8 − 2 = **+6**.

questions.question: Why do real gases deviate from ideal behaviour?
questions.solution: At high pressure the volume occupied by gas molecules is no longer negligible compared with the container volume; at low temperature intermolecular attractions become significant. Both effects make PV ≠ nRT — hence real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature.

questions.question: Explain the shape of the water molecule using VSEPR theory.
questions.solution:
In H₂O, oxygen is sp³ hybridised with **two bond pairs and two lone pairs**.

According to VSEPR, lone pair–lone pair repulsion is greater than lone pair–bond pair repulsion, which compresses the tetrahedral angle from 109.5° to about **104.5°**.

Hence the shape of H₂O is **bent (angular or V-shaped)**.

questions.question: Define ionisation energy. Why does it increase across a period?
questions.solution:
**Ionisation energy** is the minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

Across a period nuclear charge increases while the shell number stays the same, so electrons are held more strongly — more energy is needed to remove them. Hence IE increases across a period.

questions.question: What are isotopes? Give one example.
questions.solution:
**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).

Example: protium (¹₁H), deuterium (²₁H) and tritium (³₁H) — isotopes of hydrogen; also ¹²C and ¹⁴C.

questions.question: Write a short note on Graham's law of diffusion.
questions.solution:
**Graham's law:** at constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass: r ∝ 1/√M, so r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁).

Lighter gases diffuse faster — e.g. hydrogen diffuses about four times faster than oxygen.

questions.question: State Le Chatelier's principle. Predict the effect of increasing pressure on N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
questions.solution:
**Le Chatelier's principle:** when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that minimises the disturbance.

For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ there are 4 moles of gas on the left and only 2 on the right. Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium **towards the right (more ammonia)**, since fewer gas molecules means lower pressure.

questions.question: Calculate the pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution.
questions.solution:
HCl is a strong acid and dissociates completely: [H⁺] = 0.001 = 10⁻³ M.

pH = −log[H⁺] = −log(10⁻³) = **3**.

questions.question: What is a coordinate (dative) bond? Give an example.
questions.solution:
A **coordinate bond** is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by only one of the two bonded atoms (the donor), the other being the acceptor.

Example: NH₄⁺ — nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺; also H₃O⁺.

questions.question: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.
questions.solution:
**Oxidation** is the loss of electrons by an atom/ion (increase in oxidation number). **Reduction** is the gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number).

Example: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

questions.question: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and give its significance.
questions.solution:
**Heisenberg's uncertainty principle:** it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the position and the momentum of a moving microscopic particle.

Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π.

**Significance:** it rules out fixed orbits for electrons (contradicting Bohr) and leads to the concept of orbitals — regions of probability of finding the electron.

questions.question: What is the de Broglie equation? Calculate the wavelength of an electron moving at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
questions.solution:
The **de Broglie equation** λ = h/mv relates the wave nature to the particle nature of matter.

λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁶)

= 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ / 9.1 × 10⁻²⁵ ≈ **7.28 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.728 nm**.

questions.question: Why are noble gases chemically inert? Explain with reference to their electronic configuration.
questions.solution: Noble gases have completely filled outermost shells (ns² np⁶, except helium 1s²), giving maximum stability. They neither need to lose nor gain electrons, so they have high ionisation energy, almost zero electron affinity and very low reactivity.

questions.question: Distinguish between sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds.
questions.solution:
**Sigma bond:** formed by head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals; stronger; free rotation possible; only one σ bond between two atoms.

**Pi bond:** formed by sidewise (lateral) overlap of p-orbitals; weaker; rotation restricted; always present along with a σ bond (in double/triple bonds).

questions.question: Define molarity. Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH in 500 mL of solution.
questions.solution:
**Molarity (M)** is the number of moles of solute dissolved per litre of solution.

Moles of NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 500 mL = 0.5 L.

M = 0.1 / 0.5 = **0.2 M**.

questions.question: What is sp³ hybridisation? Explain the structure of methane using it.
questions.solution:
In **sp³ hybridisation** one s orbital and three p orbitals of comparable energy mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally at 109°28′.

In CH₄, carbon's one 2s electron is promoted to 2p, giving four unpaired electrons which hybridise into four sp³ orbitals; each overlaps with a hydrogen 1s orbital forming four identical C–H bonds — hence CH₄ is **tetrahedral with bond angle 109.5°**.

questions.question: State Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.
questions.solution:
**Pauli exclusion principle:** no two electrons in the same atom can have all four quantum numbers identical — an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.

**Hund's rule:** electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins before pairing begins, because this arrangement has maximum stability (maximum multiplicity).

questions.question: Why is BF₃ non-polar while NF₃ is polar?
questions.solution:
BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical: the three B–F bond dipoles cancel exactly ⇒ net dipole moment is zero ⇒ **non-polar**.

NF₃ is pyramidal (lone pair on N): the N–F bond dipoles do not cancel ⇒ net dipole moment exists ⇒ **polar**.

questions.question: What is a functional group? Write the general formula of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
questions.solution:
A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms that determines the characteristic chemical properties of an organic compound (e.g. –OH, –CHO, –COOH).

Alkanes: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; Alkenes: CₙH₂ₙ; Alkynes: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.

questions.question: Define isomerism. Draw the chain isomers of C₅H₁₂ and name them.
questions.solution:
**Isomerism** is the phenomenon in which compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements (and hence different properties).

Chain isomers of C₅H₁₂ (pentane):
1. **n-pentane** — CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃
2. **isopentane (2-methylbutane)** — (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–CH₃
3. **neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane)** — C(CH₃)₄

questions.question: Explain why the bond angle in NH₃ is greater than that in H₂O.
questions.solution:
NH₃ has one lone pair, H₂O has two. Lone pair–lone pair repulsion is stronger than lone pair–bond pair repulsion.

In H₂O the two lone pairs compress the angle more (104.5°) than the single lone pair does in NH₃ (107°). Hence **angle(NH₃) > angle(H₂O)**.

questions.question: Balance the following redox equation by ion-electron method: Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ → Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ (acidic medium).
questions.solution:
Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ …(×5)

Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O

Adding: **5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O**

questions.question: State the law of multiple proportions and explain it with an example.
questions.solution:
**Law:** when two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.

Example — carbon and oxygen form CO and CO₂. With 12 g carbon: 16 g oxygen in CO, but 32 g in CO₂. Ratio = 16 : 32 = **1 : 2**.

questions.question: What is the significance of quantum numbers? Write the four quantum numbers for the differentiating (19th) electron of potassium (Z = 19).
questions.solution:
**Significance:** principal quantum number (n) gives size/energy of shell; azimuthal (l) gives shape of orbital; magnetic (m_l) gives orientation; spin (m_s) gives spin direction. Together they completely describe an electron in an atom.

Configuration of K: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ **4s¹** — the 19th electron:

n = 4, l = 0, m_l = 0, m_s = +½.

questions.question: Why does the boiling point of water differ from that of H₂S despite both having similar molecular structures?
questions.solution: Water molecules are held together by strong **hydrogen bonds** due to the high electronegativity and small size of oxygen, so much more energy is needed to separate them. In H₂S there is no hydrogen bonding (sulphur is large and less electronegative) — only weak van der Waals forces. Hence H₂O boils far higher (100 °C) than H₂S (−60 °C).

questions.question: Define molar volume. What volume will 8 g of methane occupy at STP?
questions.solution:
**Molar volume** is the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at STP (= 22.4 L mol⁻¹).

Moles of CH₄ = 8/16 = 0.5 mol ⇒ V = 0.5 × 22.4 = **11.2 L**.

questions.question: What is the octet rule? What are its limitations?
questions.solution:
**Octet rule:** atoms tend to combine in such a way that each has eight electrons in its valence shell, attaining noble-gas configuration.

**Limitations:**
- Incomplete octet: BeCl₂, BF₃ (central atom has only 4/6 electrons).
- Expanded octet: SF₆, PCl₅ (10 or 12 electrons around central atom).
- Odd-electron molecules: NO, NO₂ cannot satisfy the rule.
- It says nothing about shape, relative stability or energy of molecules.

questions.question: Calculate the number of molecules and moles present in 5.6 L of oxygen gas at STP.
What is a homologous series? State any two characteristics.
questions.solution:
A **homologous series** is a family of organic compounds with the same general formula, same functional group and similar chemical properties, whose successive members differ by –CH₂– unit.

**Characteristics:** (i) members can be prepared by similar methods; (ii) physical properties change gradually with molecular mass; (iii) consecutive members differ by 14 in molecular mass.

questions.question: Why is the electron affinity of chlorine higher than that of fluorine?
questions.solution: Fluorine's valence shell (2p) is very compact — an incoming electron feels strong repulsion from the already present electrons. Chlorine's 3p shell is larger, so the added electron experiences much less repulsion despite lower electronegativity. Hence Cl has a **higher (more negative) electron affinity** than F.

questions.knowledgeNote: Balance oxygen with H₂O, hydrogen with H⁺, then charge with electrons until both atoms and charge agree.
questions.question: Balance the following redox reaction by the oxidation number (half-reaction) method: $MnO_4^- + C_2O_4^{2-} + H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + CO_2 + H_2O$. Give the oxidation and reduction half equations.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Reduction half equation.** Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons:

$$\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \qquad (\times 2)$$

**Step 2 — Oxidation half equation.** Carbon in $C_2O_4^{2-}$ is +3 and in $CO_2$ it is +4; two carbons lose 2 electrons:

$$\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 2e^- \qquad (\times 5)$$

**Step 3 — Equalise and cancel electrons (LCM = 10)**

$$2\text{MnO}_4^- + 16\text{H}^+ + 10e^- + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} + 10\text{CO}_2 + 10e^-$$

$$\boxed{2\text{MnO}_4^- + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + 16\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 10\text{CO}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}}$$

**Step 4 — Check.**

Mn: 2 = 2. C: 10 = 10. O: 8 + 20 = 28 on the left, 20 + 8 = 28 on the right. H: 16 = 16. Charge: $(-2 - 10 + 16) = +4$ on the left and $+4$ on the right.

questions.knowledgeNote: Oxygen in H₂O₂ has oxidation state −1, so it can be raised to 0 or lowered to −2.
questions.question: Explain why hydrogen peroxide acts both as an oxidising agent and as a reducing agent. Support your answer with balanced ionic equations, one for each role.
questions.solution:
In $H_2O_2$ oxygen has the oxidation state $-1$, which lies between $-2$ and $0$. Hence oxygen can be raised to $0$ (acting as a reducing agent) or lowered to $-2$ (acting as an oxidising agent).

**As a reducing agent — oxygen is oxidised from $-1$ to $0$:**

$$2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**As an oxidising agent — oxygen is reduced from $-1$ to $-2$:**

$$\text{H}_2\text{O}_2 + 2\text{I}^- + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

In the first, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ loses electrons and $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ accepts them, so peroxide is the oxidising agent there; in the second the roles are reversed. This is why peroxide is called an oxidising as well as a reducing agent — it is unique among common oxides.

questions.knowledgeNote: Equivalent mass equals molar mass divided by the n-factor, which for K₂Cr₂O₇ in acid is 6.
questions.question: Calculate the equivalent mass (equivalent weight) of potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇, acting as an oxidising agent in acidic (acidic medium) solution. ($A_r$: K = 39, Cr = 52, O = 16)
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Molar mass**

$$M = 2(39) + 2(52) + 7(16) = 78 + 104 + 112 = 294 \ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

**Step 2 — n-factor in acidic medium**

In acidic solution dichromate is reduced to Cr³⁺:

$$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Each chromium goes from +6 to +3, a gain of 3 electrons; with two chromium atoms the total $n$ = 2 × 3 = **6**.

**Step 3 — Equivalent mass**

$$E = \frac{M}{n} = \frac{294}{6} = \textbf{49 \ \text{g equiv}^{-1}}$$

So 49 g of K₂Cr₂O₇ will oxidise or reduce 1 mole of electrons, i.e. 49 g of Zn (equivalent mass 32.7) is oxidised by 49 g of dichromate in acid.

questions.question: State the rules for assigning oxidation numbers. Find the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄ and Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇.
questions.solution:
Key rules: free elements 0; Group 1 +1, Group 2 +2; O usually −2 (peroxides −1); H usually +1 (hydrides −1); F always −1; the sum equals the species' charge.

KMnO₄: +1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0 → Mn = **+7**.

K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(−2) = 0 → Cr = **+6**.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Balance atoms (O via H₂O, H via H⁺) first, charges with electrons last — the order that prevents most errors.
questions.question: Balance the redox reaction by the ion-electron method: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ (acidic medium).
questions.solution:
Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.

Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (×5).

Adding: **MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O**.

Check: charge −1+10+8 = +17 each side; atoms: Mn 1, Fe 5, H 8, O 4 ✓.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: 'OIL RIG' — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
questions.question: Define oxidising and reducing agents. Identify each in: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
questions.solution:
**Oxidising agent** gains electrons (is itself reduced); **reducing agent** loses electrons (is itself oxidised).

Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidised) so **Zn is the reductant**; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduced) so **CuSO₄ (Cu²⁺) is the oxidant**.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Any metal displaces metals below it in the series — the single rule behind all displacement predictions.
questions.question: What is the electrochemical series? Explain why zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
questions.solution:
The **electrochemical series** orders electrodes by standard reduction potential — higher (more positive) means easier to reduce.

Zn²⁺/Zn (−0.76 V) sits below Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V): zinc is the stronger reductant, so Zn reduces Cu²⁺ to copper metal spontaneously.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Intermediate oxidation states (−1 O, +4 S, +3 N) are the dual-role suspects — check them first.
questions.question: Hydrogen peroxide can act both as an oxidising and a reducing agent. Explain with one reaction of each type.
questions.solution:
O in H₂O₂ is at −1, midway between O₂ (0) and H₂O (−2), so it can move either way.

**Oxidant:** H₂O₂ + 2KI + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (O: −1 → −2).

**Reductant:** 5H₂O₂ + 2KMnO₄ + 3H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 8H₂O + 5O₂ (O: −1 → 0).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Standard potentials confirm it: F₂/F⁻ (+2.87 V) tops the whole electrochemical series.
questions.question: Why is fluorine the strongest oxidising agent among the halogens?
questions.solution:
Oxidising strength follows electron gain enthalpy and small size: F₂ has the highest electronegativity (4.0), the most exothermic electron affinity for its size, and a weak F–F bond that breaks easily.

So F₂ oxidises even water (to O₂) and displaces every other halogen — strength falls F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: At STP (0°C, 1 atm), 1 mol ideal gas occupies 22.4 L.
questions.question: State Boyle's law and Charles's law. Derive the ideal gas equation.
questions.solution:
**Boyle's law:** At constant T, PV = constant (P ∝ 1/V).
**Charles's law:** At constant P, V/T = constant (V ∝ T).

Combining: PV/T = constant = nR → **PV = nRT** (ideal gas equation)
where R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) or 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K).

questions.knowledgeNote: At constant pressure a gas volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature in kelvin.
questions.question: A sample of a gas occupies 500 cm³ at 27 °C and 1 atm pressure. Calculate the volume it will occupy at 127 °C if the pressure is kept constant. Assume the gas behaves ideally.
questions.solution:
At constant pressure, Charles's law applies: $\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}$, with temperature in kelvin.

**Step 1 — Convert to kelvin**

$$T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300 \ \text{K}, \qquad T_2 = 127 + 273 = 400 \ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — Apply the law**

$$\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2} \Rightarrow V_2 = V_1 \times \frac{T_2}{T_1} = 500 \times \frac{400}{300}$$

$$V_2 = 666.7 \ \text{cm}^3$$

Since $T_2 > T_1$, the volume increases, as expected for Charles's law. If a balloon burst on a hot summer afternoon, this is exactly why.
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.knowledgeNote: Both laws demand kelvin — Celsius breaks the proportionality (no true zero).
questions.question: State Boyle's law and Charles's law. Derive the ideal gas equation from them.
questions.solution:
**Boyle (T const):** P ∝ 1/V. **Charles (P const):** V ∝ T.

Combined: V ∝ T/P → PV/T = constant. For n moles the constant is nR: **PV = nRT**, with R = 8.314 J/mol·K.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Effusion through a pinhole obeys the same law — Graham covered both with one apparatus.
questions.question: State Graham's law of diffusion. Hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster than an unknown gas under identical conditions. Find the unknown gas's molar mass.
questions.solution:
**Graham's law:** diffusion rate ∝ 1/√(density) at fixed T and P.

r(H₂)/r(X) = √(Mₓ/M_H₂) → 4 = √(Mₓ/2) → Mₓ = 16 × 2 = **32 g/mol** (oxygen).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Aqueous tension rises steeply with T — the correction matters most for warm-water collections.
questions.question: State Dalton's law of partial pressures. Why is aqueous tension subtracted when a gas is collected over water?
questions.solution:
**Dalton's law:** total pressure = sum of partial pressures, P = p₁ + p₂ + ….

Gas collected over water mixes with water vapour, so P_measured = P_dry_gas + aqueous tension. The vapour's contribution (**aqueous tension**, tabulated per temperature) must be subtracted to get the dry gas pressure.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Postulate (5), ⟨KE⟩ = (3/2)kT, is the bridge from mechanics to thermometry.
questions.question: Write the postulates of the kinetic molecular theory of gases.
questions.solution: (1) Countless tiny molecules in ceaseless random motion. (2) Negligible molecular volume vs container. (3) No intermolecular forces except at collision. (4) Perfectly elastic collisions. (5) Average KE ∝ absolute temperature.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Easily liquefied gases (NH₃, CO₂ — large a) deviate most; H₂ and He least.
questions.question: Under what conditions does a real gas deviate most from ideal behaviour? Explain using van der Waals' equation.
questions.solution:
Deviations grow at **high pressure** (finite molecular volume matters) and **low temperature** (intermolecular attractions matter).

van der Waals corrects both: (P + a(n/V)²)(V − nb) = nRT — the a-term adds lost pressure from attractions, the b-term subtracts excluded volume.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Isothermal P–V is a rectangular hyperbola — doubling volume halves pressure, always.
questions.question: 2 L of a gas at 3 atm pressure expands isothermally. What volume will it occupy at 1 atm?
questions.solution: Boyle's law (T const): P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → V₂ = (3 × 2)/1 = **6 L**.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Molar mass of water = 18 g/mol (H=1×2 + O=16). At STP, 1 mol gas = 22.4 L.
questions.question: What is the mole concept? Calculate the number of molecules in 36 g of water.
questions.solution:
**Mole:** The amount of substance containing as many particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12. One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number).

Moles of H₂O = 36/18 = 2 mol
Number of molecules = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = **1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules**
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.knowledgeNote: The limiting reactant is the one present in the smaller stoichiometric amount, and it fixes the yield of product.
questions.question: 4.8 g of magnesium is burnt in 6.4 g of oxygen. Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed. ($A_r$: Mg = 24, O = 16)
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Balanced equation**

$$2\text{Mg} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}$$

**Step 2 — Moles available**

$$n(\text{Mg}) = \frac{4.8}{24} = 0.20 \ \text{mol}$$

$$n(\text{O}_2) = \frac{6.4}{32} = 0.20 \ \text{mol}$$

**Step 3 — Compare with the stoichiometric ratio**

From the equation, 2 mol Mg requires 1 mol O₂.

O₂ required for 0.20 mol Mg $= 0.20/2 = 0.10$ mol, but 0.20 mol O₂ is available. Oxygen is in excess, so **Mg is the limiting reactant**.

**Step 4 — Mass of MgO**

$$n(\text{MgO}) = n(\text{Mg}) = 0.20 \ \text{mol}, \qquad M(\text{MgO}) = 24 + 16 = 40 \ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

$$m(\text{MgO}) = 0.20 \times 40 = \textbf{8.0 \ g}$$

The extra 0.10 mol of O₂ ($= 3.2$ g) remains unreacted.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Empirical formula gives simplest whole-number ratio. Molecular formula = n × empirical formula.
questions.question: Calculate the empirical formula of a compound containing 40% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen, and 53.33% oxygen by mass.
questions.solution:
Assume 100 g of compound.
C: 40/12 = 3.33 mol
H: 6.67/1 = 6.67 mol
O: 53.33/16 = 3.33 mol

Divide by smallest (3.33):
C = 1, H = 2, O = 1

Empirical formula = **CH₂O**

questions.knowledgeNote: An empirical formula is obtained by dividing elemental mole ratios by the smallest of them and simplifying.
questions.question: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Calculate its empirical formula. ($A_r$: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.solution:
Assume 100 g of the compound, so that the masses are 40.0 g C, 6.7 g H and 53.3 g O.

**Step 1 — Convert to moles**

$$n(\text{C}) = \frac{40.0}{12} = 3.33 \ \text{mol}, \qquad n(\text{H}) = \frac{6.7}{1} = 6.7 \ \text{mol}, \qquad n(\text{O}) = \frac{53.3}{16} = 3.33 \ \text{mol}$$

**Step 2 — Divide by the smallest value (3.33)**

$$\text{C} : \text{H} : \text{O} = \frac{3.33}{3.33} : \frac{6.7}{3.33} : \frac{3.33}{3.33} = 1 : 2.01 : 1$$

**Step 3 — Round to the nearest whole numbers**

$$\text{C} : \text{H} : \text{O} = 1 : 2 : 1$$

Since the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 is already the simplest whole-number ratio, the empirical formula is

$$\boxed{\text{CH}_2\text{O}}$$

Note that 6.7/3.33 = 2.01 ≈ 2, so no further multiplication is needed.
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.knowledgeNote: M(H₂O) = 18 g/mol; at STP, 1 mol of any gas occupies 22.4 L.
questions.question: What is the mole concept? Calculate the number of molecules in 36 g of water.
questions.solution:
**Mole:** the amount containing as many particles as atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12 — one mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

Moles of H₂O = 36/18 = 2 mol. Molecules = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = **1.204 × 10²⁴**.
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.knowledgeNote: Percent → mass (per 100 g) → moles (÷ atomic mass) → simplest ratio — the fixed four-step ritual.
questions.question: Calculate the empirical formula of a compound containing 40% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen, and 53.33% oxygen by mass.
questions.solution:
Per 100 g: C = 40/12 = 3.33 mol; H = 6.67/1 = 6.67 mol; O = 53.33/16 = 3.33 mol.

Divide by 3.33: C:H:O = 1:2:1 → empirical formula **CH₂O**.

questions.knowledgeNote: Limiting reagent = the reactant exhausted first — always compare mole ratios, never gram amounts.
questions.question: 10 g of H₂ reacts with 64 g of O₂ to form water. Which is the limiting reagent, and what is the maximum mass of water formed?
questions.solution:
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Moles: H₂ = 10/2 = 5 mol; O₂ = 64/32 = 2 mol.

2 mol O₂ needs 4 mol H₂ (5 available) — **O₂ is limiting**.

Water formed = 4 mol × 18 = **72 g**.

questions.knowledgeNote: Molarity is moles per LITRE of solution — convert mL to L before dividing.
questions.question: 4 g of NaOH is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. Calculate its molarity. (NaOH = 40)

questions.knowledgeNote: Molecular = n × empirical, where n = molar mass / empirical mass — always an integer.
questions.question: A compound has empirical formula CH₂O and molar mass 180 g/mol. Find its molecular formula.
questions.solution:
Empirical mass = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30. n = 180/30 = 6.

Molecular formula = 6 × CH₂O = **C₆H₁₂O₆** (glucose).

questions.knowledgeNote: % yield never exceeds 100 — an answer above it means the product is wet or impure.
questions.question: In an experiment, the theoretical yield is 50 g but only 40 g of product is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.
questions.solution:
% yield = (actual/theoretical) × 100 = (40/50) × 100 = **80%**.

Losses come from side reactions, incomplete reaction, and handling/spillage.

questions.knowledgeNote: Critical thinking separates fact from opinion, exposes hidden assumptions, and weighs supporting and weakening evidence before accepting a conclusion.
questions.question:
A student argues in a class debate: 'Mobile phones should be banned in every school. Everybody concentrates better without them, so banning them will improve our study results.'

(i) What assumption is the speaker taking for granted that has not been proved?
(ii) Give one piece of evidence that would **support** this argument and one that would **weaken** it.
(iii) In one sentence, state the main weakness of the reasoning used.
questions.solution:
**(i) Assumption:** That mobile phones are the main cause of poor concentration and poor results, and that concentration is the only factor affecting results. The speaker also assumes that a ban is the only possible solution.

**(ii) Supporting evidence:** A study of two comparable schools, one with a full ban and one without, showing a clear fall in phone-related distractions and a rise in average internal assessment marks in the banning school.
- *Weakening evidence:* Schools in several countries removed phones from classrooms but saw **no** improvement in results, and the decline continued; or teachers report that bans simply move phone use to breaks and the corridor.

**(iii) Main weakness:** The argument moves from a plausible correlation to a certainty about cause and effect without testing other causes, so the conclusion is not logically guaranteed by the evidence given.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Survey data shows association only; to prove cause you must rule out confounding variables and check that the effect is plausible.
questions.question:
Read the following data collected by a school and answer the questions that follow.

A survey of 400 students compared mobile phone use with exam performance:
- 240 students (60%) used a phone for more than three hours a day. Of these, 110 scored below 40%.
- 160 students (40%) used a phone for less than one hour a day. Of these, 15 scored below 40%.

(i) Which group performed better on average? Support your answer with figures.
(ii) Can we conclude from this data that heavy phone use **causes** poor results? Give two reasons why not.
(iii) Write one question the school should ask next in order to test the argument fairly.
questions.solution:
**(i)** The light-user group performed much better. Only about **9%** of light users failed (15 of 160), while about **46%** of heavy users failed (110 of 240) - roughly five times the failure rate.

**(ii)** No. Two reasons:
1. **Correlation is not causation.** The survey shows the two facts occur together, but the direction of influence is unknown; poor students may also use phones more because they study less, or the results may simply reflect an already existing difference.
2. **Other possible causes (third-variable problem).** Sleep hours, home support, previous attainment, tuition, and motivation could explain both phone use and low marks. The data is also self-reported, so the phone-use figures may be inaccurate.

**(iii)** A fair next question would test a possible underlying factor, e.g. 'On an average school night, how many hours do you sleep?' or 'How many hours per week do you study with the phone in another room?'
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.knowledgeNote: Bloom's ladder (remember → create) places evaluation and creation at the top — exams increasingly target those rungs.
questions.question: What is critical thinking? Explain any three of its key skills with examples.
questions.solution:
**Critical thinking** is disciplined, evidence-based reasoning instead of accepting claims at face value.

**Skills:** (1) **Analysis** — breaking an argument into premises and conclusion. (2) **Evaluation** — testing evidence quality (a viral health claim vs a peer-reviewed trial). (3) **Inference** — drawing warranted conclusions (wet streets → it rained, barring alternatives).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Editorials blend both — spotting which sentence is which is the core critical-reading move.
questions.question: Distinguish between fact and opinion with two examples of each.
questions.solution:
**Fact** is verifiable: 'Mt. Everest is 8,848.86 m high.' 'Water boils at 100°C at sea level.'

**Opinion** expresses judgement: 'Pokhara is Nepal's most beautiful city.' 'Online classes are better than physical ones.'

Test: can evidence settle it? Yes → fact; no → opinion.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: 'Since/because' introduce premises; 'therefore/so' introduce conclusions — indicator words map arguments instantly.
questions.question: What are premises and conclusions in an argument? Identify them in: 'All students must wear uniforms since uniforms reduce economic discrimination.'
questions.solution:
**Premises** are the supporting reasons; the **conclusion** is the claim they support (flagged by 'therefore, so, since, because').

**Premise:** 'uniforms reduce economic discrimination.' **Conclusion:** 'All students must wear uniforms.'

Critical check: does the premise really entail the conclusion, or are cheaper alternatives (dress codes, subsidies) ignored?
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Strawman (distorting the opponent's view) completes the big-three fallacy set for this unit.
questions.question: What is a logical fallacy? Explain ad hominem and hasty generalisation with one example of each.
questions.solution:
A **fallacy** is reasoning that looks valid but isn't.

**Ad hominem:** attacking the person, not the claim — 'Don't trust his tax plan; he failed math.' **Hasty generalisation:** leaping from tiny samples — 'Two tourists were rude, so all tourists are rude.'
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Lateral reading — checking what OTHER reputable sites say about a source — beats judging any site by its own design.
questions.question: Write any four criteria for evaluating the credibility of an information source.
questions.solution: (1) **Authority** — qualified author/publisher? (2) **Evidence** — data and citations, or bare claims? (3) **Currency** — recent enough for the topic? (4) **Objectivity** — balanced or pushing an agenda? (+ Purpose: inform vs sell.)
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Multiple inferences can fit one observation — listing alternatives before concluding is the critical habit.
questions.question: Distinguish between observation and inference with an example.
questions.solution:
**Observation** reports direct senses: 'The classroom floor is wet.' **Inference** explains it: '…so the roof must be leaking (or someone spilled water).'

Observations are checkable facts; inferences are best-guess explanations — science advances by testing inferences against new observations.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Past perfect (had + V3) is used for the action completed before another past action.
questions.question: Fill in the blanks with correct tense: 'By the time we reached the station, the train ___ (already/leave).'
questions.solution:
'By the time we reached the station, the train **had already left**.'

Rule: Past perfect tense for the earlier action when two past actions are mentioned.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Third conditional: if + had + V3 -> would/could/might have + V3, used for unreal past situations.
questions.question: Correct the error in the following sentence and rewrite it: 'If I would have known about the flood, I would have taken the bus instead of walking through the lower bridge.'
questions.solution:
**Corrected:** If I **had known** about the flood, I would have taken the bus instead of walking through the lower bridge.

**Rule:** A third conditional describes an unreal past situation, so the *if*-clause takes **had + V3** (past perfect) and the main clause takes **would have + V3**. 'Would' is never used in the *if*-clause of a third conditional; 'if I had known' already carries the past meaning.

questions.question: Change into indirect speech: She said, 'I am very happy.'

Rules applied: 'said' stays; tense shifts (present → past); 'I' → 'she'.

questions.knowledgeNote: Modal + have + V3 speaks about the past: should have = regret, could have = missed possibility, must have = past deduction.
questions.question:
Complete the conversation with the correct form of the modal verb given in brackets:

A: I am joining a bank from tomorrow.
B: You ______ (should / not / tell) me earlier! We ______ (could / apply) together.
questions.solution:
A: I am joining a bank from tomorrow.
B: You **should have told** me earlier! We **could have applied** together.

**Rules:**
1. **should have + V3** expresses regret or reproach about a past action that did not happen. Telling happened only now, so the perfect form of the modal is required.
2. **could have + V3** expresses a real but unrealised possibility in the past. They were both free to apply together but did not.

questions.knowledgeNote: -ic forms a relational adjective (economic, historic); -al often adds the sense 'relating to' or 'thriftily' (economical, musical).
questions.question:
Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'The government's ______ report has been widely criticised by economists.'

(a) economical
(b) economic
(c) economicality
(d) economy
questions.solution:
**Correct answer: (b) economic.**

**Reasons:**
1. The suffix **-ic** turns a noun into an adjective of relation: *economy* (noun) -> **economic** (adjective), meaning 'relating to the economy'. The sentence criticises the government's *economic policy*, so the adjective is needed before the noun *report*.
2. **Economical** (suffix **-al**) means 'using money carefully; thrifty'. A report is not thrifty, so this word does not fit.
3. **Economy** is a noun and would not be placed before another noun, and **economicality** is not a standard English word.
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.knowledgeNote: Use 'an' before a vowel *sound* (an hour, an honest man) and a possessive pronoun before a noun (her promises, not hers).
questions.question:
Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'She is ______ honest girl and always keeps ______ promises she ______ made to her friends.'

(a) an / her / she
(b) a / her / she
(c) an / hers / she
(d) a / hers / her
questions.solution:
**Correct answer: (a) an / her / she.**

**Reasons:**
1. **Article:** *honest* begins with a silent *h*, so the indefinite article is **an** ('an honest girl'). The spelling 'h' is silent, so the sound, not the letter, decides.
2. **Possessive pronoun:** *promises* is a noun preceded by an adjective (*keeps ... promises*), so a possessive **pronoun** is needed: **her**, not the possessive determiner *hers*.
3. **Relative pronoun:** the missing verb is a past active verb, so the relative pronoun takes the subject form **she** to complete *she made*.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Inference questions ask what the writer implies, not what the words literally say: 'fails privately' is explained by the contrast with an apprentice, whose mistakes cost the master.
questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A generation ago a student who wanted to learn a trade had to find a master and serve an apprenticeship. Today the same skill is often learned from a screen: a video plays, the learner pauses, repeats the step, and fails privately until the hand remembers. The change looks like a small matter of convenience, but it shifts who bears the cost of learning. An apprentice's mistakes cost the master money and patience; a learner's mistakes cost only time. That protection is what makes the new learning so forgiving — and also what tempts a learner to stop before the difficult part, because nothing forces the hand to keep going except the learner's own intention.

(a) How did a student learn a trade a generation ago? (b) What does the writer mean by 'fails privately'? (c) According to the passage, what is both the advantage and the danger of learning from a screen? (d) Find a word from the passage that means 'the state of being protected from the consequences of error'.
questions.solution:
(a) A generation ago the student had to find a master and serve an apprenticeship, learning the skill by working under that master.

(b) It means the learner's mistakes are made where no one is watching or paying for them — the learner can repeat a step and fail without embarrassment, expense or a master's impatience.

(c) The advantage is that mistakes cost only time, so learning is forgiving and private; the danger is that nothing external forces the learner to continue, so a learner may stop before the difficult part unless they have their own strong intention.

(d) 'protection' — the passage says that protection (from the cost of mistakes) is what makes screen-based learning forgiving.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: A summary of a passage keeps the writer's argument and its contrast, stays within the word limit, and rewrites the wording rather than lifting sentences.
questions.question: Write a paragraph of about 100 words, in your own words, explaining the main idea of the passage in the first question. Do not copy long phrases from the passage.
questions.solution: The passage contrasts two ways of learning a practical skill. In the past an apprentice learned from a master, and every mistake had a price — money, patience and reputation. Now the same skill can be learned from recorded lessons, where mistakes cost only time, so learning becomes private, repeatable and forgiving. The writer argues that this is not merely convenient: it changes what drives the learner. Because no master insists, the learner must supply the discipline himself; the freedom that protects a beginner can also let them quit exactly where the work becomes hard.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Questions on the writer's attitude are answered from diction and imagery: 'quiet', 'without ceremony' and 'marked absent' signal sympathy and criticism, not neutrality.
questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Remittances are often described as the quiet economy of a hill village. The money arrives without ceremony, and the village converts it into brick walls, school fees and medicine. What is less visible is what leaves with the money: a generation of young hands, the songs sung at planting, and the patience to keep a field that no longer has anyone to plough it. Economists count the first and rarely the second, because a rupee that arrives can be measured while a tradition that does not is simply marked absent from the ledger.

(a) Who sends the money that the passage calls 'the quiet economy'? (b) List two things the village converts the money into. (c) Why do economists count the money but not the loss of tradition? (d) What does the phrase 'simply marked absent from the ledger' suggest about the writer's attitude?
questions.solution:
(a) Migrant workers — the young people who have left the village and send money home as remittances.

(b) Any two: brick walls (house construction), school fees, medicine.

(c) Because money that arrives can be measured and entered into accounts, while a tradition that is lost leaves nothing to count; what cannot be measured is recorded simply as absent rather than as a real loss.

(d) It suggests criticism: the writer finds it unjust that official counting treats the loss of a way of life as a blank in the accounts, as if it had no value, and implies that measures of national income are blind to what a village actually pays.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: A vocabulary question wants a context that makes the meaning unmistakable — the reader should be able to infer the word's sense from the sentence alone.
questions.question: Use the following words from the passage in sentences of your own to show their meanings clearly: (a) remittance, (b) ceremony, (c) ledger, (d) plough.
questions.solution:
(a) **remittance** — My uncle's monthly remittance from Qatar pays for my sister's tuition and my grandmother's medicine.

(b) **ceremony** — The award was given without any ceremony: the principal simply called her name in the assembly and handed over the medal.

(c) **ledger** — The shopkeeper opened his ledger and found that the customer still owed him four hundred rupees from last month.

(d) **plough** — With no one left to plough the upper terrace, the family let it go to grass and now buys the rice they once grew.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: In 'The Last Lesson' the fleeing birds and the silent blackboard are symbols of the language and identity lost when Alsace was occupied by Prussia.
questions.question:
Consider this moment in Alphonse Daudet's story 'The Last Lesson': when the order to leave the classroom comes, the mother moves her eyes from her son's face to the blackboard and back again; the master gives a strange, almost inaudible sound; and the birds fly out of the window while the Prussian soldiers seem to be passing in the street.

Explain the significance of this detail, naming at least two literary devices used in it and showing what effect each one has on the reader.
questions.solution:
**Significance:** The detail captures the moment when French, the mother tongue of Alsace, is taken away by Prussian order. Everything in the room - the blackboard with its French writing, the silent mother, the old master, the birds and the soldiers - is caught in a single second, which is why the moment is so painful and so still.

**Devices and effects:**
1. **Symbolism:** The **birds flying out of the window** stand for the sudden flight of everything familiar and innocent - the language, the joy and the childhood of the children. The **blackboard**, which is the last place French lives, becomes the symbol of a stolen language.
2. **Pathetic fallacy:** The master gives a 'strange, almost inaudible sound', which is a human feeling attributed to sound itself. Even the silence of the room behaves like a person who is trying not to cry, so the reader feels the master's suppressed grief.
3. **Personification / pathetic comparison:** The soldiers 'seem to be marching in the street' as if they were a natural, unstoppable force invading the room. War is shown not as a human argument but as an invading tide, which makes the children powerless.
4. **Contrast and silence:** The scene is described through what *does not* happen - nobody speaks, nobody cries. This deliberate silence heightens the emotion far more than direct description would.
questions.source: NEB Past

The story emphasizes patriotism, regret for wasted time, and the importance of preserving one's language and culture.

questions.knowledgeNote: Apostrophe addresses an absent person or abstract idea; Wordsworth's 'inward eye' is a metaphor for the mind's eye.
questions.question:
Read the following lines from William Wordsworth's 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' and answer the questions that follow:

'For oft, when on my couch I lie
In vacant or in pensive mood,
They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude;'

(i) What do the words 'They' and 'that inward eye' refer to?
(ii) Identify the figure of speech used in these lines and explain its effect on the reader.
(iii) What is the rhyme scheme of these four lines? Give the rhyme words that make up each rhyme.
questions.solution:
**(i) Reference:** 'They' stands for the remembered pictures of the golden daffodils - the daffodils themselves, the daffodil beds beside the lake, the child in a pink jacket, and finally the rainbow. 'That inward eye' is the **mind's eye**, that is, the memory and imagination through which a person sees things that are no longer present.

**(ii) Figure of speech:** **Apostrophe** combined with **metaphor**. The speaker does not describe the flowers; he turns and addresses an abstract thing directly - his own memory - as if it were a person standing before him ('They flash upon that inward eye'). The 'inward eye' is itself a metaphor: sight turned inwards.

**Effect:** By giving the flowers a voice and making memory an addressee, the poet suggests that the daffodils continue to live inside him and to comfort him. Solitude, which in the first stanza felt lonely and empty, is turned into 'the bliss of solitude' - the flowers have become his companions.

**(iii) Rhyme scheme:** **ABAB**.
- A = **lie** / **eye** (rhyme - the eye is the standard pronunciation, so this is an identical rhyme)
- B = **mood** / **solitude** (rhyme - both end in -u:d)

The lines are also written in **iambic tetrameter** (four feet of unstressed-stressed syllables per line), which gives the meditation a calm, rocking movement.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.question: Rewrite in passive voice: 'The gardener waters the plants every morning.'
questions.solution:
**The plants are watered by the gardener every morning.**

Rule: simple present active → am/is/are + past participle; object of the active sentence ('the plants') becomes the subject.

questions.question: Change into indirect speech: He said, 'I am learning English now.'
questions.solution:
He said that **he was learning English then**.

Rules: present continuous → past continuous; 'now' → 'then'; first person pronoun changes according to the subject of the reporting verb.

questions.question: Fill in the blanks with suitable articles: (a) … sun rises in … east. (b) She is … honest girl.
questions.solution:
(a) **The** sun rises in **the** east — unique objects take 'the'.

(b) She is **an** honest girl — 'an' is used before a vowel *sound* ('h' is silent).

questions.question: Write a paragraph of about 100 words on 'The Importance of Education'.
questions.solution:
Model answer:

**The Importance of Education**
Education is the backbone of human development. It gives people knowledge and skills to earn a living, think critically and participate responsibly in society. An educated person can distinguish right from wrong and solve problems scientifically rather than blindly following superstition. Education also reduces poverty: skilled people get better jobs and contribute to national progress. Moreover, educated mothers raise healthier families, so education benefits the next generation too. Therefore, every child — girl or boy — must get quality education, and the government should invest more in schools so that no one is left behind.

questions.question: Rewrite using the correct tense: 'When I (reach) the station, the train already (leave).'
questions.solution:
**When I reached the station, the train had already left.**

Rule: past perfect ('had left') shows the earlier of two past actions; simple past ('reached') shows the later one.

questions.question: Combine into a complex sentence: 'He is very poor. He is honest.'
questions.solution:
**Although he is very poor, he is honest.**

(Also acceptable: *Though he is very poor, he is honest.* — subordinating conjunction introduces the dependent clause.)

questions.question: Write a letter to your friend describing how you spent your last vacation.
questions.solution:
Model answer (informal letter format):

Kathmandu
15 March 2024

Dear Anita,
I hope you are fine. I am writing to tell you about my vacation. During the holidays I visited Pokhara with my family. We boated on Phewa Lake, watched the sunrise from Sarangkot and trekked part of the way to Australian Camp. The mountain views were breathtaking. Besides sightseeing, I finished two novels and helped my mother in the garden. It was refreshing after months of study.
Give my regards to your parents.

Yours lovingly,
Sita

questions.question: What is the difference between 'few' and 'a few'?
questions.solution:
**Few** = hardly any; has a negative sense (not enough). E.g. He has few friends (almost no friends).

**A few** = some; positive sense (at least some). E.g. He has a few friends (some friends).

questions.knowledgeNote: Note-making: Use abbreviations, symbols, and flow chart format. Keep it concise and organized.

Max 30 words. Key points cover health, agriculture, industry, and environment.

questions.question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions:

'The concept of global warming refers to the gradual increase in the average temperature of Earth's atmosphere, primarily due to the greenhouse effect caused by excessive emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases.'

Q: What is the main cause of global warming according to the passage?
questions.solution: **Answer:** The main cause of global warming is the excessive emission of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, which intensify the greenhouse effect and raise Earth's average temperature.

questions.knowledgeNote: To scan a notice, look first for dates, times and deadlines; words like 'must', 'before' and 'will not' carry the binding rules.
questions.question:
Read the notice below and answer the questions that follow.

NOTICE
ANNUAL SPORTS DAY - GRADE 11
All Grade 11 students must report to the east ground by 7:30 a.m. on 14 Magh. The 100-metre heats begin at 8:00 a.m. and the relay final is at 11:00 a.m. Each house team must submit its list of participants to the Physical Education teacher **before 7:15 a.m.** Students must bring their sports shoes and a water bottle. Absentees will not be allowed to compete.

(i) Sita reaches school at 7:20 a.m. Can she still submit her team's list of participants? Give a reason.
(ii) Ramesh arrives at 7:45 a.m. and asks to take part in the 100-metre race. What will happen to him, and why?
(iii) State two things a reader must look for first when scanning a notice like this one.
questions.solution:
**(i)** No. The list of participants had to be submitted **before 7:15 a.m.**, but Sita reached school only at 7:20 a.m. - five minutes after the deadline. A notice gives a fixed deadline, so arriving late makes the submission impossible.

**(ii)** Ramesh will not be allowed to compete. All students had to report to the east ground by 7:30 a.m. and the heats began at 8:00 a.m., so at 7:45 a.m. he has already missed both the reporting time and the start of his race. The notice also states clearly that absentees will not be permitted to compete.

**(iii)** Two things to look for first:
1. **Dates and times** - 14 Magh, 7:30 a.m., before 7:15 a.m., 8:00 a.m., 11:00 a.m.
2. **Deadlines and compulsory rules** - the words 'must', 'before' and 'will not be allowed', which show what the reader must do and what happens if it is not done.

questions.knowledgeNote: Ensure = make certain; assure = tell a person; insure = cover financially. Their sounds match but their meanings differ.
questions.question:
Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'Before you submit your assignment, please ______ that you have attached all the required files.'

(a) insure
(b) ensure
(c) assure
(d) endure
questions.solution:
**Correct answer: (b) ensure.**

**Rules:**
1. **Ensure** = to make certain that something happens. Here the speaker wants the files to be there, so *please ensure that ...* is correct.
2. **Insure** = to cover something financially by paying an insurance premium, so it does not fit the meaning.
3. **Assure** = to tell a person confidently that they will be safe or that something is true. Its usual pattern is *assure someone*, not *assure that something*.
4. **Endure** = to suffer something painful patiently, which is entirely unrelated.
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.knowledgeNote: Obviate means to remove an obstacle; it is not a synonym of ignore, which only means to pay no attention to it.
questions.question:
Choose the word that is nearly the same in meaning as the underlined word: 'The teacher asked us to **obviate** the difficulty we faced in solving the equation.'

(a) overcome
(b) create
(c) ignore
(d) worsen
questions.solution:
**Correct answer: (a) overcome.**

*Obviate* means to remove, get rid of or do away with something unpleasant such as a difficulty, problem or obstacle. Hence 'obviate the difficulty' = 'overcome the difficulty'.

- **(c) ignore** means to pay no attention to something; the difficulty would still be there, so it is not the same.
- **(b) create** and **(d) worsen** are the opposite meaning - they would make the situation worse.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Essay structure: Introduction (hook + thesis) → Body paragraphs (topic sentence + explanation + example) → Conclusion (summary + final thought).
questions.question: Write an essay on 'Importance of Reading Books' in about 250 words.
questions.solution:
Model essay:

Reading books is one of the most valuable habits one can develop. It broadens the mind, expands vocabulary, and deepens understanding of the world.

First, reading improves knowledge. Every book is a source of information — whether fiction or non-fiction. Reading about history helps us learn from past mistakes; reading science exposes us to new discoveries.

Second, reading enhances language skills. Regular readers have better vocabulary, grammar, and writing abilities. They can express their thoughts more clearly and confidently.

Third, reading reduces stress. Immersing oneself in a good book provides escape from daily worries and promotes mental well-being.

Finally, reading builds imagination and creativity. Stories transport us to different worlds and times, stimulating our creative thinking.

In conclusion, reading books is not merely a hobby but a lifelong necessity. It shapes character, sharpens intellect, and enriches life. Students should make reading a daily habit for overall development.
questions.source: NEB Past

questions.question: Write a letter to your friend describing your school excursion to Pokhara.
questions.solution:
Model informal letter:

Kathmandu
15 April 2024

Dear Sita,
I hope you are doing well. I am writing to share about our wonderful school excursion to Pokhara.

We left early in the morning by bus. The scenic drive through the hills was breathtaking. We reached Pokhara by afternoon and checked into our hotel.

The next day, we boated on Phewa Lake and visited the Peace Pagoda. The view of the Annapurna range from the top was magical. We also visited the World Peace Pagoda and the International Mountain Museum.

The food was delicious and the weather was cool. We returned home tired but happy.
I wish you could have joined us!

Give my regards to your family.

Your friend,
Anita

questions.knowledgeNote: In dialogue writing keep each turn short, use contractions, and show politeness through tone words rather than long speeches.
questions.question: Write a dialogue between a student and the school librarian about a book she reserved last week which still has not reached her. Your dialogue should contain at least eight exchanges and should end naturally.
questions.solution:
**Model dialogue:**

**Librarian:** Good morning. Can I help you?
**Rina:** Yes, please. I reserved *The Sound of Music* last Thursday, but nobody has told me it is ready.
**Librarian:** Let me check your record... Ah, the book is still on loan. It was due back yesterday.
**Rina:** That is exactly my problem. Even if it has come back, nobody informed me.
**Librarian:** We do send reminders, but the address you gave us is incomplete. Could you leave a phone number?
**Rina:** Certainly, I will write it here. And could you keep the book aside for me in that case?
**Librarian:** I can hold it until Monday. Please come at 10:00 a.m., after the morning reading period, because new books are issued only then.
**Rina:** I will be here at ten, thank you for the trouble.
**Librarian:** Not at all. A reminder call would have saved you both a visit.

**Techniques used:** short turns for each speaker, contractions (*I will*, *That's*), polite tone words (*please*, *thank you*), a slight difference of register between the polite librarian and the slightly irritated student, and a closing remark that ends the exchange naturally.
questions.source: NEB Model
