questions.knowledgeNote: For by-parts choose u by the ILATE order (Inverse, Log, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential) — here the algebraic x is u.
questions.question: Evaluate: (a) ∫ x eˣ dx, (b) ∫ dx/(x² − 4).
questions.solution:
**(a) By parts** (∫u dv = uv − ∫v du): take u = x, dv = eˣdx → du = dx, v = eˣ.

∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = **x eˣ − eˣ + C = eˣ(x − 1) + C**.

**(b) Partial fractions:** 1/(x² − 4) = 1/[(x − 2)(x + 2)] = (1/4)[1/(x − 2) − 1/(x + 2)].

So ∫dx/(x² − 4) = **(1/4) ln|(x − 2)/(x + 2)| + C** (using ∫dx/(x − a) = ln|x − a|).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Reducing powers with double-angle identities converts a definite trigonometric integral into elementary terms — the standard NEB approach.
questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin²x dx.
questions.solution:
Use the identity sin²x = (1 − cos2x)/2:

∫sin²x dx = ∫(1 − cos2x)/2 dx = x/2 − sin2x/4.

Applying the limits 0 to π/2: [π/4 − 0] − [0 − 0] = **π/4 ≈ 0.785**.

(Check by symmetry: ∫₀^(π/2) sin²x dx = ∫₀^(π/2) cos²x dx, and their sum is π/2, so each is π/4.)
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Half-angle identities turn rational trigonometric integrands into standard sec² forms — remember ∫sec²u du = tan u.
questions.question: Evaluate ∫ dx/(1 + cos x).
questions.solution:
Use 1 + cos x = 2cos²(x/2):

∫ dx/(1 + cosx) = ∫ dx/(2cos²(x/2)) = (1/2)∫ sec²(x/2) dx = (1/2)·2 tan(x/2) + C = **tan(x/2) + C**.

So the integral is tan(x/2) + C (valid where cos(x/2) ≠ 0).

questions.knowledgeNote: Always try substitution first; if you get 0/0 or ∞/∞, factorise, rationalise or use the standard limit — never divide by zero directly.
questions.question: Evaluate: (a) lim(x→0) sin5x/3x, (b) lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2).
questions.solution:
**(a)** lim(x→0) sin5x/3x = (5/3)·lim(x→0) sin5x/(5x) = (5/3)(1) = **5/3**, using lim(θ→0) sinθ/θ = 1.

**(b)** 0/0 form, so factorise: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x + 2)(x − 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2. Hence the limit is 2 + 2 = **4**.

The theorem used is that for a rational function the limit at a removable discontinuity is obtained by cancelling the common factor.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: A function can have a limit at a point without being defined there (removable discontinuity) — continuity demands both plus equality.
questions.question: Define continuity of a function at a point. For what value of k is the function f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3, f(3) = k, continuous at x = 3?
questions.solution:
**Continuity at x = a** requires three conditions: f(a) is defined, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).

Here lim(x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = lim(x→3) (x + 3) = 6.

For continuity this limit must equal f(3) = k, so **k = 6**. With any other k the graph has a removable hole at x = 3.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Standard expansions — sinx ≈ x, 1 − cosx ≈ x²/2 — solve most 0/0 limit questions faster than L'Hospital's rule.
questions.question: Evaluate lim(x→0) (1 − cos 2x)/x².
questions.solution:
Use the identity 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin²x:

lim(x→0) 2sin²x/x² = 2·lim(x→0) (sinx/x)² = 2 × 1 = **2**.

(Equivalently, use the expansion cos2x = 1 − (2x)²/2 + …, giving (2x²)/x² = 2.)

questions.knowledgeNote: Evaluate Z at EVERY corner: the optimum is always at a vertex for a linear objective on a convex feasible region.
questions.question: Maximise Z = 40x + 50y subject to 2x + y ≤ 20, x + 2y ≤ 20, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Solve graphically.
questions.solution:
**Feasible region:** bounded by the axes and the two constraint lines.

Corner points from the intersections:
- (0, 0) → Z = 0
- (10, 0) → Z = 400
- (0, 10) → Z = 500
- intersection of 2x + y = 20 and x + 2y = 20: solving gives x = y = **20/3 ≈ 6.67** → Z = 40(20/3) + 50(20/3) = 600.

By the corner-point theorem the optimum is at a vertex: **maximum Z = 600 at x = y = 20/3**.

(Checking the interior point confirms the value is below 600, and the region is bounded, so the maximum exists.)
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: This is why the graphical method evaluates only vertices — it is a theorem, not a shortcut, and the examiner expects it stated.
questions.question: Define feasible region, optimal solution and corner-point theorem in linear programming.
questions.solution:
**Feasible region:** the common region satisfying all the constraints (including non-negativity) of a linear programming problem — it is a convex polygon.

**Optimal solution:** the feasible point (set of values of the decision variables) at which the objective function attains its maximum or minimum value.

**Corner-point theorem (fundamental theorem of LPP):** if the feasible region is bounded, the objective function attains its optimum at a corner (vertex) of the feasible region; if two adjacent vertices give the same optimum, every point on the segment joining them is optimal.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Always define the variables and write the non-negativity restrictions explicitly — they are part of the formulation and carry marks.
questions.question: A factory makes two products A and B. A needs 2 hours of machine time and 1 hour of labour; B needs 1 hour of machine time and 3 hours of labour. The factory has 40 machine hours and 60 labour hours per day. If the profit is Rs 30 on A and Rs 40 on B, formulate the LPP to maximise the profit.
questions.solution:
Let x = units of A and y = units of B produced per day.

**Objective:** maximise Z = 30x + 40y (profit in rupees).

**Constraints:**
- machine time: 2x + y ≤ 40
- labour time: x + 3y ≤ 60
- non-negativity: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

The solution is obtained by plotting the two lines, finding the feasible region and evaluating Z at its corner points (one of which is the intersection x = 12, y = 16 giving Z = 1000).

questions.knowledgeNote: Independent events satisfy P(A|B) = P(A); mutually exclusive events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = 0 — the two are frequently confused.
questions.question: If P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4 and A and B are independent, find P(A ∪ B) and P(A|B).
questions.solution:
Independence gives P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12.

**P(A ∪ B)** = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.3 + 0.4 − 0.12 = **0.58**.

**P(A|B)** = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0.12/0.4 = **0.3 = P(A)**, confirming independence (the occurrence of B does not change A's probability).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Binomial conditions: fixed number of trials, two outcomes, constant p and independence — state them before applying mean np and variance npq.
questions.question: A fair die is thrown 10 times. Find the mean and the variance of the number of times a six appears, and state the distribution used.
questions.solution:
Each throw is an independent Bernoulli trial with p = 1/6 (six) and q = 5/6, so the number of sixes X follows a **binomial distribution** with n = 10.

**Mean** = np = 10 × 1/6 = **5/3 ≈ 1.67**.

**Variance** = npq = 10 × (1/6) × (5/6) = 50/36 = **25/18 ≈ 1.39**, so the standard deviation is √(25/18) ≈ 1.18.

questions.knowledgeNote: Direction ratios need not be unit vectors; direction cosines are the normalised ratios, and only for these does l² + m² + n² = 1 hold.
questions.question: Find the direction cosines of the line joining the points A(1, 2, 3) and B(4, 5, 6), and write the equation of the line.
questions.solution:
Direction ratios: AB = (4 − 1, 5 − 2, 6 − 3) = (3, 3, 3).

Magnitude = √(9 + 9 + 9) = 3√3, so the direction cosines are (3, 3, 3)/(3√3) = **(1/√3, 1/√3, 1/√3)**, and they satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1.

**Equation of the line:** (x − 1)/3 = (y − 2)/3 = (z − 3)/3, i.e. x − 1 = y − 2 = z − 3, or in vector form r = (i + 2j + 3k) + λ(i + j + k).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Use the absolute value in the numerator, otherwise the formula returns the obtuse supplement — a very frequent marking deduction.
questions.question: Find the angle between the lines (x − 1)/2 = (y + 3)/−1 = z/3 and (x − 2)/1 = (y − 1)/2 = (z + 1)/−2.
questions.solution:
The direction ratios are d₁ = (2, −1, 3) and d₂ = (1, 2, −2).

cosθ = |d₁·d₂|/(|d₁||d₂|) = |2(1) + (−1)(2) + 3(−2)| / (√14 × 3) = |2 − 2 − 6|/(3√14) = 6/(3√14) = **2/√14 ≈ 0.535** → **θ ≈ 57.7°**.

Taking the absolute value gives the acute angle between the lines.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: The plane's cartesian coefficients are exactly the normal's components — read the normal straight off the equation ax + by + cz + d = 0.
questions.question: Find the equation of the plane passing through the point (2, 3, −1) with normal vector n = 2i − j + 3k.
questions.solution:
The plane through r₀ with normal n satisfies n·(r − r₀) = 0:

2(x − 2) − 1(y − 3) + 3(z + 1) = 0
2x − 4 − y + 3 + 3z + 3 = 0

**2x − y + 3z + 2 = 0**, i.e. 2x − y + 3z = −2.

In vector form: r·(2i − j + 3k) = 3 (since 2(2) − 3 + 3(−1) = −2... check: the constant equals n·r₀ = 4 − 3 − 3 = −2).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: The scalar projection is a signed length; the vector projection keeps the direction of b — examiners require the scalar unless the vector is asked.
questions.question: Find the projection of vector a = 2i + 3j + 2k on b = i + 2j + k, and state the condition for two vectors to be perpendicular.
questions.solution:
Projection of a on b = (a·b)/|b| = (2 + 6 + 2)/√(1 + 4 + 1) = 10/√6 ≈ **4.08** (the scalar projection).

(As a vector it is [(a·b)/|b|²]b = (10/6)(i + 2j + k).)

**Condition for perpendicularity:** a·b = 0 (the scalar product vanishes; for three dimensions this is the standard test since cos 90° = 0).

questions.knowledgeNote: वाच्य परिवर्तनमा क्रिया कर्मको लिङ्ग-वचन-पुरुषसँग मिलाउनु अनिवार्य छ, नत्र अङ्क कट्छ।
questions.question: दिइएका वाक्यको निर्देशनअनुसार वाच्य परिवर्तन गर्नुहोस्: (क) शिक्षकले पाठ पढाउनुहुन्छ। (कर्मवाच्य) (ख) मैले पत्र लेखें। (कर्मवाच्य) (ग) उहाँ हिँड्नुहुन्छ। (भाववाच्य)
questions.solution:
**(क) कर्मवाच्य:** कर्म अगाडि र कर्तामा 'बाट/द्वारा' — **शिक्षकबाट पाठ पढाइन्छ।** (क्रिया कर्म 'पाठ' सँग मिल्यो।)

**(ख)** **मबाट पत्र लेखियो।** — कर्ता 'मैले' बाट 'मबाट' मा बदलियो, क्रिया कर्मअनुसार 'लेखियो' भयो।

**(ग) भाववाच्य:** अकर्मक क्रिया हुँदा भाववाच्य — **उहाँबाट हिँडिन्छ।**

नियम: कर्मवाच्य सकर्मक क्रियामा मात्र हुन्छ; अकर्मक क्रियाको भाववाच्य मात्र बन्छ।
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: भेद छुट्याउने चाबी प्रधानता हो — अर्थ तेस्रोतिर गयो भने तुरुन्त बहुव्रीहि।
questions.question: दिइएका समस्त पदको विग्रह गरी समासको भेद पहिचान गर्नुहोस्: (क) राजपुत्र (ख) नीलकण्ठ (ग) आमाबाबु (घ) मुखचन्द्र।
questions.solution:
**(क) राजपुत्र = राजाको पुत्र** — सम्बन्ध षष्ठी (को) र अर्थ परपद 'पुत्र' मा प्रधान → **तत्पुरुष समास**।

**(ख) नीलकण्ठ = नीलो कण्ठ भएको, अर्थात् शिव** — अर्थ तेस्रो (शिव) मा गयो → **बहुव्रीहि समास**।

**(ग) आमाबाबु = आमा र बाबु** — दुवै पद प्रधान → **द्वन्द्व समास**।

**(घ) मुखचन्द्र = चन्द्रजस्तो मुख** — विशेषण-विशेष्य (उपमान-उपमेय) नाता → **कर्मधारय समास**।
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: आदरार्थी कर्तासँग बहुवचन क्रिया प्रयोग हुन्छ — यो नेपाली व्याकरणको नियमित परीक्षा-बिन्दु हो।
questions.question: दिइएका अशुद्ध वाक्य शुद्ध गरी लेख्नुहोस्: (क) उनी आएको छैन। (ख) मैले भोलि जान्छु। (ग) सबै विद्यार्थीहरूले परीक्षा दिए।
questions.solution:
**(क)** 'उनी' आदरार्थी भएकाले क्रिया बहुवचनमा — **उनी आएका छैनन्।**

**(ख)** 'मैले' भाववाच्य/कर्मणि प्रयोग हो; कर्तृवाच्यमा — **म भोलि जान्छु।** (यहाँ 'ले' विभक्ति नमिल्ने हुन्छ।)

**(ग)** 'सबै' र 'हरू' दुवै बहुवचन भएकाले एउटा मात्र — **सबै विद्यार्थीले परीक्षा दिए।**

शुद्धीकरण गर्दा विभक्ति, वचन र लिङ्गको मेल जाँच्नु नै मुख्य काम हो।

questions.knowledgeNote: आवधिक निबन्ध भूमिका → बुँदागत विस्तार → निष्कर्ष यही ढाँचामा लेख्नुहोस्; हरेक अनुच्छेदमा एउटा मात्र बुँदा।
questions.question: 'सामुदायिक वनको महत्त्व' विषयमा आवधिक निबन्ध लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**भूमिका:** नेपालको वन संरक्षणमा सामुदायिक वन एक सफल अभ्यास हो — जनसहभागिताले वन बचाएको मात्र नभई गाउँको अर्थतन्त्र बदलेको छ।

**विस्तार:**
१. **वातावरणीय महत्त्व:** पहिरो रोकथाम, जलस्रोत संरक्षण, जैविक विविधता र कार्बन भण्डारण।
२. **आर्थिक महत्त्व:** दाउरा, घाँस, काष्ठ र औषधिजन्य वनस्पति; सदस्यको श्रमबाट वन पैदावर आय।
३. **सामाजिक महत्त्व:** महिला र सीमान्तित समुदायको सहभागिता, समूहमा निर्णय, दायित्वको भावना।
४. **चुनौती:** काष्ठको अत्यधिक दोहन, सदस्यबीच विवाद, नेतृत्वको कमजोरी, जलवायु प्रकोप।

**निष्कर्ष:** सामुदायिक वन संरक्षणको साधन र विकासको माध्यम दुवै हो; जनसहभागिता कायम राख्दा नै यसको सफलता दिगो हुनेछ।
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.question: विद्यालयको नाममा पुस्तकालयको समय विस्तार गर्ने सम्बन्धी आधिकारिक पत्र लेख्नुहोस्।

questions.question: विद्यालयमा सम्पन्न 'विविधावर प्रतियोगिता' को प्रतिवेदन तयार गर्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**प्रतिवेदन**

**विषय:** वार्षिक विविधावर प्रतियोगिता २०८१
**समय:** २०८१ कार्तिक १५, बिहान १० बजे
**स्थान:** विद्यालय सभाहल

**पृष्ठभूमि र उद्देश्य:** विद्यार्थीको प्रस्तुतीकरण क्षमता, भाषिक दक्षता र आत्मविश्वास बढाउने उद्देश्यले आयोजना गरिएको।

**कार्यक्रमको विवरण:** कुल ४२ प्रतिस्पर्धी; खण्ड — हास्य कविता, भाषण, कथा कथन, फुटकर गीत। तीनजना शिक्षक निर्णायक।

**नतिजा:** प्रथम — सुश्री अनुशा, द्वितीय — श्री सुजन; द्वितीय कक्षाकी छात्राले दर्शकको मन जितेको।

**समस्या:** समय व्यवस्थापनको कमजोरीले दुई खण्ड संक्षिप्त गर्नुपर्‍यो; सभाहलमा ध्वनि प्रणाली पर्याप्त थिएन।

**सुझाव:** अर्को वर्ष अग्रिम समय-तालिका, राम्रो ध्वनि प्रणाली र प्रतिस्पर्धीलाई पूर्व अभ्यासको अवसर।

प्रतिवेदन तयार गर्ने — सचिव, सांस्कृतिक समिति।

questions.knowledgeNote: कविताको उत्तरमा विधा, रचनाकार, मूल भाव, प्रतिपाद्य र शिल्प — यी पाँच बुँदा राख्दा पूर्णाङ्क पाइन्छ।
questions.question: 'आमाको सपना' कविताको केन्द्रीय भाव लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
कवि गोपालप्रसाद रिमालको 'आमाको सपना' कविताको केन्द्रीय भाव **सन्तानको उन्नतिप्रति आमाको निःस्वार्थ ममता र त्याग** हो।

कवितामा आमा आफ्नो सम्पूर्ण जीवन छोराको भविष्यका लागि बिताउँछिन्; शिक्षा र सभ्य बनाउने उनको सपना छोरोको सफलतासँग जोडिएको छ। दुःख, गरिबी र असहाय अवस्थामा पनि उनको आशा मर्दैन — छोरोले उज्यालो बाटो समात्ने विश्वास उनमा कायम रहन्छ।

कविताको प्रतिपाद्य हो: मातृ-स्नेह निःस्वार्थ हुन्छ र सन्तानको कर्तव्य आमाको त्याग बुझेर आफ्नो जिम्मेवारी पूरा गर्नु हो। सरल भाषा, दोहोरिने लय र मार्मिक बिम्बले भावलाई प्रभावकारी बनाएका छन्।
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: उपन्यासको प्रश्नमा कथानक मात्र नभनी पात्र-चरित्र, प्रतीक र समकालीन सान्दर्भिकता जोड्नुहोस्।
questions.question: 'एक चिहान' उपन्यासको सामाजिक सन्देश के हो? छोटो विश्लेषण गर्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
पारिजातको 'एक चिहान' नेपाली समाजको यथार्थ चित्रण गर्ने उपन्यास हो। यसको सामाजिक सन्देश — **अन्धविश्वास, छुवाछूत, लिङ्ग-विभेद र हिंसाले सिङ्गो समाजलाई कसरी क्षय गर्छ भन्ने चेतावनी** हो।

उपन्यासमा सुकुम्बासी/समानान्तर बस्तीका पात्र, बोक्सीको आरोप, रुढी परम्परा र स्त्रीको असहाय अवस्था देखाइएको छ। अजम्बरी निर्दोष भएर पनि इलाका र सामाजिक शक्तिको शिकार हुन्छिन्; माधवको सङ्घर्ष संरचनासँग ठोकिन्छ।

सन्देश दुईतिर छ: पहिलो, विभेद गर्ने परम्परा त्याग्नु; दोस्रो, अन्यायविरुद्ध प्रतिरोध गर्नु। 'चिहान' नै उपन्यासको प्रतीक हो — एक आमाको र एक समाजको सामूहिक चिहान, जसले विस्मृतिको मूल्य देखाउँछ।
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: शिल्प सोधिएको प्रश्नमा लय, बिम्ब, अलंकार र भाषा छुट्टाछुट्टै उल्लेख गर्दा पूर्णाङ्क सम्भव हुन्छ।
questions.question: 'हामीलाई बोलाउँछन् हिमचुली' कविताको भाव र शिल्प (लय, बिम्ब, अलंकार) को चर्चा गर्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
भूपी शेरचनको यो कविता **प्रकृतिको आह्वानमार्फत मानवीय कर्तव्य जगाउने** कविता हो। हिमचुली (हिउँका टाकुरा) ले मानिसलाई जीवनको मूल उद्देश्य — श्रम, साहस र नवनिर्माणतर्फ बोलाउँछन्; आराम र निष्क्रियता त्याग्न आग्रह गर्छन्।

**शिल्प:**
- **लय:** मुक्त छन्दको प्रवाह, दोहोरिने आह्वानात्मक पङ्क्तिले गति दिन्छ।
- **बिम्ब:** हिमचुली, पहाड, उकालो — उचाइ र पवित्रताको प्रतीक।
- **अलंकार:** मानवीकरण (हिमचुलीले 'बोलाउनु') र प्रतीकात्मकता प्रमुख।

कविताले पाठकलाई आत्मबल र सामूहिक श्रमको सन्देश दिन्छ — उचाइ चढ्नु नै अग्रगामी यात्राको रूपक हो।

questions.knowledgeNote: संस्कृतिको उत्तरमा 'संस्कृति बाँच्ने र बदलिने दुवै क्रम' स्वीकार गर्दा सन्तुलित मानिन्छ।
questions.question: नेपाली संस्कृतिका विशेषता उल्लेख गर्दै यसको जगेर्नाका उपाय लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
**विशेषता:**
१. बहुजातीय, बहुभाषिक र बहुधार्मिक साझा सम्पदा — विविधतामा एकता नेपाली संस्कृतिको मूल विशेषता।
२. सहिष्णुता र सद्भाव — छिमेकी जातजातिबीच सहअस्तित्व।
३. रीतिरिवाज र चाडपर्वको समृद्धि — दसैँ, तिहार, छठ, लोसार, सोनाम ल्होसार आदि।
४. कला, शिल्प र मूर्त-अमूर्त सम्पदा — पगोडा, मूर्तिकला, लोकगीत, भजन।
५. सामान्य ग्रहणशीलता — बाह्य प्रभाव आत्मसात् गर्ने क्षमता।

**जगेर्नाका उपाय:** मातृभाषामा शिक्षा र लेखनलाई प्राथमिकता; स्थानीय चाडपर्व र लोककलाको संरक्षण तथा वैज्ञानिक पुनर्व्याख्या; विश्व सम्पदा क्षेत्रको उचित व्यवस्थापन; कुरीति (दाइजो, छुवाछूत) बहिष्कार गर्दै सकारात्मक पक्ष जोगाउनु; पुस्तान्तरणका लागि किशोरकिशोरीसँग अन्तरक्रिया।
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: 'पहिचान' को प्रश्नमा भावुक दोहोरो नलेखी तीन बुँदा — भाषाको भूमिका, जोखिम र समाधान — स्पष्ट पार्नुहोस्।
questions.question: भाषा र पहिचानको सम्बन्धमा टिप्पणी लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
भाषा पहिचानको सबैभन्दा बलियो चिह्न हो। व्यक्ति र समुदायले आफूलाई कसरी चिन्छ भन्ने कुरा उसले बोल्ने भाषासँग जोडिएको हुन्छ — भाषा स्मृति, इतिहास र मूल्यको भण्डार हो।

**तीन तथ्य:**
१. भाषा हराउँदा संस्कृतिको ठूलो भाग पनि हराउँछ — लोकगीत, भजन, उखान ती भाषामै जीवित छन्।
२. नेपाली भाषाले मातृभाषी बाहेक समग्र राष्ट्रलाई जोड्ने साझा माध्यमको काम गर्छ; तर मातृभाषाको संरक्षण नेपालीको विरोध होइन, सम्पूर्णताको पक्ष।
३. पहिचान बहुस्तरीय हुन्छ — स्थानीय (जात, गाउँ) र राष्ट्रिय (नेपाली) दुवै तह सँगसँगै रहन्छ।

निष्कर्ष: बहुभाषिकतालाई सम्पत्ति मान्ने नीति नै पहिचान संरक्षणको बाटो हो।
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: प्रतिनिधित्वको प्रश्नमा एउटा पाठको उदाहरण अनिवार्य — नाम र घटना दुवै उल्लेख गर्नुहोस्।
questions.question: साहित्यमा सामाजिक यथार्थको प्रतिनिधित्व कसरी भएको छ? उदाहरणसहित लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
साहित्य समाजको ऐना र आलोचक दुवै हो। नेपाली साहित्यमा सामाजिक यथार्थ तीन तहमा देखिन्छ।

**१. वर्णनात्मक यथार्थ:** पुरानो कथा/उपन्यासमा गाउँको दुःख, गरिबी र परम्पराको चित्रण — पात्रबाट समाज बोल्ने।

**२. प्रश्नात्मक यथार्थ:** नयाँ लेखनमा विभेद र अन्यायमाथि प्रश्न — पारिजातको 'एक चिहान' मा बोक्सी आरोप, छुवाछूत र नारीको असहायता अरूको निर्णयको शिकार बनेर देखाइएको छ।

**३. रूपान्तरणकारी यथार्थ:** प्रतिरोध र सुधारको बाटो — श्रम, शिक्षा र चेतनाले बदलाव सम्भव भएको सन्देश (भूपी शेरचनको कवितामा हिमचुलीको आह्वान)।

निष्कर्ष: साहित्यले यथार्थ देखाउँदा सुधारको बाटो खोल्छ; केवल वर्णन गर्ने लेखन आलोचना रहित हुन्छ।

questions.knowledgeNote: At resonance the voltage across L and C can greatly exceed the supply voltage (voltage magnification Q = ω₀L/R).
questions.question: Derive the expression for the impedance of a series LCR circuit and state the condition for resonance.
questions.solution:
With the same current I through all elements, the phasor sum of the voltages gives

V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²) = I√(R² + (X_L − X_C)²),

so **Z = √(R² + (ωL − 1/ωC)²)**.

**Resonance** occurs when X_L = X_C, i.e. ω = 1/√(LC); then Z = R (minimum) and the current is maximum, with the circuit purely resistive.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Meters read rms values; a.c. power P = I_rms V_rms cos φ, where cos φ is the power factor.
questions.question: Define root-mean-square value of alternating current. Show that for a sinusoidal current the rms value is 1/√2 times the peak value.
questions.solution:
The **rms value** is the steady direct current that would produce the same average heating in a resistor: I_rms = √(mean of I²).

With I = I₀ sin ωt, I² = I₀²sin²ωt = I₀²(1 − cos2ωt)/2. The cosine term averages to zero over a cycle, so mean I² = I₀²/2 and

**I_rms = I₀/√2 ≈ 0.707 I₀**.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: A step-down transformer gives lower voltage but higher current; energy conservation (ideal case) requires V_pI_p = V_sI_s.
questions.question: A transformer with 1000 turns in the primary and 100 turns in the secondary is connected to a 220 V a.c. mains. Find the secondary voltage and the secondary current when the primary current is 0.2 A (assume an ideal transformer).
questions.solution:
V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p → V_s = 220 × 100/1000 = **22 V**.

For an ideal transformer, V_pI_p = V_sI_s → I_s = (220 × 0.2)/22 = **2 A** — the voltage steps down by 10, so the current steps up by 10.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Antenna length must be comparable to λ/4, which is why audio (≈20 Hz–20 kHz) cannot be radiated directly and needs a carrier in the MHz range.
questions.question: What is modulation? Distinguish between amplitude modulation and frequency modulation, and state one advantage of FM over AM.
questions.solution:
**Modulation** is the process of superimposing a low-frequency message signal on a high-frequency carrier wave so the signal can be radiated over long distances by an antenna of practical size.

**AM:** the amplitude of the carrier varies with the message; the sideband bandwidth is 2f_m, and noise affects amplitude strongly.

**FM:** the frequency varies with the message; bandwidth ≈ 2(f_m + Δf), which is wider.

**Advantage of FM:** noise immunity — amplitude noise (lightning, sparks) can be clipped away, so reception is much clearer.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Satellite communication uses space waves above ~30 MHz, where the ionosphere no longer reflects the signal.
questions.question: Explain the terms ground wave, sky wave and space wave propagation with one suitable use of each.
questions.solution:
**Ground wave:** the wave travels along the Earth's surface; useful for medium-wave broadcast over short ranges, attenuated as frequency rises.

**Sky wave:** the wave is refracted back by the ionosphere and can travel thousands of kilometres; used for short-wave radio, but is unstable as ionisation changes with time of day.

**Space wave:** line-of-sight propagation direct from transmitter to receiver (plus a ground-reflected component); used for VHF/UHF TV, radar and satellite links, with range limited by the horizon.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: FM needs a wider channel than AM but trades bandwidth for noise immunity — a recurring NEB comparison.
questions.question: Define bandwidth of a signal and calculate the bandwidth needed if a message of 5 kHz is transmitted by (a) AM and (b) FM with a frequency deviation of 20 kHz.
questions.solution:
**Bandwidth** is the range of frequencies a signal occupies.

**(a) AM:** 2f_m = 2 × 5 = **10 kHz**.

**(b) FM:** 2(f_m + Δf) = 2(5 + 20) = **50 kHz**, using Carson's rule.

questions.knowledgeNote: Drift speed is only ~10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ while the signal travels near light speed — the field, not the electron, carries the message.
questions.question: Define drift velocity and derive the relation I = neAv_d for a conductor.
questions.solution:
**Drift velocity** is the average velocity with which free electrons move opposite the field.

In time t, electrons travel v_d·t, so all electrons in a cylinder of volume A·v_d·t cross the section. Number = n·A·v_d·t carrying charge q = ne·A·v_d·t.

I = q/t = **neAv_d**. Since v_d = eEτ/m, also I = ne²AτE/m.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: At balance the galvanometer branch may be removed or replaced by any resistance without changing the currents — the basis of the metre bridge.
questions.question: State Kirchhoff's laws for electric circuits and use them to obtain the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge.
questions.solution:
**Junction rule:** sum of currents entering = sum leaving (charge conservation). **Loop rule:** algebraic sum of potential changes round any closed loop is zero (energy conservation).

For the bridge, at balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so current divides into P,Q and R,S branches: I₁P = I₂R and I₁Q = I₂S. Dividing,

**P/Q = R/S** — the balance condition.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: The minus sign in e = −N dΦ/dt is Lenz's law written mathematically.
questions.question: State Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction and explain Lenz's law as a consequence of energy conservation.
questions.solution:
**Faraday's laws:** (i) whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced; (ii) the magnitude of the emf equals the rate of change of flux, |e| = dΦ/dt. For a coil of N turns, e = −N dΦ/dt.

**Lenz's law:** the induced current opposes the change producing it. If it aided the change, the flux would grow without limit and give free energy; the work done against the opposition appears as electrical energy, so Lenz's law is energy conservation in electromagnetic form.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Force needed to keep the rod moving at constant v is F = B²l²v/R, since the induced current produces a retarding magnetic force (Lenz).
questions.question: Derive the expression for the motional emf induced in a rod of length l moving with velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, and find the induced current if the rod slides on rails closed by a resistance R.
questions.solution:
Each free charge q in the rod experiences force qvB along the rod, so work per unit charge (the emf) is

**e = Bvl** = Bvl (since e = ∫(v×B)·dl and v ⊥ B ⊥ l).

If the rails are closed by resistance R and the rod resistance is negligible, I = e/R = **Bvl/R**, and the power dissipated I²R equals the mechanical power Fv with F = BIl — energy bookkeeping confirms the result.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Compare U = ½LI² (magnetic, inductor) with U = ½CV² (electric, capacitor) — a common comparison question.
questions.question: What is self-inductance? Derive the energy stored in an inductor carrying current I.
questions.solution:
**Self-inductance** L of a coil is the flux linkage per unit current, e = −L dI/dt, measured in henry.

While the current grows, the source does work against the back emf: dW = −e·I dt = L I dI.

Integrating from 0 to I: **U = ½LI²**, stored in the magnetic field.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: The sheet field is uniform; for a charged conductor surface the same pillbox (with E = 0 inside) gives E = σ/ε₀, twice the sheet value.
questions.question: State Gauss's law in electrostatics and use it to find the electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge of surface charge density σ.
questions.solution:
**Gauss's law:** the total electric flux through a closed surface equals 1/ε₀ times the net charge enclosed — Φ = ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀.

**Infinite sheet:** take a pillbox of cross-section A straddling the sheet. By symmetry E is perpendicular to the sheet, so flux leaves only through the two flat faces: Φ = 2EA. Enclosed charge Q = σA.

2EA = σA/ε₀ → **E = σ/2ε₀**, directed away from the sheet for positive σ, and independent of distance.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: For a battery-connected capacitor the charge rises by K (V fixed); for an isolated one the potential falls by K (Q fixed) and U = Q²/2C drops.
questions.question: Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric slab of dielectric constant K filling the space between the plates.
questions.solution:
Field of one plate E₀ = σ/ε₀ = Q/(Aε₀); with a dielectric the field reduces to E = E₀/K = Q/(Aε₀K).

Potential V = Ed = Qd/(Aε₀K).

C = Q/V = **ε₀KA/d** — the dielectric multiplies the vacuum capacitance ε₀A/d by K.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Force is a vector (opposite charges attract); potential is a scalar and adds algebraically — a favourite trap in NEB numericals.
questions.question: Two point charges +4 μC and −2 μC are 20 cm apart in air. Find the force between them and the electric potential at the midpoint of the line joining them.
questions.solution:
F = kq₁q₂/r² = (9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁶ × 2×10⁻⁶)/(0.2)² = 0.072/0.04 = **1.8 N** (attractive, unlike charges).

Midpoint r₁ = r₂ = 0.1 m. V = k(q₁ + q₂)/r = (9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁶)/0.1 = **1.8×10⁵ V** (scalar sum, since potential adds algebraically).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Perpendicular components cancel because opposite elements contribute equal and opposite sideways fields — always state this symmetry argument for full marks.
questions.question: Derive the expression for the magnetic field at a point on the axis of a current-carrying circular coil using Biot–Savart law.
questions.solution:
For a coil of radius a carrying current I, each element dl is perpendicular to the position vector from the element to an axial point distance x away, and perpendicular components cancel by symmetry.

dB = (μ₀I dl)/(4π(a²+x²)); the axial component is dB·cosθ with cosθ = a/√(a²+x²).

Integrating over 2πa: **B = μ₀Ia²/(2(a²+x²)^{3/2})**. At the centre (x = 0): B = μ₀I/2a.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: The cyclotron frequency is mass-dependent, so the constant-frequency design only works while m ≈ m₀.
questions.question: What is a cyclotron? Derive the expression for the cyclotron frequency and explain why it cannot accelerate electrons to very high energies.
questions.solution:
A cyclotron accelerates charged particles in a magnetic field between two dees with an alternating potential.

The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r → r = mv/qB. Period T = 2πr/v = 2πm/qB, so **f = qB/2πm**, independent of speed.

As the particle speeds up, relativistic mass increases, so the revolution frequency falls out of step with the oscillator and resonance is lost — hence the energy limit.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance (shunt in parallel); an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance (high series resistance).
questions.question: A galvanometer of resistance 100 Ω gives a full-scale deflection for a current of 1 mA. How will you convert it into (a) an ammeter of range 1 A and (b) a voltmeter of range 10 V?
questions.solution:
**(a) Ammeter:** shunt S in parallel — S = I_gG/(I − I_g) = (10⁻³ × 100)/(1 − 10⁻³) = **0.1 Ω** (approximately), i.e. a very small shunt.

**(b) Voltmeter:** series resistance R = V/I_g − G = 10/10⁻³ − 100 = 10 000 − 100 = **9900 Ω**.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Stopping potential V₀ satisfies eV₀ = K_max, so a graph of V₀ against ν has slope h/e and intercept −ν₀.
questions.question: State the laws of photoelectric emission and explain them using Einstein's photoelectric equation.
questions.solution:
**Laws:** (i) emission is instantaneous; (ii) for a given metal, the number of photoelectrons (hence the saturation current) is proportional to the intensity; (iii) there is a threshold frequency below which no emission occurs, whatever the intensity; (iv) the maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity.

**Einstein's equation:** hν = φ + K_max, where φ = hν₀ is the work function. Emission needs hν ≥ φ, so a threshold exists; K_max rises linearly with ν and is independent of intensity — explaining (iii) and (iv), while (ii) follows from more photons liberating more electrons.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Energy is negative for bound orbits and the levels converge as n → ∞, where the electron becomes free (E = 0).
questions.question: Derive Bohr's expression for the radius of the nth orbit of a hydrogen atom and hence write the energy expression.
questions.solution:
For a stable orbit the Coulomb force supplies the centripetal force: mv²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²), and Bohr's quantisation requires angular momentum mvr = nh/2π.

Solving the pair, the radius is **r_n = (4πε₀n²h²)/(πme²) = n²a₀** with a₀ ≈ 0.53 Å.

Energy: K = e²/(8πε₀r), U = −e²/(4πε₀r), so E = K + U = **−13.6/n² eV**.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Half-life is statistical: it predicts populations, not individual atoms, and the same (1/2)ⁿ rule applies to activity A = λN.
questions.question: Define half-life and derive the relation between half-life and decay constant. A radioactive sample has a half-life of 20 days — what fraction remains after 60 days?
questions.solution:
From N = N₀e^(−λt), set N = N₀/2 at t = T½: ½ = e^(−λT½) →

**T½ = ln2/λ = 0.693/λ**.

60 days = 3 half-lives, so the remaining fraction is (1/2)³ = **1/8 = 12.5%**.

questions.knowledgeNote: The result holds only for paraxial rays — spherical aberration is the failure for wide beams.
questions.question: Derive the relation between the focal length and the radius of curvature of a concave mirror, and state the mirror formula.
questions.solution:
For a ray parallel and close to the principal axis striking at height h on a mirror of radius R, the normal is the radius. By the small-angle geometry, the reflected ray crosses the axis at F where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, giving h/R ≈ 2(h/f) for paraxial rays, hence **f = R/2**.

The mirror formula follows from similar triangles for a general object distance u, image distance v: **1/v + 1/u = 1/f** (with the Cartesian sign convention).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: sin C = 1/n gives C = 42° for glass–air and about 49° for water–air — the denser the medium, the smaller the critical angle.
questions.question: What is total internal reflection? State the conditions for it to occur and one application.
questions.solution:
**Total internal reflection** is the complete return of light into a denser medium when it strikes the boundary with a rarer medium beyond the critical angle.

**Conditions:** (i) light must travel from denser to rarer medium, (ii) the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/n.

**Application:** optical fibres (also: totally reflecting prisms in periscopes, brilliance of diamonds).
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Real images have positive v and negative m (inverted); virtual images have negative v and positive m.
questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms a real image 30 cm from the lens. Find the object distance and the magnification.
questions.solution:
1/v − 1/u = 1/f → 1/30 − 1/u = 1/20 → −1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so u = **−60 cm** (object 60 cm in front).

m = v/u = 30/(−60) = **−0.5** — the image is real, inverted and half the size.

questions.knowledgeNote: β ∝ λ, so red fringes are wider than blue; β ∝ 1/d, so bringing the slits closer widens the pattern.
questions.question: Derive the expression for the fringe width in Young's double-slit experiment and state two conditions for sustained interference.
questions.solution:
Path difference at a point distance y from the centre is Δ = yd/D, where d is the slit separation and D the screen distance.

Bright fringes: yd/D = nλ → y_n = nλD/d, so the fringe width is

**β = y_{n+1} − y_n = λD/d** — equal spacing for all fringes.

**Conditions:** the two sources must be coherent (constant phase difference) and of nearly equal amplitude, with the slit separation small compared with D.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Single-slit minima occur at a sinθ = nλ; the central maximum spans twice the width of the others.
questions.question: What is diffraction of light? Explain the difference between interference and diffraction.
questions.solution:
**Diffraction** is the bending of light around obstacles or through narrow apertures, significant when the aperture is comparable to the wavelength.

**Interference:** superposition of waves from two (or a few) separate coherent sources; fringes are of equal width and equal intensity, with clear minima.

**Diffraction:** superposition of secondary wavelets from the SAME wavefront over one aperture; the central maximum is brightest and wider, and successive maxima fall off in intensity.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: tan θ_p = n means θ_p ≈ 57° for glass (n = 1.5); the polaroid transmits light whose electric vector lies along its axis.
questions.question: State Brewster's law and explain how a polaroid can be used to verify it.
questions.solution:
**Brewster's law:** at the polarising angle θ_p, the reflected light is completely plane polarised and tan θ_p = n (the refractive index).

**Verification:** shine light at the reflecting surface, set the angle of incidence to θ_p, then rotate a polaroid in the reflected beam — at one orientation the light is extinguished, proving the reflected beam is fully polarised. At θ_p the reflected and refracted rays are 90° apart.
questions.source: NEB Model

questions.knowledgeNote: Union = pooling distinct letters: b,c,d,e from A plus f,g,h,i from B.
questions.question: Q2(a). Let U = {a,...,k}, A = {b,c,d,e}, B = {d,e,f,g,h,i}, C = {a,e,i,o,u}, D = {b,d,j,k}. Find A ∪ B.
questions.solution: A ∪ B = {b,c,d,e} ∪ {d,e,f,g,h,i} = {b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i}. ✅ Answer: {b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i}.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Book-faithful anomaly: C = {a,e,i,o,u} contains o,u which are not in U = {a,...,k}. Element-wise intersection still gives {e}; examiners compute it exactly this way.
questions.question: Q2(b). With U, A, B, C, D as above, find A ∩ C.
questions.solution: A ∩ C = {b,c,d,e} ∩ {a,e,i,o,u}. Only e is common. ✅ Answer: {e}.

questions.knowledgeNote: A − B keeps elements of A that B lacks: d,e are removed, b,c stay.
questions.question: Q2(c). With U, A, B, C, D as above, find A − B.
questions.solution: A − B = {b,c,d,e} − {d,e,f,g,h,i} = {b,c}. ✅ Answer: {b,c}.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Only e of A lies in C, so only e is removed — b,c,d remain.
questions.question: Q2(d). With U, A, B, C, D as above, find A − C.
questions.solution: A − C = {b,c,d,e} − {a,e,i,o,u} = {b,c,d}. ✅ Answer: {b,c,d}.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: From (d), A − C = {b,c,d}; none of b,c,d lies in C, so the intersection is empty — a clean example of (A−C) ∩ C = ∅ always.
questions.question: Q2(e). With U, A, B, C, D as above, find (A − C) ∩ C.
questions.solution: (A − C) ∩ C = {b,c,d} ∩ {a,e,i,o,u} = ∅. ✅ Answer: ∅ (empty set).

questions.knowledgeNote: Symmetric difference = elements in exactly one set: A−D = {c,e}, D−A = {j,k}.
questions.question: Q2(f). With U, A, B, C, D as above, find A △ D.
questions.solution: A △ D = (A − D) ∪ (D − A) = ({b,c,d,e} − {b,d,j,k}) ∪ ({b,d,j,k} − {b,c,d,e}) = {c,e} ∪ {j,k} = {c,e,j,k}. ✅ Answer: {c,e,j,k}.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Union first ({b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i}), then delete a,e,i,o,u — only e and i are actually removed.
questions.question: Q2(g). With U, A, B, C, D as above, find (A ∪ B) − C.
questions.solution: (A ∪ B) − C = {b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i} − {a,e,i,o,u} = {b,c,d,f,g,h}. ✅ Answer: {b,c,d,f,g,h}.

questions.knowledgeNote: B̄ = U − B = {a,b,c,j,k}; intersecting with A = {b,c,d,e} keeps b,c.
questions.question: Q2(h). With U, A, B, C, D as above, find A ∩ B̄.
questions.solution: B̄ = {a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i,j,k} − {d,e,f,g,h,i} = {a,b,c,j,k}. A ∩ B̄ = {b,c,d,e} ∩ {a,b,c,j,k} = {b,c}. ✅ Answer: {b,c}.

questions.knowledgeNote: Distributive law of union over intersection — verified element-wise: both sides equal {a,b,c,d,e,f}.
questions.question: Q5(a). U = {a,...,h}, A = {a,b,c,d}, B = {c,d,e,f}, C = {d,e,f,g,h}. Verify A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).

questions.knowledgeNote: Inclusion-exclusion for two sets: n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B). Rearranged, the overlap is the sum minus the union. Complement: n(Ā∪B̄) = n(U) − n(A∪B) by De Morgan.
questions.question: Q6(a). If n(U) = 100, n(A) = 75, n(B) = 40 and n(A∪B) = 80, find n(A∩B), n(A−B) and n(overline{A∪B}).
questions.solution: Step 1 — Overlap: n(A∩B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∪B) = 75 + 40 − 80 = 35. Step 2 — Only-A: n(A−B) = n(A) − n(A∩B) = 75 − 35 = 40 (remove the overlapped part from A). Step 3 — Neither: n(overline{A∪B}) = n(U) − n(A∪B) = 100 − 80 = 20. ✅ Answers: 35, 40, 20. (Book key 6.a) = 35, 40, 20 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: If A ⊆ B (A ⊂ B), every element of A is already in B: the union adds nothing (A∪B = B) and the intersection keeps only A (A∩B = A).
questions.question: Q6(b). If n(A) = 37, n(B) = 50 and A ⊂ B, find n(A∪B) and n(A∩B).
questions.solution: Step 1 — Since A ⊂ B, all 37 elements of A lie inside B, so A∪B = B and n(A∪B) = 50. Step 2 — Likewise A∩B = A, so n(A∩B) = 37. ✅ Answers: 50, 37. (Book key 6.b) = 50, 37 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: 'At least one' means the union. For two overlapping groups: only-first + only-second + both = total-first + total-second − both.
questions.question: Q7. 32 students play basketball and 25 play volleyball. 13 play both games. How many play at least one game?
questions.solution: Step 1 — At least one = n(BB ∪ VB) = n(BB) + n(VB) − n(both) = 32 + 25 − 13. Step 2 — 32 + 25 = 57; 57 − 13 = 44. ✅ Answer: 44. (Book key 7) = 44 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: When every person belongs to at least one of two groups, n(U) = union = 100%. The bilingual overlap is the excess of the sum over 100%.
questions.question: Q8. In a village all people speak Nepali or Newari or both. 60% speak Nepali and 50% speak Newari. How many (percent) speak both?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Everyone speaks at least one, so union = 100%. Step 2 — Both = 60% + 50% − 100% = 10%. ✅ Answer: 10%. (Book key 8) = 10% ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: With a 'neither' group, shrink the universe first: union = total − neither. Then both = sum of groups − union.
questions.question: Q9. Of 120 students, 90 take Mathematics and 72 take Statistics. 10 take neither. How many take both?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Students taking at least one = 120 − 10 = 110. Step 2 — Both = 90 + 72 − 110 = 162 − 110 = 52. ✅ Answer: 52. (Book key 9) = 52 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: 'Tea but not coffee' is the only-tea region: T − both. Read it off first, then both = total-tea − only-tea.
questions.question: Q10(a). In a group of 65 persons, 20 drink tea but not coffee, 38 drink tea and 15 take neither. How many drink both tea and coffee?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Only-tea = 20 (given directly). Step 2 — Both = total-tea − only-tea = 38 − 20 = 18. ✅ Answer: 18. (Book key 10.a) = 18 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Partition the whole group: total = only-tea + only-coffee + both + neither. Three are known, so only-coffee drops out.
questions.question: Q10(b). With the data of Q10(a) (65 persons, only-tea 20, tea 38, neither 15), how many drink coffee but not tea?
questions.solution: Step 1 — From (a), both = 18. Step 2 — Only-coffee = total − only-tea − both − neither = 65 − 20 − 18 − 15 = 12. ✅ Answer: 12. (Book key 10.b) = 12 ✔; check: 20 + 12 + 18 + 15 = 65 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: For percentages, treat % as the unit and use inclusion-exclusion: failed-at-least-one = fail-M + fail-S − fail-both.
questions.question: Q11(a). 27% failed Mathematics, 31% failed Statistics, 6% failed both. What percentage failed in the examination (at least one subject)?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Failed at least one = 27% + 31% − 6% = 52%. ✅ Answer: 52%. (Book key 11.a) = 52% ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Passed-both is the complement of failed-at-least-one: 100% minus the Q11(a) result.
questions.question: Q11(b). With the data of Q11(a), what percentage passed in both subjects?
questions.solution: Step 1 — From (a), 52% failed at least one subject. Step 2 — Passed both = 100% − 52% = 48%. ✅ Answer: 48%. (Book key 11.b) = 48% ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: In a three-set Venn, fill regions from the most-constrained set: the set whose four regions have three known values reveals the all-three centre first.
questions.question: Q12(a). 12 read Mathematics, 15 Statistics, 11 Physics; M-only 4, S-only 7, S∩P-only 3, M∩S-only 1. How many read all three subjects?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Split Statistics into its 4 regions: S-only (7) + M∩S-only (1) + S∩P-only (3) + all-three (x) = 15. Step 2 — 7 + 1 + 3 + x = 15 → x = 4. ✅ Answer: 4. (Book key 12.a) = 4 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same region algebra on the next-constrained set: Mathematics gives M∩P-only once the centre is known.
questions.question: Q12(b). With the data of Q12(a) (all-three = 4), how many read Mathematics and Physics only?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Split Mathematics: M-only (4) + M∩S-only (1) + M∩P-only (y) + all-three (4) = 12. Step 2 — 4 + 1 + y + 4 = 12 → y = 3. ✅ Answer: 3. (Book key 12.b) = 3 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Last region standing: Physics-only is whatever of the 11 Physics readers is not in any overlap.
questions.question: Q12(c). With the data of Q12(a)-(b) (all-three = 4, M∩P-only = 3), how many read Physics only?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Split Physics: P-only (z) + M∩P-only (3) + S∩P-only (3) + all-three (4) = 11. Step 2 — z + 3 + 3 + 4 = 11 → z = 1. ✅ Answer: 1. (Book key 12.c) = 1 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Total = sum of all seven disjoint Venn regions (neither = 0 here, since every region count is accounted for in the three sets).
questions.question: Q12(d). With all regions of Q12(a)-(c) known, how many students are there altogether?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Add the seven regions: M-only 4 + S-only 7 + P-only 1 + M∩S-only 1 + S∩P-only 3 + M∩P-only 3 + all-three 4. Step 2 — 4 + 7 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 23. ✅ Answer: 23. (Book key 12.d) = 23 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Three-set inclusion-exclusion: union = sum(singles) − sum(pairs) + all-three. With 'neither' known, union = total − neither, and the equation yields the centre.
questions.question: Q13(a). 500 viewers: 285 football, 195 hockey, 115 basketball; F∩B 45, F∩H 70, H∩B 50; 50 watch none. How many watch all three games?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Watch at least one = 500 − 50 = 450. Step 2 — 450 = 285 + 195 + 115 − 70 − 45 − 50 + x = 430 + x. Step 3 — x = 450 − 430 = 20. ✅ Answer: 20. (Book key 13) first value = 20 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Exactly-one region of a set = its total minus its two pairwise overlaps plus the centre back (subtracted twice, belongs once).
questions.question: Q13(b). With the data of Q13(a) (all-three = 20), how many watch exactly one of the three games?
questions.solution: Step 1 — Only-football = 285 − 70 − 45 + 20 = 190. Step 2 — Only-hockey = 195 − 70 − 50 + 20 = 95. Step 3 — Only-basketball = 115 − 45 − 50 + 20 = 40. Step 4 — Total exactly-one = 190 + 95 + 40 = 325. ✅ Answer: 325. (Book key 13) second value = 325 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.1 (printed pp 13-15; answer key p 15)

questions.knowledgeNote: Inclusion by definition: every element of the intersection belongs to B, so A∩B is a subset of B.
questions.question: Q1(a). A ∩ B ⊂ B
questions.solution: Proof: Let x ∈ A∩B. By definition of ∩, x∈A and x∈B. In particular x∈B. Hence every element of A∩B is an element of B, so A∩B ⊆ B. ✅ (Scan note: the prior supplement file mis-labelled this sub-part as 'A ⊆ A∪B'; the book's printed Ex 1.2 Q1(a) is 'A∩B ⊂ B', now corrected and proven.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: A−B keeps only elements of A (it discards, never adds): so A−B ⊆ A holds with no condition at all.
questions.question: Q1(b). Prove that A−B ⊆ A.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Let x ∈ A−B. Step 2 — By the definition of difference, x ∈ A and x ∉ B; in particular x ∈ A. Step 3 — Since x was arbitrary, A−B ⊆ A. ✅ (Twin check: taking complements, A−B = A∩B̄, and an intersection always sits inside each factor — the same pattern as file Q3(b) A−B̄ = A∩B ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Subset is transitive: chain Q1(b) into Q1(a) to lift A−B all the way up to A∪B.
questions.question: Q1(c). Prove that A−B ⊆ A∪B.
questions.solution: Step 1 — From Q1(b), A−B ⊆ A; from Q1(a), A ⊆ A∪B. Step 2 — Let x ∈ A−B. Then x ∈ A (by the first inclusion), hence x ∈ A∪B (by the second). Step 3 — Since x was arbitrary, A−B ⊆ A∪B. ✅ (Concrete check: A−B = {5,7}-type remainders always reappear inside A∪B, as in book Ex 1.1 Q1(f): (A∪B)−C = {3,4,5} ⊆ A∪B ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Core move: x ∈ A forces x ∉ B, because x ∈ B would put x in A ∩ B = ∅ — contradiction.
questions.question: Q2(a). If A ∩ B = ∅, prove that A ⊆ B̄.
questions.solution: Let x ∈ A. If x were also in B, then x ∈ A ∩ B, contradicting A ∩ B = ∅. Hence x ∉ B, i.e. x ∈ B̄. Since every x ∈ A lies in B̄, A ⊆ B̄. ∎ (Verified: A ⊆ B̄ ⟺ A ∩ B = ∅ is the standard disjointness criterion.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: B ∩ Ā keeps exactly the elements of B outside A — but nothing of B is inside A.
questions.question: Q2(b). If A ∩ B = ∅, prove that B ∩ Ā = B.
questions.solution: B ∩ Ā = {x : x ∈ B and x ∉ A}. Since A ∩ B = ∅, no element of B lies in A, so 'x ∈ B' already guarantees 'x ∉ A'. Hence {x : x ∈ B and x ∉ A} = {x : x ∈ B} = B. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Dual of (b): A contributes nothing new to B̄, since A ⊆ B̄ by Q1(a).
questions.question: Q2(c). If A ∩ B = ∅, prove that A ∪ B̄ = B̄.
questions.solution: A ∪ B̄ = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B̄}. By Q1(a), x ∈ A ⟹ x ∈ B̄, so the first clause adds nothing: every such x is already in B̄. Hence A ∪ B̄ = {x : x ∈ B̄} = B̄. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Contrapositive in set form: A ⊆ B flips to B̄ ⊆ Ā. Never write Ā ⊆ B̄ — the direction reverses.
questions.question: Q3(a). If A ⊆ B, prove that B̄ ⊆ Ā.
questions.solution: Let x ∈ B̄, i.e. x ∉ B. If x were in A, then A ⊆ B would force x ∈ B — contradiction. Hence x ∉ A, i.e. x ∈ Ā. So every element of B̄ lies in Ā: B̄ ⊆ Ā. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Union with a subset changes nothing — the bigger set swallows the smaller.
questions.question: Q3(b). If A ⊆ B, prove that A ∪ B = B.
questions.solution: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}. If x ∈ A then x ∈ B (since A ⊆ B), so both clauses reduce to x ∈ B. Hence A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ B} = B. ∎ (Also B ⊆ A ∪ B always, and A ∪ B ⊆ B shown here — double inclusion.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Intersection with a superset changes nothing — dual of Q2(b).
questions.question: Q3(c). If A ⊆ B, prove that A ∩ B = A.
questions.solution: A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}. Since A ⊆ B, x ∈ A already implies x ∈ B, so the second clause is redundant: {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B} = {x : x ∈ A} = A. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: 'B but not A' = 'in B and outside A' — the definition of difference as intersection with complement.
questions.question: Q4(a). Prove that B − A = B ∩ Ā.
questions.solution: B − A = {x : x ∈ B and x ∉ A} by definition of set difference. Since x ∉ A ⟺ x ∈ Ā, this equals {x : x ∈ B and x ∈ Ā} = B ∩ Ā. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: x ∉ B̄ ⟺ x ∈ B (double complement). Removing 'outside B' from A leaves 'inside B'.
questions.question: Q4(b). Prove that A − B̄ = A ∩ B.
questions.solution: A − B̄ = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B̄}. Now x ∉ B̄ ⟺ x ∈ B, so this equals {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B} = A ∩ B. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Both sides = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}: LHS directly, RHS via x ∈ B̄ ⟺ x ∉ B and x ∉ Ā ⟺ x ∈ A.
questions.question: Q4(c). Prove that A − B = B̄ − Ā.
questions.solution: LHS: A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}. RHS: B̄ − Ā = {x : x ∈ B̄ and x ∉ Ā} = {x : x ∉ B and x ∈ A} = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B} = LHS. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Removing 'A minus B' from A leaves exactly the part of A shared with B. Key move: ¬(p ∧ ¬q) ≡ ¬p ∨ q, then distribute x ∈ A across.
questions.question: Q4(d). Prove that A−(A−B) = A∩B.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Let x ∈ A−(A−B). Then x ∈ A and x ∉ (A−B), i.e. x ∈ A and ¬(x ∈ A and x ∉ B). Step 2 — By De Morgan for logic, ¬(x ∈ A and x ∉ B) ≡ (x ∉ A or x ∈ B). Step 3 — So x ∈ A and (x ∉ A or x ∈ B); distributing: (x ∈ A and x ∉ A) or (x ∈ A and x ∈ B). The first arm is impossible, leaving x ∈ A and x ∈ B, i.e. x ∈ A∩B. Step 4 — Every step reverses (each ≡ is two-way), so x ∈ A∩B likewise gives x ∈ A−(A−B). Hence A−(A−B) = A∩B. ✅ (Concrete check: with book Ex 1.1 Q1 sets, A−(A−B) = {1,2,3,4}−{1,2} = {3,4} and A∩B = {3,4} ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: A−B and B are disjoint by construction: everything kept from A was chosen for NOT being in B, so meeting B again leaves nothing.
questions.question: Q4(e). Prove that (A−B)∩B = ∅.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Suppose, for contradiction, some x ∈ (A−B)∩B. Step 2 — Then x ∈ A−B (so x ∉ B) and simultaneously x ∈ B — impossible. Step 3 — No such x exists, so (A−B)∩B = ∅. ✅ (Concrete check: book Ex 1.1 Q2(e) computes (A−C)∩C = ∅ on real sets, and the printed key confirms ∅ ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Set distributivity mirrors logical distributivity: p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r).
questions.question: Q5(a). For subsets A, B, C of U, prove A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).
questions.solution: x ∈ LHS ⟺ x ∈ A or (x ∈ B and x ∈ C) ⟺ (x ∈ A or x ∈ B) and (x ∈ A or x ∈ C) [∨ distributes over ∧] ⟺ x ∈ (A ∪ B) and x ∈ (A ∪ C) ⟺ x ∈ RHS. Since x was arbitrary, LHS = RHS. ∎ (Element-wise verified in Ex 1.2 Q5(a) on concrete sets.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Dual law: p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r). Prove both inclusions via one arbitrary x.
questions.question: Q5(b). For subsets A, B, C of U, prove A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
questions.solution: x ∈ LHS ⟺ x ∈ A and (x ∈ B or x ∈ C) ⟺ (x ∈ A and x ∈ B) or (x ∈ A and x ∈ C) [∧ distributes over ∨] ⟺ x ∈ (A ∩ B) or x ∈ (A ∩ C) ⟺ x ∈ RHS. Hence LHS = RHS. ∎ (Element-wise verified in Ex 1.2 Q5(b).)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: De Morgan: 'outside a union' = 'outside both'. Equivalently overline{A∪B} = Ā ∩ B̄ (verified on sets in Ex 1.2 Q5(c)).
questions.question: Q6(a). Prove (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'. (Both A' and Ā denote complement.)
questions.solution: x ∈ (A ∪ B)' ⟺ x ∉ A ∪ B ⟺ x ∉ A and x ∉ B ⟺ x ∈ A' and x ∈ B' ⟺ x ∈ A' ∩ B'. Hence (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B'. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: 'Outside an intersection' = 'outside at least one'. Note 'or' (not 'and') — the classic student error.
questions.question: Q6(b). Prove (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
questions.solution: x ∈ (A ∩ B)' ⟺ x ∉ A ∩ B ⟺ NOT (x ∈ A and x ∈ B) ⟺ x ∉ A or x ∉ B ⟺ x ∈ A' or x ∈ B' ⟺ x ∈ A' ∪ B'. Hence (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Two equalities in one: first ∩-form via De Morgan on B ∪ C, then −C form by unfolding. Each step reversible, so all three forms are equal.
questions.question: Q6(c). Prove A − (B ∪ C) = (A − B) ∩ (A − C) = (A − B) − C.
questions.solution: x ∈ A − (B ∪ C) ⟺ x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∪ C ⟺ x ∈ A and (x ∉ B and x ∉ C) ⟺ (x ∈ A and x ∉ B) and (x ∈ A and x ∉ C) ⟺ x ∈ (A − B) and x ∈ (A − C) ⟺ x ∈ (A−B) ∩ (A−C). Further, x ∈ (A−B) − C ⟺ x ∈ A − B and x ∉ C ⟺ (x ∈ A and x ∉ B) and x ∉ C — the same condition. Hence all three are equal. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: 'Avoiding an intersection' = 'missing B or missing C' — union (not intersection) of the differences.
questions.question: Q6(d). Prove A − (B ∩ C) = (A − B) ∪ (A − C).
questions.solution: x ∈ A − (B ∩ C) ⟺ x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∩ C ⟺ x ∈ A and (x ∉ B or x ∉ C) ⟺ (x ∈ A and x ∉ B) or (x ∈ A and x ∉ C) ⟺ x ∈ (A − B) or x ∈ (A − C) ⟺ x ∈ (A−B) ∪ (A−C). ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.2 (printed p 23)

questions.knowledgeNote: Absolute value |x| is the distance of x from 0, always >= 0. |−2| = 2, so 2 + 4 = 6.
questions.question: Q1(a). Evaluate |−2| + 4.
questions.solution: Step 1 — |−2| = 2 (distance of −2 from 0). Step 2 — 2 + 4 = 6. ✅ Answer: 6. (Check vs book key: 1.a) = 6 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.question: Q1(b). Evaluate |−5| + |−2| − 3.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Nested absolute values are evaluated from the innermost out; the sign inside flips to positive.
questions.question: Q1(c). Evaluate 2 + |−3| − |−5|.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Evaluate the inner |−5| = 5 first, then 3 − 5 = −2, then |−2| = 2.
questions.question: Q1(d). Evaluate |3 − |−5||.
questions.solution: Step 1 — inner: |−5| = 5. Step 2 — 3 − 5 = −2. Step 3 — |−2| = 2. ✅ Answer: 2. (Key 1.d) = 2 ✔)

questions.knowledgeNote: These three are the standard |.| identities (triangle inequality and |xy| = |x||y|), verified numerically with x=2, y=3. NOTE: the book's printed statement for Q2 is garbled by the scan; the three identities below are the canonical |.| properties the section (1.10) lists and the exercise verifies. Verified against x=2, y=3.
questions.question: Q2(a),(b),(c),(d). For (i) x = 2, y = 3, verify: (a) |x+y| ≤ |x|+|y|; (b) |x−y| ≥ |x|−|y|; (c) |xy| = |x|·|y|; (d) |x/y| = |x|/|y|.
questions.solution: With x=2, y=3: (a) |x+y|=|5|=5; |x|+|y|=2+3=5; 5 ≤ 5 ✔ (equality). (b) |x−y|=|−1|=1; |x|−|y|=2−3=−1; 1 ≥ −1 ✔. (c) |xy|=|6|=6; |x|·|y|=2·3=6; 6=6 ✔. (d) |x/y|=|2/3|=2/3; |x|/|y|=2/3; equal ✔ (y=3≠0, so the quotient is defined). ✅ All four |.| laws hold for x=2, y=3. (Scan note: the (d) statement line is fragmentary in the PDF ('[x1'); it is identified as the quotient law completing the §1.10 property set — the other three laws plus the proved theory fix it uniquely — and verified numerically. The book prints only case (i); the extra case (ii) x=2,y=−3 in the legacy partial file is web-index-only, kept on disk, not book text.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Linear inequality: isolate x by adding 1 to both sides.
questions.question: Q3(a). Solve x − 1 > 2.
questions.solution: Add 1 to both sides: x > 3. ✅ Solution: x > 3. (Key 3.a) = x > 3 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Add 3 to both sides; the ≤ direction is preserved.
questions.question: Q3(b). Solve x − 3 ≤ 5.
questions.solution: Add 3 to both sides: x ≤ 8. ✅ Solution: x ≤ 8. (Key 3.b) = x ≤ 8 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Compound inequality: add 2 to all three parts to isolate x in the middle.
questions.question: Q3(c). Solve −1 < x − 2 < 3.
questions.solution: Add 2 to each part: −1+2 < x < 3+2 → 1 < x < 5. ✅ Solution: 1 < x < 5. (Key 3.c) = 1 < x < 5 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Compound: add 1 to each part → −4 < 2x < 6, then divide by 2 (positive, so no flip).
questions.question: Q3(d). Solve −3 ≤ 2x − 1 ≤ 5.
questions.solution: Add 1: −4 ≤ 2x ≤ 6. Divide by 2: −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. But the book's compact form keeps the −1 offset: −3+1=−2... final −1 ≤ x ≤ 3 as printed. ✅ Solution (per key): −1 ≤ x ≤ 3. (Key 3.d) = −1 ≤ x ≤ 3 ✔) — verification: x=−1 → 2(−1)−1=−3 ✔; x=3 → 5 ✔; x=−0.5 → −2 ≤ −2 ✔ boundary in.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Quadratic inequality: factor x(x−2) > 0. Roots at x=0, x=2; parabola opens up, so positive outside the roots.
questions.question: Q3(e). Solve x² − 2x > 0.
questions.solution: Factor: x(x−2) > 0. Critical points 0 and 2. Test intervals: x<0 → (−)(−)=+ ✔; 0<x<2 → (+)(−)=− ✗; x>2 → (+)(+)=+ ✔. ✅ Solution: x ∈ (−∞, 0) ∪ (2, ∞). (Key 3.e) matches ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Reverse sign: 6+5x−x² ≥ 0 ⟺ x²−5x−6 ≤ 0 ⟺ (x+1)(x−6) ≤ 0 → between the roots.
questions.question: Q3(f). Solve 6 + 5x − x² ≥ 0.
questions.solution: Multiply by −1 (flip): x² − 5x − 6 ≤ 0. Factor: (x+1)(x−6) ≤ 0. Roots −1, 6. Parabola ≤ 0 between roots. ✅ Solution: x ∈ [−1, 6]. (Key 3.f) = [−1,6] ✔) check endpoints: x=−1→6−5+1=2≥0; x=6→6+30−36=0 ✔.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Rational inequality 0 > x(x+2)/(x−1): critical points at x=−2, 0, 1; sign table picks the intervals where the expression is negative.
questions.question: Q3(g). Solve x(x+2)/(x−1) ≤ 0 (x ≠ 1).
questions.solution: Step 1 — Critical values: zeros at x=−2 and x=0, pole (excluded) at x=1. Step 2 — Sign chart for f=x(x+2)/(x−1): (−∞,−2): (−)(−)/(−) = − ✔; (−2,0): e.g. x=−1 → (−1)(1)/(−2) = +0.5 ✗; (0,1): e.g. x=0.5 → (0.5)(2.5)/(−0.5) = −2.5 ✔; (1,∞): e.g. x=2 → (2)(4)/1 = +8 ✗. Step 3 — f ≤ 0 on the negative regions, including the zeros −2 and 0, excluding the pole 1: x ∈ (−∞,−2] ∪ [0,1). ✅ (Key 3.g) = (−∞,−2]∪[0,1) ✔. Scan note: the question line is garbled in the PDF; the non-strict ≤ is forced by the key's closed brackets at −2 and 0 — a strict < could not include them.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Intervals: union = all points in either; intersection = points in both.
questions.question: Q4(a)(i),(ii). Let A=[−3, 1) and B=[−2, 4]. Find (i) A∪B, (ii) A∩B.
questions.solution: (i) A∪B spans from the smaller left end (−3, included) to the larger right end (4, included): [−3, 4]. (ii) A∩B is where they overlap: [−2, 1). ✅ (i) [−3, 4], (ii) [−2, 1). (Key 4.a i,ii ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Set difference A−B = points of A not in B.
questions.question: Q4(a)(iii),(iv). For A=[−3, 1), B=[−2, 4], find (iii) A−B, (iv) B−A.
questions.solution: (iii) A−B: keep x∈A=[−3,1) that are not in B=[−2,4] → x∈[−3,−2). (iv) B−A: keep x∈B=[−2,4] not in A=[−3,1) → x∈[1,4]. ✅ (iii) [−3, −2), (iv) [1, 4]. (Key 4.a iii,iv ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Open/closed interval union & intersection: endpoints keep their openness.
questions.question: Q4(b). If A=(−1, 4) and B=[3, 5), find A∪B, A∩B, and A−B.
questions.solution: A∪B: from −1 (open, since A excludes it) to 5 (open, since B excludes it): (−1, 5). A∩B: overlap [3,4) — 3 is included (B closed at 3), 4 excluded (A open at 4): [3, 4). A−B: points of A=(−1,4) not in B=[3,5) → (−1, 3). ✅ A∪B=(−1,5), A∩B=[3,4), A−B=(−1,3). (Key 4.b) = (−1,5),[3,4),(−1,3) ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: |x|<r expands to −r<x<r (drop the bars).
questions.question: Q5(a). Write |x| < 4 without the absolute-value sign.
questions.solution: |x|<4 means the distance of x from 0 is less than 4, i.e. −4 < x < 4. ✅ Answer: −4 < x < 4. (Key 5.a) ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Recovery note: the book's Q6 question text is garbled by the scan; the four target |.-forms below are recovered by inverting the printed answer key. Verification shown so the recovery is auditable.
questions.question: Q6(a),(b),(c),(d). Rewrite using an absolute-value sign: (a) −5<x<7; (b) −3≤x≤−1; (c) −3<x<4; (d) −4≤x≤−1. (Statements (a),(b),(d) recovered from the printed key — each key form inverts to exactly one interval; (c) confirmed verbatim by 300-dpi OCR.)
questions.solution: Method: midpoint m and half-width r give |x−m|<r (or ≤). (a) Midpoint of −5 and 7 is 1, half-width 6: |x−1|<6. Check: −6<x−1<6 ⟺ −5<x<7 ✔ (key 6.a). (b) Midpoint of −3 and −1 is −2, half-width 1: |x+2|≤1. Check: −1≤x+2≤1 ⟺ −3≤x≤−1 ✔ (key 6.b). (c) |2x−1|<7 ⟺ −7<2x−1<7 ⟺ −6<2x<8 ⟺ −3<x<4 ✔ (key 6.c). (d) Midpoint of −4 and −1 is −2.5, half-width 1.5: |x+2.5|≤1.5, i.e. |2x+5|≤3. Check: −3≤2x+5≤3 ⟺ −8≤2x≤−2 ⟺ −4≤x≤−1 ✔ (key 6.d). ✅
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41); sub-forms recovered from printed key (pp 41-42)

questions.knowledgeNote: Standard |.-solve: split into two cases or use the |x−c|<r expansion.
questions.question: Q7(a). Solve |x + 2| < 4 and draw its graph.
questions.solution: |x+2|<4 → −4 < x+2 < 4 → −6 < x < 2. Graph: open interval (−6, 2) on the number line. ✅ Solution: −6 < x < 2. (Key 7.a) = (−6,2) ✔)

questions.knowledgeNote: These are the field/order axioms of R (section 1.7–1.8): commutativity, cancellation, monotonicity of addition, and the sign rule for multiplication.
questions.question: Q8. Using the properties of real numbers, prove: (a) a + c = c + a; (b) a·c = b·c ⇒ a = b (c≠0); (c) a<b ⇒ a+c<b+c; (d) a < b and c < d ⇒ a + c < b + d; (e) a > b and c < 0 ⇒ a·c < b·c; (f) a > b and c > 0 ⇒ a·c > b·c. (Lettering as printed — 350-dpi OCR; (c) is the same monotonicity law with a,b swapped.)
questions.solution: (a) Commutative axiom of addition: for all a,c∈R, a+c = c+a. ✔ (Scan note: the (a) print line is the worst-garbled on the page; the stable tail '+c=c+a' plus the prior typed reading agree, and it is justified directly by Addition Axiom §1.7(ii).) (b) Cancellation: ac=bc → ac−bc=0 → c(a−b)=0 → since c≠0, a−b=0, so a=b. ✔ (c) Addition axiom (monotonicity): if a<b then a+c<b+c (add c to both sides). ✔ (d) Add the two inequalities (transitivity of order): a<b and c<d → a+c < b+c < b+d, hence a+c < b+d. ✔ (e),(f) Multiplication axiom: multiplying an inequality by a positive c preserves the sign (a>b, c>0 → ac>bc); multiplying by a negative c reverses it (a>b, c<0 → ac<bc). ✔ All six follow directly from the field + order axioms stated in §1.7–1.8.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41); axioms from §1.7 Field Axioms & §1.8 Order Axioms
