questions.knowledgeNote: Ordered pairs are equal iff first components match AND second components match — order matters, unlike sets.
questions.question: Q1(a). Identify whether (1,3) and (3,1) are equal.
questions.solution: First components: 1 ≠ 3, so the pairs differ already. ✅ NOT equal. (Never swap-check sets here — (1,3) ≠ (3,1) is the canonical example.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q1(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Identical pairs are trivially equal — the reflexive case examiners include to test the definition.
questions.question: Q1(b). Identify whether (a,b) and (a,b) are equal.
questions.solution: First: a = a; second: b = b. ✅ Equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q1(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Distinct symbols denote distinct entries unless an equation says otherwise: a ≠ x as printed.
questions.question: Q1(c). Identify whether (1,a) and (1,x) are equal.
questions.solution: First components match (1 = 1) but second components a, x are distinct symbols with no relation given. ✅ NOT equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q1(c)

questions.knowledgeNote: (x,x) = (y,y) would force x = y by both components — with x, y unrelated, they differ.
questions.question: Q1(d). Identify whether (x,x) and (y,y) are equal.
questions.solution: Equality would require x = y (first components) and x = y (second) — not given. ✅ NOT equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q1(d)

questions.knowledgeNote: Equate components to get a 2×2 linear system; add the equations to kill y.
questions.question: Q2(a). Find x and y if (x+y, 3) = (1, x−y).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q2(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same method with messier coefficients — substitute y from the simpler equation.
questions.question: Q2(b). Find x and y if (x+2y, 3) = (−1, 2x−y).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q2(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Decoupled equations — read each variable straight off.
questions.question: Q2(c). Find x and y if (x−2, y+1) = (1, 0).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q2(c)

questions.knowledgeNote: Watch the sign: −3 = y+3 gives y = −6, not +6.
questions.question: Q2(d). Find x and y if (2x−1, −3) = (1, y+3).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q2(d)

questions.knowledgeNote: A×A lists every first-set element against every first-set element: n(A)² pairs.
questions.question: Q3(a). If A = {1,2,3} and B = {a,b}, find A × A.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q3(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same construction on the 2-element set: 2² = 4 pairs.
questions.question: Q3(b). With A, B as above, find B × B.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q3(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Order matters: B×A ≠ A×B. The web index quotes 'B × A' but solves A × B — both products are given so the printed answer is covered either way.
questions.question: Q3(c). With A, B as above, find B × A (web index prints 'B × A'; its worked solution shows A × B — both given).
questions.solution: B × A (first from B, second from A) = {(a,1),(a,2),(a,3),(b,1),(b,2),(b,3)} — 6 pairs. For reference, A × B = {(1,a),(1,b),(2,a),(2,b),(3,a),(3,b)}. ✅ (Flag: confirm which product the printed book asks — the two differ by order throughout.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q3(c); order ambiguity flagged vs the web index

questions.knowledgeNote: Union first, then cross: B∪C = {b,c,d}, and A supplies the first components.
questions.question: Q4(a). Let A = {a,b}, B = {b,c}, C = {c,d}. Find A × (B ∪ C).
questions.solution: B∪C = {b,c,d}. A×(B∪C) = {(a,b),(a,c),(a,d),(b,b),(b,c),(b,d)} — 6 pairs. ✅ (Web-index typo fixed: it prints (b,a), but a ∉ B∪C, so (b,a) is impossible; the correct pair is (b,b).)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q4(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Intersection first: only c survives B∩C, so just 2 pairs.
questions.question: Q4(b). With A, B, C as above, find A × (B ∩ C).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q4(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Distributive law preview: this union must equal Q4(a) — use it as a cross-check.
questions.question: Q4(c). With A, B, C as above, find (A × B) ∪ (A × C).
questions.solution: A×B = {(a,b),(a,c),(b,b),(b,c)}; A×C = {(a,c),(a,d),(b,c),(b,d)}. Union = {(a,b),(a,c),(a,d),(b,b),(b,c),(b,d)} — identical to Q4(a), as A×(B∪C) = (A×B)∪(A×C) demands. ✅
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q4(c)

questions.knowledgeNote: Only pairs present in BOTH products survive: the ones whose second component is c.
questions.question: Q4(d). With A, B, C as above, find (A × B) ∩ (A × C).
questions.solution: Common to {(a,b),(a,c),(b,b),(b,c)} and {(a,c),(a,d),(b,c),(b,d)}: (a,c) and (b,c). ✅ {(a,c),(b,c)}. (Web index omits the comma — restored.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q4(d)

questions.knowledgeNote: LHS–RHS verification: compute both sides fully, then compare as sets.
questions.question: Q5(a). Let A = {a,b}, B = {c,d}, C = {d,e}. Verify A × (B ∪ C) = (A × B) ∪ (A × C).
questions.solution: LHS: B∪C = {c,d,e}; A×that = {(a,c),(a,d),(a,e),(b,c),(b,d),(b,e)}. RHS: (A×B)∪(A×C) = {(a,c),(a,d),(b,c),(b,d)} ∪ {(a,d),(a,e),(b,d),(b,e)} = {(a,c),(a,d),(a,e),(b,c),(b,d),(b,e)}. LHS = RHS. ✅ Verified.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q5(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same drill for ∩: B∩C = {d} collapses the LHS to 2 pairs.
questions.question: Q5(b). With A, B, C as above, verify A × (B ∩ C) = (A × B) ∩ (A × C).
questions.solution: LHS: B∩C = {d}; A×{d} = {(a,d),(b,d)}. RHS: {(a,c),(a,d),(b,c),(b,d)} ∩ {(a,d),(a,e),(b,d),(b,e)} = {(a,d),(b,d)}. LHS = RHS. ✅ Verified.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q5(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Build B by evaluating the rule at each x in A — B's order follows x = 1, 2, 3.
questions.question: Q6(a). Find the Cartesian product A × B where A = {x : x = 1,2,3} and B = {y : y = 3−x}.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q6(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Squares grow fast: x = 2 gives y = 4, so B is not {0,1,2}.
questions.question: Q6(b). Find A × B where A = {x : x = 0,1,2} and B = {y : y = x²}.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.1 Q6(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Arrow-diagram test: every dot on the A side must send out exactly one arrow — a dot with none, or with two, kills the function.
questions.question: Q1(a). (Arrow diagram, see print.) State whether the diagram defines a function A→B. [Key: Yes.]
questions.solution: Each element of A sends out exactly one arrow to B — one image each, none left out. ✅ IS a function (book key: 'to each element of A there is one and only one element of B').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(a); verdict = printed Answers key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Same test on diagram (b): full coverage, single arrows.
questions.question: Q1(b). (Arrow diagram, see print.) State whether the diagram defines a function A→B. [Key: Yes.]
questions.solution: Every element of A has exactly one outgoing arrow. ✅ IS a function (book key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(b); verdict = printed Answers key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Totality failure: one element of A with no image means no function, however neat the rest is.
questions.question: Q1(c). (Arrow diagram, see print.) State whether the diagram defines a function A→B. [Key: No.]
questions.solution: The element c of A has no arrow to B — no image for c. ✅ NOT a function (book key: 'there is no element of B corresponding to the element c of A').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(c); verdict = printed Answers key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Many-to-one is legal: sharing an image never breaks function-hood.
questions.question: Q1(d). (Arrow diagram, see print.) State whether the diagram defines a function A→B. [Key: Yes.]
questions.solution: Each element of A has exactly one image (two elements happen to share one). ✅ IS a function (book key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(d); verdict = printed Answers key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Uniqueness failure: one domain element with two (here three) images is a relation, not a function.
questions.question: Q1(e). (Arrow diagram, see print.) State whether the diagram defines a function A→B. [Key: No.]
questions.solution: One element of A sends arrows to three different elements of B — three images for one input. ✅ NOT a function (book key: 'three elements of B correspond to one element of A').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(e); verdict = printed Answers key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Full coverage plus single arrows ⇒ function, even across unequal sets.
questions.question: Q1(f). (Arrow diagram, see print.) State whether the diagram defines a function A→B. [Key: Yes.]
questions.solution: Every element of A has exactly one image in B. ✅ IS a function (book key). Functions among the six: (a), (b), (d), (f) — matches key Q2-style cross-check '(c), (d), (e)' pattern of the companion question.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(f); verdict = printed Answers key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Domain restriction rules: a formula only answers inside its stated interval — outside, the value simply doesn't exist.
questions.question: Q4(i). Let f(x) = x + 2 in the interval −1 ≤ x ≤ 2 (domain of definition [−1, 2]). Find f(−1), f(0), f(1), f(2), f(−2), f(3).
questions.solution: Inside [−1,2]: f(−1) = −1+2 = 1; f(0) = 2; f(1) = 3; f(2) = 4. Outside: −2 ∉ [−1,2] and 3 ∉ [−1,2], so f(−2) and f(3) are NOT defined (not zero — undefined). ✅ 1, 2, 3, 4; f(−2), f(3) undefined (matches printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(i); answers vs printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Absolute-value split: 2|x| + 3x behaves as x (x ≥ 0) and 5x... check: x<0 gives −2x+3x = x? No: 2(−x)+3x = x. Actually both branches give x?? f(−1) = 2−3 = −1 = x. f(1) = 2+3 = 5?? 2|1|+3 = 5 ≠ 1. Recompute: x ≥ 0: 2x+3x = 5x; x < 0: −2x+3x = x. So the function is piecewise x / 5x — verify each point directly.
questions.question: Q4(ii). Let f(x) = 2|x| + 3x in the interval −1 ≤ x ≤ 2 (print reads '2|x| + 3x'; verified against key). Find f(−1), f(0), f(1), f(2), f(−2), f(3).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(ii); formula read via 300-dpi crop, answers vs printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Piecewise discipline: first ask WHICH piece the input falls in (mind the ≤ vs < at joints), then substitute.
questions.question: Q5(i). Let f(x) = 3+2x (−1/2 ≤ x < 0); 3−2x (0 ≤ x < 1/2); −3−2x (x ≥ 1/2). Find f(−1/2), f(0), f(1/2) and [f(h) − f(0)]/h for 0 ≤ h < 1/2.
questions.solution: a) x = −1/2 takes the FIRST piece (closed end): 3+2(−1/2) = 2. b) x = 0 takes the SECOND piece: 3−0 = 3. c) x = 1/2 takes the THIRD piece (x ≥ 1/2): −3−2(1/2) = −4. d) For 0 ≤ h < 1/2, f(h) = 3−2h and f(0) = 3, so [f(h)−f(0)]/h = (3−2h−3)/h = −2. ✅ 2, 3, −4, −2 (matches printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q5(i); answers vs printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: The joint x = 1 belongs to the upper piece (x ≥ 1) — a favourite examiner trap.
questions.question: Q5(ii). Let f(x) = 4x−2 (x ≥ 1); 2x (x < 1). Find f(2), f(1), f(0), f(−1) and [f(h) − f(1)]/h for h > 1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q5(ii); answers vs printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Range = the set of outputs only: evaluate at every domain point, collect distinct values.
questions.question: Q6(i). Let A = {−1, 0, 2, 4, 6}, f:A→R with f(x) = x/(x+2). Find the range of f.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q6(i); answer vs printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Zero denominator = red flag: x = −1 kills x/(x+1), so −1 contributes no output — the range skips it.
questions.question: Q6(ii). With A = {−1, 0, 2, 4, 6}, f:A→R with f(x) = x/(x+1). Find the range of f.
questions.solution: f(−1) = −1/0 — UNDEFINED (division by zero, so −1 yields no image). f(0) = 0; f(2) = 2/3; f(4) = 4/5; f(6) = 6/7. ✅ Range = {0, 2/3, 4/5, 6/7} (over the four admissible inputs; −1 excluded with reason).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q6(ii); undefined-point flagged, defined values computed

questions.knowledgeNote: Equal functions need BOTH: same domain AND same value at every point — check as sets of pairs.
questions.question: Q7. Determine whether f and g are equal: (a) f(x) = x² with domain A = {−1, −2, −3}; (b) g given by Venn diagram. [Key: equal.]
questions.solution: As a set of pairs, f = {(−1, 1), (−2, 4), (−3, 9)} (since (−1)² = 1, (−2)² = 4, (−3)² = 9). The diagram g shows exactly {(−1,1), (−2,4), (−3,9)}. Same domain, same values everywhere. ✅ f = g — the two functions are EQUAL (matches printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q7; pairs vs printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: One counterexample kills one-one: a single repeated output (f(−2) = f(2)) is enough.
questions.question: Q8(a). A = {−2,−1,0,1,2}, B = {4,0,1}, f(x) = x². Is f one-one? [Key: No.]
questions.solution: f(−2) = 4 and f(2) = 4 — two different inputs, same output (−2 ≠ 2 but f(−2) = f(2)). ✅ NOT one-one (book key: 'f(−2) = 4 = f(2) does not imply −2 = 2'). (Also f(−1) = f(1) = 1.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q8(a); reason = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: On positive integers squaring never collides: distinct bases give distinct squares.
questions.question: Q8(b). A = positive integers, B = their squares, f(x) = x². Is f one-one? [Key: Yes.]
questions.solution: For positive integers, x ≠ y ⟹ x² ≠ y² (e.g. 2² = 4 ≠ 9 = 3²; squares are strictly increasing on N). ✅ One-one (book key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q8(b); reason = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Symmetric intervals around 0 defeat x²: ±a always collide.
questions.question: Q8(c). f:[−2,2]→R, f(x) = x². Is f one-one? [Key: No.]
questions.solution: f(−2) = 4 = f(2) with −2 ≠ 2. ✅ NOT one-one (book key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q8(c); reason = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Cut off the negative half and x² becomes strictly increasing — hence one-one.
questions.question: Q8(d). f:[0,3]→R, f(x) = x². Is f one-one? [Key: Yes.]
questions.solution: On [0,3], x ≠ y ⟹ x² ≠ y² (squaring preserves order for non-negatives). ✅ One-one (book key). Compare (c): removing the negative half fixed it.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q8(d); reason = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Classify with the key's verdict: an onto-but-not-one-one map must hit everything while colliding somewhere.
questions.question: Q9(i). State whether the given function is one-one, onto, both or neither. [Print: figure-based statement, not machine-readable in scan; key verdict: onto.]
questions.solution: PRINT STATUS: the Q9(i) statement line carries a figure/diagram in this printing (unreadable even at 350-dpi crop; same family as Q1/Q8(a) figures). Book key verdict: ONTO (i.e. onto but not one-one — every B-element is hit, some output is shared). ⚠️ Confirm the exact mapping against the physical book; verdict recorded from the printed key p.84.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q9(i); verdict = printed key p.84, statement = print figure (pending physical-book read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Doubling hits only evens: one-one yes, onto no — the classic one-one-only example.
questions.question: Q9(ii). f:N→N, f(x) = 2x. One-one, onto, both or neither? [Key: one-one.]
questions.solution: One-one: 2x = 2y ⟹ x = y. Not onto: odd numbers (1, 3, 5, …) have no pre-image since f(N) = {2, 4, 6, …} ≠ N. ✅ One-one ONLY (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q9(ii); classification = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: x² on (−2,2) fails both ways: collides (±) and misses negatives.
questions.question: Q9(iii). f:(−2,2)→R, f(x) = x². One-one, onto, both or neither? [Key: neither.]
questions.solution: Not one-one: f(−1) = 1 = f(1). Not onto: e.g. −1 ∈ R has no pre-image (squares ≥ 0). ✅ NEITHER (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q9(iii); classification = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Linear maps x ↦ ax + b (a ≠ 0) over Q are bijective — invert by undoing: x = (y−5)/6 stays rational.
questions.question: Q9(iv). f:Q→Q, f(x) = 6x + 5. One-one, onto, both or neither? [Key: both.]
questions.solution: One-one: 6x+5 = 6y+5 ⟹ x = y. Onto: for any r ∈ Q, x = (r−5)/6 ∈ Q and f(x) = r. ✅ Both — ONE-ONE AND ONTO (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q9(iv); classification = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Cubing over R is strictly increasing, hence bijective with inverse ∛.
questions.question: Q9(v). f:R→R, f(x) = x³. One-one, onto, both or neither? [Key: both.]
questions.solution: One-one: x³ = y³ ⟹ x = y over R. Onto: every r ∈ R is (∛r)³. ✅ Both — ONE-ONE AND ONTO (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q9(v); classification = printed key p.84

questions.knowledgeNote: Zero denominator check first: for f(x) = 6/(x+1), x = −1 is a hard stop — flag before any range claim.
questions.question: Q10(a). f:A→B with f(x) = 6/(x+1) (fraction read with box positions at 300 dpi: numerator '6', denominator 'x+1'), A = {−2,−1,0,1,2}, B = {0, _, _} (three elements, middle/last unclear in scan). Find the range; one-one and onto both? [Key: range {0, _, 3}-family, 'onto only'.]
questions.solution: Point evaluation: f(−2) = 6/(−1) = −6; f(−1) = 6/0 — UNDEFINED (zero denominator: −1 has no image); f(0) = 6; f(1) = 3; f(2) = 2. So on the stated A the rule is not defined everywhere — as printed it is NOT a map A→B at all. ⚠️ PRINT TENSION: the key's verdict (3-element range incl. 3, 'onto only') presupposes a corrected statement (numerator or sets differ in later printings) — recorded as printed, pending physical-book confirmation. Defined-point values: {−6, 6, 3, 2}.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q10(a); formula via positioned OCR, key verdict quoted p.84, tension flagged

questions.knowledgeNote: Codomain restriction is the standard repair: a one-one map becomes bijective once B is shrunk to R(f).
questions.question: Q10(b). 'With …' — second range/one-one/onto question: find the range; if not both, how can the function be made one-one and onto both? [Key: range {−1, 0, …, 1, 2}-family; 'one-one only'. Sets/formula below scan threshold — pending.]
questions.solution: PRINT STATUS: Q10(b)'s sets and formula sit in the faint band under Q10(a) (only 'With … f(x) = [2x−1]/[…]' fragments recovered). Key verdict recorded: ONE-ONE ONLY with the stated multi-element range. General repair (asked in the question): replace the codomain B by the range R(f) — a one-one map onto its own range is bijective, i.e. one-one AND onto. ⚠️ Full statement pending physical-book confirmation.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q10(b); verdict = printed key p.84, statement pending physical-book read

questions.knowledgeNote: A relation X→Y is a function iff every element of X has exactly one image in Y — one output each, no element left without an image.
questions.question: Q1(a). Let X = {a,b,c}, Y = {p,r,s}. Is R1 = {(a,p),(a,r),(b,r),(c,s)} a function from X to Y? Give reason.
questions.solution: Check each element of X: a appears twice — (a,p) and (a,r), i.e. a has two images p and r. A function allows exactly one image per domain element. ✅ NOT a function (a violates uniqueness).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Totality matters too: every domain element must appear at least once as a first component.
questions.question: Q1(b). With X, Y as above, is R2 = {(a,p),(b,r)} a function? Give reason.
questions.solution: List first components: {a, b} — element c ∈ X has no pair, so no image for c. A function from X to Y must cover all of X. ✅ NOT a function (c has no image).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Many-to-one is allowed: distinct domain elements may share one image; only one-image-per-element and full coverage are required.
questions.question: Q1(c). With X, Y as above, is R3 = {(a,s),(b,s),(c,s)} a function? Give reason.
questions.solution: First components: a→s, b→s, c→s. Every element of X appears exactly once as a first component. ✅ IS a function (constant function; many-to-one is legal).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(c)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same test: each of a, b, c used exactly once ⇒ function, even though a and b share image p.
questions.question: Q1(d). With X, Y as above, is R4 = {(a,p),(b,p),(c,s)} a function? Give reason.
questions.solution: a→p, b→p, c→s — all three domain elements covered exactly once. ✅ IS a function.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(d)

questions.knowledgeNote: One-to-one onto a 3-element codomain subset: each domain element used once ⇒ function (bijective onto {p,r,s}).
questions.question: Q1(e). With X, Y as above, is R5 = {(a,p),(b,r),(c,s)} a function? Give reason.
questions.solution: a→p, b→r, c→s — every element of X has exactly one image. ✅ IS a function.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q1(e)

questions.knowledgeNote: Image = function value at a point: substitute and simplify, watching fraction arithmetic.
questions.question: Q2(a). If f: A→B with f(x) = 1−x, find the image of 1.
questions.solution: f(1) = 1 − 1 = 0. ✅ Image of 1 is 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q2 (x = 1)

questions.knowledgeNote: With fractions, keep a common denominator: 1 − 3/2 = (2−3)/2 = −1/2.
questions.question: Q2(b). With f(x) = 1−x as above, find the image of 3/2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q2 (x = 3/2)

questions.knowledgeNote: Minus of a minus: 1 − (−1) = 1 + 1 = 2.
questions.question: Q2(c). With f(x) = 1−x as above, find the image of −1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q2 (x = −1)

questions.knowledgeNote: Direct substitution: f(2) = 1 − 2 = −1.
questions.question: Q2(d). With f(x) = 1−x as above, find the image of 2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q2 (x = 2)

questions.knowledgeNote: Inverse by interchange: set y = f(x), swap to x = …, then solve for y.
questions.question: Q3(a). Find a formula for the inverse function f⁻¹ if f: R→R, f(x) = x + 1.
questions.solution: Step 1 — Let y = x + 1. Step 2 — Interchange: x = y + 1. Step 3 — Solve: y = x − 1. ✅ f⁻¹(x) = x − 1. (Check: f(f⁻¹(x)) = (x−1)+1 = x ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q3(a)

questions.knowledgeNote: Linear inverse: after swapping, isolate y by undoing ×2 then −3.
questions.question: Q3(b). Find f⁻¹ if f: R→R, f(x) = 2x + 3.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q3(b)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same template with constant 5: y = (x−5)/2.
questions.question: Q3(c). Find f⁻¹ if f: R→R, f(x) = 2x + 5.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q3(c)

questions.knowledgeNote: Cubic inverse uses the real cube root: x = y³+5 ⇒ y = ∛(x−5).
questions.question: Q3(d). Find f⁻¹ if f: R→R, f(x) = x³ + 5.
questions.solution: Step 1 — y = x³ + 5. Step 2 — x = y³ + 5. Step 3 — y³ = x − 5, so y = ∛(x−5). ✅ f⁻¹(x) = ∛(x−5). (Check: (∛(x−5))³+5 = x ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q3(d)

questions.knowledgeNote: Undo 3x−2 in reverse: add 2, divide by 3.
questions.question: Q3(e). Find f⁻¹ if f: R→R, f(x) = 3x − 2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q3(e)

questions.knowledgeNote: gof means apply f first: g(f(x)) = 3(2x+1)−1.
questions.question: Q4(a-i). Let f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = 3x − 1. Find gof(x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(a) gof

questions.knowledgeNote: fog reverses the order: f(g(x)) = 2(3x−1)+1. Order matters — compare with gof.
questions.question: Q4(a-ii). With f, g as above, find fog(x).
questions.solution: fog(x) = f[g(x)] = f(3x−1) = 2(3x−1) + 1 = 6x − 2 + 1. ✅ fog(x) = 6x − 1. (Note gof ≠ fog here.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(a) fog

questions.knowledgeNote: Substitute the whole quadratic into the linear outer function, then expand.
questions.question: Q4(b-i). Let f(x) = 3x² − 4 and g(x) = 2x − 5. Find gof(x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(b) gof

questions.knowledgeNote: Squaring a binomial: (2x−5)² = 4x² − 20x + 25 — middle term is 2·(2x)(−5).
questions.question: Q4(b-ii). With f, g as above, find fog(x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(b) fog

questions.knowledgeNote: Power-then-power: g(f(x)) squares the whole cubic-minus-one; leave expanded or factored as the book accepts either.
questions.question: Q4(c-i). Let f(x) = x³ − 1 and g(x) = x². Find gof(x).
questions.solution: gof(x) = (x³−1)². ✅ gof(x) = (x³ − 1)² (= x⁶ − 2x³ + 1 expanded).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(c) gof

questions.knowledgeNote: Reverse order collapses nicely: (x²)³ − 1 = x⁶ − 1.
questions.question: Q4(c-ii). With f, g as above, find fog(x).
questions.solution: fog(x) = f(x²) = (x²)³ − 1 = x⁶ − 1. ✅ fog(x) = x⁶ − 1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(c) fog

questions.knowledgeNote: Outer power 5: substitute the full quadratic-plus-one as the base.
questions.question: Q4(d-i). Let f(x) = x² + 1 and g(x) = x⁵. Find gof(x).
questions.solution: gof(x) = (x²+1)⁵. ✅ gof(x) = (x² + 1)⁵.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(d) gof

questions.knowledgeNote: (x⁵)² + 1 = x¹⁰ + 1 by the power-of-power rule.
questions.question: Q4(d-ii). With f, g as above, find fog(x).
questions.solution: fog(x) = f(x⁵) = (x⁵)² + 1 = x¹⁰ + 1. ✅ fog(x) = x¹⁰ + 1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.2 Q4(d) fog

questions.knowledgeNote: Pre-image reads the arrows backwards: f⁻¹(1) collects every domain dot whose arrow lands on 1.
questions.question: Q1. f:A→A (A = {1,2,3,4,5}) is given by the print arrow diagram, i.e. f = {(1,3),(2,1),(3,3),(4,5),(5,3)} (pairs forced by the key verdicts below). Find f⁻¹(1).
questions.solution: Only the arrow 2→1 lands on 1. ✅ f⁻¹(1) = {2} (matches printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q1(a); pairs key-reconstructed, answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Shared images collect multiple pre-images: 1, 3 and 5 all point at 3.
questions.question: Q1(b). With f as above, find f⁻¹(3).
questions.solution: Arrows landing on 3 come from 1, 3 and 5. ✅ f⁻¹(3) = {1, 3, 5} (matches printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q1(b); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Single arrow 4→5 gives a singleton pre-image.
questions.question: Q1(c). With f as above, find f⁻¹(5).
questions.solution: Only 4 maps to 5. ✅ f⁻¹(5) = {4} (matches printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q1(c); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Empty pre-image is a legal answer: nothing maps to 2, so write ∅ (the key's φ).
questions.question: Q1(d). With f as above, find f⁻¹(2).
questions.solution: No arrow lands on 2 (images are 3,1,3,5,3). ✅ f⁻¹(2) = ∅ (key's φ-fragment).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q1(d); answer = printed key (φ)

questions.knowledgeNote: Pre-image of a SET unions the individual pre-images — here it swallows the whole domain.
questions.question: Q1(e). With f as above, find f⁻¹({1, 3, 5}).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q1(e); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: ∅ ∪ ∅ = ∅: neither 2 nor 4 is ever hit.
questions.question: Q1(f). With f as above, find f⁻¹({2, 4}).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q1(f)

questions.knowledgeNote: Inverting a pair-set just swaps every pair: (a,b) becomes (b,a).
questions.question: Q2(a). f:X→Y is given in print (figure/table) with f = {(0,10),(1,13),(2,16),(3,19)} (pattern f(x) = 3x+10). Write down f⁻¹:B→A as ordered pairs.

questions.knowledgeNote: Inverse by interchange: y = x+1 ⇒ x = y+1 ⇒ y = x−1.
questions.question: Q3(a). f:R→R, f(x) = x + 1. Find a formula for f⁻¹.
questions.solution: y = x+1; interchange: x = y+1; solve: y = x−1. ✅ f⁻¹(x) = x − 1. (Check: (x−1)+1 = x ✔; matches key.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q3(a); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Undo ×2 then −3 in reverse order.

questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q3(b); answer = printed key

questions.question: Q3(c). f:R→R, f(x) = 2x + 5. Find f⁻¹.
questions.solution: y = 2x+5 → x = 2y+5 → y = (x−5)/2. ✅ f⁻¹(x) = (x−5)/2. (Check ✔; matches key.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q3(c); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Cubic inverse needs the real cube root.
questions.question: Q3(d). f:R→R, f(x) = x³ + 5. Find f⁻¹.
questions.solution: y = x³+5 → x = y³+5 → y = ∛(x−5). ✅ f⁻¹(x) = ∛(x−5). (Check: (∛(x−5))³+5 = x ✔; matches key.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q3(d); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Undo 3x−2: add 2, divide by 3.
questions.question: Q3(e). f:R→R, f(x) = 3x − 2. Find f⁻¹.
questions.solution: y = 3x−2 → x = 3y−2 → y = (x+2)/3. ✅ f⁻¹(x) = (x+2)/3. (Check ✔; matches key.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q3(e); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Scalar multiple minus constant, applied pointwise: (2f−5)(x) = 2·f(x) − 5.
questions.question: Q4(a). f(x) = 4x³ − 1, g(x) = 3x³. Find (2f − 5)(x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q4(a); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: f² means f·f (pointwise square), not f∘f — square the whole cubic.
questions.question: Q4(b). With f, g as above, find (f²)(x).
questions.solution: (f²)(x) = (4x³−1)². ✅ (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q4(b); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Watch the x³ terms cancel: 3f − 4g collapses to a constant — the question's punchline.
questions.question: Q4(c). With f, g as above, find (3f − 4g)(x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q4(c); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Product: (4x³−1)(3x³) — multiply term by term.
questions.question: Q4(d). With f, g as above, find (fg)(x).
questions.solution: (fg)(x) = (4x³−1)(3x³) = 12x⁶ − 3x³. ✅ (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q4(d); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Quotient with guard: g(x) = 3x³ = 0 at x = 0, so x ≠ 0.
questions.question: Q4(e). With f, g as above, find (f/g)(x) (g(x) ≠ 0).
questions.solution: ✅ (f/g)(x) = (4x³−1)/(3x³), x ≠ 0 (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q4(e); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: gof applies f first: g(f(x)) = 3(2x+1) − 1.
questions.question: Q5(a-i). f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = 3x − 1. Find (gof)(x).
questions.solution: g(f(x)) = 3(2x+1) − 1 = 6x + 2. ✅ (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(a) gof; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: fog reverses the order — compare with gof.
questions.question: Q5(a-ii). With f, g as above, find (fog)(x).
questions.solution: f(g(x)) = 2(3x−1) + 1 = 6x − 1. ✅ (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(a) fog; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Substitute the whole quadratic into the linear outer function.
questions.question: Q5(b-i). f(x) = 3x² − 4, g(x) = 2x − 5. Find (gof)(x).
questions.solution: g(f(x)) = 2(3x²−4) − 5 = 6x² − 13. ✅ (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(b) gof; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: (2x−5)² = 4x² − 20x + 25 — middle term 2·(2x)(−5).
questions.question: Q5(b-ii). With f, g as above, find (fog)(x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(b) fog; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Power-then-power: square the whole cubic-minus-one.
questions.question: Q5(c-i). f(x) = x³ − 1, g(x) = x². Find (gof)(x).
questions.solution: ✅ (gof)(x) = (x³−1)² (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(c) gof; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Reverse order collapses: (x²)³ − 1 = x⁶ − 1.
questions.question: Q5(c-ii). With f, g as above, find (fog)(x).
questions.solution: ✅ (fog)(x) = x⁶ − 1 (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(c) fog; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Outer power 5: substitute the full quadratic-plus-one as the base.
questions.question: Q5(d-i). f(x) = x² + 1, g(x) = x⁵. Find (gof)(x).
questions.solution: ✅ (gof)(x) = (x²+1)⁵ (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(d) gof; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: (x⁵)² + 1 = x¹⁰ + 1 by the power-of-power rule.
questions.question: Q5(d-ii). With f, g as above, find (fog)(x).
questions.solution: ✅ (fog)(x) = x¹⁰ + 1 (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q5(d) fog; answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Composite of pair-sets: chase each input through f then g, keeping pairs that survive both.
questions.question: Q6(a). f = {(1,5),(2,6),(3,7),(4,6)}, g = {(5,1),(6,2),(7,3)}. Find gof and fog.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q6(a); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Drop pairs whose middle value misses the next map: only chainable inputs survive.
questions.question: Q6(b). f = {(1,2),(3,5),(4,1)}, g = {(2,3),(5,1),(1,3)}. Find gof and fog.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q6(b); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Self-composite of a Möbius map: clear denominators by multiplying top and bottom by (1−x).
questions.question: Q7(a). f:R→R, f(x) = (x+1)/(1−x) (x ≠ 1; formula band at crop edge, computation exact). Show (fof)(x) = −1/x.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q7(a); computation verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Same phenomenon, second map: (x−1)/(x+1) also squares to −1/x — then just plug in 4.
questions.question: Q7(b). f:R→R, f(x) = (x−1)/(x+1) (x ≠ −1). Show (fof)(4) = −1/4.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q7(b); computation verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Non-constant linear maps hit every real, exactly once each.
questions.question: Q8(a). y = 3x + 1 (f:R→R). Find domain and range.
questions.solution: Defined for all real x; every real y has x = (y−1)/3. ✅ D(f) = R = (−∞,∞), R(f) = R (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(a); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: x² ≥ 0 shifts the range up by the constant: x²−1 ≥ −1.
questions.question: Q8(b). y = x² − 1. Find domain and range.
questions.solution: Defined ∀x ∈ R; x² ≥ 0 ⟹ y ≥ −1, and every y ≥ −1 occurs (x = ±√(y+1)). ✅ D = R, R = [−1,∞) (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(b); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Odd powers are onto R: every real has exactly one real cube root.
questions.question: Q8(c). y = x³. Find domain and range.
questions.solution: ✅ D = R = (−∞,∞), R = R (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(c); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Complete the square to read the maximum: −x²+4x−3 = −(x−2)²+1 ≤ 1.
questions.question: Q8(d). y = −x² + 4x − 3. Find domain and range.
questions.solution: Defined ∀x; y = −(x−2)² + 1 ≤ 1 with equality at x = 2. ✅ D = R, R = (−∞,1] (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(d); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Even root needs non-negative radicand: x − 2 ≥ 0 gates the domain.
questions.question: Q8(e). y = √(x−2). Find domain and range.
questions.solution: Need x−2 ≥ 0 ⟹ x ≥ 2; outputs cover all ≥ 0. ✅ D = [2,∞), R = [0,∞) (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(e); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Rational maps exclude the zero of the denominator AND miss one value (the horizontal asymptote).
questions.question: Q8(f). y = 1/(x+1) (read at 300 dpi with box positions). Find domain and range.
questions.solution: Undefined at x = −1 ⟹ D = R − {−1}. y = 0 never occurs, and every r ≠ 0 has x = 1/r − 1. ✅ D = R−{−1}, R = R−{0} (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(f); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Factor first: (x²−16)/(x−4) = x+4 with the hole x ≠ 4 — range misses 8.
questions.question: Q8(g). y = (x²−16)/(x−4). Find domain and range.
questions.solution: x²−16 = (x−4)(x+4), so y = x+4 for x ≠ 4. ✅ D = R−{4}, R = R−{8} (matches key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(g); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Quadratic radicand: factor (x−4)(x+2) ≥ 0 and read the sign chart — outer intervals survive.
questions.question: Q8(h). y = √(x²−2x−8). Find domain and range.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(h); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Negative quadratic under the root: 21−4x−x² = 25−(x+2)² bounds both sides.
questions.question: Q8(i). y = √(21−4x−x²). Find domain and range.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(i); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Sign function in disguise: |x−1|/(x−1) is +1 right of 1, −1 left of 1, undefined AT 1.
questions.question: Q8(j). y = |x−1|/(x−1) (key signature D = R−{1}, R = {−1,1}). Find domain and range.
questions.solution: Undefined at x = 1 (0/0) ⟹ D = R−{1}. For x > 1: (x−1)/(x−1) = 1; for x < 1: −(x−1)/(x−1) = −1. ✅ R = {−1,1} (matches key; statement attribution via the key's unique signature, pending physical-book confirmation of the exact print form).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q8(j); answer = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: c ≠ 0 is the whole engine: it lets you divide when proving one-one and when solving for onto.
questions.question: Q9. Show f:R→R, f(x) = cx + d (c ≠ 0) is one-one and onto. Find f⁻¹. Also show f(f⁻¹(x)) = f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.
questions.solution: One-one: cx₁+d = cx₂+d ⟹ c(x₁−x₂) = 0 ⟹ x₁ = x₂ (c ≠ 0). Onto: for any y, x = (y−d)/c ∈ R gives f(x) = y. So f⁻¹(x) = (x−d)/c (matches key). f(f⁻¹(x)) = c·((x−d)/c)+d = x; f⁻¹(f(x)) = (cx+d−d)/c = x. ✅
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q9; inverse = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Cross-multiply to prove one-one; solve y = 3x/(x−2) for x to prove onto and read off the inverse.
questions.question: Q10. f:R−{2}→R−{3}, f(x) = 3x/(x−2). Show f is bijective and find f⁻¹.
questions.solution: One-one: 3x₁/(x₁−2) = 3x₂/(x₂−2) ⟹ x₁(x₂−2) = x₂(x₁−2) ⟹ −2x₁ = −2x₂ ⟹ x₁ = x₂. Onto: y = 3x/(x−2) ⟹ yx−2y = 3x ⟹ x(y−3) = 2y ⟹ x = 2y/(y−3) ∈ R−{2} for y ≠ 3. So ✅ f⁻¹(x) = 2x/(x−3) (matches key) and f is bijective.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.3 Q10; inverse = printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Quotient first, then product, then power: peel the log apart layer by layer. The web index drops the '+' and '3' (prints 'log_a x log_a y'); the identity needs + 3log_a y.
questions.question: Q1(a). Prove that log_a(xy^3/z^2) = log_a x + 3log_a y - 2log_a z (x, y, z > 0, a > 0, a != 1).
questions.solution: LHS = log_a(xy^3/z^2). Quotient rule: = log_a(xy^3) - log_a(z^2). Product rule: = log_a x + log_a(y^3) - log_a(z^2). Power rule: = log_a x + 3log_a y - 2log_a z = RHS. Proved. (The web index prints this without the '+' and '3'; restored here since log_a(xy^3) = log_a x + 3log_a y. Book OCR p112 confirms '+ 3'.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(a); book p112 = PDF p137 (OCR conf 0.93) + SciPiPupil Ex-4 typed page

questions.knowledgeNote: A sum of logs is the log of a product: 3(log x - log y) folds into one cube.
questions.question: Q1(b). Prove that log_a 2x + 3(log_a x - log_a y) = log_a(2x^4/y^3).
questions.solution: LHS = log_a 2x + 3(log_a x - log_a y). Quotient rule inside: = log_a 2x + 3log_a(x/y). Power rule: = log_a 2x + log_a(x/y)^3 = log_a 2x + log_a(x^3/y^3). Product rule: = log_a(2x . x^3/y^3) = log_a(2x^4/y^3) = RHS. Proved.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(b); book p112 = PDF p137 + SciPiPupil Ex-4 typed page

questions.knowledgeNote: sqrt(x) is x^(1/2): the power rule turns 2log sqrt(x) into exactly log x.
questions.question: Q1(c). Prove that log_a x^2 - 2log_a sqrt(x) = log_a x (x > 0).
questions.solution: LHS = log_a x^2 - 2log_a sqrt(x) = log_a x^2 - 2log_a(x^(1/2)). Power rule on each: = 2log_a x - 2.(1/2)log_a x = 2log_a x - log_a x = log_a x = RHS. Proved.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(c); book p112 = PDF p137 + SciPiPupil Ex-4 typed page

questions.knowledgeNote: a^{log_a x} = x is the definition of a logarithm undone: log_a x is the exponent that turns a into x.
questions.question: Q1(d). Prove that a^{log_a x} = x (a > 0, a != 1, x > 0). [Printed flat as 'a log_a x = x'; the exponent position is restored.]
questions.solution: Let t = log_a x. By definition of logarithm, a^t = x. Substituting t back: a^{log_a x} = x. Proved. (The web index prints this flat without the superscript; the exponent form is the standard inverse property.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(d); exponent restored from standard inverse property

questions.knowledgeNote: log_a a = 1 pulls the exponent down untouched.
questions.question: Q1(e). Prove that log_a a^x = x.
questions.solution: LHS = log_a(a^x). Power rule: = x.log_a a = x . 1 = x = RHS. Proved.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(e); book p112 = PDF p137 + SciPiPupil Ex-4 typed page

questions.knowledgeNote: Difference of two squares works on logs too: U^2 - V^2 = (U+V)(U-V), then product/quotient rules.
questions.question: Q1(f). Prove that (log a)^2 - (log b)^2 = log(ab) . log(a/b) (a, b > 0).
questions.solution: LHS = (log a)^2 - (log b)^2 = (log a + log b)(log a - log b) by a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b). Product rule: log a + log b = log(ab). Quotient rule: log a - log b = log(a/b). So LHS = log(ab).log(a/b) = RHS. Proved.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(f); book p112 = PDF p137 + SciPiPupil Ex-4 typed page

questions.knowledgeNote: A numerical coincidence, NOT a rule: 1+2+3 and 1x2x3 both equal 6. Never split log of a sum in general.
questions.question: Q1(g). Verify that log(1 + 2 + 3) = log 1 + log 2 + log 3, and state why this does not make log(x+y) = log x + log y.
questions.solution: LHS = log(6). RHS = log 1 + log 2 + log 3 = 0 + log(2.3) = log 6 (product rule + log 1 = 0). So LHS = RHS = log 6. Verified. Caution: this works only because 1+2+3 = 6 = 1x2x3; in general log(x+y) != log x + log y.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(g); book p112 = PDF p137; coincidence flagged

questions.knowledgeNote: Take log of both sides: each exponent drops down and the six terms cancel in pairs.
questions.question: Q1(h). Prove that x^{log y - log z} . y^{log z - log x} . z^{log x - log y} = 1 (x, y, z > 0).
questions.solution: Let P = LHS. Take log (any base): log P = (log y - log z)log x + (log z - log x)log y + (log x - log y)log z. Expanding: = log x.log y - log x.log z + log y.log z - log y.log x + log z.log x - log z.log y = 0. So log P = 0 = log 1, hence P = 1. Proved.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(h); book p112 = PDF p137; standard cyclic-exponent proof

questions.knowledgeNote: Same trick as (h), one level up: each factor log-splits into a difference of SQUARES, and the squares telescope to zero.
questions.question: Q1(i). Prove that (yz)^{log y - log z} . (zx)^{log z - log x} . (xy)^{log x - log y} = 1 (x, y, z > 0).
questions.solution: Let P = LHS. Take log: log P = (log y - log z).log(yz) + (log z - log x).log(zx) + (log x - log y).log(xy). Since log(yz) = log y + log z: first term = (log y - log z)(log y + log z) = (log y)^2 - (log z)^2. Likewise the others give (log z)^2 - (log x)^2 and (log x)^2 - (log y)^2. Sum = 0. So log P = 0, P = 1. Proved. (Recovered from book p112 = PDF p137 OCR; the web index skips from (h) to (j).)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(i); book p112 = PDF p137 OCR conf 0.93 (web index omits it)

questions.knowledgeNote: Work from the inside out: sqrt(a^2) = a (a > 0), so each nested root collapses one layer until only log_a a = 1 is left.
questions.question: Q1(j). Prove that log_a sqrt(a sqrt(a sqrt(a^2))) = 1 (a > 0, a != 1).
questions.solution: Innermost: sqrt(a^2) = a. Then a.sqrt(a^2) = a.a = a^2, and sqrt(a^2) = a. Then a.(that) = a.a = a^2, and the outer sqrt gives a. So the whole radicand is a, and log_a a = 1. Proved. (Radicand cross-checked against book p112 OCR 'a/a/a^2' fragments and the web typed page.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q1(j); book p112 = PDF p137 + SciPiPupil Ex-4 typed page

questions.knowledgeNote: Set t = ab: the fraction 2t/(1+t^2) is built so its (1+t)/(1-t) form becomes a perfect square - the log doubles.
questions.question: Q2. If f(x) = log((1+x)/(1-x)) (-1 < x < 1), show that f(2ab/(1+a^2b^2)) = 2f(ab), where |ab| < 1. (The print orders the fraction as (1-x)/(1+x); the identity holds for either sign - both sides only change sign.)
questions.solution: Put t = ab (|t| < 1, so f is defined). LHS = f(2t/(1+t^2)) = log((1 + 2t/(1+t^2))/(1 - 2t/(1+t^2))) = log(((1+t^2+2t)/(1+t^2))/((1+t^2-2t)/(1+t^2))) = log((1+t)^2/(1-t)^2) = 2log((1+t)/(1-t)) = 2f(t) = 2f(ab). Shown. (Statement decoded from a 220-dpi band crop of PDF p137: 'f(x) = log(1-x/1+x), show ... = 2f(ab), 2ab/1+a^2b^2, |ab|<1'. Proved for the (1+x)/(1-x) form; with the flipped fraction both sides negate.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q2; book p112 = PDF p137, statement via 220-dpi band OCR

questions.knowledgeNote: Write each log in one base (natural log): xyz collapses to a single ratio and the claim becomes ordinary algebra.
questions.question: Q3. If x = log_{2a} a, y = log_{3a} 2a and z = log_{4a} 3a, prove that xyz + 1 = 2yz.
questions.solution: Write all three in natural logs: x = ln a/ln 2a, y = ln 2a/ln 3a, z = ln 3a/ln 4a. Then xyz = ln a/ln 4a and yz = ln 2a/ln 4a. Claim xyz + 1 = 2yz becomes (ln a + ln 4a)/ln 4a = 2ln 2a/ln 4a, i.e. ln(4a^2)... check: ln a + ln 4a = ln(4a^2)? No: ln a + ln 4a = ln(4a^2) is wrong; ln a + ln 4a = ln(4a^2/a)... recompute: need ln a + ln 4a = 2ln 2a = ln(4a^2). LHS = ln(a.4a) = ln(4a^2). RHS = ln((2a)^2) = ln(4a^2). Equal. Proved. (Valid for a > 0 with all bases positive and != 1.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q3; book p112 = PDF p137 OCR; change-of-base chain

questions.knowledgeNote: One common value k ties the three logs together; the weighted sum x.logx + y.logy + z.logz then telescopes to zero.
questions.question: Q4. If (log x)/(y-z) = (log y)/(z-x) = (log z)/(x-y), prove that x^x . y^y . z^z = 1.
questions.solution: Put each ratio = k: log x = k(y-z), log y = k(z-x), log z = k(x-y). Take log of P = x^x.y^y.z^z: log P = x.log x + y.log y + z.log z = k[x(y-z) + y(z-x) + z(x-y)] = k[xy - xz + yz - yx + zx - zy] = 0. So log P = 0 = log 1, hence P = 1. Proved.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Book Ex 2.4 Q4; book p112 = PDF p137 OCR '(logx)/(y-z)...prove x^x.y^y.z^z = 1'

questions.knowledgeNote: a^2 + b^2 = 2ab rearranges to (a-b)^2 = 0, forcing a = b; both sides then collapse to log a. APPENDIX: this is the guide-edition's Ex 2.4 Q2 (SciPiPupil typed page) - it does NOT occur in the 2075-print Ex 2.4 (book p112 = PDF p137); kept here so no web-indexed question is ever dropped.
questions.question: A1 (printing variant). If a^2 + b^2 = 2ab (a, b > 0), show that log((a+b)/2) = (log a + log b)/2.
questions.solution: Given a^2 + b^2 = 2ab, so a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = 0, i.e. (a-b)^2 = 0, hence a = b. LHS = log((a+a)/2) = log(2a/2) = log a. RHS = (log a + log a)/2 = log a. LHS = RHS. Shown.
questions.source: Guide-edition Ex 2.4 Q2 (SciPiPupil typed page; absent from 2075-print p112); proof via (a-b)^2 = 0

questions.knowledgeNote: A x B pairs every element of A with every element of B: |A x B| = |A| x |B| = 9 here.
questions.question: AQ1(a). Let A = {a, b, c} and B = {x, y, z}. Find A x B.
questions.solution: A x B = {(a,x),(a,y),(a,z),(b,x),(b,y),(b,z),(c,x),(c,y),(c,z)} - 9 ordered pairs.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q1; book pp112-113 = PDF pp137-140

questions.knowledgeNote: Break the function rule on purpose: give one input two outputs (or leave an input with none).
questions.question: AQ1(b)(i). Give a relation from A to B which is NOT a function.
questions.solution: E.g. R = {(a,x),(a,y),(b,z)}: the input 'a' has two images (x and y), so R is not a function. (Any relation where some element of A maps to two elements of B, or an element of A maps to nothing, works.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q1; book pp112-113 = PDF pp137-140

questions.knowledgeNote: A constant map (everything to one output) is the simplest function; a matching pairs all three.
questions.question: AQ1(b)(ii). Give relations from A to B which ARE functions.
questions.solution: E.g. R1 = {(a,x),(b,x),(c,x)} (constant function - every input maps to x) and R2 = {(a,x),(b,y),(c,z)} (one-one matching). In each, every element of A has exactly one image in B, so both are functions.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q1; book pp112-113 = PDF pp137-140

questions.knowledgeNote: Integers only: [1,6) contributes {1,2,3,4,5}. Evaluate piece by piece.
questions.question: AQ2. A function f is defined on the set of integers by f(x) = 1+x (1<=x<2), 2x-1 (2<=x<4), 3x-10 (4<=x<6). (a) Find the domain of f. (b) Find the range of f. (c) Is f one-one?
questions.solution: (a) Integer x with 1<=x<6: domain = {1,2,3,4,5}. (b) f(1) = 2; f(2) = 3, f(3) = 5; f(4) = 2, f(5) = 5. Range = {2,3,5}. (c) No: f(1) = f(4) = 2 with 1 != 4. Matches the printed Answers key (p115): 'Domain = {1,2,3,4,5), Range = {2,3,5); No'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q2; book pp112-113 = PDF pp137-140; every value matches printed Answers key p115 (PDF p142)

questions.knowledgeNote: Equal gaps (1,3,5,7...) mean linear: slope = step = 2.
questions.question: AQ3. Is f = {(1,1),(2,3),(3,5),(4,7)} a function? If it is defined by f(x) = ax + b, find a and b.
questions.solution: Yes: each x (1,2,3,4) occurs once, so f is a function. a(1)+b = 1 and a(2)+b = 3 give a = 2, b = -1. Check: f(3) = 5 and f(4) = 7. So a = 2, b = -1. Matches the printed Answers key (p115): 'a = 2, b = -1'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q3; book pp112-113 = PDF pp137-140; matches printed Answers key p115 (PDF p142)

questions.knowledgeNote: Read each arrow diagram three ways: every input hit exactly once (function?), outputs covering B (onto?), distinct outputs (one-one?).
questions.question: AQ4. Three print arrow diagrams are given. State whether each is (i) one-one and onto, (ii) an into function, (iii) an onto-only function; show by diagram and give the domain and range of each.
questions.solution: Method (diagrams are print figures - pending physical-book read): (i) one-one and onto = every element of A maps to a distinct element of B and every element of B is hit (bijective, sets match in size); (ii) into = some element of B is never hit (range is a proper subset of B); (iii) onto-only = every element of B is hit but two inputs share an output (many-one). Domain = the full left set; range = the hit elements of B in each diagram. FLAGGED: exact sets pending figure read.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q4; book p113 = PDF pp138-140; statements are print figures

questions.knowledgeNote: Squares forget signs: (-1)^2 = 1^2 kills one-one immediately.
questions.question: AQ5 (T.U. 2049). Let A = {-1,-2,0,1,2} and f:A->B be defined by f(x) = x^2/2. Find the range of f. Is the function one-one?
questions.solution: f(-1) = 1/2, f(-2) = 2, f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1/2, f(2) = 2. Range = {0, 1/2, 2}. Not one-one: f(-1) = f(1) = 1/2 with -1 != 1. Matches the printed Answers key (p115): 'Range = {0,1/2,2}, No'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q5 (T.U. 2049); book p113 = PDF pp138-140; matches printed Answers key p115 (PDF p142)

questions.knowledgeNote: Six inputs, six distinct outputs: one-one holds, but B has a seventh member (1) nobody hits - so 'both' fails.
questions.question: AQ6 (T.U. 2050, 2058S). Let f:A->B be defined by f(x) = (x-1)/(x+2) with A = {-1,0,1,2,3,4} and B = {-2,1,-1/2,0,1/2,1/4,2/5}. Find the range of f. Is f one-one and onto both? If not, how can it be made so?
questions.solution: f(-1) = -2, f(0) = -1/2, f(1) = 0, f(2) = 1/4, f(3) = 2/5, f(4) = 1/2. Range = {-2,-1/2,0,1/4,2/5,1/2}. All six outputs are distinct, so f is one-one; but 1 in B is never hit, so f is not onto (hence not both). Fix: replace B by the range (drop 1); then f:A->range is one-one and onto. Matches the printed Answers key (p115).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q6 (T.U. 2050, 2058S); book p113 = PDF pp138-140; matches printed Answers key p115 (PDF p142)

questions.knowledgeNote: The print renders f(x) = x/(x+2) (OCR reads it as '(2+x)/x'; the printed Answers key forces x/(x+2) - every value matches).
questions.question: AQ7 (T.U. 2051). Let f:A->B be defined by f(x) = x/(x+2) with A = {-1,0,1,2,3,4} and B = {-1,0,1,1/3,1/2,3/5,2/3}. Find the range of f. Is f one-one and onto both? If not, how can it be made so?
questions.solution: f(-1) = -1, f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1/3, f(2) = 1/2, f(3) = 3/5, f(4) = 2/3. Range = {-1,0,1/3,1/2,3/5,2/3}. All six distinct: one-one yes; 1 in B is never hit: onto no (so not both). Fix: replace B by the range (drop 1); then f is one-one and onto. Matches the printed Answers key (p115). (Print-form note: the scan renders the rule ambiguously; x/(x+2) is adopted because it reproduces the key exactly.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q7 (T.U. 2051); book p113 = PDF pp138-140; rule adopted via printed Answers key p115 (PDF p142)

questions.knowledgeNote: Linear with nonzero slope is always bijective on Q: solve y = 3x+5 for x to exhibit the pre-image of every y.
questions.question: AQ8. Let Q be the set of all rational numbers. Show that f:Q->Q with f(x) = 3x + 5 is one-one and onto. (The book prints a full model solution.)
questions.solution: One-one: let x1, x2 in Q with f(x1) = f(x2): 3x1+5 = 3x2+5 gives 3x1 = 3x2, so x1 = x2. Onto: for each y in Q, x = (y-5)/3 is in Q and f(x) = y. Hence f is one-one and onto. (Reproduces the book's printed solution, book p113.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q8; book p113 = PDF pp138-140 (solution printed in book)

questions.knowledgeNote: On [-2,0] every number is non-positive, so x1^2 = x2^2 forces x1 = x2 - the sign ambiguity of squares disappears.
questions.question: AQ9(a). Show that f:[-2,0]->R defined by f(x) = x^2 is one-one but not onto.
questions.solution: One-one: let x1, x2 in [-2,0] with x1^2 = x2^2. Then |x1| = |x2|; since both are <= 0, x1 = -|x1| = -|x2| = x2. So f is one-one. Not onto: f(x) = x^2 >= 0 always (range is [0,4]), so e.g. -1 in R has no pre-image. Hence one-one but not onto.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q9(a); book p114 = PDF p141 OCR conf 0.94

questions.knowledgeNote: Read the codomain carefully: |x| on [0,inf) never goes negative, so 'onto R' as printed is FALSE - the intended codomain is [0,inf).
questions.question: AQ9(b). Let f:[0,inf)->R be defined by f(x) = |x|. The print asks to 'show it is one-one and onto' - assess honestly.
questions.solution: One-one: on [0,inf), |x| = x, so f(x1) = f(x2) gives x1 = x2 - one-one holds. Onto R FAILS: range is [0,inf), so e.g. -1 in R has no pre-image. VERDICT: one-one yes, onto R no (print overstates). With the corrected codomain [0,inf), f(x) = x is bijective. FLAGGED as a print tension.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q9(b); book p114 = PDF p141 OCR; onto-R disproved, corrected codomain given

questions.knowledgeNote: f(f(x)) = x makes a function its own inverse - bijectivity follows for free.
questions.question: AQ10. Let R0 be the set of non-zero real numbers and f:R0->R0 be defined by f(x) = 1/x. Show that f is one-one and onto.
questions.solution: One-one: 1/x1 = 1/x2 gives x1 = x2 (multiply by x1.x2 != 0). Onto: for each y in R0, x = 1/y is in R0 and f(x) = y. So f is one-one and onto (indeed f(f(x)) = x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q10; book p114 = PDF p141 OCR conf 0.94

questions.knowledgeNote: Swap x and y, solve for y: the inverse undoes each operation in reverse order.
questions.question: AQ11. Define an inverse of a function. What condition makes a function have its inverse? Let f:R->R be defined by f(x) = 2x - 4. Find f^-1 and show that f(f^-1(x)) = f^-1(f(x)) = x.
questions.solution: A function has an inverse iff it is one-one and onto (bijective); f^-1 reverses every arrow. Here y = 2x - 4; swapping roles x = 2y - 4 gives y = (x+4)/2, so f^-1(x) = (x+4)/2 (the book prints this hint). Check: f(f^-1(x)) = 2.(x+4)/2 - 4 = x; f^-1(f(x)) = ((2x-4)+4)/2 = x.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q11; book p114 = PDF p141 OCR (hint printed in book)

questions.knowledgeNote: Odd powers preserve order: cubes keep distinct numbers distinct and hit every real.
questions.question: AQ12 (T.U. 2053). Let f:R->R be defined by f(x) = x^3. Show that f is one-one and onto. Hence find f^-1.
questions.solution: One-one: x1^3 = x2^3 gives (taking real cube roots) x1 = x2. Onto: for each y in R, x = cubert(y) is real with f(x) = y. Hence bijective; f^-1(x) = cubert(x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q12 (T.U. 2053); book p114 = PDF p141 OCR

questions.knowledgeNote: The inverse exists only if a != 0 (a = 0 makes f constant) - the book's 'a, b real' needs this hypothesis added.
questions.question: AQ13. Let f:R->R be defined by f(x) = ax + b (a, b real). Find f^-1 and show that f(f^-1(x)) = f^-1(f(x)) = x.
questions.solution: Requires a != 0 (else f is constant, not bijective - hypothesis added). y = ax + b gives x = ay + b, so y = (x-b)/a: f^-1(x) = (x-b)/a. Check: f(f^-1(x)) = a.(x-b)/a + b = x; f^-1(f(x)) = ((ax+b)-b)/a = x.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q13; book p114 = PDF p141 OCR; a != 0 hypothesis added

questions.knowledgeNote: Order matters in composition: doubling after adding 1 differs from adding 1 after doubling.
questions.question: AQ14 (HSEB 2054). Let f:R->R be defined by f(x) = 2x and g:R->R by g(x) = x + 1. Find (fog)(x) and (gof)(x). Are they one-one?
questions.solution: (fog)(x) = f(x+1) = 2x + 2. (gof)(x) = g(2x) = 2x + 1. Both are non-zero-slope linears, hence one-one: yes and yes. Matches the printed Answers key (p115): '2x+2, 2x+1; yes'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q14 (HSEB 2054); book p114 = PDF p141 OCR; matches printed Answers key p115 (PDF p142)

questions.knowledgeNote: Four compositions, one pair: expand each and match against the key - the key itself pins down f.
questions.question: AQ15. With f(x) = 2x^2 - 3 and g(x) = 3x + 2 determine (i) (fog)(x), (ii) (gof)(x), (iii) (fof)(x), (iv) (gog)(x). (f is cut off in the scan; 2x^2-3 is forced by the printed answers.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q15; book p114 = PDF p141 OCR (f reconstructed); all four match printed Answers key p115 (PDF p142)

questions.knowledgeNote: p AND (NOT p) is always false - negating it is always true. That is the whole proof.
questions.question: AQ16(a). Prove that ~(p ^ (~p)) is a tautology.
questions.solution: Truth table: p=T: ~p=F, p^(~p)=F, ~(F)=T. p=F: ~p=T, p^(~p)=F, ~(F)=T. All-true column: tautology. Matches the printed key table (p115-116).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q16(a); book pp114-115 = PDF pp141-142; matches printed key table

questions.knowledgeNote: p OR (NOT p) is always true - negating it is always false.
questions.question: AQ16(b). Prove that ~(p v (~p)) is a contradiction.
questions.solution: Truth table: p=T: ~p=F, p v (~p)=T, ~(T)=F. p=F: ~p=T, p v (~p)=T, ~(T)=F. All-false column: contradiction. Matches the printed key table.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q16(b); book pp114-115 = PDF pp141-142; matches printed key table

questions.knowledgeNote: If p is false, ~p is true and already makes the big OR true; if p is true, p itself does.
questions.question: AQ16(c). Prove that (p v q) v (~p) is a tautology.
questions.solution: Truth table over p,q: whenever p=T, (p v q)=T so the whole is T; whenever p=F, ~p=T so the whole is T. All four rows true: tautology. Matches the printed key table.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q16(c); book pp114-115 = PDF pp141-142; matches printed key table

questions.knowledgeNote: (~q) AND q can never both hold - the whole conjunction dies whatever p is.
questions.question: AQ16(d). Prove that ((~q) ^ p) ^ q is a contradiction. (Print header garbled as '((~q)~p)q'; the AND-AND reading is forced by the all-false key table.)
questions.solution: Truth table: the factor (~q)^q is F in every row (q=T: ~q=F; q=F: q=F), so ((~q)^p)^q is F in all four rows: contradiction. Matches the printed key table (all-false column, p116). FLAGGED: connective reading adopted via key; pending physical-book check.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q16(d); book pp114-115 = PDF pp141-142; reading via printed key table (all false)

questions.knowledgeNote: Solve y = 2x/(x-1) for x: the forbidden denominator x = 1 maps exactly to the forbidden value y = 2.
questions.question: AQ17. If f:R-{1}->R-{2} is defined by f(x) = 2x/(x-1), prove that f is one-one and onto.
questions.solution: One-one: 2x1/(x1-1) = 2x2/(x2-1) gives x1(x2-1) = x2(x1-1), i.e. x1 = x2. Onto: for y != 2, y = 2x/(x-1) gives x(y-2) = y... solve: yx - y = 2x, x(y-2) = y, x = y/(y-2) (defined since y != 2); and x != 1 since y/(y-2) = 1 would give y = y-2, impossible. So every y in R-{2} has pre-image y/(y-2) in R-{1}: onto.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q17; book p115 = PDF p142 OCR (two consistent reads)

questions.knowledgeNote: Modus tollens: being an integer is necessary for being a natural number, so failing it rules out the conclusion.
questions.question: AQ18. Is the following argument valid? All natural numbers are integers. x is not an integer. Therefore, x is not a natural number.
questions.solution: Valid (modus tollens). Form: P -> Q (natural -> integer); ~Q (x not integer); therefore ~P (x not natural). Denying the consequent necessarily denies the antecedent.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q18; book p115 = PDF p142 OCR

questions.knowledgeNote: 'Some' does not cover all: Prakash may sit in the non-smart part of the class.
questions.question: AQ19. Is the following argument valid? Some students of class XI are smart. Prakash is a student of class XI. Therefore, Prakash is smart.
questions.solution: Invalid. 'Some students are smart' only guarantees a smart subset; Prakash may belong to the complementary (non-smart) subset. The middle term is undistributed - no conclusion about Prakash follows.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q19; book p115 = PDF p142 OCR

questions.knowledgeNote: Strictly increasing (derivative 6x^2 >= 0, zero only at a point) means injective; odd-degree means surjective.
questions.question: AQ20. Prove that f:R->R defined by f(x) = 2x^3 - 1 is one-one and onto. Also find f^-1.
questions.solution: One-one: 2x1^3-1 = 2x2^3-1 gives x1^3 = x2^3, so x1 = x2 (real cube roots unique). Onto: for each y, x = cubert((y+1)/2) is real with f(x) = y. Inverse: y = 2x^3-1 gives x = ((y+1)/2)^(1/3), so f^-1(x) = ((x+1)/2)^(1/3). Matches the printed Answers key (p116): '((x+1)/2)^1/3'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q20; book p115 = PDF p142 OCR; matches printed Answers key p116 (PDF p143, root glyph confirmed)

questions.knowledgeNote: Compute both orders and compare: (4x-1)^3+2 versus 4x^3+7 are nowhere equal.
questions.question: AQ21 [HSEB 2065]. If f,g:R->R are defined by f(x) = x^3 + 2 and g(x) = 4x - 1, find (fog)(x) and (gof)(x) and show that the composite functions are not commutative.
questions.solution: (fog)(x) = f(4x-1) = (4x-1)^3 + 2 = 64x^3-48x^2+12x+1. (gof)(x) = g(x^3+2) = 4(x^3+2)-1 = 4x^3+7. They differ (e.g. at x=0: 1 vs 7), so fog != gof: not commutative. Matches the printed Answers key (p116): 'No'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q21 [HSEB 2065]; book p115 = PDF pp141-142 (ask confirmed by 350-dpi crop); matches key

questions.knowledgeNote: Cubes preserve order, so both composites inherit one-one-ness from f and g.
questions.question: AQ22 [HSEB 2061]. From f(x) = 2x^3 - 3 and g(x) = 3x + 2 (x in R), determine (fog)(x) and (gof)(x). Are they one-one?
questions.solution: (fog)(x) = 2(3x+2)^3 - 3 = 54x^3+108x^2+72x+13. (gof)(x) = 3(2x^3-3) + 2 = 6x^3-7. One-one: (fog)'(x) = 18(3x+2)^2 >= 0 with equality only at x = -2/3, so strictly increasing: yes. (gof)'(x) = 18x^2 >= 0 with equality only at 0, so strictly increasing: yes.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q22 [HSEB 2061]; book p115 = PDF p141 (statement confirmed by 350-dpi line image)

questions.knowledgeNote: Read the tiny -1s: the first ask inverts f, the second inverts g. Each answer checks by direct substitution.
questions.question: AQ23. If f(x) = x^3 - 1 and g(x) = 2x - 3, compute (f^-1 o g)(2) and (f o g^-1)(1). (Notation read from a 350-dpi line image; OCR alone merges the -1s.)
questions.solution: f^-1(x) = cubert(x+1); g^-1(x) = (x+3)/2. (f^-1 o g)(2) = f^-1(g(2)) = f^-1(1) = cubert(2) (since (cubert2)^3-1 = 1: verified). (f o g^-1)(1) = f(g^-1(1)) = f(2) = 7 (verified). Exact answers: cubert(2) and 7. NOTE: the printed key (p116) shows '23. 2, 7' - the '2' is almost certainly a dropped cube-root sign (cubert(2)), since the key's Q20 line proves the compositor prints ^{1/3}; pending physical-book confirmation.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q23; book p115 = PDF p141 (statement via 350-dpi image read); key p116 checked visually

questions.knowledgeNote: Evaluate inside-out: +1, then exponential, then log - the natural log exactly undoes e^.
questions.question: AQ24. If f,g,h:R->R are defined by f(x) = x + 1, g(x) = e^x and h(x) = log x, find the value of (h o (g o f))(1).
questions.solution: f(1) = 2; g(2) = e^2; h(e^2) = log(e^2) = 2 (natural log). So (h o (g o f))(1) = 2. Matches the printed Answers key (p116): '24. 2'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.2 Additional Q24; book p115 = PDF p141 OCR; matches printed Answers key p116 (PDF p143)
