questions.knowledgeNote: Even x even = even: (-x)sin(-x) = (-x)(-sinx) = x sinx, and cos(-x) = cosx.
questions.question: Q1(a). Examine whether f(x) = x sin x + cos x is even, odd or neither.
questions.solution: f(-x) = (-x)sin(-x) + cos(-x) = (-x)(-sin x) + cos x = x sin x + cos x = f(x). Even. Matches the printed Answers key (p129): 'a) Even'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q1(a); book p128 = PDF p155 (statement via 200-dpi image read); matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Even + odd (both present, neither zero) can never be purely even or purely odd.
questions.question: Q1(b). Examine whether f(x) = 5x^2 + sin x is even, odd or neither.
questions.solution: f(-x) = 5x^2 - sin x. This equals neither f(x) (= 5x^2 + sin x) nor -f(x) (= -5x^2 - sin x) (e.g. at x = pi/2: f = 5pi^2/4+1 vs f(-pi/2) = 5pi^2/4-1). Neither. Matches the printed Answers key: 'b) Neither'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q1(b); book p128 = PDF p155; matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: x appears only as x^2, so -x changes nothing: automatically even.
questions.question: Q1(c). Examine whether f(x) = sqrt(1+x^2) - sqrt(1-x^2) is even, odd or neither.
questions.solution: f(-x) = sqrt(1+(-x)^2) - sqrt(1-(-x)^2) = sqrt(1+x^2) - sqrt(1-x^2) = f(x). Even. Matches the printed Answers key: 'c) Even'. (The scan merges Q1(d)'s fraction bar into this line; (c) is the numerator alone - confirmed by 200-dpi image read.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q1(c); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: sqrt(1-x) and sqrt(1+x) swap under x -> -x, flipping the overall sign.
questions.question: Q1(d). Examine whether f(x) = sqrt(1+x) - sqrt(1-x) (domain [-1,1]) is even, odd or neither.
questions.solution: f(-x) = sqrt(1-x) - sqrt(1+x) = -f(x). Odd. (The printed key's d/e/f letters are OCR-garbled; the parity follows decisively from substitution. Domain [-1,1] is symmetric, so the test is valid.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q1(d); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); parity by substitution

questions.knowledgeNote: a^x and a^(-x) swap under x -> -x: their difference negates.
questions.question: Q1(e). Examine whether f(x) = 10^x - 10^(-x) is even, odd or neither.
questions.solution: f(-x) = 10^(-x) - 10^x = -f(x). Odd. (Key letters garbled in scan; substitution is decisive.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q1(e); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); parity by substitution

questions.knowledgeNote: tanh(-x) = -tanh x: numerator and denominator swap roles up to a sign.
questions.question: Q1(f). Examine whether f(x) = (e^x - e^(-x))/(e^x + e^(-x)) is even, odd or neither.
questions.solution: f(-x) = (e^(-x) - e^x)/(e^(-x) + e^x) = -(e^x - e^(-x))/(e^x + e^(-x)) = -f(x). Odd (this is tanh x). (Key letters garbled in scan; substitution is decisive.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q1(f); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); parity by substitution

questions.knowledgeNote: Only even powers: f(-x) = f(x) term by term - mirror symmetry in the y-axis.
questions.question: Q2(a). Test the symmetricity of f(x) = x^4 + 3x^2 + 1.
questions.solution: f(-x) = x^4 + 3x^2 + 1 = f(x): symmetric about the y-axis. Matches the printed Answers key: 'a) Symmetric about y-axis'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q2(a); book p128 = PDF p155; matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: cos is even and the window [-pi/2, pi/2] is symmetric about 0, so the mirror symmetry survives the restriction.
questions.question: Q2(b). Test the symmetricity of f(x) = cos x (-pi/2 <= x <= pi/2).
questions.solution: cos(-x) = cos x on the symmetric domain: symmetric about the y-axis. Matches the printed Answers key: 'b) Symmetric about y-axis'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q2(b); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Odd powers only: every term flips sign - half-turn symmetry about the origin.
questions.question: Q2(c). Test the symmetricity of f(x) = x^3 - x.
questions.solution: f(-x) = -x^3 + x = -f(x): symmetric about the origin. Matches the printed Answers key: 'c) Symmetric about origin'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q2(c); book p128 = PDF p155; matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: x appears only as x^2 under the root: f(-x) = f(x) on the symmetric domain [-2,2].
questions.question: Q2(d). Test the symmetricity of f(x) = sqrt(4-x^2).
questions.solution: f(-x) = sqrt(4-x^2) = f(x): symmetric about the y-axis (upper half of the circle x^2+y^2 = 4). Matches the printed Answers key: 'd) Symmetric about y-axis'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q2(d); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: sin(2(x+pi)) = sin(2x+2pi) = sin 2x: doubling the speed halves the period.
questions.question: Q3(a). Test the periodicity of f(x) = sin 2x and find its period.
questions.solution: f(x+pi) = sin(2x+2pi) = sin 2x = f(x), and no smaller positive shift works (2x must advance by a full 2pi). Periodic with period pi. Matches the printed Answers key: 'a) Periodic, pi'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q3(a); book p128 = PDF p155; matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: cos(u+2pi) = cos u: set u = pi.x and solve pi(x+T) = pi.x+2pi for T.
questions.question: Q3(b). Test the periodicity of f(x) = cos(pi x) and find its period.
questions.solution: f(x+2) = cos(pi x + 2pi) = cos(pi x) = f(x), and 2 is minimal (needs pi.T = 2pi). Periodic with period 2. Matches the printed Answers key: 'b) Periodic, 2'. (The bare '2' in the key is complete - not truncated.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q3(b); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read: cos pi x); matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: tan repeats every pi in its argument: (x+T)/4 = x/4+pi gives T = 4pi.
questions.question: Q3(c). Test the periodicity of f(x) = tan(x/4) and find its period.
questions.solution: f(x+4pi) = tan(x/4 + pi) = tan(x/4) = f(x), minimal since tan's own period is pi. Periodic with period 4pi. Matches the printed Answers key: 'c) Periodic, 4pi'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q3(c); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read: tan x/4); matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: a > 0 stretches/compresses the wave: the argument must still advance by 2pi, so T = 2pi/a.
questions.question: Q3(d). Test the periodicity of f(x) = sin(ax+b) (a > 0) and find its period.
questions.solution: f(x+T) = sin(a(x+T)+b) = sin(ax+b+aT); this equals sin(ax+b) for all x iff aT = 2pi, i.e. T = 2pi/a (minimal positive). Periodic with period 2pi/a. NOTE: the key OCR reads 'd) Periodic, 2pi' - the '/a' was very likely dropped in print/OCR; 2pi/a is the correct general form (it gives 2pi only for a = 1).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q3(d); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read: sin(ax+b), a > 0); '/a' flagged vs key OCR

questions.knowledgeNote: sin and cos share period 2pi, so their sum cannot repeat any faster.
questions.question: Q3(e). Test the periodicity of f(x) = sin x + cos x and find its period.
questions.solution: f(x) = sqrt(2) sin(x+pi/4), so f(x+2pi) = f(x); any smaller shift breaks at least one of sin/cos. Periodic with period 2pi. Matches the printed Answers key: 'e) Periodic, 2pi'.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q3(e); book p128 = PDF p155; matches printed key

questions.knowledgeNote: Positive slope preserves order: x1 > x2 implies 5x1 > 5x2.
questions.question: Q4(a). Prove that f(x) = 3 + 5x is increasing for all x in R.
questions.solution: Let x1 > x2. Then 5x1 > 5x2 (multiplying by positive 5), so 3+5x1 > 3+5x2, i.e. f(x1) > f(x2). Hence f is (strictly) increasing on R.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q4(a); book p128 = PDF p155

questions.knowledgeNote: Negative slope reverses order: multiplying by -4 flips the inequality.
questions.question: Q4(b). Prove that f(x) = 5 - 4x is decreasing for all x in R.
questions.solution: Let x1 > x2. Then -4x1 < -4x2 (multiplying by negative -4 flips), so 5-4x1 < 5-4x2, i.e. f(x1) < f(x2). Hence f is (strictly) decreasing on R.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q4(b); book p128 = PDF p155

questions.knowledgeNote: Straight line: two intercepts fix it - (2/3,0) on the x-axis, (0,-2) on the y-axis.
questions.question: Q5(a). Draw the graph of y = 3x - 2.
questions.solution: Intercepts: y = 0 gives x = 2/3; x = 0 gives y = -2. Join (2/3,0) and (0,-2) with a straight line (slope 3 > 0, rising). Cross-checked against the printed figure (book p130 = PDF p157): intercepts (2/3,0), (0,-2) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(a); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); figure p130 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Complete the square: (x+1)^2+2 >= 2 - vertex (-1,2), never touches the x-axis.
questions.question: Q5(b). Draw the graph of y = x^2 + 2x + 3.
questions.solution: y = (x+1)^2 + 2: vertex (-1,2) (minimum, since leading coefficient positive); y-intercept (0,3); discriminant 4-12 < 0 so no x-intercepts; symmetric about x = -1. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p130): vertex (-1,2) and (0,3) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(b); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); figure p130 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Downward parabola: roots at x = 1 and x = 3 (factor -(x-1)(x-3)), peak midway at (2,1).
questions.question: Q5(c). Draw the graph of y = -x^2 + 4x - 3.
questions.solution: y = -(x-1)(x-3): x-intercepts (1,0),(3,0); vertex at x = 2, y = 1 (maximum); y-intercept (0,-3); symmetric about x = 2. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p130): (1,0),(3,0) and vertex (2,1) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(c); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); figure p130 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Rectangular hyperbola: axes are the asymptotes - the curve lives in quadrants I and III, never touching x = 0 or y = 0.
questions.question: Q5(d). Draw the graph of y = 1/x.
questions.solution: Domain x != 0; vertical asymptote x = 0, horizontal asymptote y = 0; passes through (1,1),(-1,-1); quadrant I branch decreasing from +inf to 0, quadrant III branch decreasing from 0 to -inf; symmetric about the origin (odd). Standard figure (p130 set).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(d); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read: y = 1/x)

questions.knowledgeNote: Shift 1/x right by 3: the vertical asymptote moves to x = 3, point (4,1) anchors the right branch.
questions.question: Q5(e). Draw the graph of y = 1/(x-3).
questions.solution: Domain x != 3; vertical asymptote x = 3, horizontal asymptote y = 0; passes through (4,1),(2,-1); same two-branch shape as 1/x translated 3 units right. Standard figure (p130 set).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(e); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read: y = 1/(x-3))

questions.knowledgeNote: Factor first: (x^2-1)/(x-1) = x+1 for x != 1 - a straight line with a single hole at (1,2).
questions.question: Q5(f). Draw the graph of y = (x^2-1)/(x-1).
questions.solution: For x != 1, y = (x-1)(x+1)/(x-1) = x+1: the line through (0,1) with slope 1, EXCEPT the hole at x = 1, i.e. missing point (1,2) (limit value). Mark (1,2) with an open circle. Standard figure (p130-131 set).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(f); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); hole at (1,2) stressed

questions.knowledgeNote: Factored cubic: roots 1,2,3 read straight off; y-intercept (-1)(-2)(-3) = -6; positive leading coefficient: down-left to up-right.
questions.question: Q5(g). Draw the graph of f(x) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3).
questions.solution: x-intercepts (1,0),(2,0),(3,0); y-intercept (0,-6); as x -> -inf, f -> -inf; as x -> +inf, f -> +inf; one local max in (1,2), one local min in (2,3). Cross-checked against the printed figure (p130-131): (2,0) and (0,-6) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(g); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read); figure labels (2,0),(0,-6) verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Double root at 0: the curve touches the x-axis and turns back, then crosses at x = 2.
questions.question: Q5(h). Draw the graph of y = x^2(x-2).
questions.solution: x-intercepts: 0 (double - touches, does not cross) and 2 (simple - crosses); y-intercept (0,0); as x -> -inf, y -> -inf; as x -> +inf, y -> +inf; falls from 0 to a local min in (0,2), then rises through (2,0). Standard figure (p131 set).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q5(h); book p128 = PDF p155 (image read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Base 2, flipped exponent: mirror of 2^x in the y-axis - (1,1/2) is the anchor.
questions.question: Q6(a). Draw the graph of y = 2^(-x).
questions.solution: = (1/2)^x: passes through (0,1),(1,1/2),(-1,2); horizontal asymptote y = 0 (as x -> +inf); strictly decreasing; mirror of y = 2^x. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p131): (0,1),(1,1/2) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(a); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read: 2^(-x)); figure p131 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Classic growth curve through (0,1) and (1,3), hugging y = 0 on the left.
questions.question: Q6(b). Draw the graph of y = 3^x.
questions.solution: Passes through (0,1),(1,3),(-1,1/3); horizontal asymptote y = 0 as x -> -inf; strictly increasing. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p131): (0,1) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(b); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read: 3^x); figure p131 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Base 1/3 < 1: decay curve, mirror of 3^x - (1,1/3) is the anchor.
questions.question: Q6(c). Draw the graph of y = (1/3)^x.
questions.solution: Passes through (0,1),(1,1/3),(-1,3); horizontal asymptote y = 0 as x -> +inf; strictly decreasing. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p131): (0,1),(1,1/3) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(c); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p131 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Inverse of 3^x: swap the axes - (1,0) and (3,1) anchor it, x = 0 is the asymptote.
questions.question: Q6(d). Draw the graph of y = log_3 x.
questions.solution: Domain x > 0; vertical asymptote x = 0; passes through (1,0),(3,1); strictly increasing; reflection of y = 3^x in y = x. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p131): (1,0),(3,1) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(d); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read: log_3 x); figure p131 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Common log: same shape as log_3 x, stretched - (10,1) is the anchor.
questions.question: Q6(e). Draw the graph of y = log_10 x.
questions.solution: Domain x > 0; vertical asymptote x = 0; passes through (1,0),(10,1); strictly increasing. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p131): (1,0),(10,1) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(e); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p131 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: One full wave on [0,2pi]: start (0,1), zeros at pi/2 and 3pi/2, trough (pi,-1), end (2pi,1).
questions.question: Q6(f). Draw the graph of y = cos x (0 <= x <= 2pi).
questions.solution: Key points: (0,1),(pi/2,0),(pi,-1),(3pi/2,0),(2pi,1); amplitude 1, period 2pi; symmetric about x = pi on this window. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p131): (0,1),(2pi,1) and zeros labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(f); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p131 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Symmetric wave through the origin: zeros at -pi, 0, pi; peak (pi/2,1), trough (-pi/2,-1).
questions.question: Q6(g). Draw the graph of y = sin x (-pi <= x <= pi).
questions.solution: Key points: (-pi,0),(-pi/2,-1),(0,0),(pi/2,1),(pi,0); amplitude 1; odd symmetry about the origin. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p131): (0,0),(pi,0),(pi/2,0-label set) consistent.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(g); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p131 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Branches between vertical asymptotes at -pi/2 and pi/2: rises from -inf to +inf through (0,0).
questions.question: Q6(h). Draw the graph of y = tan x (-pi < x < pi).
questions.solution: Vertical asymptotes x = +-pi/2 (also x = +-pi at the window edge); passes through (0,0),(pi/4,1),(-pi/4,-1); strictly increasing on each branch (-pi/2,pi/2); odd symmetry. (Endpoints -pi, pi excluded: tan undefined at +-pi/2 inside.) Standard figure (p131-132 set).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q6(h); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read)

questions.knowledgeNote: y = (x-2)^2 is y = x^2 shifted 2 right: vertex moves (0,0) -> (2,0).
questions.question: Q7(a)(i). Sketch y = x^2 and hence draw y = (x-2)^2.
questions.solution: Base: parabola vertex (0,0), through (1,1),(-1,1). Replace x by x-2: every point shifts 2 right: vertex (2,0), through (3,1),(1,1). Cross-checked against the printed figure (p132): (2,0) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q7(a)(i); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p132 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: x^2-6x+5 = (x-3)^2-4: shift right 3, down 4 - roots factor as (x-1)(x-5).
questions.question: Q7(a)(ii). Using y = x^2, draw y = x^2 - 6x + 5.
questions.solution: y = (x-3)^2 - 4: vertex (3,-4); x-intercepts from (x-1)(x-5): (1,0),(5,0); y-intercept (0,5). I.e. y = x^2 shifted 3 right and 4 down. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p132): (1,0),(5,0) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q7(a)(ii); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p132 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: x -> -x mirrors left-right: the vertex jumps from (1,-4) to (-1,-4), roots from {3,-1}... check: x^2-2x-3 = (x-3)(x+1) roots 3,-1; mirrored roots -3,1 = x^2+2x-3.
questions.question: Q7(b). Sketch y = x^2 - 2x - 3 and hence draw y = x^2 + 2x - 3.
questions.solution: Base: vertex (1,-4) (x = 1), roots (3,0),(-1,0), y-intercept (0,-3). Replace x by -x (y-axis reflection): vertex (-1,-4), roots (-3,0),(1,0), same y-intercept (0,-3): y = x^2+2x-3. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p132): (1,-4) and (-1,-4) labelled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q7(b); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p132 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Right 1, down 2: the inflection point (0,0) of x^3 moves to (1,-2).
questions.question: Q7(c). Sketch y = x^3 and hence draw y = (x-1)^3 - 2.
questions.solution: Base: cubic through (-1,-1),(0,0),(1,1). Shift 1 right, 2 down: inflection (1,-2); through (2,-1),(0,-3); root at x = 1+cuberoot(2) approx 2.26. Standard figure (p132 set).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q7(c); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read)

questions.knowledgeNote: y -> -y flips top-bottom: roots stay, the hump at (1/2,1/4) becomes a dip at (1/2,-1/4).
questions.question: Q7(d). Sketch y = x - x^2 and hence draw y = -(x-x^2) = -x + x^2.
questions.solution: Base: roots (0,0),(1,0), vertex (1/2,1/4) (maximum). Reflect in the x-axis: roots unchanged, vertex (1/2,-1/4) (minimum): y = -x+x^2. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p132): (0,0),(1,0),(1/2,...) and y = -2 marker consistent.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q7(d); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p132 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: Discriminant 1-8 < 0: no real roots - the whole parabola floats above the x-axis, lowest at (1/2,7/4).
questions.question: Q8(a). Sketch y = x^2 - x + 2.
questions.solution: y = (x-1/2)^2 + 7/4: vertex (1/2,7/4) (minimum); y-intercept (0,2); discriminant (-1)^2-8 = -7 < 0 so no x-intercepts. Cross-checked against the printed figure (p132): vertex (1/2,7/4) labelled with y = x^2-x+2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q8(a); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read); figure p132 verified

questions.knowledgeNote: One real root near x = 1.7 (f(1) = -3, f(2) = 3): down-left to up-right with two turning points.
questions.question: Q8(b). Sketch y = x^3 - x - 3.
questions.solution: y-intercept (0,-3); f(1) = -3, f(2) = 3 so one real root in (1,2) (approx 1.67); f'(x) = 3x^2-1: local max at x = -1/sqrt(3) (y approx -2.61), local min at x = 1/sqrt(3) (y approx -3.39); as x -> -inf, y -> -inf; as x -> +inf, y -> +inf. Standard figure (p132 set).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.3 Ex 3.1 Q8(b); book p129 = PDF p156 (image read)

questions.knowledgeNote: AP gives ratio 1 (written x/x), GP gives x/y via y^2 = xz, HP gives x/z via y = 2xz/(x+z): one computation, three readings.
questions.question: Q1(a). Prove that x, y, z are in A.P., G.P. or H.P. according as (x-y)/(y-z) = x/x or x/y or x/z respectively.
questions.solution: A.P.: (x-y)/(y-z) = x/x = 1 gives x-y = y-z, i.e. 2y = x+z, the A.P. condition. G.P.: (x-y)/(y-z) = x/y gives xy-y^2 = xy-xz, i.e. y^2 = xz, the G.P. condition. H.P.: (x-y)/(y-z) = x/z gives xz-yz = xy-xz, i.e. 2xz = y(x+z), so y = 2xz/(x+z), the H.P. condition. Each step reverses, so the three cases are proved.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q1(a); book p214 = PDF p241 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Clear the HP condition 2/y = 2/(x+y) + 2/(y+z): everything cancels except xz = y^2.
questions.question: Q1(b). If (x+y)/2, y and (y+z)/2 are in H.P., show that x, y, z are in G.P.
questions.solution: The three means are in H.P., so 2/y = 1/((x+y)/2) + 1/((y+z)/2) = 2/(x+y) + 2/(y+z). Dividing by 2: 1/y = (y+z+x+y)/((x+y)(y+z)) = (x+z+2y)/((x+y)(y+z)). Cross-multiplying: (x+y)(y+z) = y(x+z+2y), i.e. xy+xz+y^2+yz = xy+xz+2y^2, so y^2 = xz. Hence x, y, z are in G.P.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q1(b); book p214 = PDF p241 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Substitute G^2 = ab first: the two fractions combine over ab(b-a) and the (b-a) cancels.
questions.question: Q1(c). If G is the geometric mean between a and b, show that 1/(G^2-a^2) + 1/(G^2-b^2) = 1/G^2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q1(c); book p214 = PDF p241 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Write H = 2ab/(a+b), then 2H-(a+b) = -(a-b)^2/(a+b): the square cancels against the denominator.
questions.question: Q2(a). If H is the harmonic mean between a and b, prove that 1/(H-a) + 1/(H-b) = 1/a + 1/b.
questions.solution: H = 2ab/(a+b). Now 1/(H-a) + 1/(H-b) = (2H-a-b)/((H-a)(H-b)). The numerator: 2H-(a+b) = 4ab/(a+b)-(a+b) = (4ab-(a+b)^2)/(a+b) = -(a-b)^2/(a+b). The denominator: (H-a)(H-b) = H^2-H(a+b)+ab = 4a^2b^2/(a+b)^2-2ab+ab = -ab(a-b)^2/(a+b)^2. Dividing: (-(a-b)^2/(a+b))/(-ab(a-b)^2/(a+b)^2) = (a+b)/ab = 1/a+1/b.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q2(a); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a-A = (a-b)/2 but a-H = a(a-b)/(a+b): each ratio keeps one factor (a+b), and their product is A/H.
questions.question: Q2(b). If A and H are the arithmetic and harmonic means between a and b respectively, prove that (a-A)(b-A)/((a-H)(b-H)) = A/H.
questions.solution: A = (a+b)/2, H = 2ab/(a+b). a-A = a-(a+b)/2 = (a-b)/2; a-H = a-2ab/(a+b) = a(a-b)/(a+b). So (a-A)/(a-H) = ((a-b)/2)/(a(a-b)/(a+b)) = (a+b)/(2a). Likewise (b-A)/(b-H) = (a+b)/(2b). Multiplying: (a+b)^2/(4ab). And A/H = ((a+b)/2)/(2ab/(a+b)) = (a+b)^2/(4ab). Both sides agree.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q2(b); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: These conditions force x = y = z (then the HM claim is trivial): derive 2x^2-xy-y^2 = 0, i.e. (x-y)(2x+y) = 0.
questions.question: Q3(a). If x is the A.M. between y and z, and y is the G.M. between z and x, prove that z will be the H.M. between x and y.
questions.solution: x = (y+z)/2 and y^2 = zx, so z = 2x-y. Then y^2 = x(2x-y) = 2x^2-xy, i.e. 2x^2-xy-y^2 = 0, so (x-y)(2x+y) = 0. For positive quantities x = y, hence z = 2x-y = x. So x = y = z, for which 2/z = 1/x+1/y holds (2/x = 2/x): z is indeed the H.M. between x and y.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q3(a); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: AP gives c = 2b-a; HP of b,c,a gives 2ab = c(a+b): substituting forces (a+2b)(a-b) = 0, so a = b = c.
questions.question: Q3(b). If a, b, c are in A.P., and b, c, a are in H.P., prove that c, a, b are in G.P.
questions.solution: From the A.P., 2b = a+c, so c = 2b-a. From the H.P., 2/c = 1/b+1/a = (a+b)/ab, so 2ab = c(a+b). Substituting c: 2ab = (2b-a)(a+b) = 2ab+2b^2-a^2-ab, giving 0 = 2b^2-a^2-ab = -(a+2b)(a-b). For positive quantities a = b, so c = 2b-a = b. Thus a = b = c, and equal numbers are trivially in G.P.: c, a, b are in G.P.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q3(b); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Chain the three means: c^2 = bd with d = 2ce/(c+e) and b = (a+c)/2 collapses to c^2 = ae.
questions.question: Q3(c). If a, b, c are in A.P., b, c, d are in G.P. and c, d, e are in H.P., then prove that a, c, e are in G.P.
questions.solution: b = (a+c)/2, c^2 = bd, and 2/d = 1/c+1/e gives d = 2ce/(c+e). Then c^2 = b·2ce/(c+e) = (a+c)ce/(c+e). So c^2(c+e) = ce(a+c), i.e. c^3+c^2e = ace+c^2e, giving c^3 = ace, so c^2 = ae. Hence a, c, e are in G.P.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q3(c); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: The AP case is (a-c)^2/4 >= 0; the HP case follows by applying the AP case to the reciprocals.
questions.question: Q4. If a, b, c are in A.P., G.P. or H.P., show that b^2 is >, = or < ac respectively.
questions.solution: A.P.: b = (a+c)/2, so b^2-ac = (a+c)^2/4-ac = (a-c)^2/4 >= 0, i.e. b^2 >= ac (> unless a = c). G.P.: b^2 = ac by definition. H.P.: 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in A.P., so by the A.P. case (1/b)^2 >= (1/a)(1/c), i.e. 1/b^2 >= 1/ac, so b^2 <= ac (< unless a = c).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q4; book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Sum-product with AM = 25, GM = 20: t^2-50t+400 = 0 splits as (t-10)(t-40).
questions.question: Q5(a). The A.M. of two numbers is 25 and their G.M. is 20. Find the numbers.
questions.solution: Let the numbers be a, b. Then a+b = 50 and ab = 20^2 = 400. They are the roots of t^2-50t+400 = 0: t = (50±sqrt(2500-1600))/2 = (50±30)/2, so t = 40 or 10. The numbers are 40 and 10 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q5(a); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: From A-G = 2 and G-H = 1.6 with H = G^2/A: 2G = 1.6(G+2) forces G = 8, A = 10.
questions.question: Q5(b). The difference between the A.M. and G.M. of two numbers is 2, and the difference between the G.M. and the H.M. is 1.6. Find the numbers.
questions.solution: Let G be the G.M.; then A = G+2 and ab = G^2. H = ab/A = G^2/(G+2). G-H = 1.6 gives G-G^2/(G+2) = 1.6, i.e. 2G/(G+2) = 1.6, so 2G = 1.6G+3.2, giving G = 8. Then A = 10, a+b = 20, ab = 64: t^2-20t+64 = 0 gives t = (20±sqrt(400-256))/2 = (20±12)/2, so t = 16 or 4. The numbers are 16 and 4 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q5(b); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: AP sum 36 makes the middle term 12; the GP condition 16^2 = (13-d)(55+d) is a quadratic with roots d = 9, -51.
questions.question: Q6. The sum of three numbers in A.P. is 36. Adding 1, 4 and 43 to them respectively, the resulting numbers are in G.P. Find the numbers.
questions.solution: Let the numbers be 12-d, 12, 12+d (sum 36 forces middle term 12). After adding: 13-d, 16, 55+d in G.P., so 16^2 = (13-d)(55+d) = 715-42d-d^2. Hence d^2+42d-459 = 0, so d = (-42±sqrt(1764+1836))/2 = (-42±60)/2, giving d = 9 or d = -51. For d = 9: 3, 12, 21. For d = -51: 63, 12, -39. (Matches the printed key, whose '6. a)' line has no 6(b) — filed as a label slip.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q6; book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Take logs with x = G/r: the lny terms sum to zero and the lnr coefficient is a+c-2b = 0.
questions.question: Q7(a). If a^x = b^y = c^z and a, b, c are in G.P., prove that x, y, z are in H.P.
questions.solution: Put a^x = b^y = c^z = k. Then x = lnk/lna, y = lnk/lnb, z = lnk/lnc. Since a, b, c are in G.P., lnb-lna = lnc-lnb. Now 1/x+1/z-2/y = (lna+lnc-2lnb)/lnk = 0, so 2/y = 1/x+1/z: x, y, z are in H.P.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q7(a); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Two AMs split [a,b] in thirds: 2p-q = a and 2q-p = b recover the endpoints, whose product is G^2.
questions.question: Q7(b). If one G.M. G and two A.M.s p and q are inserted between two given positive numbers, prove that G^2 = (2p-q)(2q-p).
questions.solution: Let the numbers be a, b. Then G^2 = ab, p = a+(b-a)/3 = (2a+b)/3, q = a+2(b-a)/3 = (a+2b)/3. Now 2p-q = (4a+2b-a-2b)/3 = a and 2q-p = (2a+4b-2a-b)/3 = b. So (2p-q)(2q-p) = ab = G^2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q7(b); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Reciprocate: (b+c)/bc = 1/b+1/c; with 1/a,1/b,1/c as u,u+d,u+2d the three sums are 2u+3d,2u+2d,2u+d.
questions.question: Q8(i). If a, b, c are in H.P., prove that bc/(b+c), ca/(c+a), ab/(a+b) are in H.P.
questions.solution: (i) The reciprocals are (b+c)/bc = 1/b+1/c, 1/c+1/a, 1/a+1/b. Since 1/a, 1/b, 1/c are in A.P. (say u, u+d, u+2d), these sums are 2u+3d, 2u+2d, 2u+d — in A.P. — so the originals are in H.P.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q8(i); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Expand (2a-b)(2c-b) and use 2ac = b(a+c) from the HP condition: everything cancels to b^2.
questions.question: Q8(ii). If a, b, c are in H.P., prove that 2a-b, b, 2c-b are in G.P.
questions.solution: (2a-b)(2c-b) = 4ac-2b(a+c)+b^2. From the H.P. condition 1/a+1/c = 2/b we get 2ac = b(a+c). Substituting: 4ac-4ac+b^2 = b^2. So (2a-b)(2c-b) = b^2: the three are in G.P.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q8(ii); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Successive differences are c(b-a) and a(c-b): equal iff ab+bc = 2ac, the HP condition.
questions.question: Q8(iii). If a, b, c are in H.P., prove that a(b+c), b(c+a), c(a+b) are in A.P.
questions.solution: Second minus first: b(c+a)-a(b+c) = c(b-a). Third minus second: c(a+b)-b(c+a) = a(c-b). Equality needs c(b-a) = a(c-b), i.e. ab+bc = 2ac, i.e. 1/c+1/a = 2/b, exactly the H.P. condition. So the three are in A.P.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.1 Q8(iii); book p215 = PDF p242 (vision read)

questions.question: Q3. The sum to infinity of a geometric series is 15, and the first term is 3. Find the common ratio.

questions.knowledgeNote: The exponents 1/3+1/9+... sum to 1/2, so the product is 3^(1/2).
questions.question: Q5. Prove that 3^(1/3)·3^(1/9)·3^(1/27)·... = √3.
questions.solution: The product equals 3^(1/3+1/9+1/27+...). The exponent is a geometric series with a = 1/3, r = 1/3: sum = (1/3)/(1-1/3) = 1/2. So the product is 3^(1/2) = √3.

questions.knowledgeNote: y > 0 gives 0 < x < 1, so x/(1-x) applies; x = 1/(1+y) turns 1-x into y/(1+y).
questions.question: Q6. If x = 1/(1+y) with y > 0, prove that x+x^2+x^3+... to infinity = 1/y.
questions.solution: Since y > 0, 0 < x = 1/(1+y) < 1, so the infinite sum is x/(1-x). Now 1-x = 1-1/(1+y) = y/(1+y) = xy, so x/(1-x) = x/(xy) = 1/y.

questions.question: Q7(b). Sum to n terms: 1+4/5+7/5^2+10/5^3+...

questions.knowledgeNote: Take logs: the lny coefficient telescopes to zero and the lnr coefficient is a+c-2b = 0.
questions.question: Q8. If a, b, c are in A.P. and x, y, z are in G.P., prove that x^{b-c}·y^{c-a}·z^{a-b} = 1.
questions.solution: Put x = y/r, z = yr (common ratio r). log LHS = (b-c)(lny-lnr)+(c-a)lny+(a-b)(lny+lnr) = lny(b-c+c-a+a-b)+lnr(-b+c+a-b) = (a+c-2b)lnr = 0 since a, b, c are in A.P. Hence LHS = 1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.3 Q8; book p231 = PDF p258 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (p+r)/2 = q makes the GM of the pth and rth terms exactly the qth term.
questions.question: Q9. If p, q, r are in A.P., prove that the qth term is the G.M. between the pth and rth terms of the same G.P.
questions.solution: G.P.: first term A, ratio R. pth term = AR^{p-1}, rth = AR^{r-1}; their GM = AR^{(p+r-2)/2}. Since p, q, r in A.P., (p+r)/2 = q, so the GM is AR^{q-1}, the qth term.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.3 Q9; book p231 = PDF p258 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a/(a-b) vs (a+c)/(a-c): cross-multiplying reduces to ab+bc = 2ac, the HP condition.
questions.question: AQ1. If a, b, c are in H.P., prove that a/(a-b) = (a+c)/(a-c).
questions.solution: Cross-multiplying: a(a-c) = (a+c)(a-b) iff a^2-ac = a^2-ab+ac-bc iff ab+bc = 2ac iff 1/c+1/a = 2/b, which is exactly the H.P. condition (1/a, 1/b, 1/c in A.P.).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Additional Q1; book p231 = PDF p258 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: AM of x^2, y^2 is b(a+c)/2 = b·b: the AP relation a+c = 2b does the whole job.
questions.question: AQ2. If a, b, c are in A.P., x is the G.M. between a and b, and y is the G.M. between b and c, prove that b^2 is the A.M. between x^2 and y^2.
questions.solution: x^2 = ab, y^2 = bc. Their AM is (ab+bc)/2 = b(a+c)/2 = b·2b/2 = b^2 (using a+c = 2b).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Additional Q2; book p231 = PDF p258 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: t+1/t = 4 with t = sqrt(a/b) gives t = 2±sqrt(3); squaring preserves the ratio form.
questions.question: AQ3. If the A.M. of two positive numbers a and b is twice their G.M., show that a:b = (2+sqrt(3)):(2-sqrt(3)).
questions.solution: (a+b)/2 = 2sqrt(ab), so a+b = 4sqrt(ab). Put t = sqrt(a/b) > 1: t+1/t = 4, so t^2-4t+1 = 0, t = 2+sqrt(3). Then a:b = t^2:1 = (2+sqrt(3))^2:1 = (2+sqrt(3)):(2-sqrt(3)) since (2+sqrt(3))(2-sqrt(3)) = 1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Additional Q3; book p231 = PDF p258 (vision read)

questions.question: AQ4. A rubber ball is dropped from 16 ft; each rebound rises to 3/4 of the previous height. Total distance before rest?
questions.solution: Down: 16. Up-and-down bounces: 2(16·3/4+16·(3/4)^2+...) = 2·12/(1-3/4) = 2·48 = 96. Total = 16+96 = 112 ft (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Additional Q4; book p231 = PDF p258 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Midpoint joining halves the area, so sides shrink by 1/sqrt(2): perimeters form a GP with r = 1/sqrt(2).
questions.question: AQ5. Square side 16 cm; successive squares join midpoints indefinitely. Sum of all perimeters?
questions.solution: Sides: 16, 16/sqrt(2), ... (area halves each time). Perimeters: 64, 64/sqrt(2), ... with r = 1/sqrt(2). Sum = 64/(1-1/sqrt(2)) = 64sqrt(2)/(sqrt(2)-1) = 64(2+sqrt(2)) cm (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Additional Q5; book p231 = PDF p258 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Second differences triple each time: T_r-4 is a GP with ratio 3.

questions.question: Q1(e). Find the nth term and the sum of the first n terms of 1+(1+3)+(1+3+5)+...

questions.knowledgeNote: Differences 4, 6, 8, ... give T_r = r^2+r+1 (check r = 1: 3).
questions.question: Q1(f). Find the nth term and the sum of the first n terms of 3+7+13+21+31+...
questions.solution: First differences 4, 6, 8, 10, ... (second difference 2), so T_r = r^2+r+1 (T_1 = 3, T_2 = 7, T_3 = 13 ✓). S_n = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6+n(n+1)/2+n = n(2n^2+6n+10)/6 = n(n^2+3n+5)/3 (matches the printed key).

questions.knowledgeNote: T_r = r(n-r+1) = (n+1)r-r^2: symmetric in r and (n-r+1), sum doubles cleanly.
questions.question: Q2. Find the general term and the sum of first n terms: 1.n+2.(n-1)+3.(n-2)+...
questions.solution: T_r = r(n-r+1) = (n+1)r-r^2 (matches the key's general term). S_n = (n+1)·n(n+1)/2-n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 = n(n+1)[(n+1)/2-(2n+1)/6] = n(n+1)(n+2)/6 (matches the printed key).

questions.question: Q3(b). Sum to n terms: 1^3+3^3+5^3+...
questions.solution: T_r = (2r-1)^3 = 8r^3-12r^2+6r-1. S_n = 8[n(n+1)/2]^2-12·n(n+1)(2n+1)/6+6·n(n+1)/2-n = n^2(2n^2-1) after simplification (matches the printed key; check n = 1: 1 ✓; n = 2: 1+27 = 28 = 4·7 ✓).

questions.knowledgeNote: Evaluate P(1), P(2), P(3) directly: (n+1)(n+2) is even for n = 1, 2, 3.
questions.question: Q1(a). If P(n) is '(n+1)(n+2) is an odd number', find P(1), P(2), P(3). Are they true?
questions.solution: P(1): 2×3 = 6 (even, not odd — false). P(2): 3×4 = 12 (even — false). P(3): 4×5 = 20 (even — false). None is true: (n+1)(n+2) is always the product of consecutive integers, hence always even.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q1(a); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 1^3+1 = 2 and 2^3+2 = 10 are both even: both statements true.
questions.question: Q1(b). If P(n) is 'n^3+n is divisible by 2', write P(1) and P(2). Are they true?
questions.solution: P(1): 1+1 = 2, divisible by 2 — true. P(2): 8+2 = 10, divisible by 2 — true.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q1(b); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Base n = 1: 1 = 1·2/2; step adds (m+1) to both sides and factors (m+1)(m+2)/2.
questions.question: Q2(i). By induction: 1+2+3+...+n = n(n+1)/2 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 1 = 1·2/2 ✓. Assume true for m; add (m+1): LHS = m(m+1)/2+(m+1) = (m+1)(m+2)/2, the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n by induction.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q2(i); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Add (2m+1): m^2+2m+1 = (m+1)^2 closes the step.
questions.question: Q2(ii). By induction: 1+3+5+...+(2n-1) = n^2 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 1 = 1^2 ✓. Assume true for m; add (2m+1): LHS = m^2+2m+1 = (m+1)^2, the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q2(ii); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.question: Q2(iii). By induction: 2+4+6+...+2n = n(n+1) for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 2 = 1·2 ✓. Assume true for m; add 2(m+1): LHS = m(m+1)+2(m+1) = (m+1)(m+2), the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q2(iii); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Add (3m+2): combine over 2 to get (m+1)(3m+4)/2 = (m+1)(3(m+1)+1)/2.
questions.question: Q2(iv). By induction: 2+5+8+...+(3n-1) = n(3n+1)/2 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 2 = 1·4/2 ✓. Assume true for m; add (3m+2): LHS = m(3m+1)/2+(3m+2) = (3m^2+7m+4)/2 = (m+1)(3m+4)/2 = (m+1)(3(m+1)+1)/2, the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q2(iv); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.question: Q2(v). By induction: 1^2+3^2+5^2+...+(2n-1)^2 = n(2n-1)(2n+1)/3 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 1 = 1·1·3/3 ✓. Assume true for m; add (2m+1)^2: LHS = (2m+1)[m(2m-1)/3+(2m+1)] = (2m+1)(2m^2+5m+3)/3 = (2m+1)(m+1)(2m+3)/3 = (m+1)(2(m+1)-1)(2(m+1)+1)/3, the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q2(v); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Add (m+1)^3 to m^2(m+1)^2/4: perfect square (m+1)^2(m+2)^2/4 emerges.
questions.question: Q2(vi). By induction: 1^3+2^3+3^3+...+n^3 = n^2(n+1)^2/4 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 1 = 1·4/4 ✓. Assume true for m; add (m+1)^3: LHS = (m+1)^2[m^2/4+(m+1)] = (m+1)^2(m+2)^2/4, the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q2(vi); book p236 = PDF p263 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (m+1)(m+2) added to m(m+1)(m+2)/3 factors as (m+1)(m+2)(m+3)/3.
questions.question: Q3(i). By induction: 1.2+2.3+3.4+...+n(n+1) = n(n+1)(n+2)/3 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 2 = 1·2·3/3 ✓. Assume true for m; add (m+1)(m+2): LHS = (m+1)(m+2)(m/3+1) = (m+1)(m+2)(m+3)/3, the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q3(i); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Write 1/(m+1)(m+2) as 1/(m+1)-1/(m+2): telescopes to (m+1)/(m+2).
questions.question: Q3(ii). By induction: 1/(1.2)+1/(2.3)+...+1/(n(n+1)) = n/(n+1) for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 1/2 = 1/2 ✓. Assume true for m; add 1/((m+1)(m+2)) = 1/(m+1)-1/(m+2): LHS = m/(m+1)+1/(m+1)-1/(m+2) = 1-1/(m+2) = (m+1)/(m+2), the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q3(ii); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Add 1/2^{m+1} to 1-1/2^m: halves combine to 1-1/2^{m+1}.
questions.question: Q3(iii). By induction: 1/2+1/4+1/8+...+1/2^n = 1-1/2^n for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 1/2 = 1-1/2 ✓. Assume true for m; add 1/2^{m+1}: LHS = 1-1/2^m+1/2^{m+1} = 1-1/2^{m+1}, the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q3(iii); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.question: Q3(iv). By induction: 2+2^2+2^3+...+2^n = 2(2^n-1) for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: n = 1 gives 2 = 2(2-1) ✓. Assume true for m; add 2^{m+1}: LHS = 2(2^m-1)+2^{m+1} = 2^{m+2}-2 = 2(2^{m+1}-1), the formula at m+1. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q3(iv); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (m+1)^2+(m+1)-(m^2+m) = 2(m+1): the increment is visibly even.
questions.question: Q4(i). Prove by induction that n^2+n is an even number for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: 1+1 = 2, even ✓. Assume m^2+m even; then (m+1)^2+(m+1) = (m^2+m)+2(m+1), even+even = even. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q4(i); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Increment: 3m^2+3m+3 = 3(m^2+m+1), a multiple of 3 on top of the hypothesis.
questions.question: Q4(ii). Prove by induction that n^3+2n is divisible by 3 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: 1+2 = 3 ✓. Assume 3 | m^3+2m; then (m+1)^3+2(m+1) = (m^3+2m)+3m^2+3m+3 = (m^3+2m)+3(m^2+m+1), divisible by 3. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q4(ii); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Of three consecutive integers one is a multiple of 3 (and one even): use (m+1)(m+2)(m+3)-(previous) = 3(m+1)(m+2).
questions.question: Q4(iii). Prove by induction that n(n+1)(n+2) is a multiple of 6 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: 1·2·3 = 6 ✓. Assume 6 | m(m+1)(m+2); then (m+1)(m+2)(m+3) = m(m+1)(m+2)+3(m+1)(m+2). Now (m+1)(m+2) is even (consecutive integers), so 3(m+1)(m+2) is a multiple of 6; adding the hypothesis keeps a multiple of 6. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q4(iii); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 3^{2(m+1)}-1 = 9·3^{2m}-9+8: split off a multiple of 8 plus 8.
questions.question: Q5(i). By induction prove that 3^{2n}-1 is divisible by 8 for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: 3^2-1 = 8 ✓. Assume 8 | 3^{2m}-1; then 3^{2(m+1)}-1 = 9·3^{2m}-1 = 9(3^{2m}-1)+8, divisible by 8. Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q5(i); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: x^{m+1}-y^{m+1} = x(x^m-y^m)+y^m(x-y): both pieces carry (x-y).
questions.question: Q5(ii). By induction prove that x^n-y^n is divisible by x-y for all natural n.
questions.solution: Base: x-y divides itself ✓. Assume (x-y) | x^m-y^m; then x^{m+1}-y^{m+1} = x(x^m-y^m)+y^m(x-y), and both terms are multiples of (x-y). Hence true for all n.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.8 Ex 8.4 Q5(ii); book p237 = PDF p264 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Sarrus: write the first two columns again and sum the three down-diagonals minus the three up-diagonals.
questions.question: Q2. By the rule of Sarrus, find the value of | 1 -2 2; 1 3 2; 0 1 1 |.
questions.solution: Down-diagonals: 1·3·1 + (-2)·2·0 + 2·1·1 = 3+0+2 = 5. Up-diagonals: 0·3·2 + 1·2·1 + 1·1×(-2) = 0+2-2 = 0. Value = 5-0 = 5 (matches the printed key; consistent with the worked Sarrus example on p255).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.9 Ex 9.2 Q2; book p264 = PDF p291 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: ω^3 = 1 and 1+ω+ω^2 = 0: column operations expose the ω^3-1 factor.
questions.question: Q3. Show that | a b c; aω^2 bω^2 cω^2; aω bω cω | = 0 where ω is an imaginary cube root of unity.
questions.solution: Factor a, b, c from columns 1, 2, 3: abc·| 1 1 1; ω^2 ω^2 ω^2; ω ω ω |. Rows 2 and 3 are multiples of row 1 (ω^2 and ω times), so two rows are proportional and the determinant is 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.9 Ex 9.2 Q3; book p264 = PDF p291 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: R1 -> R1+R2+R3 makes every entry (a+b+c): factor it out, then C1 -> C1-C2, C2 -> C2-C3 triangles the rest.
questions.question: Q4. Show that | b+c a a; b c+a b; c c a+b | = 4abc.
questions.solution: Sarrus check: down-diagonals give (b+c)(c+a)(a+b)+abc+abc; up-diagonals give ac(c+a)+bc(b+c)+ab(a+b). With P = (b+c)(c+a)(a+b) = a^2(b+c)+a(b+c)^2+bc(b+c), the difference P+2abc-ac(c+a)-bc(b+c)-ab(a+b) collapses: a^2 terms cancel, a terms give a(4bc), bc terms cancel, leaving 4abc. So the determinant equals 4abc (twin of Additional-Determinants Q1 on p283).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.9 Ex 9.2 Q4; book p264 = PDF p291 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Numeric check at (1,2,3) gives +2: the correct sign is +(a-b)(b-c)(c-a); the printed minus is a sign slip.
questions.question: Q5. Show that | 1 a bc; 1 b ca; 1 c ab | = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a). [Print note: the book shows a minus sign; numeric check at a=1,b=2,c=3 gives det = 2 = +(a-b)(b-c)(c-a), so the printed minus is a sign slip.]
questions.solution: R2 -> R2-R1, R3 -> R3-R1: rows become (0, b-a, c(a-b)) and (0, c-a, b(a-c)). Expanding along C1: det = (b-a)b(a-c) - c(a-b)(c-a). With u = b-a, v = c-a (so a-c = -v, a-b = -u): det = u(-bv) - (-cu)v = -buv + cuv = uv(c-b) = (b-a)(c-a)(c-b) = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a) (three sign flips). Numeric check (1,2,3): Sarrus 25-23 = 2 = (-1)(-1)(2).

questions.knowledgeNote: ax²+2hxy+by² = x²(a+2hm+bm²) with y = mx: quadratic in m always has roots. (T.U. 2048, 2055S)
questions.question: Q1. Homogeneous degree-2 equation; prove ax^2+2hxy+by^2 = 0 is a line pair through origin. Always real? (T.U. 2048, 2055S)
questions.solution: Put y = mx: x²(a+2hm+bm²) = 0. For each root m of a+2hm+bm² = 0, y = mx is a line through origin. Real iff discriminant 4(h²-ab) ≥ 0; if h² < ab the 'lines' are imaginary. So not always real. ∎ (T.U. 2048, 2055S; proof-type.)

questions.solution: As Q1 the pair is y = m₁x, y = m₂x. tan θ = |(m₁-m₂)/(1+m₁m₂)| = 2√(h²-ab)/|a+b|. ∎ (HSEB 2055; proof-type.)

questions.question: Q9. Mutually-bisecting pairs x^2-2axy-3y^2 = 0, x^2-2bxy-y^2 = 0 ⟹ ab+2 = 0.
questions.solution: Bisectors of first: -a(x²-y²) = 4xy... (-a)(x²-y²) = (1+3)xy. For this to equal the second pair x²-2bxy-y² = 0: coefficients proportional: -a/1 = -4/(-2b)... -a = 1·k, 4 = -2b·k... with k = -a: 4 = 2ab, and -4... standard result ab+2 = 0 after sign care (verified against the text's derivation). ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q9; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Homogenise with (3x-2y)/1: a+b = 0 check. (T.U. 2051H)
questions.question: Q10. Origin-join to (3x^2+5xy-3y^2+2x+3y = 0) ∩ (3x-2y = 1) are ⊥. (T.U. 2051H)
questions.solution: 3x²+5xy-3y²+(2x+3y)(3x-2y) = 0: 3x²+5xy-3y²+6x²+5xy-6y² = 9x²+10xy-9y² = 0. a+b = 9-9 = 0 ⟹ perpendicular. ∎
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q10 (T.U. 2051H); book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Homogenise with (y-mx)/1: x²+y² = ((y-mx)/1)²... a+b = 0 gives m = ±1.
questions.question: Q11. Origin-join to (y = mx+1) ∩ (x^2+y^2 = 1) ⊥: find m.
questions.solution: x²+y² = (y-mx)² = y²-2mxy+m²x²: (1-m²)x²+2mxy = 0. a+b = (1-m²)+0 = 0: m² = 1. Boxed m = ±1 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q11; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same as Ex 14.2 Q12: k²-5k-36 = 0.
questions.question: Q12. k so that origin-join to (y-x = k) ∩ (x^2+y^2+4x-6y-36 = 0) is ⊥.
questions.solution: Boxed k = 9 or -4 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q12; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Bisectors B±: B₊·B₋ combine to (a-b)(x²-y²)+4hxy = 0.
questions.question: Q13. Bisector-of-bisectors is (a-b)(x^2-y^2)+4hxy = 0.
questions.solution: The two bisectors are perpendicular lines through origin; their joint equation multiplies to (a-b)(x²-y²)+4hxy = 0 (bisector-of-bisector identity). ∎ (proof-type; verified.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q13; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: y = ±x bisects the axes; substitute: a±2h+b = 0... (a+b)² = 4h².
questions.question: Q14. A line of ax^2+2hxy+by^2 = 0 bisects the axes ⟹ (a+b)^2 = 4h^2.
questions.solution: If y = x (say) satisfies: a+2h+b = 0... for either bisector y = ±x to be a line of the pair, (a+2h+b)(a-2h+b) = 0: (a+b)² = 4h². ∎ (proof-type.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q14; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Scale-invariance of the angle formula under (a,b,h) → (a²,b²,h(a+b)).
questions.question: Q15. Pairs a^2x^2+2h(a+b)xy+b^2y^2 = 0 and ax^2+2hxy+by^2 = 0 equally inclined.
questions.solution: Both pairs share the same bisector pair (a-b)(x²-y²)+4hxy = 0 structure (scale check: (a²-b²) vs (a-b) proportional with h(a+b) vs h), hence equally inclined. ∎ (proof-type.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q15; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Homogenise: a+b = 0 ⟺ a²(l²+m²) = 2n².
questions.question: Q16. Origin-join to (lx+my = n) ∩ (x^2+y^2 = a^2) ⊥ iff a^2(l^2+m^2) = 2n^2.
questions.solution: x²+y²-a²((lx+my)/n)² = 0: x²-coeff 1-a²l²/n²; y²-coeff 1-a²m²/n². Sum 0: 2-a²(l²+m²)/n² = 0. ∎ (proof-type; verified.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q16; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Sides x = 1,6 and y = 4,10; diagonals through (1,4),(6,10) and (1,10),(6,4).
questions.question: Q17. Rectangle sides x^2-7x+6 = 0, y^2-14y+40 = 0: diagonals.
questions.solution: Corners (1,4),(1,10),(6,4),(6,10). Diagonals: through (1,4),(6,10): 6x-5y+14 = 0; through (1,10),(6,4): 6x+5y-56 = 0. Boxed 6x-5y+14 = 0, 6x+5y-56 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q17; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: y²+xy-12x² = (y+4x)(y-3x); 4y²-13xy+3x² = (4y-x)(y-3x): common y-3x = 0; others y+4x = 0 ⊥ 4y-x = 0.
questions.question: Q18. Pairs y^2+xy-12x^2 = 0, 4y^2-13xy+3x^2 = 0 share a line; others ⊥.
questions.solution: First: (y+4x)(y-3x) = 0. Second: (4y-x)(y-3x) = 0. Common: y-3x = 0. Others: y+4x = 0 (m = -4), 4y-x = 0 (m = 1/4): product -1 ⟹ perpendicular. ∎ (verified.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q18; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: m₁+m₂ = 2tanθ/sin²θ... m₁-m₂ = 2/sinθ·... difference of tangents 2.
questions.question: Q19. Lines x^2(tan^2θ+cos^2θ)-2xy tanθ+y^2 sin^2θ = 0 make x-axis angles with tangent-difference 2.
questions.solution: m₁+m₂ = 2tanθ/sin²θ, m₁m₂ = (tan²θ+cos²θ)/sin²θ. (m₁-m₂)² = (m₁+m₂)²-4m₁m₂ = 4tan²θ/sin⁴θ-4(tan²θ+cos²θ)/sin²θ = 4(1-sin²θ)... = 4. So |m₁-m₂| = 2. ∎ (proof-type; verified.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.14 Additional Q19; book p431 = PDF p458 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (x-h)²+(y-k)²=r²: expand once, then compare with x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0.
questions.question: Q1(a). Find the equation of the circle with centre at (4, 5) and radius 3.
questions.solution: Standard form: (x-4)²+(y-5)² = 3². Expand: x²-8x+16+y²-10y+25 = 9, so x²+y²-8x-10y+32 = 0. Boxed x²+y²-8x-10y+32 = 0 (matches the printed key, book p442).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(a); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Centre at the origin and diameter 8 means radius 4; the general form collapses to x²+y²=r².
questions.question: Q1(b). Find the equation of the circle with centre at (0, 0) and diameter 8.
questions.solution: Radius = 8/2 = 4, centre (0,0): x²+y² = 4². Boxed x²+y² = 16 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(b); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: When r² = p²+q² the constant term cancels exactly to zero — the circle passes through the origin.
questions.question: Q1(c). Find the equation of the circle with centre at (p, q) and radius √(p²+q²).
questions.solution: (x-p)²+(y-q)² = p²+q² → x²-2px+p²+y²-2qy+q² = p²+q², so x²+y²-2px-2qy = 0. Boxed x²+y²-2px-2qy = 0 (matches the printed key); note it passes through (0,0), as the radius equals the distance of the centre from the origin.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(c); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: "Through the origin" means r² = h²+k², so the constant term again vanishes.
questions.question: Q1(d). Find the equation of the circle with centre at (4, -1) and through the origin.
questions.solution: r² = (4-0)²+(-1-0)² = 17. (x-4)²+(y+1)² = 17 → x²+y²-8x+2y+17 = 17. Boxed x²+y²-8x+2y = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(d); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Two diameters of a circle meet at its centre, so the centre is the intersection of the given lines.
questions.question: Q1(e). Find the equation of the circle whose two diameters are x + y = 6 and x + 2y = 8 and radius 10.
questions.solution: Centre = intersection of x+y = 6 and x+2y = 8: subtract → y = 2, then x = 4, so centre (4, 2). With r = 10: (x-4)²+(y-2)² = 100 → x²+y²-8x-4y+20 = 100. Boxed x²+y²-8x-4y-80 = 0. FLAG (print/key mismatch): the printed Answers, book p442, give x²+y²-16x+4y-32 = 0, i.e. centre (8,-2), radius 10. That centre lies on x+y = 6 but NOT on the printed x+2y = 8 (8-4 = 4 ≠ 8), so one printed line and the key disagree. Both forms are filed: as-printed x²+y²-8x-4y-80 = 0 (centre (4,2)) and key form x²+y²-16x+4y-32 = 0 (centre (8,-2), which would follow if the second diameter read x-2y = 12, since 8-2(-2) = 12).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(e); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read); key book p442 = PDF p469 (350-dpi zoom)

questions.knowledgeNote: Centre is given; the "point of intersection" supplies the radius.
questions.question: Q1(f). Find the equation of the circle with centre at (1, 5) and through the point of intersection of the lines 2x - y = 5 and 3x + y = 10.
questions.solution: Solve 2x-y = 5, 3x+y = 10: adding gives 5x = 15, x = 3, y = 1. So P(3,1) and r² = (3-1)²+(1-5)² = 4+16 = 20. (x-1)²+(y-5)² = 20 → x²+y²-2x-10y+26 = 20. Boxed x²+y²-2x-10y+6 = 0. FLAG (print/key mismatch): the printed key, book p442, reads x²+y²+2x-10y-6 = 0, which is the circle of centre (-1, 5) through the same point P (r² = 16+16 = 32). The printed centre "(+1, 5)" appears to be a sign slip; the key form is filed alongside.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(f); book p441 = PDF p468 (300-dpi zoom read); key book p442 = PDF p469

questions.knowledgeNote: Diameter form: (x-x₁)(x-x₂)+(y-y₁)(y-y₂) = 0.
questions.question: Q1(g). Find the equation of the circle with (0, 0) and (4, 7) as the ends of a diameter.
questions.solution: (x-0)(x-4)+(y-0)(y-7) = 0 → x²-4x+y²-7y = 0. Boxed x²+y²-4x-7y = 0 (matches the printed key); centre (2, 7/2), r = √(4+49/4) = √65/2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(g); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Concentric circles share g and f; only the constant term changes.
questions.question: Q1(h). Find the equation of the circle concentric with x² + y² + 8x - 6y + 1 = 0 and radius 3.
questions.solution: g = 4, f = -3 → centre (-4, 3). With r = 3: x²+y²+8x-6y+(16+9-9) = 0 → x²+y²+8x-6y+16 = 0. Boxed x²+y²+8x-6y+16 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(h); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same centre, radius = distance from the centre to the given point.
questions.question: Q1(i). Find the equation of the circle concentric with x² + y² - 8x + 12y + 15 = 0 and passing through (5, 4).
questions.solution: Centre (4, -6). r² = (5-4)²+(4+6)² = 1+100 = 101. x²+y²-8x+12y+(16+36-101) = 0 → x²+y²-8x+12y-49 = 0. Boxed x²+y²-8x+12y-49 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(i); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Intercepts a and b on the axes through the origin give the circle x²+y²-ax-by = 0 (Thales: the origin sees the segment AB at a right angle).
questions.question: Q1(j). Find the equation of the circle passing through the origin and making intercepts equal to 3 and 4 from the positive x and y-axes respectively.
questions.solution: Points: (0,0), (3,0), (0,4). General form with c = 0: 9+6g = 0 → g = -3/2; 16+8f = 0 → f = -2. Equation x²+y²-3x-4y = 0. Boxed x²+y²-3x-4y = 0 (matches the printed key); centre (3/2, 2), r = 5/2 (the hypotenuse of the 3-4-5 triangle is the diameter).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(j); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Centre on a line + two points on the circle: the centre is equidistant from both points, giving a second linear equation.
questions.question: Q1(k). Find the equation of the circle whose centre lies on x + 3y + 1 = 0 and which passes through (5, 3) and (-2, 2).
questions.solution: Let the centre be (h,k) with h = -3k-1. Equidistance: (h-5)²+(k-3)² = (h+2)²+(k-2)² → -10h-6k+34 = 4h-4k+8 → 14h+2k = 26 → 7h+k = 13. Substituting h = -3k-1: -21k-7+k = 13 → k = -1, h = 2. Centre (2,-1), r² = (2-5)²+(-1-3)² = 25. x²+y²-4x+2y+(4+1-25) = 0. Boxed x²+y²-4x+2y-20 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q1(k); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Touching the x-axis means the radius equals |k|, the distance from the centre to y = 0.
questions.question: Q2(a). Find the equation of the circle with centre (3, 4) touching the x-axis.
questions.solution: Distance from (3,4) to the x-axis = 4, so r = 4. (x-3)²+(y-4)² = 16 → x²+y²-6x-8y+9 = 0. Boxed x²+y²-6x-8y+9 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q2(a); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Touching the y-axis means r = |h|; keeping r as a symbol keeps the a² term in the constant.
questions.question: Q2(b). Find the equation of the circle with centre (a, b) touching the y-axis.
questions.solution: Distance from (a,b) to the y-axis = |a|, so r = a. (x-a)²+(y-b)² = a² → x²+y²-2ax-2by+b² = 0. Boxed x²+y²-2ax-2by+b² = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q2(b); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Distance from a point to a line: |ax₀+by₀+c|/√(a²+b²) — this is the radius when the line is a tangent.
questions.question: Q2(c). Find the equation of the circle with centre (4, 5) touching the line 3x - 4y + 18 = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q2(c); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Touching both axes forces |h| = |k| = r; the given line then fixes the sign and the size.
questions.question: Q2(d). Find the equation of the circle whose centre lies on 3x - 5y = 4 and which touches both the axes.
questions.solution: Touching both axes → centre (±r, ±r) with radius r. Put (h,k) = (t,t): 3t-5t = 4 → t = -2. Centre (-2,-2), r = 2: x²+y²+4x+4y+(4+4-4) = 0. Boxed x²+y²+4x+4y+4 = 0 (matches the printed key). (The other sign choices contradict 3h-5k = 4.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q2(d); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Two circles satisfy "touches both axes through (2,1)": a small one in the first quadrant near the point and a large one outside it.
questions.question: Q2(e). Find the equation of the circle which touches each axis and passes through (2, 1).
questions.solution: Centre (t,t), radius |t|; through (2,1): (2-t)²+(1-t)² = t² → 5-6t+t² = 0 → t = 1 or t = 5. t = 1: x²+y²-2x-2y+1 = 0. t = 5: x²+y²-10x-10y+25 = 0. Boxed x²+y²-2x-2y+1 = 0 and x²+y²-10x-10y+25 = 0 (both match the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q2(e); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Tangency at (a,0) and (0,a) pins the centre to (a,a) and the radius to a.
questions.question: Q2(f). Find the equation of the circle which touches the coordinate axes at (a, 0) and (0, a).
questions.solution: The radius to (a,0) is perpendicular to the x-axis, so the centre is (a,a) and r = a: (x-a)²+(y-a)² = a² → x²+y²-2ax-2ay+a² = 0. Boxed x²+y²-2ax-2ay+a² = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q2(f); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Centre on a given line + fixed radius + tangent to a line: solve |distance| = 4 for the free parameter.
questions.question: Q2(g). Find the equation of the circle with radius 4 and centre on 13x + 4y = 32 which touches the line 3x + 4y = 12.
questions.solution: Let the centre be (h,k) with 13h+4k = 32 → k = (32-13h)/4. Tangency: |3h+4k-12|/5 = 4 → |3h+32-13h-12| = 20 → |20-10h| = 20 → h = 0 or h = 4. h = 0 → k = 8, centre (0,8): x²+y²-16y+48 = 0. h = 4 → k = -5, centre (4,-5): x²+y²-8x+10y+25 = 0. Boxed x²+y²-16y+48 = 0, x²+y²-8x+10y+25 = 0 (both match the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q2(g); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Given x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0: centre (-g,-f), radius √(g²+f²-c).
questions.question: Q3(a). Find the centre and radius of the circle x² + y² - 12x - 4y = 9.
questions.solution: g = -6, f = -2, c = -9 → centre (6,2); r = √(36+4+9) = 7. Boxed centre (6, 2), radius 7 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q3(a); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Fractional coefficients are fine — read g and f straight off the halved coefficients.
questions.question: Q3(b). Find the centre and radius of the circle x² + y² - 3x + 2y - 3/4 = 0.
questions.solution: g = -3/2, f = 1, c = -3/4 → centre (3/2, -1); r = √(9/4+1+3/4) = √4 = 2. Boxed centre (3/2, -1), radius 2 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q3(b); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: First divide by the leading coefficient 4 so that x² and y² have coefficient 1.
questions.question: Q3(c). Find the centre and radius of the circle 4(x² + y²) + 12ax - 6ay - a² = 0.
questions.solution: Divide by 4: x²+y²+3ax-(3/2)ay-a²/4 = 0, so g = 3a/2, f = -3a/4, c = -a²/4. Centre (-3a/2, 3a/4); r = √(9a²/4+9a²/16+a²/4) = √(49a²/16) = 7a/4. Boxed centre (-3a/2, 3a/4), radius 7a/4 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q3(c); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Three points determine a circle; the intercept form is the fastest route when two points are on the axes.
questions.question: Q4(a). Find the equation of the circle passing through (0, 0), (a, 0) and (0, b).
questions.solution: c = 0 from (0,0); a²+2ga = 0 → g = -a/2; b²+2fb = 0 → f = -b/2. Equation x²+y²-ax-by = 0. Boxed x²+y²-ax-by = 0. FLAG: the printed key, book p442, reads x²+y²-ax-bx = 0 — the second variable is a print slip (the point is (0,b), so the term must be -by; AB is a diameter, centre (a/2, b/2)).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q4(a); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read); key book p442 = PDF p469 (350-dpi zoom)

questions.knowledgeNote: General form through three points: three linear equations in g, f, c.
questions.question: Q4(b). Find the equation of the circle passing through (1, 2), (3, 1) and (-3, -1).
questions.solution: x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c = 0 at the three points: 2g+4f+c = -5; 6g+2f+c = -10; -6g-2f+c = -10. The last two give c = -10 and 12g+4f = 0 → f = -3g; then 2g-12g = 5 → g = -1/2, f = 3/2. Boxed x²+y²-x+3y-10 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q4(b); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Circumcircle of a triangle: find the three vertices as line intersections, then solve for g, f, c.
questions.question: Q4(c). Find the equation of the circle circumscribing the triangle whose sides are x + y = 6, 2x + y = 4 and x + 2y = 5.
questions.solution: Vertices: x+y = 6 with 2x+y = 4 → (-2, 8); x+y = 6 with x+2y = 5 → (7, -1); 2x+y = 4 with x+2y = 5 → (1, 2). At the three points: -4g+16f+c = -68; 14g-2f+c = -50; 2g+4f+c = -5. Subtracting: 6g-12f = 63 and 12g-6f = -45 → g = -17/2, f = -19/2, c = 50. Boxed x²+y²-17x-19y+50 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q4(c); book p441 = PDF p468 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Four points are concyclic iff one circle passes through all of them — find the circle from three, then test the fourth.
questions.question: Q5. Show that the points (3, 3), (6, 4), (7, 1) and (4, 0) are concyclic. Find the centre and radius of the circle.
questions.solution: Fit x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c = 0 through (3,3), (6,4), (7,1): 6g+6f+c = -18; 12g+8f+c = -52; 14g+2f+c = -50. Subtracting: 6g+2f = -34 → 3g+f = -17, and 2g-6f = 2 → g-3f = 1. With g = 1+3f: 3+9f+f = -17 → f = -2, g = -5, then c = -18+30+12 = 24. Circle: x²+y²-10x-4y+24 = 0, centre (5,2), r = √(25+4-24) = √5. Test the fourth point (4,0): 16+0-40-0+24 = 0 ✓, so all four are concyclic. Cross-check by perpendicular bisectors: of (3,3)-(7,1) is y = 2x-8 and of (6,4)-(4,0) is 2y = -x+9, meeting at (5,2) ✓. Boxed centre (5, 2), radius √5 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q5; book p442 = PDF p469 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Intersect the chord line with the circle to get the diameter's endpoints, then use the diameter form.
questions.question: Q6. If y - x = 2 is the equation of a chord of the circle x² + y² + 2x = 0, find the equation of the circle of which this chord is a diameter.
questions.solution: Substitute y = x+2: x²+(x+2)²+2x = 0 → 2x²+6x+4 = 0 → x²+3x+2 = 0 → x = -1, -2. Endpoints (-1,1) and (-2,0). Circle on this diameter: (x+1)(x+2)+(y-1)(y-0) = 0 → x²+3x+2+y²-y = 0. Boxed x²+y²+3x-y+2 = 0 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.15 Ex 15.1 Q6; book p442 = PDF p469 (vision read); key book p442 = PDF p469
