questions.knowledgeNote: Both terms differentiate to 1/(2 sqrt .); the constant sqrt(a) differentiates to 0.
questions.question: Q7(iv). Find dy/dx when sqrt(x) + sqrt(y) = sqrt(a).
questions.solution: Differentiate: 1/(2 sqrt x) + (1/(2 sqrt y)) y' = 0, so y' = -sqrt(y)/sqrt(x) = -sqrt(y/x). Boxed (printed key p534: -y^(1/2)/x^(1/2)).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(iv); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: Logarithmic differentiation cancels the common factor (4y - 3x); the answer collapses to y/x.
questions.question: Q7(v). Find dy/dx when x^2 y^3 = (x + 2y)^5.
questions.solution: Take logs: 2 log x + 3 log y = 5 log(x + 2y). Differentiate: 2/x + 3y'/y = 5(1 + 2y')/(x + 2y). Collect y': y'[10/(x + 2y) - 3/y] = 2/x - 5/(x + 2y). Left bracket = [10y - 3(x + 2y)]/[y(x + 2y)] = (4y - 3x)/[y(x + 2y)]; right side = [2(x + 2y) - 5x]/[x(x + 2y)] = (4y - 3x)/[x(x + 2y)]. Hence y' = y/x (for 4y != 3x). Boxed y/x (printed key p534: y/x).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(v); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: The x^2 cancels the -1/x^2 of the inner derivative, leaving -cos(1/x) + 2x sin(1/x).
questions.question: Q7(vi). Find dy/dx when y = x^2 sin(1/x).
questions.solution: Product + chain rule: y' = 2x sin(1/x) + x^2 cos(1/x)(-1/x^2) = 2x sin(1/x) - cos(1/x). Boxed (printed key p534: -cos(1/x) + 2x sin(1/x)).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(vi); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: 1 - (3x-4x^3)^2 factors as (1-x^2)(1-4x^2)^2; the modulus gives +-3/sqrt(1-x^2), i.e. 3/sqrt(1-x^2) on the branch |x| < 1/2.
questions.question: Q7(vii). Find dy/dx when y = sin^-1(3x - 4x^3). (T.U. 2048)
questions.solution: y' = 3(1 - 4x^2)/sqrt(1 - (3x - 4x^3)^2). Now 1 - (3x - 4x^3)^2 = 1 - 9x^2 + 24x^4 - 16x^6 = (1 - x^2)(1 - 4x^2)^2, so y' = 3(1 - 4x^2)/[|1 - 4x^2| sqrt(1 - x^2)] = 3/sqrt(1 - x^2) when |x| < 1/2. Boxed 3/sqrt(1 - x^2) (printed key p534: 3/sqrt(1-x^2)); for 1/2 < |x| < 1 the derivative is -3/sqrt(1 - x^2) because |1 - 4x^2| = -(1 - 4x^2) there. The printing states the |x| < 1/2 branch, on which 3x - 4x^3 = sin 3(theta) with x = sin theta; no book error, only the branch qualifier added.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(vii); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: Parametric rule dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); the common (1+t^3)^2 and the factor 3 cancel.
questions.question: Q7(viii). Find dy/dx when x = 3t/(1 + t^3), y = 3t^2/(1 + t^3). (T.U. 2048 H)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(viii); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: The cycloid's tangent slope is cot(theta/2) after the half-angle identities.
questions.question: Q7(ix). Find dy/dx when x = a(theta - sin theta), y = a(1 - cos theta).
questions.solution: dx/dtheta = a(1 - cos theta), dy/dtheta = a sin theta. dy/dx = sin theta/(1 - cos theta) = [2 sin(theta/2)cos(theta/2)]/[2 sin^2(theta/2)] = cot(theta/2). Boxed (printed key p534: cot(theta/2)).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(ix); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: Three-factor logarithmic differentiation: each factor contributes its exponent times (inner derivative)/(factor).
questions.question: Q7(x). Find dy/dx when y = x^2 sqrt(2x + 3) / cbrt(4x + 1).
questions.solution: Take logs: log y = 2 log x + (1/2)log(2x + 3) - (1/3)log(4x + 1). Differentiate: y'/y = 2/x + 1/(2x + 3) - 4/[3(4x + 1)]. Hence y' = y[2/x + 1/(2x + 3) - 4/(3(4x + 1))]. Boxed (printed key p534: y[2/x + 1/(2x+3) - 4/(3(4x+1))]).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(x); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: The half from the square root multiplies the whole bracket; numerator logs are added, denominator logs subtracted.
questions.question: Q7(xi). Find dy/dx when y = sqrt((x + 1)(x + 2)/((x - 3)(x - 4))).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q7(xi); book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: f(0) fixes the intercept c, f'(0) fixes the gradient m; then evaluate at x = 2.
questions.question: Q8. If f(x) = mx + c and f(0) = f'(0) = 1, what is f(2)?
questions.solution: f(0) = c = 1. f'(x) = m for every x, so f'(0) = m = 1. Hence f(x) = x + 1 and f(2) = 3. Boxed 3 (printed key p534: 3).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q8; book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: Differentiate term by term twice; the constant 3 vanishes and the linear term gives the constant -8.
questions.question: Q9. If f(x) = 4x^3 - 8x + 3, find f'(0) and f''(1).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q9; book p532-534 = PDF p559-561; key book p533-534

questions.knowledgeNote: Implicit differentiation, then replace x by sin y/sin(a+y); the bracket collapses to sin a/sin(a+y).
questions.question: Q10(a). If sin y = x sin(a + y), prove that dy/dx = sin^2(a + y)/sin a.
questions.solution: Differentiate implicitly with respect to x: cos y * y' = sin(a + y) + x cos(a + y) * y'. Collect y': y'[cos y - x cos(a + y)] = sin(a + y). Eliminate x using the given relation x = sin y/sin(a + y): cos y - x cos(a + y) = [cos y sin(a + y) - sin y cos(a + y)]/sin(a + y) = sin[(a + y) - y]/sin(a + y) = sin a/sin(a + y). Therefore y' = sin(a + y) * sin(a + y)/sin a = sin^2(a + y)/sin a. Boxed (printed key, book p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q10(a); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Same pattern as Q10(a): the difference formula cos y cos T + sin y sin T = cos(T - y) is the whole proof.
questions.question: Q10(b). If sin y = x cos(a + y), show that dy/dx = cos^2(a + y)/cos a.
questions.solution: Differentiate: cos y * y' = cos(a + y) - x sin(a + y) * y', so y'[cos y + x sin(a + y)] = cos(a + y). With x = sin y/cos(a + y): cos y + x sin(a + y) = [cos y cos(a + y) + sin y sin(a + y)]/cos(a + y) = cos[(a + y) - y]/cos(a + y) = cos a/cos(a + y). Hence y' = cos(a + y) * cos(a + y)/cos a = cos^2(a + y)/cos a. Boxed (printed key, book p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q10(b); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Squaring makes the quotient differentiation trivial; the identity (1-x)^2 y^2 = 1-x^2 converts the result to y/(1-x^2).
questions.question: Q11. If y = sqrt((1 + x)/(1 - x)), prove that dy/dx = y/(1 - x^2).
questions.solution: Square: y^2 = (1 + x)/(1 - x). Differentiate implicitly: 2y y' = [(1 - x) + (1 + x)]/(1 - x)^2 = 2/(1 - x)^2, so y' = 1/[(1 - x)^2 y]. Now (1 - x)^2 y^2 = (1 - x)(1 + x) = 1 - x^2, hence (1 - x)^2 y = (1 - x^2)/y and y' = y/(1 - x^2). Boxed (printed key, book p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q11; book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Variable base and variable exponent (x^sin x): take logs first, then y' = y[v' log u + v u'/u].
questions.question: Q12(i). Find the derivative of x^(sin x).
questions.solution: Logarithmic differentiation: log y = sin x * log x, so y'/y = cos x log x + sin x/x. Hence y' = x^(sin x)(sin x/x + cos x log x). Boxed (printed key p534: x^(sin x)((sin x)/x + cos x log x)).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(i); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: (sin x)^x: the bracket is log u + x u'/u = log sin x + x cot x.
questions.question: Q12(ii). Find the derivative of (sin x)^x.
questions.solution: log y = x log(sin x), so y'/y = log(sin x) + x cot x. Hence y' = (sin x)^x (x cot x + log sin x). Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(ii); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Product of two logs: differentiate log x and log sin x separately, each against the other factor.
questions.question: Q12(iii). Find the derivative of (sin x)^(log x).
questions.solution: log y = log x * log(sin x), so y'/y = (1/x)log(sin x) + log x * cot x. Hence y' = (sin x)^(log x) [(1/x)log sin x + cot x log x]. Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(iii); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Tower e^(x^x): differentiate the inner tower x^x logarithmically, then apply the outer chain rule.
questions.question: Q12(iv). Find the derivative of e^(x^x).
questions.solution: Let u = x^x. Then log u = x log x and u' = x^x(1 + log x). Chain rule: y' = e^(x^x) * u' = e^(x^x) * x^x(1 + log x). Boxed (printed key p534: e^(x^x).x^x(1 + log x)).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(iv); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: x^(e^x): product rule on e^x log x gives e^x(log x + 1/x).
questions.question: Q12(v). Find the derivative of x^(e^x).
questions.solution: log y = e^x log x, so y'/y = e^x log x + e^x/x = e^x(log x + 1/x). Hence y' = x^(e^x) e^x(log x + 1/x). Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(v); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Nested log: d/dx log(log x) = 1/(x log x) supplies the second term.
questions.question: Q12(vi). Find the derivative of (log x)^(tan x).
questions.solution: log y = tan x * log(log x), so y'/y = sec^2 x log(log x) + tan x * 1/(x log x). Hence y' = (log x)^(tan x){sec^2 x log(log x) + tan x/(x log x)}. Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(vi); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: (tan x)^(log x): the u'/u part is sec^2 x/tan x, which multiplies log x.
questions.question: Q12(vii). Find the derivative of (tan x)^(log x). (T.U. 2048 H)
questions.solution: log y = log x * log(tan x), so y'/y = (1/x)log(tan x) + log x * sec^2 x/tan x. Hence y' = (tan x)^(log x){(1/x)log tan x + (sec^2 x/tan x)log x}. Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(vii); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: x^(sec x): sec x differentiates to sec x tan x, and sec x/x survives from the log x term.
questions.question: Q12(viii). Find the derivative of x^(sec x).
questions.solution: log y = sec x * log x, so y'/y = sec x tan x log x + sec x/x = sec x(tan x log x + 1/x). Hence y' = x^(sec x) sec x(tan x log x + 1/x). Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(viii); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: (sin x)^(cos x): the derivative of cos x is -sin x, which is why the log term is subtracted.
questions.question: Q12(ix). Find the derivative of (sin x)^(cos x). (T.U. 2053)
questions.solution: log y = cos x * log(sin x), so y'/y = -sin x log(sin x) + cos x * cot x. Hence y' = (sin x)^(cos x){cos x cot x - sin x log(sin x)}. Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q12(ix); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: y = x^y: differentiate the base and the exponent separately, then use x^y = y to simplify y.x^(y-1) to y^2/x.
questions.question: Q13(i). Find dy/dx when y = x^y.
questions.solution: Differentiate with respect to x, treating the exponent as a variable: dy/dx = y x^(y-1) + x^y log x * dy/dx (product rule on x^y). So y'[1 - x^y log x] = y x^(y-1). Using x^y = y: y x^(y-1) = y * y/x = y^2/x, hence y' = (y^2/x)/(1 - y log x) = y^2/[x(1 - y log x)]. Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q13(i); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: The product of two powers becomes a sum of logs; the implicit derivative then collects y' against (log x + x/y).
questions.question: Q13(ii). Find dy/dx when x^y . y^x = 1. (T.U. 2051 H)
questions.solution: Take logs: y log x + x log y = 0. Differentiate: y' log x + y/x + log y + x y'/y = 0, so y'(log x + x/y) = -(y/x + log y). Hence y' = -(y/x + log y)/(log x + x/y) = -y(y + x log y)/[x(y log x + x)]. Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q13(ii); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Homogeneous-type relation: the common factor (my - nx) cancels, leaving the symmetric answer y/x.
questions.question: Q13(iii). Find dy/dx when x^m y^n = (x + y)^(m+n).
questions.solution: Take logs: m log x + n log y = (m + n)log(x + y). Differentiate: m/x + n y'/y = (m + n)(1 + y')/(x + y). Collect y': y'[(m + n)/(x + y) - n/y] = m/x - (m + n)/(x + y). Left bracket = [(m + n)y - n(x + y)]/[y(x + y)] = (my - nx)/[y(x + y)]; right side = [m(x + y) - (m + n)x]/[x(x + y)] = (my - nx)/[x(x + y)]. Hence y' = y/x (for my != nx). Boxed y/x (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q13(iii); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Each exponential contributes its chain factor: cos x on the left, cos y on the right.
questions.question: Q13(iv). Find dy/dx when e^(sin x) + e^(sin y) = 1.
questions.solution: Differentiate: e^(sin x) cos x + e^(sin y) cos y * y' = 0, so y' = -e^(sin x) cos x / (e^(sin y) cos y). Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q13(iv); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: x^y = y^x is the classic log case; collect y' against (log x - x/y).
questions.question: Q13(v). Find dy/dx when x^y = y^x. (T.U. 2048)
questions.solution: Take logs: y log x = x log y. Differentiate: y' log x + y/x = log y + x y'/y, so y'(log x - x/y) = log y - y/x. Hence y' = (log y - y/x)/(log x - x/y) = y(x log y - y)/[x(y log x - x)]. Boxed (printed key p534).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.17 Additional Questions (Derivative) Q13(v); book p533-534 = PDF p560-561; key book p534 = PDF p561

questions.knowledgeNote: Symmetry: the same expression appears on each side; the missing x^(sin x)/y^(sin y) factor is 1 by the hypothesis.
questions.question: Q13(vi). Find dy/dx when x^(sin x) = y^(sin y). (T.U. 2049)
questions.solution: Take logs: sin x log x = sin y log y. Differentiate both sides with respect to x: cos x log x + sin x/x = [cos y log y + sin y/y] * y'. Hence y' = [cos x log x + sin x/x]/[cos y log y + sin y/y] = y(x cos x log x + sin x)/[x(y cos y log y + sin y)]. Boxed (printed key p534). Note: the full implicit form carries the factor x^(sin x)/y^(sin y), which equals 1 by the given equation — that is why the key has no such factor.

questions.knowledgeNote: Sign of f' at the point decides it: f' = 30x - 14 is negative at x = 2/5 and positive at x = 5/2.
questions.question: Q1(i). Examine whether the function f(x) = 15x^2 - 14x + 1 is increasing or decreasing at x = 2/5 and x = 5/2.
questions.solution: A differentiable function increases at a point when f'(x) > 0 there and decreases when f'(x) < 0. f'(x) = 30x - 14. At x = 2/5: f'(2/5) = 30(2/5) - 14 = 12 - 14 = -2 < 0, so f is decreasing at x = 2/5. At x = 5/2: f'(5/2) = 30(5/2) - 14 = 75 - 14 = 61 > 0, so f is increasing at x = 5/2. Boxed decreasing at 2/5, increasing at 5/2 (printed key p551: 'Decreasing at x = 2/5 and increasing at x = 5/2').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q1(i); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f' = 6(x^2 - 4): positive outside the interval [-2, 2], negative inside it. 3 lies outside, 3/2 inside.
questions.question: Q1(ii). Show that the function f(x) = 2x^3 - 24x + 15 is increasing at x = 3 and decreasing at x = 3/2.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 6x^2 - 24 = 6(x^2 - 4). At x = 3: f'(3) = 6(9 - 4) = 30 > 0, so f is increasing at x = 3. At x = 3/2: f'(3/2) = 6(9/4 - 4) = 6(-7/4) = -21/2 < 0, so f is decreasing at x = 3/2. Boxed as required (no separate key entry: stated as a 'show that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q1(ii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f' = 4(x-1) has a single zero at x = 1; to the right of it the parabola 2x^2-4x+3 rises.
questions.question: Q2(i). Test whether the function f(x) = 2x^2 - 4x + 3 is increasing or decreasing on the interval (1, 4].
questions.solution: f'(x) = 4x - 4 = 4(x - 1). For every x in (1, 4], x - 1 > 0, hence f'(x) > 0 on the whole interval: f is increasing on (1, 4]. Boxed increasing (printed key p551: 'Increasing').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q2(i); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f' = 4(4 - x^2) is negative exactly when |x| > 2; the interval (-inf, -2) lies in that region.
questions.question: Q2(ii). Examine whether the function f(x) = 16x - (4/3)x^3 is increasing or decreasing on the interval (-infinity, -2).
questions.solution: f'(x) = 16 - 4x^2 = 4(4 - x^2) = 4(2 - x)(2 + x). For x < -2 both factors (2 - x) and (2 + x) are positive and negative respectively: 2 - x > 0 and 2 + x < 0, so f'(x) < 0 throughout (-infinity, -2). Hence f is decreasing there. Boxed decreasing (printed key p551: 'Decreasing').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q2(ii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Complete the square inside the bracket: 3x^2-12x+13 = 3(x-2)^2+1 > 0 always, so f' < 0 identically.
questions.question: Q2(iii). Show that the function f(x) = -x^3 + 6x^2 - 13x + 20 is decreasing for all x in R.
questions.solution: f'(x) = -3x^2 + 12x - 13 = -[3x^2 - 12x + 13] = -[3(x - 2)^2 + 1]. The bracket is at least 1 for every real x, so f'(x) <= -1 < 0 for all x. Hence f is strictly decreasing on R. Boxed (no separate key entry: 'show that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q2(iii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f' = 4 + 9/x^2 is always positive; the excluded point x = 0 is simply outside the domain, not a sign change.
questions.question: Q2(iv). Show that the function f(x) = 4x - 9/x + 6 is increasing for all x in R except at x = 0.
questions.solution: The function is defined only for x != 0. f'(x) = 4 + 9/x^2. Since 9/x^2 > 0 for every x != 0, f'(x) > 4 > 0 on each of the intervals (-infinity, 0) and (0, infinity). Hence f is increasing on both branches; at x = 0 the function has no value (vertical asymptote). Boxed (no separate key entry: 'show that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q2(iv); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: A single zero at x = 1 for f' = 6(x-1): the parabola falls up to its vertex and rises afterwards.
questions.question: Q3(i). Find the intervals in which f(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + 5 is increasing or decreasing.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 6x - 6 = 6(x - 1). Sign chart: f' < 0 for x < 1 and f' > 0 for x > 1. Hence f is decreasing on (-infinity, 1) and increasing on (1, infinity). Boxed (printed key p551: 'Increasing on (1, infinity) and decreasing on (-infinity, 1)').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q3(i); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: x^2 never changes the sign; the turning value is x = 1/4 where 4x - 1 changes sign.
questions.question: Q3(ii). Find the intervals in which f(x) = x^4 - (1/3)x^3 is increasing or decreasing.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 4x^3 - x^2 = x^2(4x - 1). The factor x^2 >= 0 always (zero only at x = 0), so the sign of f' is the sign of (4x - 1). Hence f' < 0 for x < 1/4 and f' > 0 for x > 1/4. Thus f is decreasing on (-infinity, 1/4) and increasing on (1/4, infinity). Boxed (printed key p551: 'Increasing on (1/4, infinity) and decreasing on (-infinity, 1/4)').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q3(ii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Up-down-up cubic: the derivative changes sign at x = -3 and x = 3.
questions.question: Q3(iii). Find the intervals in which f(x) = 5x^3 - 135x + 22 is increasing or decreasing.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 15x^2 - 135 = 15(x^2 - 9) = 15(x - 3)(x + 3). Sign chart: positive for x < -3, negative for -3 < x < 3, positive for x > 3. Hence f is increasing on (-infinity, -3), decreasing on (-3, 3), increasing on (3, infinity). Boxed (printed key p551: 'Increasing on (-infinity, -3) U (3, infinity) and decreasing on (-3, 3)').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q3(iii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: The leading coefficient is negative, so the pattern is down-up-down; f' > 0 between the roots -1 and 2.
questions.question: Q3(iv). Find the intervals in which f(x) = 6 + 12x + 3x^2 - 2x^3 is increasing or decreasing.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 12 + 6x - 6x^2 = -6(x^2 - x - 2) = -6(x - 2)(x + 1). The factor (x - 2)(x + 1) is negative on (-1, 2) and positive outside, so f'(x) > 0 on (-1, 2) and f'(x) < 0 on (-infinity, -1) U (2, infinity). Hence f is increasing on (-1, 2), decreasing on (-infinity, -1) and on (2, infinity). Boxed (printed key p551: 'Decreasing on (-infinity, -1) U (2, infinity) and increasing on (-1, 2)').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q3(iv); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: The cubic's own intervals are intersected with the given domain [-3, 5].
questions.question: Q3(v). Find the intervals in which f(x) = x^3 - 12x is increasing or decreasing, where x is defined on [-3, 5].
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12 = 3(x^2 - 4) = 3(x - 2)(x + 2). On the restricted domain [-3, 5]: f' > 0 for -3 <= x < -2 and for 2 < x <= 5; f' < 0 for -2 < x < 2. Hence f is increasing on [-3, -2) and on (2, 5], and decreasing on (-2, 2). Boxed (printed key p551: 'Increasing on [-3, -2) U (2, 5] and decreasing on (-2, 2)').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q3(v); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: On a closed interval, compare f at the endpoints and at every interior stationary point; here 13 > 4 > 1.
questions.question: Q4(i). Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of f(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + 4 on [-1, 2].
questions.solution: Closed-interval method: f'(x) = 6x - 6 = 0 gives x = 1, an interior critical point. Evaluate: f(-1) = 3 + 6 + 4 = 13; f(1) = 3 - 6 + 4 = 1; f(2) = 12 - 12 + 4 = 4. The largest value is 13 and the smallest is 1. Boxed absolute maximum 13, absolute minimum 1 (printed key p551: 'Absolute max = 13, Absolute min = 1').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q4(i); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Two critical points plus two endpoints give the four candidates; the endpoint -2 is where the cubic bottoms out.
questions.question: Q4(ii). Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 on [-2, 4].
questions.solution: f'(x) = 6x^2 - 18x = 6x(x - 3) = 0 at x = 0 and x = 3, both inside [-2, 4]. Values: f(-2) = -16 - 36 = -52; f(0) = 0; f(3) = 54 - 81 = -27; f(4) = 128 - 144 = -16. Largest 0, smallest -52. Boxed absolute maximum 0, absolute minimum -52 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q4(ii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Both 0 and 3 give the value 0, so the minimum is attained twice; the maximum is at the right endpoint.
questions.question: Q4(iii). Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x on [0, 5].
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3) = 0 at x = 1 and x = 3. Values: f(0) = 0; f(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 = 4; f(3) = 27 - 54 + 27 = 0; f(5) = 125 - 150 + 45 = 20. Largest 20, smallest 0. Boxed absolute maximum 20, absolute minimum 0 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q4(iii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: The endpoint x = 4 wins here: the cubic rises again after x = 3, overtaking the local maximum 38.
questions.question: Q4(iv). Find the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of f(x) = 2x^3 - 15x^2 + 36x + 10 on [1, 4].
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q4(iv); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Quadratic: f'' is a nonzero constant, so the single stationary point is a minimum and no inflection exists.
questions.question: Q5(i). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + 3.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 6x - 6 = 0 gives x = 1. f''(x) = 6 > 0 at every point, so x = 1 is a local minimum, and the value there is f(1) = 3 - 6 + 3 = 0. A point of inflection needs f''(x) = 0 with a sign change of f''; here f'' = 6 never vanishes, so there is no point of inflection. Boxed minimum value 0 at x = 1, no point of inflection (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(i); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Second-derivative test: f'' < 0 gives the maximum at x = -2, f'' > 0 the minimum at x = 2; f'' changes sign at 0.
questions.question: Q5(ii). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = x^3 - 12x + 8.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12 = 3(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0 at x = -2 and x = 2. f''(x) = 6x: f''(-2) = -12 < 0 so x = -2 gives a local maximum f(-2) = -8 + 24 + 8 = 24; f''(2) = 12 > 0 so x = 2 gives a local minimum f(2) = 8 - 24 + 8 = -8. f''(x) = 0 at x = 0 and changes sign there (- to +), so (0, f(0)) = (0, 8) is the point of inflection. Boxed max 24 at x = -2, min -8 at x = 2, inflection at x = 0 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(ii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f'' = 6x - 12: negative before 2, positive after; the maximum sits at 0, the minimum at 4.
questions.question: Q5(iii). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 3.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x = 3x(x - 4) = 0 at x = 0 and x = 4. f''(x) = 6x - 12: f''(0) = -12 < 0, so x = 0 gives a local maximum f(0) = 3; f''(4) = 12 > 0, so x = 4 gives a local minimum f(4) = 64 - 96 + 3 = -29. f''(x) = 0 at x = 2 with a sign change, so (2, f(2)) = (2, -13) is the point of inflection. Boxed max 3 at x = 0, min -29 at x = 4, inflection at x = 2 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(iii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Very flat maximum (33) beside the minimum (32): the two stationary values differ by only 1, which is why the inflection sits exactly midway at 5/2.
questions.question: Q5(iv). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = 2x^3 - 15x^2 + 36x + 5. (HSEB 2050, 052)
questions.solution: f'(x) = 6x^2 - 30x + 36 = 6(x - 2)(x - 3) = 0 at x = 2 and x = 3. f''(x) = 12x - 30: f''(2) = -6 < 0, so x = 2 gives a local maximum f(2) = 16 - 60 + 72 + 5 = 33; f''(3) = 6 > 0, so x = 3 gives a local minimum f(3) = 54 - 135 + 108 + 5 = 32. f''(x) = 0 at x = 5/2 with a sign change, so (5/2, f(5/2)) = (5/2, 32.5) is the point of inflection. Boxed max 33 at x = 2, min 32 at x = 3, inflection at x = 5/2 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(iv); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f' = 6(x-4)(x+1): up to the maximum at -1, down to the minimum at 4; the inflection is the midpoint 3/2.
questions.question: Q5(v). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 - 24x + 3.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 6x^2 - 18x - 24 = 6(x^2 - 3x - 4) = 6(x - 4)(x + 1) = 0 at x = 4 and x = -1. f''(x) = 12x - 18: f''(-1) = -30 < 0, so x = -1 gives a local maximum f(-1) = -2 - 9 + 24 + 3 = 16; f''(4) = 30 > 0, so x = 4 gives a local minimum f(4) = 128 - 144 - 96 + 3 = -109. f''(x) = 0 at x = 3/2 with a sign change, so (3/2, f(3/2)) = (3/2, -36.75) is the point of inflection. Boxed max 16 at x = -1, min -109 at x = 4, inflection at x = 3/2 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(v); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Keep fractional values exact: f(1/2) = 39/4, and the inflection abscissa is the average (1/2 + 2)/2 = 5/4.
questions.question: Q5(vi). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = 4x^3 - 15x^2 + 12x + 7. (HSEB 2051)
questions.solution: f'(x) = 12x^2 - 30x + 12 = 6(2x^2 - 5x + 2) = 6(2x - 1)(x - 2) = 0 at x = 1/2 and x = 2. f''(x) = 24x - 30: f''(1/2) = -18 < 0, so x = 1/2 gives a local maximum f(1/2) = 1/2 - 15/4 + 6 + 7 = 39/4; f''(2) = 18 > 0, so x = 2 gives a local minimum f(2) = 32 - 60 + 24 + 7 = 3. f''(x) = 0 at x = 5/4 with a sign change, so (5/4, f(5/4)) is the point of inflection. Boxed max 39/4 at x = 1/2, min 3 at x = 2, inflection at x = 5/4 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(vi); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: All three critical abscissas -1/2, 1/2, 3/2 lie in (-1, 2); the maximum and minimum values are 7/2 and -25/2.
questions.question: Q5(vii). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = 4x^3 - 6x^2 - 9x + 1 on the interval (-1, 2).
questions.solution: f'(x) = 12x^2 - 12x - 9 = 3(4x^2 - 4x - 3) = 3(2x - 3)(2x + 1) = 0 at x = 3/2 and x = -1/2, both inside (-1, 2). f''(x) = 24x - 12: f''(-1/2) = -24 < 0, so x = -1/2 gives a local maximum f(-1/2) = -1/2 - 3/2 + 9/2 + 1 = 7/2; f''(3/2) = 24 > 0, so x = 3/2 gives a local minimum f(3/2) = 27/2 - 27/2 - 27/2 + 1 = -25/2. f''(x) = 0 at x = 1/2, inside the interval and with a sign change, so (1/2, f(1/2)) is the point of inflection. Boxed max 7/2 at x = -1/2, min -25/2 at x = 3/2, inflection at x = 1/2 (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(vii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f' = 1 - 100/x^2 has the two roots +-10; the second derivative has a fixed sign on each branch, so no inflection.
questions.question: Q5(viii). Find the local maxima and minima and points of inflection of f(x) = x + 100/x - 5.
questions.solution: Domain x != 0. f'(x) = 1 - 100/x^2 = 0 gives x^2 = 100, i.e. x = 10 or x = -10. f''(x) = 200/x^3: f''(10) = 200/1000 > 0, so x = 10 gives a local minimum f(10) = 10 + 10 - 5 = 15; f''(-10) = -200/1000 < 0, so x = -10 gives a local maximum f(-10) = -10 - 10 - 5 = -25. f''(x) = 200/x^3 is never zero, so there is no point of inflection. Boxed min 15 at x = 10, max -25 at x = -10, no point of inflection (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q5(viii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Complete the square: x^2 - 4x + 8 = (x-2)^2 + 4 > 0, so f' > 0 everywhere — strictly increasing, so no extremum.
questions.question: Q6(i). Show that f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 24x + 4 has neither maximum nor minimum value.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 24 = 3[(x - 2)^2 + 4] > 0 for every real x (the square is non-negative and 4 > 0). Since f' never vanishes and is always positive, f is strictly increasing on R: there is no point where the function turns, hence neither a maximum nor a minimum. Boxed (no separate key entry: 'show that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q6(i); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f' = 3(x-2)^2 touches zero without changing sign: a horizontal inflection at x = 2, values rise on both sides.
questions.question: Q6(ii). Show that f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 12x - 3 has neither maximum nor minimum value.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 12 = 3(x - 2)^2 >= 0, and f'(x) = 0 only at x = 2. At x = 2 the derivative does not change sign (it is non-negative on both sides), so x = 2 is a stationary point of inflection, not an extremum. Hence the function has neither a maximum nor a minimum. Boxed (no 'show that' key entry).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q6(ii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f'' = 12x(x-1): positive outside [0,1], negative inside — the curve is a 'cup' outside and a 'cap' between 0 and 1.
questions.question: Q7(i). Determine where the graph of f(x) = x^4 - 2x^3 + 5 is concave upwards and where concave downwards.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 6x^2, f''(x) = 12x^2 - 12x = 12x(x - 1). Concavity follows the sign of f'': f'' > 0 for x < 0 and for x > 1 (concave upwards), f'' < 0 for 0 < x < 1 (concave downwards). Boxed concave upwards on (-infinity, 0) U (1, infinity), concave downwards on (0, 1) (printed key p551: 'Concave upwards for x > 1, concave upwards for x < 0 and concave downwards for 0 < x < 1').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q7(i); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f'' = 12(x-1)(x-3): outside [1,3] the graph is concave up; between 1 and 3 it is concave down.
questions.question: Q7(ii). Determine where the graph of f(x) = x^4 - 8x^3 + 18x^2 - 24 is concave upwards and where concave downwards. (HSEB 2056)
questions.solution: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 24x^2 + 36x, f''(x) = 12x^2 - 48x + 36 = 12(x^2 - 4x + 3) = 12(x - 1)(x - 3). Hence f'' > 0 for x < 1 and x > 3 (concave upwards), and f'' < 0 for 1 < x < 3 (concave downwards). Boxed concave upwards on (-infinity, 1) U (3, infinity), concave downwards on (1, 3) (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q7(ii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: y'' = 60x(x^2+1): the quadratic factor is always positive, so only the sign of x matters.
questions.question: Q7(iii). Determine where the graph of y = 3x^5 + 10x^3 + 15x is concave upwards and where concave downwards.
questions.solution: y' = 15x^4 + 30x^2 + 15, y'' = 60x^3 + 60x = 60x(x^2 + 1). Since x^2 + 1 > 0 always, the sign of y'' is the sign of x: y'' > 0 for x > 0 (concave upwards), y'' < 0 for x < 0 (concave downwards). Boxed concave upwards on (0, infinity), concave downwards on (-infinity, 0) (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q7(iii); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: f'' = 6(x-3): the concavity changes at x = 3, and the domain cuts the branches at -2 and 5.
questions.question: Q7(iv). Determine where the graph of f(x) = x^3 - 9x^2 is concave upwards and where concave downwards, given x is in [-2, 5].
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 18x, f''(x) = 6x - 18 = 6(x - 3). On the stated domain: f'' > 0 for 3 < x <= 5 (concave upwards), f'' < 0 for -2 <= x < 3 (concave downwards). Boxed concave upwards on (3, 5], concave downwards on [-2, 3) (printed key p551).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q7(iv); book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Fixed perimeter means the maximum rectangle is the square: 36 m x 36 m, area 1296 m^2.
questions.question: Q8. A man who has 144 metres of fencing material wishes to enclose a rectangular garden. Find the maximum area he can enclose. (HSEB 2054)
questions.solution: Let the sides be x and y with 2(x + y) = 144, so x + y = 72 and y = 72 - x. The area is A(x) = x(72 - x) = 72x - x^2, 0 < x < 72. A'(x) = 72 - 2x = 0 gives x = 36, and A''(x) = -2 < 0, so this is a maximum. Then y = 36 and A = 36 * 36 = 1296. Boxed maximum area 1296 sq. m (printed key p552).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q8; book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: A' = P/2 - 2x gives x = P/4 for both sides — the square — and A'' = -2 confirms a maximum.
questions.question: Q9. Show that the rectangle of largest possible area, for a given perimeter, is a square. (HSEB 2058)
questions.solution: Let the perimeter be P (fixed) and the sides x and y, so 2(x + y) = P and y = P/2 - x. Area A(x) = x(P/2 - x) = Px/2 - x^2. A'(x) = P/2 - 2x = 0 gives x = P/4, and A''(x) = -2 < 0, so it is a maximum. Then y = P/2 - P/4 = P/4 = x: the rectangle is a square, with area P^2/16. Boxed (no separate key entry: 'show that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q9; book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Perimeter 2h + 2r + pi r = 9; substituting h turns A into a quadratic in r, and A' = 9 - (4 + pi)r gives r = 9/(4+pi).
questions.question: Q10. A window is in the form of a rectangle surmounted by a semi-circle. If the total perimeter is 9 metres, find the radius of the semi-circle for the greatest window area. (HSEB 2055)
questions.solution: Let the semi-circle have radius r, so the rectangle has width 2r and height h. The perimeter is the two vertical sides, the base, and the semi-circular arc: 2h + 2r + pi r = 9, so h = (9 - 2r - pi r)/2. Area = rectangle + semi-circle = 2rh + (1/2)pi r^2 = 2r * (9 - 2r - pi r)/2 + (1/2)pi r^2 = 9r - (2 + pi)r^2 + (pi/2)r^2 = 9r - (2 + pi/2)r^2. Then A'(r) = 9 - (4 + pi)r = 0, giving r = 9/(4 + pi). A''(r) = -(4 + pi) < 0, so this is a maximum (h = (9 - (2 + pi) * 9/(4 + pi))/2 > 0, so the window is geometrically possible). Boxed r = 9/(4 + pi) metres (printed key p552: 9/(4 + pi) metres).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q10; book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: S = 2 pi r^2 + 104/r; S' = 0 gives r^3 = 26/pi and the volume condition then forces h = 2r.
questions.question: Q11. A closed cylindrical can is to be made so that its volume is 52 cm^3. Find its dimensions if the surface is to be a minimum.
questions.solution: Let the radius be r and height h. Volume: pi r^2 h = 52, so h = 52/(pi r^2). The total surface of a closed can is S = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h = 2 pi r^2 + 104/r. Then S'(r) = 4 pi r - 104/r^2 = 0 gives 4 pi r^3 = 104, i.e. r^3 = 26/pi, so r = (26/pi)^(1/3). S''(r) = 4 pi + 208/r^3 > 0, so this is a minimum. The height is h = 52/(pi r^2); using pi r^3 = 26 we get pi r^2 = 26/r, hence h = 52/(26/r) = 2r. Boxed radius (26/pi)^(1/3) cm with height = 2 radius (printed key p552: 'height = 2 radius where radius = (26/pi)^(1/3)').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q11; book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Three parallel fences of length y plus two of length x: 2x + 3y = 120; maximising xy gives x = 30, y = 20.
questions.question: Q12. A gardener having 120 m of fencing wishes to enclose a rectangular plot of land and also to erect a fence across the land parallel to two of the sides. Find the maximum area he can enclose.
questions.solution: Let the plot be x by y with the dividing fence parallel to the sides of length y. The fencing used is 2x + 3y = 120, so y = (120 - 2x)/3. Area A(x) = xy = x(120 - 2x)/3 = (120x - 2x^2)/3. A'(x) = (120 - 4x)/3 = 0 gives x = 30, hence y = (120 - 60)/3 = 20. A''(x) = -4/3 < 0, so it is a maximum. A = 30 * 20 = 600. Boxed 600 sq. m (printed key p552: 600 m^2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q12; book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: S = x^2 + (10-x)^2 is a convex quadratic with vertex at x = 5; equal halves minimise the sum of squares.
questions.question: Q13. Find two numbers whose sum is 10 and the sum of whose squares is minimum.
questions.solution: Let the numbers be x and 10 - x. Then S(x) = x^2 + (10 - x)^2 = 2x^2 - 20x + 100. S'(x) = 4x - 20 = 0 gives x = 5, and S''(x) = 4 > 0, so this is a minimum. The second number is 10 - 5 = 5. Boxed 5 and 5 (printed key p552: 5, 5).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.1 Q13; book p550-551 = PDF p577-578; key book p551-552 = PDF p578-579

questions.knowledgeNote: Differentiate s once for velocity (m/s) and twice for acceleration (m/s^2); a constant second derivative means uniform acceleration.
questions.question: Q1(a). A particle moves in a straight line. The distance s (in metre) covered in time t (in second) is s = 2t^2 + 5t - 4. Find the velocity and the acceleration of the particle at t = 6 sec.
questions.solution: Velocity is the time-derivative of displacement and acceleration the time-derivative of velocity. v = ds/dt = 4t + 5; at t = 6: v = 24 + 5 = 29 m/s. a = dv/dt = d^2s/dt^2 = 4 (constant); at t = 6: a = 4 m/s^2. Boxed 29 m/s and 4 m/s^2 (printed key p559: 29 m/s, 4 m/s^2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q1(a); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: The displacement is quadratic, so the acceleration is a constant -30 m/s^2 (uniformly retarded motion).
questions.question: Q1(b). The displacement of a particle varies with time as x = -15t^2 + 20t + 30. Find the velocity and the acceleration of the particle at t = 1/2 second (distance in metre, time in second).
questions.solution: v = dx/dt = -30t + 20; at t = 1/2: v = -15 + 20 = 5 m/s. a = dv/dt = -30 m/s^2 for every t, so at t = 1/2: a = -30 m/s^2. Boxed 5 m/s and -30 m/s^2 (printed key p559: 5 m/s, -30 m/s^2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q1(b); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Related rates: differentiate the geometric relation with respect to time, then substitute the instantaneous values.
questions.question: Q2(a). The side of a square sheet is increasing at the rate of 5 cm/min. At what rate is the area increasing when the side is 12 cm long?
questions.solution: Let the side be x and the area A = x^2. Differentiate with respect to t: dA/dt = 2x dx/dt. Given dx/dt = 5 cm/min and x = 12 cm: dA/dt = 2(12)(5) = 120. Boxed 120 cm^2/min (printed key p559: 120 cm^2/min).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q2(a); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Note 2 * 52.5 = 105 and 105 / 7 = 15, so the 22/7 cancels neatly to 330.
questions.question: Q2(b). A stone thrown into a pond produces circular ripples which expand from the point of impact. If the radius of the ripple increases at the rate of 3.5 cm/sec, how fast is the area growing when the radius is 15 cm? (pi = 22/7)
questions.solution: A = pi r^2, so dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt. With r = 15, dr/dt = 3.5 and pi = 22/7: dA/dt = 2 * (22/7) * 15 * 3.5 = 2 * (22/7) * 52.5 = 330. Boxed 330 cm^2/sec (printed key p559: 330 cm^2/sec).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q2(b); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Only the cross-sectional area pi r^2 multiplies dh/dt; the total height 40 cm is redundant data in this printing.
questions.question: Q3(a). From a cylindrical drum containing oil and kept vertical, the oil is leaking so that the level of the oil is decreasing at the rate of 2 cm/min. If the radius and the height of the drum are 10.5 cm and 40 cm respectively, find the rate at which the volume of the oil is decreasing. (pi = 22/7)
questions.solution: V = pi r^2 h with r constant (10.5 cm): dV/dt = pi r^2 dh/dt. Given dh/dt = -2 cm/min (level decreasing), dV/dt = (22/7)(10.5)^2(-2) = (22/7)(110.25)(-2) = -(22/7)(220.5) = -693. Hence the volume decreases at 693 cm^3/min. Boxed 693 cm^3/min (printed key p560: 693 cm^3/min). The drum's height 40 cm is not needed: the level is falling with the full cross-section pi r^2 throughout.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q3(a); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: The rising speed is the flow rate divided by the base area 64 pi cm^2.
questions.question: Q3(b). Water is poured into a right circular cylinder of radius 8 cm at the rate of 18 cu.cm/min. Find the rate at which the level of water is rising in the cylinder.
questions.solution: V = pi r^2 h with r = 8 cm fixed, so dV/dt = 64 pi dh/dt. Given dV/dt = 18: 64 pi dh/dt = 18, dh/dt = 18/(64 pi) = 9/(32 pi). Boxed 9/(32 pi) cm/min (printed key p560: 9/(32 pi) cm/min).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q3(b); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Same pattern as Q3(b): rate of rise = flow rate / base area (81 pi).
questions.question: Q3(c). Gasoline is pumped into a vertical cylindrical tank at the rate of 24 cu.cm/min. The radius of the tank is 9 cm. How fast is the surface rising?
questions.solution: V = pi r^2 h with r = 9 cm fixed: dV/dt = 81 pi dh/dt. Given dV/dt = 24: dh/dt = 24/(81 pi) = 8/(27 pi). Boxed 8/(27 pi) cm/min (printed key p560: 8/(27 pi) cm/min).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q3(c); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: The surface area 4 pi r^2 is the conversion factor between volume rate and radius rate.
questions.question: Q4(a). A spherical balloon is inflated at the rate of 18 cu.cm/sec. At what rate is the radius increasing when the radius is 8 cm?
questions.solution: V = (4/3) pi r^3, so dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 dr/dt. With dV/dt = 18 and r = 8: 18 = 4 pi (64) dr/dt = 256 pi dr/dt, so dr/dt = 18/(256 pi) = 9/(128 pi). Boxed 9/(128 pi) cm/sec (printed key p560: 9/(128 pi) cm/sec).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q4(a); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Write dV/dt two ways — as S dr/dt and as -kS — then cancel S; the radius rate is the constant -k.
questions.question: Q4(b). A spherical ball of salt is dissolving in water in such a way that the rate of decrease of volume at any instant is proportional to its surface. Prove that the radius is decreasing at a constant rate.
questions.solution: Let r be the radius. Volume V = (4/3) pi r^3 and surface S = 4 pi r^2, so dV/dt = 4 pi r^2 dr/dt = S dr/dt. The hypothesis says dV/dt = -k S for a positive constant k (the rate of decrease is proportional to the surface). Hence S dr/dt = -k S, and since S > 0 for r > 0, dr/dt = -k: the radius decreases at the constant rate k. Boxed (no separate key entry: 'prove that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q4(b); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Eliminate r using r = h/3 first, so V depends on h alone: V = pi h^3/27 and dV/dt = (pi h^2/9) dh/dt.
questions.question: Q5(a). The radius of a conical tank is 1/3 of the height. Water flows into an inverted conical tank at the rate of 4.4 cu.cm/sec. How fast is the level rising when the height of the water is 3.5 cm? (pi = 22/7)
questions.solution: With r = h/3, the water volume is V = (1/3) pi r^2 h = (1/3) pi (h^2/9) h = pi h^3/27. Differentiate: dV/dt = (pi h^2/9) dh/dt. Given dV/dt = 4.4 and h = 3.5: (22/7)(12.25)/9 * dh/dt = 4.4, and (22/7)(12.25) = 38.5, so (38.5/9) dh/dt = 4.4, giving dh/dt = 4.4 * 9/38.5 = 39.6/38.5 = 36/35. Boxed 36/35 cm/sec (printed key p560: 36/35 cm/sec).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q5(a); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: The tank's own dimensions fix the cone ratio r/h = 1/2; after that it is the same one-variable computation as Q5(a).
questions.question: Q5(b). Water flows into an inverted conical tank at the rate of 42 cm^3/sec. When the depth of the water is 8 cm, how fast is the level rising? Assume that the height of the tank is 12 cm and the radius of the top is 6 cm.
questions.solution: Similar triangles give r/h = 6/12 = 1/2, so r = h/2 and V = (1/3) pi (h^2/4) h = pi h^3/12. Then dV/dt = (pi h^2/4) dh/dt. With dV/dt = 42 and h = 8: 42 = (pi * 64/4) dh/dt = 16 pi dh/dt, so dh/dt = 42/(16 pi) = 21/(8 pi). Boxed 21/(8 pi) cm/sec (printed key p560: 21/(8 pi) cm/sec).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q5(b); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Find the edge from the given surface first, get dx/dt from the volume rate, then convert to dS/dt = 12x dx/dt.
questions.question: Q6. If the volume of the expanding cube is increasing at the rate of 24 cm^3/min, how fast is its surface area increasing when the surface area is 216 cm^2?
questions.solution: Surface area S = 6x^2 = 216 gives x^2 = 36, so the edge is x = 6 cm. Volume V = x^3 gives dV/dt = 3x^2 dx/dt: 24 = 3(36) dx/dt = 108 dx/dt, so dx/dt = 2/9 cm/min. Surface area S = 6x^2 gives dS/dt = 12x dx/dt = 12(6)(2/9) = 16. Boxed 16 cm^2/min (printed key p560: 16 cm^2/min).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q6; book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: A = pi(R^2 - r^2): the outer circle gains 210 cm^2/sec of area while the inner loses 240, so the annulus shrinks.
questions.question: Q7. Two concentric circles are expanding in such a way that the radius of the inner circle is increasing at the rate of 10 cm/sec and that of the outer circle at the rate of 7 cm/sec. At a certain time the radii of the inner and the outer circles are respectively 24 cm and 30 cm. At that time, is the area between the circles increasing or decreasing? How fast?
questions.solution: Let R be the outer and r the inner radius; the area between them is A = pi(R^2 - r^2). Then dA/dt = 2 pi (R dR/dt - r dr/dt). With R = 30, dR/dt = 7, r = 24, dr/dt = 10: dA/dt = 2 pi (30 * 7 - 24 * 10) = 2 pi (210 - 240) = -60 pi. The negative sign means the area is decreasing at 60 pi cm^2/sec. Boxed decreasing at 60 pi cm^2/sec (printed key p560: '60 pi cm^2/sec (decreasing)').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q7; book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Similar triangles give s = x/2 independently of x; the shadow grows at half the walking speed (the 42 cm data is not needed).
questions.question: Q8. A man of height 1.5 m walks away from a lamp post of height 4.5 m at the rate of 20 cm/sec. How fast is his shadow lengthening when the man is 42 cm from the post?
questions.solution: Let x be the man's distance from the post and s the length of his shadow (from his feet to its tip, measured away from the post). The lamp post and the man give similar triangles: s/(x + s) = 1.5/4.5 = 1/3. Hence 3s = x + s, i.e. 2s = x, so s = x/2. Differentiate: ds/dt = (1/2) dx/dt = (1/2)(20) = 10 cm/sec. Boxed 10 cm/sec (printed key p560: 10 cm/sec). The instantaneous distance 42 cm does not affect the answer, because the ratio s = x/2 is fixed for the given heights.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q8; book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Chain rule along the curve gives dy/dt = y'(x) dx/dt = 12 * 2 = 24; then differentiate D^2 to get dD/dt = (x x' + y y')/D at D = 2 sqrt 5.
questions.question: Q9. A point is moving along the curve y = 2x^3 - 3x^2 in such a way that its x-coordinate is increasing at the rate of 2 cm/sec. Find the rate at which the distance of the point from the origin is increasing when the point is at (2, 4).
questions.solution: Let the point be (x, y) with y = 2x^3 - 3x^2, and let D be its distance from the origin: D^2 = x^2 + y^2. At (2, 4): D = sqrt(4 + 16) = sqrt(20) = 2 sqrt(5). Differentiate D^2 = x^2 + y^2: 2D dD/dt = 2x dx/dt + 2y dy/dt, i.e. dD/dt = (x dx/dt + y dy/dt)/D. Now dy/dt = (6x^2 - 6x) dx/dt; at x = 2, dy/dx = 24 - 12 = 12, so dy/dt = 12(2) = 24 cm/sec. Hence dD/dt = (2(2) + 4(24))/(2 sqrt 5) = 100/(2 sqrt 5) = 50/sqrt 5 = 10 sqrt 5. Boxed 10 sqrt 5 cm/sec (printed key p560: 10 sqrt 5 cm/sec).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q9; book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Pythagoras with fixed height: at L = 25 the horizontal leg is 7 m, so the cord pays out at (7/25) of the kite's speed.
questions.question: Q10(a). A kite is 24 m high and there are 25 metres of cord out. If the kite moves horizontally at the rate of 36 km/hr directly away from the person who is flying it, how fast is the cord out?
questions.solution: Let x be the horizontal distance and L the length of cord; the kite height 24 m stays fixed, so L^2 = x^2 + 24^2. When L = 25: x^2 = 625 - 576 = 49, so x = 7 m. Differentiate: 2L dL/dt = 2x dx/dt, i.e. dL/dt = (x/L) dx/dt = (7/25)(36) = 10.08. Boxed 10.08 km/hr (printed key p560: 10.08 km/hr).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q10(a); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Keep the units consistent (250 cm, 200 cm, hence 150 cm); the foot speeds up as the top comes down because dx/dt = -(y/x)dy/dt.
questions.question: Q10(b). A 2.5 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. If the top slides downwards at the rate of 12 cm/sec, find the speed of the lower end when it is 2 m from the wall.
questions.solution: Let x be the distance of the foot from the wall and y the height of the top, both in cm: x^2 + y^2 = 250^2. When x = 200 cm, y^2 = 62500 - 40000 = 22500, so y = 150 cm. Differentiate: 2x dx/dt + 2y dy/dt = 0, so dx/dt = -(y/x) dy/dt = -(150/200)(-12) = 9 cm/sec. Boxed 9 cm/sec (printed key p560: 9 cm/sec).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Exercise 18.2 (Rate of change / rate measure) Q10(b); book p558-559 = PDF p585-586; key book p559-560 = PDF p586-587

questions.knowledgeNote: Extremum = stationary point where f' changes sign; second derivative decides (f'' < 0 max, f'' > 0 min, 0 inconclusive).
questions.question: Q1. What are the maximum and minimum values of a function at a point? What are the criteria to be satisfied in order to have maximum and minimum values of a function?
questions.solution: Definitions. A function f has a local maximum at x = a if f(a) >= f(x) for all x in some open interval around a; it has a local minimum at x = a if f(a) <= f(x) on such an interval. The maximum and minimum values themselves are f(a). Criteria. (1) Necessary condition: if f is differentiable at a and has an extremum there, then f'(a) = 0 (a is a stationary point). (2) First-derivative (sign) test: if f' changes from + to - at a, f(a) is a maximum; if f' changes from - to + at a, f(a) is a minimum; if f' does not change sign, a is a point of inflection. (3) Second-derivative test: at a stationary point, f''(a) < 0 gives a maximum, f''(a) > 0 gives a minimum, and f''(a) = 0 is inconclusive (fall back to the sign test). (4) For an absolute extremum on a closed interval [a, b], compare the values of f at all interior stationary points with f(a) and f(b). Boxed (definition question - no numeric key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q1; book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: An even power: the graph bottoms out at x = 3 with value 0 and rises without bound on both sides.
questions.question: Q2(i). Find the maximum and minimum values of y = (x - 3)^4.
questions.solution: y' = 4(x - 3)^3 = 0 gives x = 3. y'' = 12(x - 3)^2 >= 0, and in fact y''(3) = 0, so the second-derivative test is inconclusive; use the sign test: for x < 3, y' < 0, and for x > 3, y' > 0, so y' changes from - to + at x = 3 and the point is a minimum. The value is y(3) = 0. Since y = (x - 3)^4 >= 0 for every x, 0 is also the absolute minimum, and there is no maximum. Boxed minimum value 0 at x = 3 (printed key p561).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q2(i); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Factor out (x + 2): y' = (x+2)(3x), and y'' = 6x + 6 decides which stationary point is which.
questions.question: Q2(ii). Find the maximum and minimum values of y = (x - 1)(x + 2)^2.
questions.solution: y' = (x + 2)^2 + 2(x - 1)(x + 2) = (x + 2)[(x + 2) + 2(x - 1)] = (x + 2)(3x) = 3x(x + 2) = 0 at x = 0 and x = -2. y'' = 6x + 6: y''(0) = 6 > 0, so x = 0 gives a minimum y(0) = (-1)(4) = -4; y''(-2) = -6 < 0, so x = -2 gives a maximum y(-2) = (-3)(0) = 0. Boxed minimum -4 at x = 0, maximum 0 at x = -2 (printed key p561: 'min. value = -4 at x = 0; max. value = 0 at x = -2').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q2(ii); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: The sign chart comes from (x-4)(x-16) alone; note the maximum (1) is numerically smaller than the minimum (25) because the branch across x = 10 is separate.
questions.question: Q2(iii). Find the maximum and minimum values of y = (x^2 - 7x + 6)/(x - 10).
questions.solution: Quotient rule: y' = [(2x - 7)(x - 10) - (x^2 - 7x + 6)]/(x - 10)^2 = (2x^2 - 27x + 70 - x^2 + 7x - 6)/(x - 10)^2 = (x^2 - 20x + 64)/(x - 10)^2 = (x - 4)(x - 16)/(x - 10)^2. Critical points x = 4 and x = 16 (x = 10 is not in the domain). Values: y(4) = (16 - 28 + 6)/(4 - 10) = (-6)/(-6) = 1; y(16) = (256 - 112 + 6)/(16 - 10) = 150/6 = 25. The denominator (x - 10)^2 > 0, so the sign of y' is the sign of (x - 4)(x - 16): positive outside [4, 16], negative between. Hence x = 4 gives a maximum 1 and x = 16 a minimum 25. Boxed max 1 at x = 4, min 25 at x = 16 (printed key p561).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q2(iii); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: The vertex formula: x = -b/(2a), value (4ac - b^2)/(4a); the sign of a decides maximum versus minimum.
questions.question: Q2(iv). Find the maximum and minimum values of y = ax^2 + bx + c.
questions.solution: y' = 2ax + b = 0 gives the single stationary point x = -b/(2a) (a != 0). Its value is y = a b^2/(4a^2) - b^2/(2a) + c = c - b^2/(4a) = (4ac - b^2)/(4a). The second derivative is y'' = 2a, so if a > 0 the parabola opens upward and the point is a minimum; if a < 0 it opens downward and the point is a maximum. Boxed minimum (4ac - b^2)/(4a) at x = -b/(2a) when a > 0; maximum (4ac - b^2)/(4a) at x = -b/(2a) when a < 0 (printed key p561).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q2(iv); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Classic cubic with two turning points symmetric about the origin; f(-1) = 2 and f(1) = -2.
questions.question: Q2(v). Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = x^3 - 3x.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1) = 0 at x = 1 and x = -1. f''(x) = 6x: f''(-1) = -6 < 0, so x = -1 gives a maximum f(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2; f''(1) = 6 > 0, so x = 1 gives a minimum f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2. Boxed maximum 2 at x = -1, minimum -2 at x = 1 (printed key p561).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q2(v); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Both turning points lie on the negative axis, one unit apart; the vertical gap is only 1.
questions.question: Q2(vi). Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = 2x^3 + 9x^2 + 12x + 2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q2(vi); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Factor the cubic derivative as (x+1)(x-3)(x+2); the quartic has one maximum between two minima, the deeper one at x = 3.
questions.question: Q2(vii). Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = x^4 - 14x^2 - 24x + 1.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 28x - 24 = 4(x^3 - 7x - 6) = 4(x + 1)(x - 3)(x + 2) = 0 at x = -1, x = -2 and x = 3. f''(x) = 12x^2 - 28: f''(-1) = -16 < 0, so x = -1 gives a maximum f(-1) = 1 - 14 + 24 + 1 = 12; f''(-2) = 20 > 0, so x = -2 gives a local minimum f(-2) = 16 - 56 + 48 + 1 = 9; f''(3) = 80 > 0, so x = 3 gives a local minimum f(3) = 81 - 126 - 72 + 1 = -116. Boxed maximum 12 at x = -1; minima 9 at x = -2 and -116 at x = 3 (printed key p561: 'max. value = 12 at x = -1; min. value = 9 at x = -2; min. value = -116 at x = 3').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q2(vii); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: The double root x^2 in f' means no sign change at 0; the simple roots 1 and 3 are certified by the second derivative -10 and +90.
questions.question: Q3. Show that x^5 - 5x^4 + 5x^3 - 1 is maximum when x = 1, minimum when x = 3, and neither when x = 0.
questions.solution: Let f(x) = x^5 - 5x^4 + 5x^3 - 1. f'(x) = 5x^4 - 20x^3 + 15x^2 = 5x^2(x^2 - 4x + 3) = 5x^2(x - 1)(x - 3), so the stationary points are x = 0 (double root), x = 1, x = 3. f''(x) = 20x^3 - 60x^2 + 30x = 10x(2x^2 - 6x + 3). At x = 1: f''(1) = 20 - 60 + 30 = -10 < 0, so f(1) = 1 - 5 + 5 - 1 = 0 is a maximum. At x = 3: f''(3) = 540 - 540 + 90 = 90 > 0, so f(3) = 243 - 405 + 135 - 1 = -28 is a minimum. At x = 0: f''(0) = 0, and near 0 the factor 5x^2 is positive on both sides while (x - 1)(x - 3) is positive, so f' > 0 immediately left and right of 0: no sign change, hence neither maximum nor minimum (a stationary point of inflection). Boxed as required (no separate key entry: 'show that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q3; book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: A.M. >= G.M. also gives it instantly: x + 100/x >= 2 sqrt(100) = 20 with equality at x = 10.
questions.question: Q4(i). Find two positive numbers whose product is 100 and whose sum is as small as possible. What is the minimum sum?
questions.solution: Let the numbers be x and 100/x (positive). Sum S(x) = x + 100/x. S'(x) = 1 - 100/x^2 = 0 gives x^2 = 100, x = 10 (positive). S''(x) = 200/x^3 > 0 at x = 10, so the sum is a minimum there; the other number is also 10 and the sum is 20. Boxed the numbers 10 and 10, minimum sum 20 (printed key p562: '10, 10; 20').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q4(i); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: The sum of squares is convex with vertex at the midpoint: equal halves minimise it.
questions.question: Q4(ii). Divide 60 into two parts such that the sum of the squares of the two parts is minimum.
questions.solution: Let the parts be x and 60 - x. Then S(x) = x^2 + (60 - x)^2 = 2x^2 - 120x + 3600. S'(x) = 4x - 120 = 0 gives x = 30, and S''(x) = 4 > 0, so this is a minimum; the other part is 30. Boxed 30 and 30 (printed key p562: '30, 30').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q4(ii); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: An interior maximum of a differentiable function forces f'(1) = 0; the value a = 120 is then confirmed by comparing f(1) = 68 with the endpoints.
questions.question: Q5. It is given that at x = 1 the function x^4 - 62x^2 + ax + 9 attains its maximum value on the interval [0, 2]. Find the value of a.
questions.solution: Since the maximum is attained at the interior point x = 1 and the polynomial is differentiable, x = 1 must be a stationary point: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 124x + a, so f'(1) = 4 - 124 + a = 0, giving a = 120. Check: with a = 120, f'(x) = 4x^3 - 124x + 120 and f''(x) = 12x^2 - 124, so f''(1) = -112 < 0 - a maximum, and f(1) = 1 - 62 + 120 + 9 = 68 exceeds f(0) = 9 and f(2) = 16 - 248 + 240 + 9 = 17, so 68 really is the maximum on [0, 2]. Boxed a = 120 (printed key p562: 120).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q5; book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: f'' = 12x(x+2) has roots -2 and 0; upward outside that interval, downward inside it.
questions.question: Q6(i). Determine where the graph of f(x) = x^4 + 4x^3 - 1 is concave upwards and where it is concave downwards.
questions.solution: f'(x) = 4x^3 + 12x^2, f''(x) = 12x^2 + 24x = 12x(x + 2). f'' > 0 for x < -2 and for x > 0 (concave upwards); f'' < 0 for -2 < x < 0 (concave downwards). Boxed concave upwards on (-infinity, -2) U (0, infinity), concave downwards on (-2, 0) (printed key p562).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q6(i); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: The product form matters only through the expanded quartic; concavity changes at x = +-1.
questions.question: Q6(ii). Determine where the graph of y = (x^2 - 1)(x^2 - 5) is concave upwards and where it is concave downwards.
questions.solution: Expand: y = x^4 - 6x^2 + 5, so y' = 4x^3 - 12x and y'' = 12x^2 - 12 = 12(x - 1)(x + 1). Hence y'' > 0 for x < -1 and x > 1 (concave upwards), y'' < 0 for -1 < x < 1 (concave downwards). Boxed concave upwards on (-infinity, -1) U (1, infinity), concave downwards on (-1, 1) (printed key p562).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q6(ii); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: x^2 y >= 0 on the feasible segment, and u = 0 at x = 0 (y = 7); the interior critical point x = 14/3 is the maximum 1372/27.
questions.question: Q7(i). Find the minimum value of x^2 y when x + y = 7.
questions.solution: From x + y = 7 we get y = 7 - x, so the quantity is u(x) = x^2(7 - x) = 7x^2 - x^3. u'(x) = 14x - 3x^2 = x(14 - 3x) = 0 at x = 0 and x = 14/3 (y = 7/3). At x = 14/3, u'' = 14 - 6x = -14 < 0, a maximum, not a minimum. The minimum is at x = 0, where y = 7 and u = 0; indeed u = x^2 y >= 0 whenever y >= 0, and u = 0 also at x = 7, y = 0. Boxed minimum value 0 (printed key p562: 'Min. value = 0').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q7(i); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Splitting a in the ratio 2:1 maximises x^2 y; the value is 4a^3/27.
questions.question: Q7(ii). If x + y = a (a > 0), find the maximum value of x^2 y.
questions.solution: y = a - x, so u(x) = x^2(a - x) = ax^2 - x^3. u'(x) = 2ax - 3x^2 = x(2a - 3x) = 0 at x = 0 and x = 2a/3. u''(x) = 2a - 6x: u''(2a/3) = 2a - 4a = -2a < 0, so x = 2a/3 gives the maximum, with y = a - 2a/3 = a/3 and u = (4a^2/9)(a/3) = 4a^3/27. Boxed maximum value 4a^3/27 at x = 2a/3, y = a/3 (printed key p562: 4a^3/27).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q7(ii); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Solving 36x^2 = 4(2-x)^2 gives the two branches x = 1/2 and x = -1; the modulus-free squaring is why both must be examined.
questions.question: Q7(iii). Find the maximum and minimum values of u = 4/x + 36/y where x + y = 2.
questions.solution: Put y = 2 - x: u(x) = 4/x + 36/(2 - x). u'(x) = -4/x^2 + 36/(2 - x)^2 = 0 gives 36x^2 = 4(2 - x)^2, i.e. 6x = +-2(2 - x). The positive branch: 6x = 4 - 2x, so x = 1/2 and y = 3/2, giving u = 8 + 24 = 32. The negative branch: 6x = -4 + 2x, so x = -1 and y = 3, giving u = -4 + 12 = 8. Classifying with the second derivative u''(x) = 8/x^3 + 72/(2 - x)^3: at x = 1/2, u'' = 64 + 216/3.375 = 64 + 64 > 0, a minimum; at x = -1, u'' = -8 + 72/27 = -8 + 8/3 < 0, a maximum. Boxed maximum 8 at x = -1, minimum 32 at x = 1/2 (printed key p562: 'Max. value = 8 at x = -1, Min. value = 32 at x = 1/2').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q7(iii); book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Constant dA/dt means dr/dt = k/(2 pi r); multiplying by 2 pi gives dP/dt = k/r.
questions.question: Q8. If the area of a circle increases at a uniform rate, prove that the rate of increase of the perimeter varies inversely as the radius.
questions.solution: Let r be the radius, A = pi r^2 the area and P = 2 pi r the perimeter. The hypothesis gives dA/dt = k, a constant. Differentiating A: dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt = k, so dr/dt = k/(2 pi r). Then dP/dt = 2 pi dr/dt = 2 pi * k/(2 pi r) = k/r. Hence dP/dt is proportional to 1/r: the perimeter's rate of increase varies inversely as the radius. Boxed (no separate key entry: 'prove that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q8; book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: cos 120 deg = -1/2 makes the cosine rule add: d^2 = 3v^2t^2, so d grows linearly at sqrt(3) v.
questions.question: Q9. Two cars start at the same time from the junction of two roads, one on each road, with uniform speed v m.p.s. If the roads are inclined at 120 degrees, show that the distance between them increases at the rate of sqrt(3) v m.p.s.
questions.solution: After t seconds each car has travelled vt metres. The distance d between them satisfies the cosine rule with the included angle 120 degrees: d^2 = (vt)^2 + (vt)^2 - 2(vt)(vt) cos 120 degrees = 2v^2t^2 + v^2t^2 = 3v^2t^2 (since cos 120 degrees = -1/2, so -2(vt)^2(-1/2) = +(vt)^2). Hence d = sqrt(3) vt, and dd/dt = sqrt(3) v. Boxed (no separate key entry: 'show that').
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q9; book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Positions (9t, 0) and (0, -12(t-1)); differentiate d^2 = 81t^2 + 144(t-1)^2 at t = 2 with d = 6 sqrt 13.
questions.question: Q10. A ship leaves a port at noon and travels east at the rate of 9 km/hr. Another ship leaves the same port after one hour and sails south at the rate of 12 km/hr. How fast are they separating at 2 PM?
questions.solution: Measure t in hours after noon. The first ship is at (9t, 0). The second ship has been sailing for (t - 1) hours, so it is at (0, -12(t - 1)). The square of their separation is d^2 = (9t)^2 + [12(t - 1)]^2 = 81t^2 + 144(t - 1)^2. At 2 PM, t = 2: d^2 = 324 + 144 = 468, so d = sqrt(468) = 6 sqrt(13). Differentiate d^2: 2d dd/dt = 162t + 288(t - 1), so at t = 2, 2d dd/dt = 324 + 288 = 612, giving dd/dt = 612/(2 * 6 sqrt 13) = 51/sqrt(13) km/hr. Boxed 51/sqrt(13) km/hr (printed key p562: 51/sqrt(13) km/hr).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q10; book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Both the man and the shadow tip move, so the tip's speed is (3/2)v = 30 cm/sec, while the shadow only lengthens at v/2 = 10 cm/sec.
questions.question: Q11. A man of height 1.5 m walks away from a lamp post of height 4.5 m at the rate of 20 cm/sec. How fast does the end of his shadow move?
questions.solution: Let x be the man's distance from the post at time t and s the shadow length. Similar triangles: s/(x + s) = 1.5/4.5 = 1/3, so 3s = x + s, i.e. s = x/2. The tip of the shadow is at distance x + s = 3x/2 from the post. Differentiate: d/dt(x + s) = (3/2) dx/dt = (3/2)(20) = 30 cm/sec. Boxed 30 cm/sec (printed key p562: 30 cm/sec). Compare Exercise 18.2 Q8, where the shadow's *length* grows at 10 cm/sec: the tip moves three times as fast as the man.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.18 Additional Questions (Maxima, Minima and Rate Measure) Q11; book p560-561 = PDF p587-588; key book p561-562 = PDF p588-589

questions.knowledgeNote: Power rule plus constant multiple: 5x^3 integrates to (5/4)x^4; the +c records the family of antiderivatives.
questions.question: Q1(i). Find the indefinite integral: integral of 5x^3 dx.
questions.solution: Use the power rule integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c for n = 3, then the constant multiple rule: integral 5x^3 dx = 5 * x^4/4 + c = (5/4)x^4 + c. Check by differentiating: d/dx[(5/4)x^4] = (5/4)(4x^3) = 5x^3. Boxed (5/4)x^4 + c (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: Term-by-term integration of a polynomial; one constant c for the whole sum.
questions.question: Q2(i). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (x^2 + 2) dx.
questions.solution: Integrate term by term: integral x^2 dx = x^3/3 and integral 2 dx = 2x. Sum: (1/3)x^3 + 2x + c. Check: d/dx[(1/3)x^3 + 2x] = x^2 + 2. Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: The coefficients 3 and 2 are exactly cancelled by the power-rule denominators 3 and 2.
questions.question: Q2(ii). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (3x^2 + 2x + 1) dx.
questions.solution: Integrate each term: 3 * x^3/3 = x^3, 2 * x^2/2 = x^2, integral 1 dx = x. Sum: x^3 + x^2 + x + c. Check by differentiation: 3x^2 + 2x + 1. Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: There is no product rule for integrals, so multiply the brackets out before integrating.
questions.question: Q2(iv). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (2x + 1)(3x + 2) dx.
questions.solution: Expand first: (2x + 1)(3x + 2) = 6x^2 + 4x + 3x + 2 = 6x^2 + 7x + 2. Integrate: 6x^3/3 + 7x^2/2 + 2x = 2x^3 + (7/2)x^2 + 2x + c. Check: d/dx = 6x^2 + 7x + 2. Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: A negative power integrates to a smaller negative power: x^(-2) -> x^(-1)/(-1) = -1/x, so the minus signs give +1/x.
questions.question: Q2(v). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (x^2 - 1/x^2) dx.
questions.solution: Write 1/x^2 as x^(-2): integral x^2 dx - integral x^(-2) dx = x^3/3 - x^(-1)/(-1) = (1/3)x^3 + 1/x + c. Check: d/dx[(1/3)x^3 + x^(-1)] = x^2 - x^(-2). Boxed (printed key p571: (1/3)x^3 + 1/x + c).

questions.knowledgeNote: Convert the surds to powers before integrating; note the minus sign survives on the second term.
questions.question: Q2(vi). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (sqrt(x) - 1/sqrt(x)) dx.
questions.solution: Rewrite with fractional indices: sqrt(x) = x^(1/2) and 1/sqrt(x) = x^(-1/2). Then integral x^(1/2) dx = (2/3)x^(3/2) and integral x^(-1/2) dx = x^(1/2)/(1/2) = 2x^(1/2). Hence (2/3)x^(3/2) - 2x^(1/2) + c. Check: d/dx = x^(1/2) - x^(-1/2). Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: Either expand or substitute y = x - 3; both give (1/3)x^3 - 3x^2 + 9x + c, equal to (x-3)^3/3 + c.
questions.question: Q2(viii). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (x - 3)^2 dx.
questions.solution: Expand: (x - 3)^2 = x^2 - 6x + 9. Integrate: x^3/3 - 3x^2 + 9x + c. Check: d/dx = x^2 - 6x + 9 = (x - 3)^2. Boxed (printed key p571). (The substitution y = x - 3 gives the same answer in the compact form (x - 3)^3/3 + c.)

questions.question: Q2(ix). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (3x^2 - 5x + 2)/x dx.
questions.solution: Divide term by term: (3x^2 - 5x + 2)/x = 3x - 5 + 2/x. Integrate: 3x^2/2 - 5x + 2 log x + c. Check: d/dx = 3x - 5 + 2/x, which is the integrand. Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: Three separate standard integrals: constant -> ax, 1/x -> log x, x^(-2) -> -1/x.
questions.question: Q2(x). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (ax^2 + bx + c)/x^2 dx.
questions.solution: Divide by x^2: (ax^2 + bx + c)/x^2 = a + b/x + c x^(-2). Integrate: ax + b log x + c x^(-1)/(-1) = ax + b log x - c/x + k. Check by differentiating: a + b/x + c/x^2. Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: Linear inner function: divide by the inner derivative 3, hence the 1/15.
questions.question: Q3(i). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (3x + 5)^4 dx.
questions.solution: Substitute y = 3x + 5, so dy = 3 dx and dx = dy/3. Then integral (3x + 5)^4 dx = (1/3) integral y^4 dy = (1/3) y^5/5 + c = (3x + 5)^5/15 + c. Check: d/dx[(3x+5)^5/15] = (5(3x+5)^4 * 3)/15 = (3x+5)^4. Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.knowledgeNote: The inner derivative is -b, so the answer carries the factor -1/b.
questions.question: Q3(ii). Find the indefinite integral: integral of (a - bx)^5 dx.
questions.solution: Put y = a - bx, dy = -b dx, so dx = -dy/b. Then integral (a - bx)^5 dx = -(1/b) integral y^5 dy = -(1/b) y^6/6 + c = -(a - bx)^6/(6b) + c. Check: d/dx[-(a-bx)^6/(6b)] = -(6(a-bx)^5(-b))/(6b) = (a-bx)^5. Boxed (printed key p571).

questions.question: Q3(iv). Find the indefinite integral: integral of dx/sqrt(2x + 7).

questions.question: Q3(v). Find the indefinite integral: integral of [x + 1/(x + 3)^2] dx.
