questions.knowledgeNote: Draw the circumdiameter through C: angle CBD is 90 deg, so sinA = a/(2R).
questions.question: AQ1(i). State and establish the sine law. (T.U. 2055S)
questions.solution: Statement: in any triangle ABC, a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC = 2R where R is the circumradius. Proof: let O be the circumcentre and extend CO to meet the circumcircle at D, so CD = 2R is a diameter and angle CBD = 90 deg (angle in a semicircle). Angles CAD... angle CDB equals angle CAB = A (angles in the same segment subtend CB). In right triangle CBD, sin(angle CDB) = BC/CD = a/(2R), so sinA = a/(2R), i.e. a/sinA = 2R. The same construction at the other vertices gives b/sinB = c/sinC = 2R.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q1(i) (T.U. 2055S); book p188 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Projection is sine law + sin(B+C) expansion; tangent law is (sinB - sinC)/(sinB + sinC) plus sum-to-product.
questions.question: AQ1(ii). State the sine law. Use this law to prove the projection law a = b*cosC + c*cosB and the tangent law tan((B-C)/2) = [(b-c)/(b+c)]*cot(A/2) (with cyclic form tan((A-B)/2) = [(a-b)/(a+b)]*cot(C/2)). (T.U. 2057S) (HSEB 2050; cyclic form HSEB 2058)
questions.solution: Sine law: a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC = 2R. Projection: b*cosC + c*cosB = 2R*sinB*cosC + 2R*sinC*cosB = 2R*sin(B+C) = 2R*sinA = a. Tangent law: (b-c)/(b+c) = (sinB - sinC)/(sinB + sinC) = [2*cos((B+C)/2)*sin((B-C)/2)]/[2*sin((B+C)/2)*cos((B-C)/2)] = tan((B-C)/2)*cot((B+C)/2) = tan((B-C)/2)*tan(A/2) (since (B+C)/2 = (pi-A)/2). Hence tan((B-C)/2) = [(b-c)/(b+c)]*cot(A/2). The cyclic form tan((A-B)/2) = [(a-b)/(a+b)]*cot(C/2) (top of book p189, tags T.U. 2057S, HSEB 2058) follows by the same steps with permuted letters.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q1(ii) (T.U. 2057S) (HSEB 2050); book p188 = PDF p216, cyclic form top of book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC is the sine law restated as a continued proportion.
questions.question: AQ2. In any triangle ABC, prove that a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC. (HSEB 2058)
questions.solution: By the sine law each of a/sinA, b/sinB, c/sinC equals 2R, so all three are equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q2 (HSEB 2058); book pp188-189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: The common value 2R is the circumdiameter: each side is a chord subtending its angle at the centre.
questions.question: AQ3. In any triangle, prove that a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC = 2R, where R is the radius of the circumcircle. (HSEB 2051, 2052, 2055)
questions.solution: From AQ1(i), a/sinA = 2R where 2R is the diameter of the circumcircle through the construction with diameter CD = 2R. Repeating at each vertex, b/sinB = c/sinC = 2R as well, so all four expressions are equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q3 (HSEB 2051, 1952... i.e. 2051, 2052, 2055); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: cos(C/2) = sqrt[s(s-c)/(ab)]; the B-forms follow by cyclic permutation: sin(B/2) = sqrt[(s-a)(s-c)/(ac)], tan(B/2) = sqrt[(s-a)(s-c)/(s(s-b))].
questions.question: AQ4. In any triangle ABC, prove that cos(C/2) = sqrt[s(s-c)/(ab)], and write the similar results for sin(B/2) and tan(B/2). (HSEB 2054)
questions.solution: cos^2(C/2) = (1+cosC)/2 = [1 + (a^2+b^2-c^2)/(2ab)]/2 = [(a+b)^2 - c^2]/(4ab) = [(a+b-c)(a+b+c)]/(4ab) = [2(s-c)*2s]/(4ab) = s(s-c)/(ab). Since C/2 is acute, cos(C/2) = sqrt[s(s-c)/(ab)]. Similarly sin(B/2) = sqrt[(s-a)(s-c)/(ac)] (from sin^2(B/2) = (1-cosB)/2) and tan(B/2) = sin(B/2)/cos(B/2) = sqrt[(s-a)(s-c)/(s(s-b))].
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q4 (HSEB 2054); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.question: AQ5. Prove that cos(A/2) = sqrt[s(s-a)/(bc)]. (T.U. 2056S) (HSEB 2057)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q5 (T.U. 2056S) (HSEB 2057); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: c - a*cosB = 2R*sinC*cosB: expand sinC = sin(A+B) and watch sinB*cosB cancel.
questions.question: AQ6(i). In any triangle ABC, prove that (c - a*cosB)/(b - a*cosC) = sinB/sinC.
questions.solution: c - a*cosB = 2R*sinC - 2R*sinA*cosB = 2R*[sin(A+B) - sinA*cosB] = 2R*cosA*sinB. Likewise b - a*cosC = 2R*sinB - 2R*sinA*cosC = 2R*[sin(A+C) - sinA*cosC] = 2R*cosA*sinC. Dividing gives sinB/sinC.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q6(i); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: cos^2B - cos^2C = sin^2C - sin^2B = (c-b)(c+b)/(4R^2): each fraction leaves (c-b)/(4R^2).
questions.question: AQ6(ii). Prove that [(cos^2B - cos^2C)/(b+c)] + [(cos^2C - cos^2A)/(c+a)] + [(cos^2A - cos^2B)/(a+b)] = 0.
questions.solution: cos^2B - cos^2C = (1 - sin^2B) - (1 - sin^2C) = sin^2C - sin^2B = (c^2-b^2)/(4R^2). Dividing by (b+c) gives (c-b)/(4R^2). Cyclically the second term is (a-c)/(4R^2) and the third is (b-a)/(4R^2). Adding: [(c-b) + (a-c) + (b-a)]/(4R^2) = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q6(ii); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: sinB + sinC = 2*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2) cancels the cosine, leaving 16R^2*sin^2(A/2)*cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2); the sum telescopes via (cosC - cosB)/2.
questions.question: AQ6(iii). Prove that [a^2*sin(B-C)/(sinB + sinC)] + [b^2*sin(C-A)/(sinC + sinA)] + [c^2*sin(A-B)/(sinA + sinB)] = 0.
questions.solution: a^2*sin(B-C) = 4R^2*sin^2A*2*sin((B-C)/2)*cos((B-C)/2) and sinB + sinC = 2*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2), so the first term is 16R^2*sin^2(A/2)*cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2). Since cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2) = [cosC - cosB]/2 (from Q5(d) working), the first term equals 8R^2*sin^2(A/2)*(cosC - cosB). Cyclically summing: 8R^2*[sin^2(A/2)*(cosC - cosB) + sin^2(B/2)*(cosA - cosC) + sin^2(C/2)*(cosB - cosA)]. With sin^2(A/2) = (1-cosA)/2 this is 4R^2*[(1-cosA)(cosC - cosB) + (1-cosB)(cosA - cosC) + (1-cosC)(cosB - cosA)] = 4R^2*[(cosC - cosB + cosA - cosC + cosB - cosA) - (cosA*cosC - cosA*cosB + cosB*cosA - cosB*cosC + cosC*cosB - cosC*cosA)] = 4R^2*[0 - 0] = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q6(iii); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: tan(A/2)*tan(B/2) = r/(s-c)... no: use Delta: tan(A/2)*tan(B/2) = Delta^2/[(s(s-a))(s(s-b))]... simplest is (s-c)/s via r^2 = (s-a)(s-b)(s-c)/s.
questions.question: AQ6(iv). Prove that tan(A/2)*tan(B/2) = (a+b-c)/(a+b+c).
questions.solution: tan(A/2)*tan(B/2) = sqrt[(s-b)(s-c)/(s(s-a))] * sqrt[(s-a)(s-c)/(s(s-b))] = (s-c)/s. And (a+b-c)/(a+b+c) = 2(s-c)/(2s) = (s-c)/s. Both sides agree.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q6(iv); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (b-c)*cot(A/2) = 4R*cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2) = 2R*(cosC - cosB): cyclic sum vanishes.
questions.question: AQ6(v). Prove that (b-c)*cot(A/2) + (c-a)*cot(B/2) + (a-b)*cot(C/2) = 0.
questions.solution: (b-c)*cot(A/2) = 2R*(sinB - sinC)*cos(A/2)/sin(A/2) = 2R*2*cos((B+C)/2)*sin((B-C)/2)*cos(A/2)/sin(A/2) = 4R*sin((B-C)/2)*cos(A/2) = 2R*[cosC - cosB] (using 2*sin((B-C)/2)*cos(A/2) = cosC - cosB from Q5(d) working). Cyclically the others are 2R*(cosA - cosC) and 2R*(cosB - cosA). Adding: 2R*[(cosC - cosB) + (cosA - cosC) + (cosB - cosA)] = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q6(v); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Expand with cos^2(C/2) = (s(s-c))/(ab) style halves, or collect: LHS - c^2 = (a-b)^2 - 4ab*sin^2(C/2) - ... = 0 by the cosine rule.
questions.question: AQ6(vi). Prove that (a-b)^2*cos^2(C/2) + (a+b)^2*sin^2(C/2) = c^2.
questions.solution: With cos^2(C/2) = (1+cosC)/2 and sin^2(C/2) = (1-cosC)/2, the left side is [(a-b)^2*(1+cosC) + (a+b)^2*(1-cosC)]/2 = [(a-b)^2 + (a+b)^2]/2 + cosC*[(a-b)^2 - (a+b)^2]/2 = (2a^2+2b^2)/2 + cosC*(-4ab)/2 = (a^2+b^2) - 2ab*cosC = c^2 by the cosine rule.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q6(vi); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Angles 1:2:3 of 180 deg are 30/60/90: sides go as sin30:sin60:sin90 = 1:sqrt(3):2.
questions.question: AQ7(i). If the angles of a triangle are to one another as 1:2:3, prove that the corresponding sides are 1:sqrt(3):2.
questions.solution: Let the angles be k, 2k, 3k with k + 2k + 3k = 180 deg, so k = 30 deg: angles 30, 60, 90 deg. By the sine rule a:b:c = sin30:sin60:sin90 = (1/2):(sqrt(3)/2):1 = 1:sqrt(3):2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(i); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Smallest side sqrt(13) is opposite the smallest angle: cosine rule gives cos = sqrt(3)/2.
questions.question: AQ7(ii). If the sides of a triangle are 7 cms, 4*sqrt(3) cms, sqrt(13) cms, prove that the smallest angle is 30 deg.
questions.solution: The smallest angle is opposite the smallest side sqrt(13). By the cosine rule, cos = [7^2 + (4*sqrt(3))^2 - (sqrt(13))^2]/[2*7*4*sqrt(3)] = (49 + 48 - 13)/(56*sqrt(3)) = 84/(56*sqrt(3)) = 3/(2*sqrt(3)) = sqrt(3)/2. Hence the smallest angle is 30 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(ii); book p189 = PDF p216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Angles in A.P. force the middle to 60 deg; then b:c = sinB:sinC pins C = 45 deg.
questions.question: AQ7(iii). The angles of a triangle ABC are in A.P., and it is given that b:c = sqrt(3):sqrt(2). Find angle A. (Printed Answers line reads '7.(ii) 75 deg' - a label slip for 7.(iii); 7.(ii) is a proof with no numeric answer.)
questions.solution: Angles in A.P.: 2B = A + C with A + B + C = 180 deg gives 3B = 180, so B = 60 deg. Then b:c = sinB:sinC gives sqrt(3):sqrt(2) = (sqrt(3)/2):sinC, so sinC = sqrt(2)/2 and C = 45 deg (C = 135 deg impossible with B = 60). Hence A = 180 - 60 - 45 = 75 deg. (Filed: the printed answer '75 deg' belongs to this part (iii), not (ii).)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(iii); book p189 = PDF p216-217 (vision read); answer-label slip documented

questions.knowledgeNote: Try B = 90 deg first: sinB:sinC = 1:sin60 = 2:sqrt(3) matches instantly.
questions.question: AQ7(iv). In triangle ABC, if angle A = 30 deg and b:c = 2:sqrt(3), find angle B.
questions.solution: B + C = 150 deg and sinB:sinC = 2:sqrt(3). With B = 90 deg, C = 60 deg: sinB:sinC = 1:(sqrt(3)/2) = 2:sqrt(3). This satisfies the ratio, and monotonicity of sinB/sin(150 deg - B) on (0, 150 deg) makes it unique. So B = 90 deg. Matches the printed Answers: 90 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(iv); book p189 = PDF p216-217 (vision read); matches key

questions.knowledgeNote: sin3B = 2sinB gives sinB*(1 - 4sin^2B) = 0: with B under 60 deg, sinB = 1/2.
questions.question: AQ7(v). If a = 2b and A = 3B, find the angles of the triangle.
questions.solution: a:b = sinA:sinB gives 2:1 = sin3B:sinB, so sin3B = 2sinB. With sin3B = 3sinB - 4sin^3B: 3sinB - 4sin^3B = 2sinB, i.e. sinB*(1 - 4sin^2B) = 0. Since B is a triangle angle with 3B < 180 deg, sinB != 0, so sin^2B = 1/4 and (B acute) sinB = 1/2: B = 30 deg. Then A = 90 deg, C = 60 deg. Matches the printed Answers: 90, 30, 60 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q7(v); book p189 = PDF p216-217 (vision read); matches key
questions.answer: A = 90 deg, B = 30 deg, C = 60 deg

questions.knowledgeNote: Mirror of Ex Q8 with a, b swapped: (a+c)^2 - b^2 = 3ca factors to cosB = 1/2.
questions.question: AQ8. If 1/(a+b) + 1/(b+c) = 3/(a+b+c), show that angle B = 60 deg.

questions.knowledgeNote: b + c = 2R*(sinB + sinC) = 4R*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2): with A = 60 deg, cos(A/2) = a/(2R).
questions.question: AQ9(i). If in a triangle ABC, A = 60 deg, show that b + c = 2a*cos((B-C)/2).
questions.solution: b + c = 2R*(sinB + sinC) = 4R*sin((B+C)/2)*cos((B-C)/2) = 4R*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2). With A = 60 deg, cos(A/2) = cos30 = sqrt(3)/2 and a = 2R*sin60 = 2R*sqrt(3)/2 = R*sqrt(3), so 4R*cos(A/2) = 4R*sqrt(3)/2 = 2*R*sqrt(3) = 2a. Hence b + c = 2a*cos((B-C)/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q9(i); book p189 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (a+c)^2 - b^2 = 3ca rearranges to a^2 + c^2 - b^2 = ca: read off cosB.
questions.question: AQ9(ii). In a triangle ABC, if angle B = 60 deg, prove that (a+b+c)*(a-b+c) = 3ca.
questions.solution: (a+b+c)*(a-b+c) = (a+c)^2 - b^2 = a^2 + c^2 + 2ac - b^2. With B = 60 deg, cosB = (a^2+c^2-b^2)/(2ac) = 1/2 gives a^2 + c^2 - b^2 = ac. Substituting: ac + 2ac = 3ca.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q9(ii); book p189 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a:b:c = 2:3:4 with s = 27 forces a = 12, b = 18, c = 24: Heron gives sqrt(27*15*9*3) = 27*sqrt(15).
questions.question: AQ10(i). If in any triangle a:b:c = 2:3:4 and s = 27, find the area of the triangle.
questions.solution: 2k + 3k + 4k = 2s = 54 gives k = 6: a = 12, b = 18, c = 24. Delta = sqrt[27*(27-12)*(27-18)*(27-24)] = sqrt(27*15*9*3) = sqrt(10935) = sqrt(729*15) = 27*sqrt(15) sq. units. Matches the printed Answers: 27*sqrt(15) sq. units.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q10(i); book pp189-190 = PDF p217 (vision read); matches key

questions.knowledgeNote: Delta = (1/2)*a*b*sinC: (1/2)*5*6*sin30 = 7.5 directly.
questions.question: AQ10(ii). In a triangle ABC, a = 5, b = 6 and C = 30 deg; show that its area is 7.5 sq. units.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q10(ii); book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 2^2 + 3^2 ... (sqrt(2))^2 + (sqrt(3))^2 = (sqrt(5))^2: right triangle, legs sqrt(2), sqrt(3).
questions.question: AQ10(iii). In a triangle ABC, if a = sqrt(2), b = sqrt(3) and c = sqrt(5), show that its area is (1/2)*sqrt(6) sq. units.
questions.solution: a^2 + b^2 = 2 + 3 = 5 = c^2, so the triangle is right angled at C. Delta = (1/2)*a*b = (1/2)*sqrt(2)*sqrt(3) = (1/2)*sqrt(6) sq. units.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q10(iii); book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: s = 21: sin(A/2) = sqrt[(s-b)(s-c)/(bc)] = sqrt(1/5); everything else follows by doubling.
questions.question: AQ11. In any triangle ABC, if a = 13 cms, b = 14 cms, c = 15 cms, find sin(A/2), cos(A/2), sinA, cosA and tan(A/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q11; book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a, b, c in A.P. means 2sinB = sinA + sinC: divide by 2cos(B/2) to get 2sin(B/2) = cos((A-C)/2), then use tan product formula.
questions.question: AQ12(i). If a, b, c are in A.P., prove that 3*tan(A/2)*tan(C/2) = 1.
questions.solution: 2b = a + c gives 2sinB = sinA + sinC, i.e. 4*sin(B/2)*cos(B/2) = 2*sin((A+C)/2)*cos((A-C)/2) = 2*cos(B/2)*cos((A-C)/2), so 2*sin(B/2) = cos((A-C)/2). Now tan(A/2)*tan(C/2) = [cos((A-C)/2) - cos((A+C)/2)]/[cos((A-C)/2) + cos((A+C)/2)]. Since cos((A+C)/2) = sin(B/2), this is [2*sin(B/2) - sin(B/2)]/[2*sin(B/2) + sin(B/2)] = sin(B/2)/[3*sin(B/2)] = 1/3. Hence 3*tan(A/2)*tan(C/2) = 1.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q12(i); book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 2a = b + c becomes 2sinA = 2cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2): cancel cos(A/2).
questions.question: AQ12(ii). If b, a, c are in A.P., prove that cos((B-C)/2) = 2*sin(A/2).
questions.solution: 2a = b + c gives 2sinA = sinB + sinC = 2*sin((B+C)/2)*cos((B-C)/2) = 2*cos(A/2)*cos((B-C)/2). Since 2sinA = 4*sin(A/2)*cos(A/2), dividing by 2*cos(A/2) gives 2*sin(A/2) = cos((B-C)/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q12(ii); book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: c + (b-a)*cosB = b*(cosA + cosB) = 2b*cos((A+B)/2)*cos((A-B)/2): the sine-rule ratio collapses to cot((B-A)/2).
questions.question: AQ13. If b - a = mc, prove that cot((B-A)/2) = (1 + m*cosB)/(m*sinB).
questions.solution: m = (b-a)/c. Then (1 + m*cosB)/(m*sinB) = [c + (b-a)*cosB]/[(b-a)*sinB]. Numerator: c + (b-a)*cosB = (a*cosB + b*cosA) + (b-a)*cosB (projection law) = b*(cosA + cosB) = 2b*cos((A+B)/2)*cos((A-B)/2) = 2b*sin(C/2)*cos((B-A)/2). Denominator: (b-a)*sinB = 2R*(sinB - sinA)*sinB = 2R*2*cos((A+B)/2)*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB = 4R*sin(C/2)*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB. Ratio: [2b*sin(C/2)*cos((B-A)/2)]/[4R*sin(C/2)*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB] = [2*2R*sinB*cos((B-A)/2)]/[4R*sin((B-A)/2)*sinB] = cos((B-A)/2)/sin((B-A)/2) = cot((B-A)/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Additional Questions (I) Q13; book p190 = PDF p217 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (b-c)/a = sin((B-C)/2)/cos(A/2): sum-to-product on both differences.
questions.question: Q5(a). In any triangle, prove that [(b-c)/a]*cos(A/2) = sin((B-C)/2).
questions.solution: (b-c)/a = (sinB - sinC)/sinA = [2*cos((B+C)/2)*sin((B-C)/2)]/[2*sin(A/2)*cos(A/2)] = [2*sin(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2)]/[2*sin(A/2)*cos(A/2)] = sin((B-C)/2)/cos(A/2). Multiplying by cos(A/2) gives sin((B-C)/2).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q5(a); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: cos^2(A/2) = (1+cosA)/2, then the projection law finishes it: b*cosA + a*cosB = c.
questions.question: Q5(b). In any triangle, prove that b*cos^2(A/2) + a*cos^2(B/2) = (a+b+c)/2.
questions.solution: b*cos^2(A/2) + a*cos^2(B/2) = b*(1+cosA)/2 + a*(1+cosB)/2 = [(a+b) + (b*cosA + a*cosB)]/2. By the projection law b*cosA + a*cosB = c, so this equals (a+b+c)/2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q5(b); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read; s written as (a+b+c)/2 in print)

questions.knowledgeNote: cosB - cosC = -2*cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2) and c - b = -4R*sin(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2): the sine factors cancel.
questions.question: Q5(c). In any triangle, prove that a*(cosB - cosC) = 2*(c-b)*cos^2(A/2).
questions.solution: Left: a*(cosB - cosC) = 2R*sinA*[-2*sin((B+C)/2)*sin((B-C)/2)] = 2R*2*sin(A/2)*cos(A/2)*[-2*cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2)] = -8R*sin(A/2)*cos^2(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2). Right: 2*(c-b)*cos^2(A/2) = 4R*(sinC - sinB)*cos^2(A/2) = 4R*2*cos((B+C)/2)*sin((C-B)/2)*cos^2(A/2) = 8R*sin(A/2)*[-sin((B-C)/2)]*cos^2(A/2). Both sides agree.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q5(c); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Each weighted term becomes (cosC - cosB)/2: the three differences telescope to zero.
questions.question: Q5(d). In any triangle, prove that [(b-c)/a]*cos^2(A/2) + [(c-a)/b]*cos^2(B/2) + [(a-b)/c]*cos^2(C/2) = 0.
questions.solution: From Q5(a), (b-c)/a = sin((B-C)/2)/cos(A/2), so the first term is sin((B-C)/2)*cos(A/2) = [sin((B-C+A)/2) + sin((B-C-A)/2)]/2 = [sin((pi-2C)/2) + sin((-(pi-2B))/2)]/2 = (cosC - cosB)/2. Cyclically the second is (cosA - cosC)/2 and the third is (cosB - cosA)/2. Adding: [(cosC - cosB) + (cosA - cosC) + (cosB - cosA)]/2 = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q5(d); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Halve with (1+cosA)/2, then use bc*cosA + ca*cosB + ab*cosC = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2.
questions.question: Q5(e). In any triangle, prove that bc*cos^2(A/2) + ca*cos^2(B/2) + ab*cos^2(C/2) = s^2, where 2s = a+b+c.
questions.solution: The left side is [bc*(1+cosA) + ca*(1+cosB) + ab*(1+cosC)]/2 = [(ab+bc+ca) + (bc*cosA + ca*cosB + ab*cosC)]/2. Now bc*cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2 and cyclically, so the bracket sum is (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2. Hence the left side is [(ab+bc+ca) + (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2]/2 = (a+b+c)^2/4 = s^2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q5(e); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: tan^2(A/2) = (s-b)(s-c)/[s(s-a)]: multiply the three and one factor cancels.
questions.question: Q5(f). In any triangle, prove that tan^2(A/2)*tan^2(B/2)*tan^2(C/2) = [(s-a)/s]*[(s-b)/s]*[(s-c)/s], where 2s = a+b+c.
questions.solution: By the half-angle formula tan^2(A/2) = (s-b)(s-c)/[s(s-a)], and cyclically for B and C. Multiplying: numerator (s-b)(s-c)*(s-c)(s-a)*(s-a)(s-b) = [(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)]^2; denominator s^3*(s-a)(s-b)(s-c). Cancelling one factor (s-a)(s-b)(s-c) gives (s-a)(s-b)(s-c)/s^3 = [(s-a)/s]*[(s-b)/s]*[(s-c)/s].
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q5(f); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: cot(B/2) + cot(C/2) = sinA/[sin(B/2)*sin(C/2)]: half-angles are compulsory (full angles fail: test the 3-4-5 triangle).
questions.question: Q5(g). In any triangle, prove that (b+c-a)*[cot(B/2) + cot(C/2)] = 2a*cot(A/2).
questions.solution: cot(B/2) + cot(C/2) = sin((B+C)/2)/[sin(B/2)*sin(C/2)] = cos(A/2)/[sin(B/2)*sin(C/2)], so the left side is 2(s-a)*cos(A/2)/[sin(B/2)*sin(C/2)]. Now (s-a) = 4R*cos(A/2)*sin(B/2)*sin(C/2) (from r = 4R*sin(A/2)*sin(B/2)*sin(C/2) and tan(A/2) = r/(s-a)). Substituting: 2*4R*cos(A/2)*sin(B/2)*sin(C/2)*cos(A/2)/[sin(B/2)*sin(C/2)] = 8R*cos^2(A/2). The right side is 2a*cot(A/2) = 4R*sinA*cos(A/2)/sin(A/2) = 8R*cos^2(A/2). Both sides agree. (Check on 3-4-5 with A = 90 deg: left = 2*(cot(B/2)+cot(C/2)) = 2*(2.414+0.414) = 5.657 = 2*5*cot45.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q5(g); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read; half-angles confirmed in print)

questions.knowledgeNote: a^2*cotA = R*a*(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(bc): summing gives R*(2*sum a^2b^2 - sum a^4)/(abc) = 4*Delta by Heron.
questions.question: Q13(a). In any triangle, prove that a^2*cotA + b^2*cotB + c^2*cotC = 4*Delta.
questions.solution: a^2*cotA = a^2*cosA/sinA = a^2*[(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2bc)]/(a/2R) = R*a*(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(bc) = R*a^2*(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(abc). Summing cyclically gives R/(abc)*[sum a^2*(b^2+c^2-a^2)] = R/(abc)*[2*(a^2*b^2+b^2*c^2+c^2*a^2) - (a^4+b^4+c^4)]. By Heron's form 16*Delta^2 = 2*sum a^2b^2 - sum a^4, so this is R*16*Delta^2/(abc) = 16R*Delta^2/(4R*Delta) = 4*Delta (using abc = 4R*Delta).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q13(a); book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Equality holds because a/sinA = 2R is constant: both sides equal 4R^2*(sum sin^2)^2.
questions.question: Q13(b). In any triangle, prove that (a*sinA + b*sinB + c*sinC)^2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2)*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C).
questions.solution: Since a = 2R*sinA (and cyclically), the left side is [2R*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C)]^2 = 4R^2*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C)^2. The right side is [4R^2*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C)]*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C), which is the same. (This is Cauchy-Schwarz with equality, because (a, b, c) is proportional to (sinA, sinB, sinC).)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q13(b); book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: sinA + sinB + sinC = (a+b+c)/(2R) = s/R: just add the three sine-rule fractions.
questions.question: Q13(c). In any triangle, prove that sinA + sinB + sinC = s/R, where 2s = a+b+c.
questions.solution: sinA + sinB + sinC = a/(2R) + b/(2R) + c/(2R) = (a+b+c)/(2R) = 2s/(2R) = s/R.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q13(c); book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Expand a*cosB*cosC with a = y+z style substitution: sum = [sum a^2 - sum(b-c)^2 ... ]/(4R) = Delta/R.
questions.question: Q13(d). In any triangle, prove that a*cosB*cosC + b*cosC*cosA + c*cosA*cosB = Delta/R.
questions.solution: a*cosB*cosC = 2R*sinA*cosB*cosC, so the left side is 2R*[sinA*cosB*cosC + sinB*cosC*cosA + sinC*cosA*cosB]. Dividing the bracket by cosA*cosB*cosC gives tanA + tanB + tanC, which equals tanA*tanB*tanC (standard A+B+C = pi identity). Hence the bracket is cosA*cosB*cosC*tanA*tanB*tanC = sinA*sinB*sinC, and the sum is 2R*sinA*sinB*sinC = 2R*(abc/8R^3) = abc/(4R^2) = Delta/R (using abc = 4R*Delta).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q13(d); book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Move everything left: (a^2+b^2-c^2)^2 = 2a^2b^2, then cosC = +-1/sqrt(2).
questions.question: Q6. If a^4 + b^4 + c^4 = 2c^2*(a^2+b^2), prove that C = 45 deg or 135 deg. (T.U. 2051) (HSEB 2056)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q6 (T.U. 2051) (HSEB 2056); book pp187-188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: (b+c)^2 - a^2 = 3bc factors to b^2+c^2-a^2 = bc: read off cosA = 1/2.
questions.question: Q7. If (a+b+c)*(b+c-a) = 3bc, show that A = 60 deg.
questions.solution: (a+b+c)*(b+c-a) = (b+c)^2 - a^2 = b^2 + c^2 + 2bc - a^2. Setting this equal to 3bc gives b^2 + c^2 - a^2 = bc, so cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2bc) = 1/2. With 0 < A < pi, A = 60 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q7; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Clear denominators: (a+c)+(b+c) over product form collapses to (a+b)^2 = c^2 + 3ab.
questions.question: Q8. If 1/(a+c) + 1/(b+c) = 3/(a+b+c), show that C = 60 deg. (T.U. 2054, HSEB 2053)
questions.solution: Combining: [(b+c) + (a+c)]/[(a+c)(b+c)] = 3/(a+b+c), i.e. (a+b+2c)(a+b+c) = 3[(a+c)(b+c)]. Put s1 = a+b: (s1+2c)(s1+c) = 3[c^2 + c*s1 + ab], i.e. s1^2 + 3c*s1 + 2c^2 = 3c^2 + 3c*s1 + 3ab, so s1^2 = c^2 + 3ab. Hence (a+b)^2 = c^2 + 3ab, i.e. a^2 + b^2 - c^2 = ab, so cosC = 1/2 and C = 60 deg.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q8 (T.U. 2054, HSEB 2053); book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: cosA/a = cosB/b becomes sinB*cosA = sinA*cosB, i.e. sin(B-A) = 0.
questions.question: Q9. If the cosines of two of the angles of a triangle are proportional to the opposite sides, prove that the triangle is isosceles.
questions.solution: Suppose cosA/a = cosB/b (the same argument works for any pair). Then b*cosA = a*cosB, i.e. 2R*sinB*cosA = 2R*sinA*cosB, so sinB*cosA - sinA*cosB = sin(B-A) = 0. With angles in (0, pi), B - A = 0, so A = B and the triangle is isosceles.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q9; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Either cosA = 0 (right-angled) or the sine factors force B = C: factor, never divide blindly.
questions.question: Q10. If (cosA + 2cosC):(cosA + 2cosB) = sinB:sinC, prove that the triangle is either isosceles or right-angled.
questions.solution: Cross-multiplying: (cosA + 2cosC)*sinC = (cosA + 2cosB)*sinB, i.e. cosA*(sinC - sinB) = 2*(sinB*cosB - sinC*cosC) = sin2B - sin2C. Now sin2B - sin2C = 2*cos(B+C)*sin(B-C) = -2*cosA*sin(B-C), and sinC - sinB = 2*cos((B+C)/2)*sin((C-B)/2) = 2*sin(A/2)*sin((C-B)/2). So 2*cosA*sin(A/2)*sin((C-B)/2) = -2*cosA*sin(B-C) = 4*cosA*sin((C-B)/2)*cos((C-B)/2). If cosA = 0 then A = 90 deg (right-angled). Otherwise divide by 2*cosA*sin((C-B)/2) (zero only if B = C, isosceles): sin(A/2) = 2*cos((C-B)/2). But |(C-B)/2| < (B+C)/2 = (pi-A)/2 gives cos((C-B)/2) > cos((pi-A)/2) = sin(A/2), so 2*cos((C-B)/2) > sin(A/2) always and this case never occurs. Hence B = C (isosceles) or A = 90 deg (right-angled).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q10; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 2*sinC*cosA = sinB expands to sin(C-A) = 0 via sinB = sin(A+C).
questions.question: Q11. If 2cosA = sinB/sinC, show that the triangle is isosceles.
questions.solution: 2*sinC*cosA = sinB = sin(A+C) = sinA*cosC + cosA*sinC. Subtracting cosA*sinC: sinC*cosA = sinA*cosC, i.e. sinC*cosA - sinA*cosC = sin(C-A) = 0. With angles in (0, pi), C = A, so the triangle is isosceles.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q11; book p188 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Translate both sides to cos2: the condition becomes cos2A + cos2C = 2cos2B, the AP condition.
questions.question: Q12. Prove that a^2, b^2, c^2 are in A.P. if sinA:sinC = sin(A-B):sin(B-C).
questions.solution: a^2, b^2, c^2 in A.P. means 2*sin^2B = sin^2A + sin^2C (dividing by 4R^2), i.e. (1-cos2B) = (1-cos2A)/2 + (1-cos2C)/2, i.e. cos2A + cos2C = 2cos2B. The given condition: sinA*sin(B-C) = sinC*sin(A-B). Left: [cos(A-B+C) - cos(A+B-C)]/2 = [cos(pi-2B) - cos(pi-2C)]/2 = (cos2C - cos2B)/2. Right: [cos(C-A+B) - cos(C+A-B)]/2 = [cos(pi-2A) - cos(pi-2B)]/2 = (cos2B - cos2A)/2. Equality gives cos2C - cos2B = cos2B - cos2A, i.e. cos2A + cos2C = 2cos2B, exactly the A.P. condition.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q12 (condition continues on book p188); book p188 = PDF pp215-216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a^2+b^2+c^2 = 4R^2*(sum sin^2) = 8R^2*(1 + cosA*cosB*cosC): the 8R^2 forces a zero cosine.
questions.question: Q14. If 8R^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2, prove that the triangle is right angled. (T.U. 2057S)
questions.solution: a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 4R^2*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C). Since sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C = 2 + 2*cosA*cosB*cosC (standard identity), this equals 8R^2*(1 + cosA*cosB*cosC). Setting it equal to 8R^2 gives cosA*cosB*cosC = 0, so one angle is 90 deg: the triangle is right angled.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q14 (T.U. 2057S); book p188 = PDF p215-216 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 6-8-10 is the scaled 3-4-5 right triangle: s = 12, Delta = 24, R = 5 fall out immediately.

questions.knowledgeNote: b*cosC - c*cosB collapses to (b^2-c^2)/a: clear the denominators first.
questions.question: Q1(a). In any triangle, prove that a(b*cosC - c*cosB) = b^2 - c^2.
questions.solution: By the cosine rule cosC = (a^2+b^2-c^2)/(2ab) and cosB = (a^2-b^2+c^2)/(2ac). So b*cosC - c*cosB = (a^2+b^2-c^2)/(2a) - (a^2-b^2+c^2)/(2a) = (2b^2-2c^2)/(2a) = (b^2-c^2)/a. Multiplying by a gives a(b*cosC - c*cosB) = b^2 - c^2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q1(a); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: All three expressions equal the same symmetric value (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc): prove one, the others follow by cyclic symmetry.
questions.question: Q1(b). In any triangle, prove that cosA/a + a/(bc) = cosB/b + b/(ca) = cosC/c + c/(ab).
questions.solution: cosA/a + a/(bc) = (bc*cosA + a^2)/(abc). Since bc*cosA = bc*(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2bc) = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2, the numerator is (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2 + a^2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2. Hence the first expression equals (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc). The second and third are the same computation with cyclically permuted letters, so all three are equal to (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q1(b); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Put everything over abc and use bc*cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2: the six terms pair up.
questions.question: Q1(c). In any triangle, prove that cosA/a + cosB/b + cosC/c = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc).
questions.solution: With common denominator abc the left side is (bc*cosA + ca*cosB + ab*cosC)/(abc). Now bc*cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2, ca*cosB = (c^2+a^2-b^2)/2, ab*cosC = (a^2+b^2-c^2)/2, whose sum is (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2. Dividing by abc gives (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2abc).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q1(c); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a^3 = 8R^3*sin^3A turns the whole sum into a telescoping sine product.
questions.question: Q2(a). In any triangle, prove that a^3*(sin^3B - sin^3C) + b^3*(sin^3C - sin^3A) + c^3*(sin^3A - sin^3B) = 0.
questions.solution: By the sine rule a = 2R*sinA, so a^3 = 8R^3*sin^3A (and cyclically). The left side becomes 8R^3*[sin^3A*(sin^3B - sin^3C) + sin^3B*(sin^3C - sin^3A) + sin^3C*(sin^3A - sin^3B)] = 8R^3*[sin^3A*sin^3B - sin^3A*sin^3C + sin^3B*sin^3C - sin^3B*sin^3A + sin^3C*sin^3A - sin^3C*sin^3B] = 0, since the six terms cancel in pairs.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q2(a); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Each fraction simplifies to 4R^2*sinA*sin(B-C); the sine-product sum telescopes to zero.
questions.question: Q2(b). In any triangle, prove that [a^2*sin(B-C)]/sinA + [b^2*sin(C-A)]/sinB + [c^2*sin(A-B)]/sinC = 0. (T.U. 2052)
questions.solution: Since a^2 = 4R^2*sin^2A, the first term is 4R^2*sinA*sin(B-C) (and cyclically). Now sinA*sin(B-C) = [cos(A-B+C) - cos(A+B-C)]/2 = [cos(pi-2B) - cos(pi-2C)]/2 = (cos2C - cos2B)/2. Summing cyclically: (1/2)*[(cos2C - cos2B) + (cos2A - cos2C) + (cos2B - cos2A)] = 0. Hence the whole sum is 4R^2*0 = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q2(b) (T.U. 2052); book p186 = PDF p213 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Each fraction equals the constant 1/(2R), so all three are equal: b^2-c^2 = 4R^2*sin(B-C)*sinA is the key step.
questions.question: Q2(c). In any triangle, prove that [a*sin(B-C)]/(b^2-c^2) = [b*sin(C-A)]/(c^2-a^2) = [c*sin(A-B)]/(a^2-b^2). (T.U. 2051H)
questions.solution: b^2 - c^2 = 4R^2*(sin^2B - sin^2C) = 4R^2*sin(B-C)*sin(B+C) = 4R^2*sin(B-C)*sinA. So the first fraction is 2R*sinA*sin(B-C)/[4R^2*sin(B-C)*sinA] = 1/(2R). The same computation cyclically gives 1/(2R) for the second and third fractions, so all three are equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q2(c) (T.U. 2051H); book p186 = PDF p213-214 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Regroup into the three projection pairs: (b*cosA + a*cosB) = c and friends.
questions.question: Q3(a). In any triangle, prove that (b+c)*cosA + (c+a)*cosB + (a+b)*cosC = a + b + c.
questions.solution: Regroup the left side as (b*cosA + a*cosB) + (c*cosB + b*cosC) + (a*cosC + c*cosA). By the projection law b*cosA + a*cosB = c, c*cosB + b*cosC = a, and a*cosC + c*cosA = b. Adding gives c + a + b = a + b + c.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q3(a); book p186 = PDF p213-214 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Write everything with a = 2R*sinA: both sides become 8R^2*sinA*sinB*sinC.
questions.question: Q3(b). In any triangle, prove that b^2*sin2C + c^2*sin2B = 2ab*sinC. (T.U. 2051H)
questions.solution: Left side: b^2*2*sinC*cosC + c^2*2*sinB*cosB = 8R^2*sin^2B*sinC*cosC + 8R^2*sin^2C*sinB*cosB = 8R^2*sinB*sinC*(sinB*cosC + cosB*sinC) = 8R^2*sinB*sinC*sin(B+C) = 8R^2*sinA*sinB*sinC. Right side: 2*(2R*sinA)*(2R*sinB)*sinC = 8R^2*sinA*sinB*sinC. Both sides agree.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q3(b) (T.U. 2051H); book p186 = PDF p214 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: The trick is (b*cosC + c*cosB)^2 = a^2: expand it to isolate c^2*cos^2B + b^2*cos^2C.
questions.question: Q3(c). In any triangle, prove that c^2*cos^2B + b^2*cos^2C + bc*cos(B-C) = (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)/2. (T.U. 2058S)
questions.solution: From the projection law a = b*cosC + c*cosB, squaring gives a^2 = b^2*cos^2C + c^2*cos^2B + 2bc*cosB*cosC, so c^2*cos^2B + b^2*cos^2C = a^2 - 2bc*cosB*cosC. Substituting: left side = a^2 - 2bc*cosB*cosC + bc*cos(B-C) = a^2 - 2bc*cosB*cosC + bc*(cosB*cosC + sinB*sinC) = a^2 - bc*(cosB*cosC - sinB*sinC) = a^2 - bc*cos(B+C) = a^2 + bc*cosA. Since bc*cosA = (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2, this is a^2 + (b^2+c^2-a^2)/2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q3(c) (T.U. 2058S); book p186 = PDF p214 (vision read; the 1/2 on the right confirmed in print)

questions.knowledgeNote: c - b*cosA = 2R*sinA*cosB: the sinA factor cancels in the ratio.
questions.question: Q3(d). In any triangle, prove that (c - b*cosA)/(b - c*cosA) = cosB/cosC. (HSEB 2064)
questions.solution: c - b*cosA = 2R*sinC - 2R*sinB*cosA = 2R*[sin(A+B) - sinB*cosA] = 2R*sinA*cosB. Likewise b - c*cosA = 2R*sinB - 2R*sinC*cosA = 2R*[sin(A+C) - sinC*cosA] = 2R*sinA*cosC. Dividing (cosA != 0; if cosA = 0 both numerator and denominator reduce via the projection law) gives cosB/cosC.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q3(d) (HSEB 2064); book pp186-187 = PDF pp213-214 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same 2R expansion as Q3(d): a - b*cosC = 2R*sinC*cosB, and the cosB cancels.
questions.question: Q3(e). In any triangle, prove that (a - b*cosC)/(c - b*cosA) = sinC/sinA.
questions.solution: a - b*cosC = 2R*sinA - 2R*sinB*cosC = 2R*[sin(B+C) - sinB*cosC] = 2R*cosB*sinC. From Q3(d), c - b*cosA = 2R*sinA*cosB. Dividing gives (2R*sinC*cosB)/(2R*sinA*cosB) = sinC/sinA.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q3(e); book p187 = PDF p214 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Use cosB = (a^2+c^2-b^2)/(2ac): each product a^3*b*cosC collapses to a^2*(a^2+b^2-c^2)/2.
questions.question: Q4(a). In any triangle, prove that a^3*sin(B-C) + b^3*sin(C-A) + c^3*sin(A-B) = 0.
questions.solution: Write sin(B-C) = sinB*cosC - cosB*sinC = (b*cosC - c*cosB)/(2R), so a^3*sin(B-C) = a^3*(b*cosC - c*cosB)/(2R). Summing cyclically and multiplying by 2R gives [a^3*b*cosC + b^3*c*cosA + c^3*a*cosB] - [a^3*c*cosB + b^3*a*cosC + c^3*b*cosA]. Now a^3*b*cosC = a^3*b*(a^2+b^2-c^2)/(2ab) = a^2*(a^2+b^2-c^2)/2, and cyclically; their sum is (1/2)*[sum a^4 + sum a^2*b^2 - sum a^2*c^2] = (1/2)*sum a^4 since the two mixed sums are equal. Likewise a^3*c*cosB = a^2*(a^2+c^2-b^2)/2, summing to the same (1/2)*sum a^4. Their difference is 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q4(a); book p187 = PDF p214 (vision read; cubes confirmed: a^3, b^3, c^3)

questions.knowledgeNote: [(b^2-c^2)/a^2]*sin2A reduces to 2*sin(B-C)*cosA; then sin(B-C)*cosA = (sin2C - sin2B)/2 telescopes.
questions.question: Q4(b). In any triangle, prove that [(b^2-c^2)/a^2]*sin2A + [(c^2-a^2)/b^2]*sin2B + [(a^2-b^2)/c^2]*sin2C = 0.
questions.solution: (b^2-c^2)/a^2 = 4R^2*sin(B-C)*sinA/(4R^2*sin^2A) = sin(B-C)/sinA, so the first term is [sin(B-C)/sinA]*2*sinA*cosA = 2*sin(B-C)*cosA (and cyclically). Now 2*sin(B-C)*cosA = 2*[sin(B-C+A) + sin(B-C-A)]/2 = sin(pi-2C) + sin(-(pi-2B)) = sin2C - sin2B. Summing cyclically: (sin2C - sin2B) + (sin2A - sin2C) + (sin2B - sin2A) = 0.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q4(b); book p187 = PDF p214 (vision read; denominators a^2, b^2, c^2 confirmed)

questions.knowledgeNote: Each leg equals abc/R: (a^2-b^2+c^2)*tanB = 2ac*sinB.
questions.question: Q4(c). In any triangle, prove that (a^2-b^2+c^2)*tanB = (a^2+b^2-c^2)*tanC = (b^2+c^2-a^2)*tanA.
questions.solution: a^2 - b^2 + c^2 = 2ac*cosB by the cosine rule, so the first expression is 2ac*cosB*tanB = 2ac*sinB = 2ac*(b/2R) = abc/R. Cyclically the second is 2ab*sinC = abc/R and the third is 2bc*sinA = abc/R. All three equal abc/R, hence are equal.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q4(c); book p187 = PDF pp214-215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Sum-to-product on top and bottom: cosB - cosC = -2*cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2), cosA + 1 = 2*cos^2(A/2).
questions.question: Q4(d). In any triangle, prove that (cosB - cosC)/(cosA + 1) = (c - b)/a.
questions.solution: cosB - cosC = -2*sin((B+C)/2)*sin((B-C)/2) = -2*cos(A/2)*sin((B-C)/2), and cosA + 1 = 2*cos^2(A/2). So the left side is -sin((B-C)/2)/cos(A/2). Meanwhile (c-b)/a = (sinC - sinB)/sinA = [2*cos((B+C)/2)*sin((C-B)/2)]/[2*sin(A/2)*cos(A/2)] = [2*sin(A/2)*(-sin((B-C)/2))]/[2*sin(A/2)*cos(A/2)] = -sin((B-C)/2)/cos(A/2). Both sides agree.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q4(d); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Numerator = 2R*sum sin^2, denominator = abc/(2R^2): their ratio is exactly R*(a^2+b^2+c^2)/(abc).
questions.question: Q4(e). In any triangle, prove that (a*sinA + b*sinB + c*sinC)/(a*cosA + b*cosB + c*cosC) = R*(a^2+b^2+c^2)/(abc).
questions.solution: Numerator: a*sinA + b*sinB + c*sinC = 2R*(sin^2A + sin^2B + sin^2C) = 2R*(a^2+b^2+c^2)/(4R^2) = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2R). Denominator: a*cosA + b*cosB + c*cosC = 2R*(sinA*cosA + sinB*cosB + sinC*cosC) = R*(sin2A + sin2B + sin2C) = R*4*sinA*sinB*sinC = 4R*(a/2R)*(b/2R)*(c/2R) = abc/(2R^2). Dividing: [(a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2R)]/[abc/(2R^2)] = R*(a^2+b^2+c^2)/(abc).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.6 Ex 6.1 Q4(e); book p187 = PDF p215 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Name the two given angles A and C so the computed third angle sits in the middle: a:b:c then reads straight off as sin105:sin60:sin15.
questions.question: Q1(i). The angles of a triangle are 105° and 15°; find the ratio of its sides.
questions.solution: The third angle is 180° - (105° + 15°) = 60°. Call the given angles A = 105° and C = 15°, so B = 60°. By the sine rule a:b:c = sinA:sinB:sinC = sin105°:sin60°:sin15°. Now sin105° = sin(60°+45°) = sin60°cos45° + cos60°sin45° = (√6+√2)/4, sin60° = √3/2 = 2√3/4, sin15° = sin(60°-45°) = (√6-√2)/4. Hence a:b:c = (√6+√2):2√3:(√6-√2). Since √6+√2 = √2(√3+1), √6-√2 = √2(√3-1) and 2√3 = √2·√6, dividing by √2 gives a:b:c = (√3+1):√6:(√3-1). Check: largest angle 105° faces the largest side √3+1 ≈ 2.73, smallest angle 15° faces √3-1 ≈ 0.73.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q1(i); book p196 = PDF p223 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: sin75°/sin45° collapses to (√3+1)/2: expand sin75° = sin(45°+30°) rather than reaching for a calculator.
questions.question: Q1(ii). If A = 45°, B = 60°, show that a:c = 2:(√3+1).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q1(ii); book p196 = PDF p223 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Angles in ratio 1:3 with A = 60° give B = 30°, C = 90° at once: assign the 60° to the middle angle so a:b:c reads 1:√3:2.
questions.question: Q1(iii). If one angle of a triangle is 60° and the ratio of the other two is 1:3, find all the angles and the ratio of the sides.
questions.solution: Let the other two angles be x and 3x. Then x + 3x = 180° - 60° = 120°, so x = 30°. The three angles are 30°, 60°, 90°. Put B = 60° (the given angle), A = 30°, C = 90°. By the sine rule a:b:c = sin30°:sin60°:sin90° = (1/2):(√3/2):1 = 1:√3:2. Check: hypotenuse c = 2 opposite 90° is the longest side. ✓
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q1(iii); book p196 = PDF p223 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: 2+3+7 = 12 parts, so one part is 15°: the angles are 30°, 45°, 105° and the sine ratio simplifies with a factor of √2.
questions.question: Q1(iv). The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:7. Prove that the sides are in the ratio √2:2:(√3+1).
questions.solution: 2 + 3 + 7 = 12 parts = 180°, so one part is 15° and the angles are 30°, 45°, 105°. By the sine rule a:b:c = sin30°:sin45°:sin105° = (1/2):(1/√2):((√6+√2)/4). Multiplying by 4 gives 2:2√2:(√6+√2); dividing by √2 gives √2:2:(√3+1). Largest angle 105° faces √3+1 ≈ 2.73, the longest side. ✓
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q1(iv); book p196 = PDF p223 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: cosA = 4/5, cosB = 3/5 is the 3-4-5 triangle in disguise: cos(A+B) = 0 forces C = 90°.
questions.question: Q1(v). If cosA = 4/5 and cosB = 3/5, find a:b:c.
questions.solution: sinA = 3/5 and sinB = 4/5 (A, B acute). cos(A+B) = cosAcosB - sinAsinB = (4/5)(3/5) - (3/5)(4/5) = 0, so A+B = 90° and C = 90°, sinC = 1. By the sine rule a:b:c = sinA:sinB:sinC = (3/5):(4/5):1 = 3:4:5. Check: 3² + 4² = 5², consistent with C = 90°. ✓
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q1(v); book p196 = PDF p223 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: c = √3+1 is the longest side, so expect C obtuse: cosine gives C = 105° directly, then sine for A and angle-sum for B.
questions.question: Q2(i). Given a = 2, b = √2, c = √3+1, solve the triangle. (HSEB 2058)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q2(i) (HSEB 2058); book p196 = PDF p223 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: a = 3+√3 is the longest side: cosine gives A = 105° at once; factor √3 out of (3+√3) when simplifying sinB.
questions.question: Q2(ii). If a = 3+√3, b = 2√3, c = √6, solve the triangle.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q2(ii); book p196-197 = PDF p223-224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same 45°-60°-75° triangle as the worked Example 5: c = √3+1 is longest, so cosine for C first, then sine for A.
questions.question: Q2(iii). If three sides of a triangle are proportional to 2:√6:√3+1, find all the angles. (HSEB 2056)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q2(iii) (HSEB 2056); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Two angles given: the third is 105° and both unknown sides scale off c/sinC = 12√2; keep sin105° in surd form until the last step.
questions.question: Q3(i). If C = 30°, B = 45°, c = 6√2, solve the triangle.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q3(i); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: A = 60° makes a/sinA simplify to 4: b and c then drop out as (√6+√2) and 2√2 with no calculator.
questions.question: Q3(ii). If A = 60°, B = 75°, a = 2√3, solve the triangle.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q3(ii); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Mirror of Q3(i) with the known side b = 2: the common factor b/sinB = 2√2 clears both denominators.
questions.question: Q3(iii). If A = 30°, B = 45°, b = 2, solve the triangle.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q3(iii); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: SAS with a:b = 1:2 and included 60°: c = 2√3 first, then sinA = 1/2 with A < C forces the acute value A = 30°.
questions.question: Q4(i). If a = 2, b = 4, C = 60°, find A and B.
questions.solution: c² = a²+b²-2ab·cosC = 4+16-2·2·4·(1/2) = 20-8 = 12, so c = 2√3. Then sinA = a·sinC/c = 2(√3/2)/(2√3) = 1/2, giving A = 30° or 150°; A = 150° is impossible with C = 60° (sum > 180°), and a < c confirms A acute: A = 30°. B = 180° - (30°+60°) = 90°. Answer: A = 30°, B = 90° (matches the printed key; indeed 2²+(2√3)² = 4²).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q4(i); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: The sine rule alone gives sinA ≈ 0.966 (75° or 105°): the cosine rule breaks the tie — a is the longest side, so A = 105°. Classic exam trap.
questions.question: Q4(ii). Two sides of a triangle are √3+1 and √3-1 and the included angle is 60°; solve the triangle.
questions.solution: Put a = √3+1, b = √3-1, C = 60°. c² = a²+b²-2ab·cos60° = (4+2√3)+(4-2√3)-(3-1) = 8-2 = 6, so c = √6 (matches the key). By the sine rule sinA = a·sinC/c = (√3+1)(√3/2)/√6 = (√3+1)/(2√2) ≈ 0.966, so A = 75° or 105°. Tie-break with cosine: a² = 4+2√3 ≈ 7.46 > b²+c² = (4-2√3)+6 ≈ 6.54, so A is obtuse: A = 105°. Then B = 180° - (105°+60°) = 15°. Answer: c = √6, A = 105°, B = 15° (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q4(ii); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Area + cosine rule give bc = 8 and b²+c² = 65: (b+c)² = 81 turns it into the quadratic t²-9t+8 = 0.
questions.question: Q4(iii). Given a = √57, A = 60° and area Δ = 2√3, find b and c.
questions.solution: Δ = (1/2)bc·sinA gives 2√3 = (1/2)bc(√3/2), so bc = 8. From the cosine rule a² = b²+c²-2bc·cosA: 57 = b²+c²-2·8·(1/2) = b²+c²-8, so b²+c² = 65. Then (b+c)² = 65+2·8 = 81, so b+c = 9. b, c are the roots of t²-9t+8 = 0, i.e. {8, 1}. Answer: b, c are 8 and 1 in some order (matches the printed key). Check: (1/2)·8·1·sin60° = 2√3. ✓
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q4(iii); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: SSA with a < b but a > b·sinA: two triangles. B = 60° gives the right-angled one (c = 6); B = 120° gives C = 30° and c = a = 3.
questions.question: Q5(i). Given a = 3, b = 3√3, A = 30°, solve the triangle. In which case is the solution ambiguous?
questions.solution: sinB = b·sinA/a = 3√3·(1/2)/3 = √3/2, so B = 60° or 120°; both satisfy A+B < 180°, so this case is AMBIGUOUS with two solutions. If B = 60°: C = 90° and c = a/sinA = 3/(1/2) = 6. If B = 120°: C = 30° and c = a·sinC/sinA = 3 (equal angles give equal sides). Answer: B = 60°, C = 90°, c = 6; or B = 120°, C = 30°, c = 3 (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q5(i) (ambiguous case); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: Same ambiguous pattern with surds: sinB = (√3+1)/(2√2) ≈ 0.966 gives B = 75°/105°. The printed key writes 'a = √6 / √2' but a = 2 is given — it means c (flag filed).
questions.question: Q5(ii). Given a = 2, b = √3+1, A = 45°, solve the triangle. In which case is the solution ambiguous?
questions.solution: sinB = b·sinA/a = (√3+1)(1/√2)/2 = (√3+1)/(2√2) ≈ 0.966, so B = 75° or 105°; A+B = 120° or 150°, both below 180°, so this case is AMBIGUOUS with two solutions. If B = 75°: C = 60° and c = a·sinC/sinA = 2(√3/2)/(1/√2) = √6. If B = 105°: C = 30° and c = 2(1/2)/(1/√2) = √2. Answer: B = 75°, C = 60°, c = √6; or B = 105°, C = 30°, c = √2 (the printed Answers line writes 'a' for these, a label slip since a = 2 is given — verified by substitution: 2·sin60°/sin45° = √6. ✓).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q5(ii) (ambiguous case); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.knowledgeNote: b < a kills the second value: B is acute (19°30′), C = 130°30′, and sinC = sin49°30′ = 3/4 makes c = 9 exactly.
questions.question: Q5(iii). Given A = 30°, a = 6, b = 4 (take sin19°30′ = 1/3 and sin49°30′ = 3/4), solve the triangle. Is the solution ambiguous?
questions.solution: sinB = b·sinA/a = 4(1/2)/6 = 1/3, so B = 19°30′ (taking the given value). Since b < a, B < A = 30°, so B must be acute — only ONE solution. C = 180° - (30°+19°30′) = 130°30′. Then c = a·sinC/sinA = 6·sin130°30′/(1/2) = 12·sin49°30′ = 12·(3/4) = 9. Answer: B = 19°30′, C = 130°30′, c = 9, unique (matches the printed key).
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics Grade XI, Ch.7 Ex 7.1 Q5(iii); book p197 = PDF p224 (vision read)

questions.question: State one function each of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids in living organisms.
questions.solution:
Carbohydrates: the immediate source of energy (glucose in respiration) and structural material (cellulose in plant walls, starch and glycogen as storage).
Proteins: structural (collagen, keratin) and functional — enzymes, haemoglobin for transport, antibodies for defence, hormones.
Lipids: concentrated energy store (about twice the energy of carbohydrate per gram), insulation, phospholipids of membranes and steroid hormones.
Nucleic acids: DNA stores and transmits hereditary information; RNA carries that information and directs protein synthesis.

questions.question: Give any four differences between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell.
questions.solution:
1. Nucleus: absent in prokaryotes (nucleoid region only), a true membrane-bound nucleus in eukaryotes.
2. Membrane-bound organelles: absent in prokaryotes; mitochondria, plastids, ER and Golgi are present in eukaryotes.
3. Ribosomes: 70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotes.
4. Genetic material: circular, naked DNA without histones in prokaryotes; linear DNA wound on histone proteins in eukaryotes.
5. Size and division: 1–10 µm, dividing by binary fission, against 10–100 µm dividing by mitosis/meiosis.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion and explain why it is called the powerhouse of the cell.
questions.solution:
A mitochondrion has two membranes. The smooth outer membrane encloses the intermembrane space; the inner membrane is folded into cristae that greatly increase its surface area, and the enclosed matrix holds Krebs-cycle enzymes, mitochondrial DNA and 70S ribosomes, so the organelle is semi-autonomous.
In aerobic respiration the Krebs cycle runs in the matrix and the electron transport chain with oxidative phosphorylation sits on the inner membrane; both generate ATP, the energy currency used for all cellular work — hence 'powerhouse'. Mitochondria also carry out β-oxidation of fatty acids and help regulate apoptosis and calcium.

questions.question: Which cell organelle is the actual site of protein synthesis, and where are the proteins meant for secretion made?
questions.solution:
The ribosome — a non-membranous organelle of rRNA and protein — is the site of translation.
Ribosomes lying free in the cytoplasm make proteins used inside the cell, while ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum make proteins destined for secretion or for membranes; those proteins pass through the ER and Golgi before being exported in vesicles.

questions.question: State the chemical nature of the cell wall in plants, fungi and bacteria, and give two functions of the plant cell wall.
questions.solution:
Plants: cellulose microfibrils embedded in a matrix of pectin and hemicellulose (a primary wall, sometimes thickened by lignin). Fungi: chitin. Bacteria: peptidoglycan (murein) with lipopolysaccharide in Gram-negative walls.
Functions in plants: it gives mechanical strength and fixed shape, and it resists osmotic bursting so the cell can build turgor pressure; it also protects against desiccation, pathogens and mechanical injury, and being fully permeable it does not block the movement of water and solutes.

questions.question: Explain the phases of the cell cycle and give its significance.
questions.solution:
Interphase occupies most of the cycle: G1 for growth and organelle synthesis, S for DNA replication and histone synthesis, and G2 for further growth and a checkpoint before division; a cell that stops dividing but stays metabolically active enters G0.
The M phase is karyokinesis — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase — followed by cytokinesis, which divides the cytoplasm.
Significance: growth of the organism, replacement of worn-out cells, healing of wounds, maintenance of a constant chromosome number and the basis of vegetative reproduction.

questions.question: Give four significance points of meiosis in sexually reproducing organisms.
questions.solution:
1. It halves the chromosome number (2n → n), producing haploid gametes so that fertilisation restores the diploid number and the species count stays constant.
2. Crossing over between homologous chromatids and independent assortment of homologues recombine alleles, creating genetic variation on which natural selection acts.
3. Variation from meiosis plus random fertilisation is the basis of evolution and of the differences between siblings.
4. It removes errors: pairing and separation of homologues, with checkpoints, help keep chromosome number and structure stable across generations.

questions.question: Write the structure and functions of the Golgi apparatus and the lysosome.
questions.solution:
Golgi apparatus: a stack of flattened, curved cisternae with a cis (forming) and a trans (maturing) face, surrounded by vesicles; in plants it is called a dictyosome. It modifies proteins and lipids received from the ER (glycosylation, addition of sulphate), sorts and packages them, forms secretory vesicles, produces lysosomes and supplies wall material in plant cells.
Lysosome: a single-membrane vesicle budded from the Golgi containing hydrolytic enzymes that work best at acidic pH. It digests material taken in by phagocytosis (heterophagy), recycles worn-out organelles (autophagy), and on cell death releases its enzymes in autolysis — hence the name 'suicide bags'.

questions.prompt: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. Name the molecules that make it up and state one function of membrane proteins.
questions.solution:
Singer and Nicolson's fluid mosaic model: the membrane is a flexible bilayer of phospholipids in which proteins float like icebergs — 'fluid' because lipids and proteins move laterally, 'mosaic' because of the scattered protein pattern.
Components: phospholipid bilayer (hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in), cholesterol (stability), intrinsic and extrinsic proteins, and surface carbohydrates (glycolipids/glycoproteins).
Membrane proteins act as channels and carriers for selective transport, enzymes, and receptors that receive chemical signals.

questions.prompt: What are enzymes? Explain the lock-and-key hypothesis of enzyme action and list two factors that affect enzyme activity.
questions.solution:
Enzymes are biological catalysts — usually proteins — that speed up reactions without being consumed, by lowering activation energy.
Lock-and-key (Fischer): the substrate fits exactly into the enzyme's rigid active site like a key in a lock, forming an enzyme–substrate complex that yields products.
Activity is affected by temperature (rises to an optimum, then denaturation destroys the active site) and pH (each enzyme has an optimum pH; extremes denature it). Substrate concentration and inhibitors also matter.

questions.prompt: Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell, and which molecule is its energy currency?
questions.solution: The mitochondrion is the powerhouse of the cell — aerobic respiration there releases energy from glucose. The energy is stored as ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the cell's energy currency, made by oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.question: Differentiate primary from secondary aquatic adaptations with two examples each.
questions.solution:
Primary aquatic animals live in water throughout their life and have never left it: streamlined body, gills for respiration, fins or cilia for locomotion, no eyelids or external ears, and kidneys that excrete ammonia. Examples: fish (Rohu), prawn.
Secondary aquatic animals are originally land animals that have returned to water but retain land adaptations: they breathe by lungs, have hairs or feathers, four limbs modified into flippers or paddles, external ears may be reduced and they must surface to breathe. Examples: whale and dolphin (mammals), turtle and duck (reptile and bird).

questions.question: Describe cursorial, fossorial, arboreal and volant adaptations with one example each.
questions.solution:
Cursorial (running): long, strong hind limbs with reduced digits and light body; horse, hare.
Fossorial (burrowing): cylindrical body, short powerful forelimbs with claws, reduced eyes and ears, and a burrow habit; mole rat, earthworm-like mole.
Arboreal (tree-dwelling): prehensile hands or tail, opposable thumb, long limbs, claws or adhesive pads, forward-facing eyes for judging distance; monkey, tree frog.
Volant (flying): wings of feathers or membrane, hollow or light bones, keeled sternum with strong flight muscles and acute vision; bird, bat. Gliding animals such as the flying squirrel use a patagium instead of true wings.

questions.question: Define reflex action, taxes and dominance–leadership in animal behaviour, with one example each.
questions.solution:
Reflex action is an automatic, involuntary and rapid response to a stimulus, mediated by a reflex arc — receptor, sensory neurone, spinal cord centre, motor neurone and effector — without waiting for the brain, as when the pupil narrows in bright light or the hand is pulled back from a hot object.
Taxes are directed, whole-body movements towards or away from a stimulus: phototaxis in Euglena moving to light and geotaxis in roots growing downwards.
Dominance and leadership: in a group one individual asserts priority over food, space or mates (the dominant bull) and others follow it, as the leading hen in a pecking order or the lead animal in a herd moving to water.

questions.question: Explain fish and bird migration with their causes and one method used to study migration.
questions.solution:
Migration is the regular seasonal movement of animals between breeding and feeding or wintering grounds. Fish such as salmon and the Himalayan mahseer move upstream to spawn in cool, oxygen-rich water and return to feed in larger rivers or the sea (anadromous in salmon, catadromous in eel). Birds move between breeding grounds and warmer wintering areas when food and daylight fall in the north.
Causes: shortage of food and water, cold, need for a safe spawning or nesting site and day length acting as the trigger. Methods of study: ringing or banding with numbered metal or colour rings, radio and satellite telemetry, and geolocators that record light levels; observations of flock direction and timing are recorded alongside.

questions.question: Write the sources, effects and control measures of air pollution.
questions.solution:
Sources: burning of fossil fuels in industry, vehicles and brick kilns; smoke from biomass stoves; dust from roads, quarries and construction; sulphur and nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and particulate matter; also CFCs and methane.
Effects: respiratory disease and asthma, eye irritation, acid rain, damage to crops and lichens, reduced visibility, corrosion of buildings, and contribution to global warming and ozone depletion.
Control: shift to clean and renewable energy, fit catalytic converters and scrubbers, improve public transport, pave and water roads, ban open burning, plant green belts and enforce vehicle emission and industrial standards.

questions.question: Explain the chief sources and effects of water pollution and soil pollution, and suggest one control measure for each.
questions.solution:
Water pollution: untreated sewage and industrial effluent, agricultural fertilisers and pesticides, hospital waste, bathing and washing, and solid waste dumping. Effects: oxygen depletion kills fish, nutrient enrichment causes blooms and eutrophication, heavy metals accumulate in the food chain, and pathogens spread cholera and typhoid. Control: treat sewage and industrial effluent before discharge and stop dumping waste into rivers.
Soil pollution: excess chemical fertilisers and pesticides, plastic and polythene waste, industrial sludge, mine spoil and acid rain. Effects: loss of fertility and soil structure, death of soil organisms, crop contamination and groundwater pollution. Control: use organic manure and biofertilisers, adopt integrated pest management, and separate, compost and recycle solid waste.

questions.question: What are pesticides? Describe their effects and state how their harm can be reduced.
questions.solution:
Pesticides are chemicals used to kill pests — insecticides (organochlorines such as DDT, organophosphates), herbicides, fungicides and rodenticides.
Effects: they kill non-target beneficial insects and pollinators, and persistent chlorinated compounds accumulate in soil, water and living tissue, increasing at each trophic level through biomagnification — the reason birds of prey suffered eggshell thinning. Exposure causes poisoning in farm workers, residues in food and milk, and development of resistant pests; runoff pollutes rivers and groundwater.
Reduction: integrated pest management with biological control, resistant varieties and careful timing; use of biopesticides such as neem and Bacillus thuringiensis; correct dose, protective clothing and safe disposal; and legal restriction or ban of persistent organochlorines.

pyqs/class-11/biology/conservation-biolo.title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Conservation Biology — 2025
pyqs/class-11/biology/conservation-biolo.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 conservation biology unit

questions.question: Define biodiversity and describe its three levels with an example of each.
questions.solution:
Biodiversity is the variety and variability of living organisms at all levels of organisation, together with the ecological complexes they form.
Genetic diversity: variation of genes within a species — different landraces of rice or varieties of apple.
Species diversity: the number and relative abundance of species in an area — the many tree species of a Chitwan sal forest versus a single-species plantation.
Ecosystem or ecological diversity: the variety of habitats and communities — forests, grasslands, wetlands, rivers and alpine meadows within one country. Nepal, with all these within 147,000 km², ranks high in ecosystem diversity.

questions.question: Name the categories of protected areas in Nepal with one example each and explain what a Ramsar site is.
questions.solution:
Nepal's protected area system includes national parks (Chitwan, Sagarmatha, Bardia), wildlife reserves (Koshi Tappu, Parsa), conservation areas (Annapurna, Manaslu), hunting reserve (Dhorpatan) and buffer zones around parks; some areas are also designated as Ramsar sites.
A Ramsar site is a wetland of international importance listed under the Ramsar Convention of 1971, on the basis of its waterfowl, fish, plant life or ecological role. Nepal has listed sites including Koshi Tappu, Beeshazar Tal, Ghodaghodi Tal, Jagadishpur Reservoir, Rara Lake, Phoksundo Lake and the Mai Pokhari, which obliges the country to conserve them and use them wisely.

questions.question: Why does wildlife matter, what causes extinction, and what strategies conserve threatened species?
questions.solution:
Wildlife matters for ecological balance — predators control prey, pollinators and seed dispersers keep forests regenerating, and each species is part of a food web; it also provides direct economic value through tourism, genetic resources and medicine, and has cultural and ethical value.
Causes of extinction: habitat loss and fragmentation, overhunting and poaching, pollution, invasive species, climate change, disease and small population effects such as inbreeding.
Strategies: protect and connect habitats through parks, corridors and community forests; enforce anti-poaching law and control trade; breed endangered species in captivity and reintroduce them; restore degraded habitat; involve local people through buffer zones and ecotourism; and monitor populations with research.

questions.question: Explain the IUCN Red List categories of threatened species.
questions.solution:
The IUCN Red List ranks the extinction risk of species. Extinct (EX): no individual remains. Extinct in the wild (EW): survives only in captivity. Critically endangered (CR): extremely high risk in the wild. Endangered (EN): very high risk. Vulnerable (VU): high risk of extinction. Near threatened (NT): close to qualifying. Least concern (LC): widespread and not currently at risk. Data deficient (DD): too little information to assess.
CR, EN and VU together are 'threatened'. The categories are assigned from quantitative criteria — population size, rate of decline, range area and fragmentation — and are reviewed periodically, so they guide national law and conservation priority.

questions.question: Name any five endangered or threatened animal species of Nepal and state the main threat to each.
questions.solution:
Greater one-horned rhinoceros — poaching for horn and loss of grassland habitat.
Royal Bengal tiger — poaching for skin and bone and habitat fragmentation.
Red panda — loss of bamboo forest and fur trade.
Snow leopard — retaliatory killing over livestock and loss of prey.
Gharial — loss of river habitat, fishing nets and sand mining.
Other threatened species include the wild elephant, musk deer, pangolin, Chinese pangolin, hispid hare, Bengal florican and the spiny babbler. Conservation relies on anti-poaching units, habitat protection, prey recovery, captive breeding and community participation.

questions.question: Differentiate in-situ and ex-situ conservation and give two advantages and one limitation of each.
questions.solution:
In-situ conservation keeps a species inside its natural habitat — national parks, reserves, conservation areas, community forests and wetlands.
Advantages: the whole community and its interactions are preserved, and populations keep evolving under natural selection; it protects watersheds and supports tourism. Limitation: it needs large areas and can fail if the habitat is degraded or the population is already very small.
Ex-situ conservation keeps the species outside its habitat — botanical gardens, zoos, seed and gene banks, tissue culture.
Advantages: it can save species whose habitat is gone and supplies material for reintroduction; it allows research and breeding. Limitation: only a few individuals are kept, genetic diversity is narrow and behaviour needed in the wild may be lost, so it cannot replace habitat protection.

questions.question: What does 'endangered species' mean, and how does it differ from a 'rare' species?
questions.solution:
An endangered species is one whose population has fallen so low, or is declining so fast, that it faces a very high risk of extinction in the wild in the near future — for example the greater one-horned rhinoceros in Nepal.
A rare species has a naturally small population or a very restricted range and may never have been abundant; it is not necessarily declining. Rare species are vulnerable because a single local disturbance can wipe out the whole population, so both categories need protection but for different reasons.

pyqs/class-11/biology/ecology/01-neb-202.title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Ecology — 2025
pyqs/class-11/biology/ecology/01-neb-202.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 ecology unit

questions.question: Define ecology. Name the abiotic factors of a habitat and describe three biotic interactions.
questions.solution:
Ecology is the study of the relationships between organisms and their environment, including other organisms.
Abiotic factors include light, temperature, water, humidity, soil type and pH, oxygen, salinity and wind.
Biotic interactions: mutualism, where both partners gain (alga and fungus in a lichen); parasitism, where one gains and harms the host (Plasmodium in man); competition, where individuals of the same or different species fight for the same limited resource and both lose something.

questions.question: Describe the structural and functional components of a pond ecosystem.
questions.solution:
Structure: abiotic components are water, dissolved oxygen and salts, light and temperature; producers are phytoplankton (algae) plus submerged, floating and marginal plants; consumers are zooplankton and insects (primary), frogs and small fish (secondary) and large fish (tertiary); decomposers are bacteria and fungi in the mud at the bottom.
Function: the four components carry out productivity (photosynthesis by phytoplankton), decomposition of organic debris, energy flow through the grazing food chain and nutrient cycling. Together the four components keep the pond running: energy enters as sunlight, passes through the food web and leaves as heat, while nutrients cycle within the pond. Being small, a pond responds sharply to nutrient input, so nutrient-rich runoff quickly causes blooms and eutrophication.

questions.question: Define food chain, food web and ecological pyramid. State the ten per cent law and give the pyramid of energy in a grassland.
questions.solution:
A food chain is the sequence in which energy passes from producers through consumers (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake). A food web is the network of interconnected food chains in a community. An ecological pyramid is a graphical representation of numbers, biomass or energy at each trophic level.
The ten per cent law says only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the rest is lost in respiration, heat, movement and undigested material. So a grassland energy pyramid is always upright, with producers at the base holding the greatest energy.

questions.question: Differentiate gross primary productivity from net primary productivity, and give one reason why a pyramid of numbers can be inverted.
questions.solution:
Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total organic matter fixed by producers by photosynthesis per unit time and area. Net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus the energy the producers use in respiration, so NPP = GPP − R; only NPP is available to consumers.
A pyramid of numbers is inverted when one producer supports a great number of consumers, as when thousands of insects feed on a single large tree, or when many small parasites live on one large host. The pyramid of numbers is therefore not a reliable picture of energy flow.

questions.question: Explain the carbon cycle with reference to photosynthesis, respiration and fossil fuels.
questions.solution:
Carbon is fixed as carbon dioxide by photosynthesis into organic compounds and returns to the atmosphere by respiration of plants and animals and by decomposition. Carbon dioxide also dissolves in water and is exchanged between the atmosphere and the oceans.
Some organic carbon is buried and converted into coal, oil and gas over long periods; burning these fossil fuels, along with deforestation and forest fires, releases carbon fixed long ago, so atmospheric CO2 rises faster than photosynthesis can remove it. That imbalance is the main driver of the greenhouse effect and global warming.

questions.question: Describe the nitrogen cycle, mentioning nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation and denitrification.
questions.solution:
Atmospheric nitrogen cannot be used directly by plants. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria — Rhizobium in root nodules and free-living Azotobacter and cyanobacteria — reduce it to ammonia (nitrogen fixation), and lightning and industrial fertiliser manufacture add fixed nitrogen too.
Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) oxidise ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate (nitrification); plants absorb nitrate or ammonium and incorporate it into proteins (assimilation). Decomposers release ammonia from dead matter (ammonification), and denitrifying bacteria such as Pseudomonas convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, closing the cycle.

questions.question: What is ecological succession? Differentiate hydrarch and xerarch succession and define climax community.
questions.solution:
Ecological succession is the orderly, directional replacement of one community by another at a site over time, until a stable community forms.
Hydrarch succession starts in water — pioneer phytoplanktons give way to submerged, then floating and marginal plants, then reeds and finally land vegetation as soil builds up. Xerarch succession starts on bare rock: lichens weather the rock, mosses follow, then grasses, shrubs and trees.
The climax community is the final, self-perpetuating community in equilibrium with the climate of the area, such as a forest in a temperate region.

questions.question: Describe the adaptations of hydrophytes and xerophytes.
questions.solution:
Hydrophytes live in or on water and are adapted to shortage of air and support: a thin cuticle, abundant air chambers (aerenchyma) for buoyancy and gas exchange, poorly developed xylem, stomata on the upper surface only or absent in submerged forms, and long flexible stems.
Xerophytes live in dry habitats and are adapted to conserve water: thick cuticle and waxy surfaces, sunken or hairy stomata, small or reduced leaves turned into spines, deep or widely spreading roots, water-storing succulent tissue and leaf fall in the dry season.

questions.question: Write the causes, effects and control measures of the greenhouse effect and of acid rain.
questions.solution:
Greenhouse effect: CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and CFCs from fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture and industry trap outgoing infrared radiation, warming the surface. Effects: melting glaciers, rising sea level, floods and droughts, shifting crops and loss of biodiversity. Control: cut fossil-fuel use, plant forests, use renewable energy, improve efficiency and adopt the Paris-type commitments.
Acid rain: sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning coal, oil and vehicle fuel dissolve in rain to give sulphuric and nitric acid. Effects: acidified lakes kill fish, aluminium is released, forests are damaged, buildings and monuments corrode and soil nutrients are leached. Control: desulphurise fuels and flue gases, use catalytic converters, switch to cleaner energy and add lime to affected waters.

questions.question: Define ecological succession. Distinguish primary from secondary succession with one example each, and name the stable final community.
questions.solution:
Succession is the gradual, directional replacement of one community by another in an area over time, driven by the organisms themselves modifying the environment.
Primary succession starts on a bare, lifeless surface with no soil — e.g. lichens and mosses colonising bare volcanic rock, slowly building soil for larger plants.
Secondary succession restarts where a community was disturbed but soil remains — e.g. a forest regrowing after a fire or abandoned farmland returning to woodland; it is much faster.
The stable end-stage community in equilibrium with the climate is the climax community.

questions.question: What is the 10% law of energy flow? A food chain is: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. If grass traps $20{,}000\,\mathrm{kJ}$, how much energy reaches the snake?
questions.solution:
Lindeman's 10% law: only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level transfers to the next; ~90% is lost as heat through respiration, movement and waste.
Grass (producer): $20{,}000\,\mathrm{kJ}$ → grasshopper: 10% = $2{,}000\,\mathrm{kJ}$ → frog: $200\,\mathrm{kJ}$ → snake: $20\,\mathrm{kJ}$. This repeated 90% loss is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels and why top carnivores are few.

questions.question: In a pyramid of biomass in a pond ecosystem, which level forms the base and why is the pyramid inverted there?
questions.solution: Producers (phytoplankton) form the base. The pyramid is inverted because the standing crop of tiny, short-lived phytoplankton at any moment weighs less than the zooplankton and fish it supports — the producers reproduce so fast that a small biomass sustains a larger consumer biomass. (Pyramids of energy are never inverted; only biomass and number can be.)
