pyqs/class-11/biology/evolutionary-biolo.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 evolutionary biology unit

questions.question: Describe the Oparin–Haldane hypothesis of the origin of life and explain the significance of the Miller–Urey experiment.
questions.solution:
Oparin and Haldane proposed that the primitive Earth had a reducing atmosphere of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour with no free oxygen, together with intense ultraviolet radiation, lightning and volcanic heat. These energy sources converted simple gases into organic molecules, which accumulated in the warm ocean as a 'hot dilute soup'; the molecules aggregated into coacervates — membranes enclosing a chemical system — and these became the first primitive cells.
Miller and Urey passed electric sparks through a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour and obtained amino acids, proving experimentally that the organic building blocks of life can form abiotically under such conditions.

questions.question: Discuss any four lines of evidence of evolution.
questions.solution:
Palaeontological: fossils in rock strata show a sequence of forms and connecting links such as Archaeopteryx, which has both reptilian and avian characters.
Morphological and anatomical: homologous organs — forelimbs of a man, whale, bat and horse built on the same plan — indicate common ancestry, whereas analogous organs (wing of an insect and of a bird) show convergent adaptation.
Embryological: vertebrate embryos share gill slits and a tail at early stages, pointing to common descent.
Biochemical and molecular: the same genetic code, similar proteins such as cytochrome c and similar blood pigments across species show relatedness, and the degree of difference measures how long lineages have been separate.

questions.question: Explain Lamarckism and state why it is rejected.
questions.solution:
Lamarck proposed that organisms have an inborn urge to become more complex, that use of an organ strengthens it while disuse weakens it (use and disuse), and that such acquired characters are inherited by the offspring — the long neck of the giraffe arising from generations of stretching for high leaves.
It is rejected because acquired changes in body cells do not alter the genes of germ cells, so they are not inherited: Weismann cut the tails of mice for many generations and no tailless young appeared, and a blacksmith's strong arms do not produce strong-armed children. The theory also cannot explain why structures useless to the organism exist.

questions.question: State Darwin's theory of natural selection and explain how neo-Darwinism differs from it.
questions.solution:
Darwin's theory rests on overproduction of offspring, variation among them, a struggle for existence, survival of the fittest and inheritance of favourable variations, so that populations gradually change — descent with modification. Later forms of the theory add the modern understanding of heredity.
Neo-Darwinism (the modern synthesis) explains variation as mutation and recombination rather than vague 'variation', identifies genes as the unit of inheritance, and treats evolution as a change in allele frequency in a population under selection, genetic drift, gene flow and mutation, supported by population genetics and the fossil record.

questions.question: Give the position of man in the animal kingdom with the characters that justify it.
questions.solution:
Man (Homo sapiens) is placed in Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Subphylum Vertebrata, Class Mammalia, Order Primates, Family Hominidae, Genus Homo, Species sapiens.
Justification: animal — heterotrophic, no cell wall, moves; chordate — notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and gill slits at some stage; vertebrate — vertebral column and internal skeleton; mammal — hair, mammary glands, warm blood, diaphragm, three middle-ear bones and a four-chambered heart; primate — grasping hands, opposable thumb, forward-facing eyes with stereoscopic vision, large brain, nails instead of claws and usually one young per birth.

questions.question: Give four differences between old-world monkeys and new-world monkeys.
questions.solution:
1. Nose: narrow, downward-pointing nostrils in old-world monkeys; broad, flat, sideways-facing nostrils in new-world monkeys.
2. Tail: never prehensile in old-world monkeys; often prehensile (gripping) in new-world monkeys.
3. Distribution: Africa and Asia against Central and South America.
4. Teeth and thumb: old-world monkeys have two premolars and opposable thumbs; new-world monkeys have three premolars and thumbs that do not oppose as fully.
Examples: rhesus monkey and baboon (old world); spider monkey and marmoset (new world).

questions.question: Differentiate apes from man, and trace the evolution of modern man from the anthropoid ancestor.
questions.solution:
Apes have a semi-erect posture with longer arms than legs, a prognathous face with a prominent brow ridge, a C-shaped spine, a smaller brain (about 400–500 cm³), no chin and body hair; man is fully erect with longer legs, a flat face, an S-shaped spine, a brain of about 1,350–1,400 cm³, a chin and sparse hair, and possesses speech and culture.
The line runs Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus → Australopithecus africanus (bipedal, small brain) → Homo habilis (stone tools, 650 cm³) → Homo erectus (fire, larger brain, Java and Peking man) → Neanderthal man (burial, cold adaptation) → Cro-Magnon and finally Homo sapiens, with brain size, tool use and culture increasing along the line.

questions.question: Distinguish homologous from analogous organs with one example each, and state what each proves.
questions.solution:
Homologous organs have the same basic structure and embryonic origin but different functions — the forelimbs of man, bat, whale and horse. They show divergent evolution from a common ancestor.
Analogous organs have different structure and origin but similar function — the wing of an insect and the wing of a bird, or the eye of an octopus and of a fish. They show convergent evolution, in which unrelated organisms adapt to a similar way of life; they are evidence of adaptation, not of ancestry.

questions.question: Give an outline classification of Protista and the diagnostic features of Protozoa up to class with one example of each class.
questions.solution:
Kingdom Protista is divided into protozoans (animal-like), algae (plant-like) and slime moulds (fungus-like).
Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotic heterotrophs without a cell wall, moving by pseudopodia, flagella or cilia and often forming cysts.
Classes: Rhizopoda or Sarcodina — move by pseudopodia, e.g. Amoeba; Mastigophora or Flagellata — move by flagella, e.g. Trypanosoma, Euglena; Ciliophora — move by cilia, e.g. Paramecium; Sporozoa — no locomotory organelle, parasitic with spore-like stages, e.g. Plasmodium.

questions.question: Describe the structure and reproduction of Paramecium caudatum.
questions.solution:
Paramecium is a slipper-shaped ciliate covered by a pellicle with cilia; it has two nuclei — a large macronucleus for metabolism and a small micronucleus for reproduction — a contractile vacuole for osmoregulation at each end, food vacuoles and a cytostome with an oral groove.
Asexual reproduction is by transverse binary fission, sometimes preceded by conjugation. Sexual reproduction is conjugation: two individuals join at the oral grooves, their macronuclei degenerate and micronuclei undergo meiosis; a haploid nucleus from each migrates into the other, fuses to form a synkaryon, and the cells separate and divide — a way of exchanging genetic material and restoring vigour.

questions.question: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium vivax and name the vector.
questions.solution:
The cycle has two hosts. In the female Anopheles mosquito (definitive host) gametocytes taken up with a blood meal fuse in the gut to form a zygote, which becomes a motile ookinete and then an oocyst full of sporozoites; these migrate to the salivary glands.
When the mosquito bites, sporozoites enter the human liver and multiply asexually in liver cells (pre-erythrocytic phase), releasing merozoites into the blood. There they invade red cells, grow as trophozoites and divide into more merozoites, bursting the cells and causing the fever cycle; some become gametocytes, which are picked up by the next mosquito. Relapse follows from hypnozoites left in the liver.

questions.question: State the economic importance of Plasmodium falciparum.
questions.solution:
P. falciparum causes falciparum malaria, the most severe and often fatal form, with cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, kidney failure and pulmonary oedema. Its economic importance is entirely destructive: it removes productive days from adults, keeps children out of school, and reduces work capacity and learning; it drains household income for treatment and travel, and national budgets for drugs, nets and spraying.
In Nepal it threatens the Terai and inner-Terai districts and complicates irrigation and settlement projects, so malaria control is a public-health and development priority rather than a resource.

questions.question: Explain the levels of body organisation, body symmetry, body cavity and segmentation in animals with examples.
questions.solution:
Organisation: cellular (Porifera), tissue (Cnidaria), organ (Platyhelminthes), organ system (Nematoda onwards).
Symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (Hydra, starfish) and bilateral, where the body has a right and left half, a dorsal and ventral side and anterior and posterior ends — typical of active animals.
Body cavity: acoelomate, with no cavity between gut and body wall (Platyhelminthes); pseudocoelomate, a cavity not lined by mesoderm (Nematoda); coelomate, a true cavity lined by mesoderm (Annelida onwards).
Segmentation: metameric repetition of body parts along the axis, seen clearly in the earthworm, and as jointed segments in arthropods.

questions.question: Give the diagnostic features of any five animal phyla with one example each.
questions.solution:
Porifera: cellular level, no organs, body wall perforated by ostia and a spongocoel with collar cells; Sycon.
Cnidaria: radial symmetry, tissue level, one opening surrounded by tentacles bearing nematocysts; Hydra, Aurelia.
Platyhelminthes: flat, bilaterally symmetrical, acoelomate, with flame cells and often a parasitic life cycle; Fasciola, Taenia.
Nematoda: unsegmented, cylindrical, pseudocoelomate, covered by a cuticle, sexes usually separate; Ascaris.
Annelida: metamerically segmented coelomate worms with setae and a closed circulatory system; Pheretima, Hirudinaria.
Arthropoda: jointed appendages, chitinous exoskeleton, segmented body and open circulation; Palaemon, butterfly.
Mollusca: soft body with a fleshy foot and mantle, often a calcareous shell and a radula; Pila, Octopus.

questions.question: Describe the digestive system of earthworm.
questions.solution:
The alimentary canal is a straight tube: mouth in the first segment, buccal cavity, muscular pharynx that pumps in soil, oesophagus, muscular gizzard that grinds the food, and stomach, followed by the intestine which runs to the anus.
The intestine has an internal fold, the typhlosole, that increases absorptive surface, and its wall secretes enzymes; chloragogen cells store food and neutralise toxins. Digestion is extracellular: proteases, amylase and lipase act in the intestine at pH favourable for the enzymes. The worm feeds on soil rich in decayed organic matter and the undigested soil is egested as a cast — an albuminous soil deposit valuable to farmers.

questions.question: Describe the excretory and nervous systems of earthworm.
questions.solution:
Excretion is by nephridia of three kinds: pharyngeal micronephridia, integumentary nephridia scattered on the body wall, and septal nephridia attached to the septa behind the clitellum. A nephridium has a nephrostome ciliated funnel, a coiled tubule and an external nephridiopore; it removes nitrogenous waste as urea, and the chloragogen cells help by converting ammonia into urea.
The nervous system is a dorsal cerebral ganglion in the third segment, a circumpharyngeal connectives ring and a ventral nerve cord with a ganglion in each segment; sense organs include photoreceptor cells, taste buds and epidermal receptor cells, and giant nerve fibres allow rapid withdrawal.

questions.question: Describe the reproductive system of earthworm and state four of its economic benefits.
questions.solution:
Earthworm is hermaphrodite: male organs are two pairs of testes in segments 10 and 11, with seminal vesicles and vasa deferentia opening at the prostatic pores of segment 18; female organs are a pair of ovaries in segment 13 with oviducts opening at segment 14. Four pairs of spermathecae in segments 6–9 store sperm during mutual cross-fertilisation; two worms lie head to tail, exchange sperm, and later the clitellum secretes a cocoon into which eggs and stored sperm are shed, so fertilisation is external in the cocoon.
Benefits: casts improve soil fertility and structure, burrows aerate and drain soil, worms are protein feed for poultry and fish, and they help degrade organic waste in vermicomposting; they also serve as bait and in the food chain.

questions.question: Describe the digestive and respiratory systems of frog.
questions.solution:
Digestive: the mouth has a sticky tongue attached in front and numerous small, backwardly directed teeth on the upper jaw, with the internal nares opening into the buccal cavity. The oesophagus leads to a stomach with cardiac and pyloric parts, then the small intestine (duodenum, ileum) and large intestine opening into the cloaca. The liver with gall bladder, pancreas and salivary glands pour in secretions; digestion is completed in the intestine with absorption through villi.
Respiratory: in water by moist skin and buccal lining; on land by lungs — a pair of simple sacs with internal folds, linked to the buccal cavity by the larynx and bronchi. Breathing is a buccal pump: air is drawn into the buccal cavity, the nares close, the floor rises and air is forced into the lungs, which is why a frog throbs even when resting.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a frog's heart and explain the working of the circulation.
questions.solution:
The heart is three-chambered — two atria and one ventricle — lying in the pericardial cavity. The sinus venosus receives venous blood and opens into the right atrium; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs; the ventricle is thin-walled with internal ridges that reduce mixing, and the truncus arteriosus leaves it and divides into carotid, systemic and pulmocutaneous arches.
Working: the sinus venosus pumps deoxygenated blood into the right atrium while pulmonary veins fill the left; both atria contract, sending blood into the ventricle. During ventricular contraction the blood is directed so that the pulmocutaneous arches receive the deoxygenated part (to lungs and skin) and the carotids receive the oxygenated part (to head), so mixing is partly avoided. Blood returns through the venae cavae and pulmonary veins, and the flow is unidirectional because of valves at each chamber junction.

questions.question: Describe the male and female reproductive systems of frog.
questions.solution:
Male: a pair of yellowish oval testes attached to the kidney by the mesorchium, with vasa efferentia that run through the kidney into the ureter, which becomes the urinogenital duct opening into the cloaca; a vocal sac and nuptial thumb pad develop in breeding season.
Female: a pair of triangular ovaries above the kidneys with long, much-coiled oviducts, each opening into the coelom by a ciliated funnel and opening into the cloaca, plus a swollen oviduct during breeding. During amplexus, the male clasps the female and she releases eggs into the water, which the male fertilises externally; the zygotes hatch into tadpoles.

pyqs/class-11/biology/floral-diversity/0.title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Floral Diversity — 2025
pyqs/class-11/biology/floral-diversity/0.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 floral diversity unit

questions.question: Name the three domains of life and state the rules of binomial nomenclature with one example.
questions.solution:
The three domains are Archaea (prokaryotes of extreme habitats, with ether-linked membrane lipids and no peptidoglycan), Bacteria (prokaryotes with peptidoglycan walls) and Eukarya (nucleus and membrane-bound organelles).
Binomial nomenclature, given by Linnaeus, names every organism with two Latinised words: the genus with a capital letter and the species in lower case, both italicised in print and underlined when handwritten, e.g. Mangifera indica for mango. The name is Latin, follows the rule of priority, and is the same worldwide, which is why scientific names avoid the confusion of local names.

questions.question: State the basis of Whittaker's five kingdom classification, name the kingdoms with one example each, and give one merit and one demerit of the system.
questions.solution:
Basis: cell structure (prokaryote or eukaryote), thallus organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.
Kingdoms: Monera (bacteria), Protista (Euglena), Fungi (Rhizopus), Plantae (mango), Animalia (earthworm).
Merit: it separates prokaryotes from eukaryotes and autotrophs from heterotrophs, placing fungi in a kingdom of their own. Demerit: Protista and Fungi remain heterogeneous groups, and bacteria and cyanobacteria are kept together although they differ greatly.

questions.question: Give the diagnostic features of the four classes of fungi with one example each.
questions.solution:
Phycomycetes: aseptate, coenocytic hyphae, spores non-motile or motile; Rhizopus and Mucor.
Ascomycetes (sac fungi): septate hyphae, sexual spores as ascospores inside an ascus, often budding; Penicillium, yeast.
Basidiomycetes (club fungi): septate hyphae, basidiospores borne on a basidium; mushroom Agaricus, puffball.
Deuteromycetes (fungi imperfecti): septate hyphae, only asexual reproduction by conidia, sexual stage unknown; Alternaria, Trichoderma.

questions.question: Describe reproduction in Mucor and in yeast.
questions.solution:
Mucor reproduces vegetatively by fragmentation of the mycelium, asexually by non-motile sporangiospores formed inside a sporangium on a sporangiophore, and sexually by conjugation of two opposite strains: gametangia fuse, a thick-walled zygospore forms, undergoes meiosis and germinates into a new mycelium.
Yeast (Saccharomyces) multiplies mainly by budding — a small bud grows out, receives a nucleus and separates — and sometimes by fission. Sexually two haploid cells fuse and the diploid cell undergoes meiosis to form four ascospores inside an ascus.

questions.question: How are edible mushrooms distinguished from poisonous ones, and what is the economic importance of fungi?
questions.solution:
There is no single reliable field test. Edible forms such as Agaricus campestris and Pleurotus (oyster) are identified by species; deadly ones such as Amanita phalloides and A. muscaria carry amatoxins and must never be eaten. Warnings are only hints, not proof — never judge by colour, ring or volva alone.
Economic importance: food rich in protein and B vitamins, flavour and enzymes, antibiotics (penicillin), organic acids, vitamins, mycorrhizal partners for crops, decomposers that recycle nutrients and yeasts for bakery and brewing; on the other hand fungi spoil food, rot timber and cause crop and skin diseases.

questions.question: What is a lichen? Name its two partners and state why lichens are used as pollution indicators.
questions.solution:
A lichen is a symbiotic association of a fungus (mycobiont) and an alga or cyanobacterium (phycobiont). The fungus provides shelter, water and minerals; the alga photosynthesises and supplies food.
Lichens absorb water and gases directly over their whole surface and have no protective cuticle, so they accumulate sulphur dioxide and other pollutants and die or change form when air is polluted. Their presence therefore indicates clean air and their disappearance indicates pollution.

questions.question: Give the characteristic pigments and reserve foods of green, brown and red algae, and describe reproduction in Spirogyra.
questions.solution:
Chlorophyceae (green): chlorophyll a and b, reserve starch. Phaeophyceae (brown): chlorophyll a and c with fucoxanthin, reserve laminarin and mannitol. Rhodophyceae (red): chlorophyll a and d with phycoerythrin, reserve floridean starch.
Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga with spiral chloroplasts. It multiplies asexually by fragmentation; sexually it reproduces by conjugation — in scalariform conjugation two filaments lie side by side and form a conjugation tube through which one gamete passes, and in lateral conjugation gametes of adjacent cells fuse. The zygote becomes a zygospore, undergoes meiosis and germinates into a new filament.

questions.question: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom? Describe the structure and reproduction of Marchantia.
questions.solution:
Bryophytes live on land but need a film of water for the male gametes to swim to the archegonia, so they are called amphibians of the plant kingdom. The gametophyte is the dominant plant, vascular tissue is absent, and the sporophyte is dependent on the gametophyte.
Marchantia has a dorsiventral thallus with a midrib, rhizoids and scales below, and pores on the upper surface. It reproduces asexually by gemmae formed in gemma cups, and sexually by antheridia and archegonia borne on umbrella-shaped gametophores; water carries the sperm, the zygote becomes a sporophyte whose capsule releases spores.

questions.question: State the distinguishing features of pteridophytes and describe the life cycle of Dryopteris.
questions.solution:
Pteridophytes are the first true vascular plants: the sporophyte is dominant with true roots, stem and compound leaves, and spores are produced in sporangia, so they never form seeds.
In Dryopteris the sporophyte has a rhizome and large fronds whose underside bears sori with sporangia. Spores fall on damp soil and grow into a heart-shaped prothallus (gametophyte) bearing antheridia and archegonia; water carries the sperm to the egg, the zygote develops into a new sporophyte, and the prothallus dies — a clear alternation of generations.

questions.question: Why are gymnosperms called naked-seeded plants? Describe reproduction in Pinus and give two economic uses.
questions.solution:
Their ovules lie exposed on the megasporophylls of a cone, and after fertilisation the seeds remain uncovered on the cone scales because there is no ovary to enclose them.
Pinus is monoecious and heterosporous. Male cones bear microsporophylls producing pollen with air sacs that is carried by wind; female cones bear ovules with archegonia. Pollination occurs when pollen reaches the ovule, but fertilisation follows about a year later; the zygote develops into an embryo and the whole structure becomes a winged seed between the scale.
Uses: timber and pulp, resin, turpentine and rosin, and edible seeds (chilgoza from Pinus gerardiana).

questions.question: Give four differences between a root and a stem, and name one modification of each with the plant.
questions.solution:
1. Position: the root grows downwards under the soil, the stem grows upwards into air.
2. Nodes and internodes: absent in the root, present in the stem.
3. Leaves and buds: the root bears neither, the stem bears both.
4. Branching and geotropism: root branching is endogenous and negatively phototropic; stem branching is exogenous and positively phototropic.
Modifications: the tap root of carrot is swollen for food storage; the stem of potato becomes an underground tuber while that of cucumber becomes a tendril for climbing.

questions.question: Write the taxonomic hierarchy and give the floral formula, one diagnostic flower character and one example of the families Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae.
questions.solution:
Hierarchy: Kingdom → Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
Brassicaceae: Br, ⊕, K 2+2, C 4, A 2+4, G(2); tetradynamous stamens and a siliqua fruit; Brassica campestris.
Fabaceae: Br, %, K(5), C 1+2+(2), A(9)+1, G 1; papilionaceous corolla and a legume pod with root nodules; Pisum sativum.
Solanaceae: Br, ⊕, K(5), C(5), A 5, G(2); persistent calyx with axile placentation and a berry or capsule; Solanum tuberosum.
Liliaceae: Br, ⊕, P 3+3, A 3+3, G(3); trimerous perianth with a superior ovary; Allium cepa.

pyqs/class-11/biology/introduction-to-bi.title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Introduction To Biology — 2025
pyqs/class-11/biology/introduction-to-bi.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 introduction to biology unit

questions.question: Define biology. Name its major branches and state the fields studied under pure and applied biology.
questions.solution:
Biology is the science of living things — their structure, function, growth, origin, evolution, distribution and classification.
Major branches: morphology, anatomy, physiology, cytology, genetics, evolution, taxonomy and ecology, split by group into botany, zoology and microbiology.
Pure biology studies life for knowledge — taxonomy, genetics, evolution, physiology — while applied biology uses that knowledge for practical ends: medicine, agriculture, animal husbandry, forestry, fisheries, biotechnology, pharmacy and environmental management.

questions.question: Explain the relationship of biology with chemistry, physics, mathematics and geography, giving one example each.
questions.solution:
Chemistry: explains the molecules of life — the structure of DNA and the action of enzymes are chemistry applied to living systems, and biochemistry grew from this link.
Physics: explains how organisms work — osmosis and diffusion, the optics of the eye, the mechanics of muscle and bone, the electricity of nerve impulses.
Mathematics: turns observations into testable models — Mendelian ratios, population growth equations, statistics used to test whether results are significant.
Geography and geology: explain where organisms live — climate, soil and landforms decide vegetation, and fossils in rock strata document evolution.

questions.question: What is the scientific method, and why is a control group necessary in an experiment?
questions.solution:
The scientific method is an orderly way of gaining reliable knowledge: observation, a question, a hypothesis, a controlled experiment, collection and analysis of data, and a conclusion that may support or reject the hypothesis, after which results are reported so others can repeat them.
A control group is treated exactly like the experimental group except for the one variable being tested. It shows what would have happened without the treatment, so any difference can be credited to that variable rather than to temperature, age or chance.

questions.question: Why is the study of biology important for Nepal? Give four points.
questions.solution:
1. Agriculture: most Nepalis depend on farming, so knowledge of crops, soil, pests, seeds and animal husbandry raises production and food security.
2. Health: understanding pathogens, immunity and nutrition supports disease control, vaccination and public-health planning in remote districts.
3. Natural resource management: forests, medicinal plants, biodiversity and watersheds need biological survey and conservation planning; biology also underlies ecotourism.
4. Biotechnology and environment: tissue culture, biofertilisers, biogas and bioremediation open new employment and help control pollution, while biology teaches how to protect the Himalayan ecosystems on which the country's water and climate depend.

pyqs/class-11/biology/introductory-micro.title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Introductory Microbiology — 2025
pyqs/class-11/biology/introductory-micro.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 introductory microbiology unit

questions.question: Describe the structure of a bacterial cell and state the function of any three parts.
questions.solution:
A bacterial cell has a cell envelope of capsule (in some), cell wall of peptidoglycan and plasma membrane; inside lie the nucleoid — a single circular DNA without histones — 70S ribosomes, plasmids, inclusion bodies and storage granules. Many bear flagella for movement, pili for attachment and conjugation, and some form endospores.
Functions: the capsule protects against drying and phagocytosis and helps adhesion; the cell wall gives shape and resists osmotic lysis; flagella provide motility; pili transfer DNA during conjugation; ribosomes carry out protein synthesis.

questions.question: Explain the modes of nutrition in bacteria and describe the bacterial growth curve.
questions.solution:
Autotrophic bacteria make their own food — photoautotrophs use light (cyanobacteria) and chemoautotrophs oxidise inorganic compounds (Nitrosomonas). Heterotrophic bacteria depend on organic matter: saprophytes decompose dead material, parasites live on hosts and pathogens cause disease.
In a closed culture the growth curve has four phases: lag (cells adapt and enzymes are induced, no division), log or exponential (fastest doubling under ample food), stationary (growth equals death as nutrients fall and waste accumulates) and decline or death phase.

questions.question: Give the characteristic features of cyanobacteria and their economic importance.
questions.solution:
Cyanobacteria are prokaryotic, photosynthetic and mostly blue-green; they contain chlorophyll a with phycocyanin and phycoerythrin, have no flagella, and store food as cyanophycean starch. Some form filaments with heterocysts for nitrogen fixation, and many secrete mucilage.
Importance: they fix atmospheric nitrogen (Anabaena, Nostoc) and are used as biofertiliser in paddy fields, add organic matter and improve soil fertility, serve as protein-rich food (Spirulina) and are used in sewage treatment. On the other hand, heavy growth in nutrient-rich water causes blooms that deoxygenate the water and release toxins.

questions.question: Draw the general structure of a virus and explain why viruses are regarded as a link between living and non-living things.
questions.solution:
A virus has a nucleic acid core — either DNA or RNA, never both — enclosed in a protein coat, the capsid, built of subunits called capsomeres; some also have an envelope derived from the host membrane.
They behave as non-living outside a host: they have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolism, do not respire, cannot reproduce independently and can be crystallised and stored like a chemical (tobacco mosaic virus). Yet inside a suitable host they replicate, mutate and evolve and show host specificity, so they sit on the border between living and non-living.

questions.question: Describe the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage.
questions.solution:
1. Adsorption: the phage tail fibres recognise and attach to specific receptors on the bacterial wall.
2. Penetration: the tail sheath contracts and injects the phage DNA into the bacterium, leaving the capsid outside.
3. Biosynthesis: host DNA is degraded and the phage DNA directs the host machinery to make phage DNA and proteins.
4. Maturation: heads, tails and DNA are assembled into new virions.
5. Lysis: phage lysozyme bursts the cell, releasing many progeny phages that infect new bacteria.
In the lysogenic cycle the phage DNA instead integrates into the bacterial chromosome as a prophage and is copied with it until induction triggers the lytic cycle.

questions.question: State four impacts of biotechnology in the field of microbiology.
questions.solution:
1. Recombinant bacteria such as E. coli produce human insulin, growth hormone and interferon, giving pure products in bulk.
2. Fermentation industries use microbes to make antibiotics (penicillin from Penicillium), alcohol, citric acid, vitamins and enzymes.
3. Gene cloning, PCR and DNA probes let pathogens be detected quickly and vaccines and gene therapy developed.
4. Engineered microbes carry out bioremediation of oil spills and industrial waste and produce biogas, while microbial genomics helps trace outbreaks.
Risks such as escape of engineered strains and antibiotic-resistance genes mean such work needs strict containment.

pyqs/class-11/biology/vegetation/01-neb-.title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Vegetation — 2025
pyqs/class-11/biology/vegetation/01-neb-.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 vegetation unit

questions.question: Define vegetation and describe the main types of vegetation found in Nepal.
questions.solution:
Vegetation means the plant cover of a region — the assemblage of plant communities growing there naturally, as distinct from a single flora or species list.
Nepal's vegetation follows altitude and rainfall: tropical and subtropical sal and mixed hardwood forests in the Terai and inner Terai up to about 1,000 m; temperate forests of oak, rhododendron, chestnut and alder from about 1,000–3,000 m; coniferous forests of pine, fir, spruce and juniper with birch higher up; alpine shrubs, meadows and cushion plants above the treeline; and almost no vegetation on the high Himalaya, where only mosses, lichens and snow algae survive.

questions.question: Differentiate in-situ from ex-situ conservation and give two examples of each in Nepal.
questions.solution:
In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, where they continue to evolve with the ecosystem: national parks and wildlife reserves (Chitwan National Park, Sagarmatha National Park), conservation areas and Ramsar sites, plus community forests and sacred groves.
Ex-situ conservation keeps species outside their habitat when the wild population is too small or its habitat is gone: botanical gardens (Godavari, Mahendra Ratna), seed banks, tissue-culture and zoo collections and captive breeding. In-situ is preferred because it preserves the whole community, while ex-situ is a safety net and a source of material for reintroduction.

questions.question: Explain how human activities affect natural vegetation and suggest three measures to reduce the damage.
questions.solution:
People clear forest for farmland, settlements, roads and hydropower, cut trees for fuelwood and timber, overgraze pastures, set fires and quarry hillsides. Plantations of a single species replace mixed forest, invasive species such as Mikania and Lantana spread, and pollution plus climate change shift the tree line. The result is deforestation, soil erosion and landslides, drying of springs, loss of habitat and extinction of species.
Measures: protect remaining forest through community forestry and strict law enforcement, promote fuel alternatives, terrace farming, agroforestry and reforestation with native species, and plan roads and dams with environmental impact assessment and habitat corridors.

questions.question: Which forest type dominates the Terai region of Nepal and which dominates the upper temperate zone?
questions.solution:
The Terai, below about 1,000 m with high rainfall and warm temperature, carries tropical and subtropical deciduous forest dominated by sal (Shorea robusta) with sissoo, khair and tall grasses.
The upper temperate zone, roughly 2,000–3,000 m, carries broad-leaved temperate forest of oak, rhododendron and laurel, passing into conifers — pine, fir, spruce and hemlock — and finally birch and juniper near the treeline.

questions.question: Why is Nepal rich in floral diversity? Mention the role of protected areas in conserving vegetation.
questions.solution:
Nepal spans only about 147,000 km² but rises from 60 m to 8,848 m, so it carries tropical, subtropical, temperate, subalpine and alpine climates within short distances; the monsoon adds a strong east–west rainfall gradient, and varied geology and soils add further niches. This is why the country holds a large share of the Himalayan flora, including many endemic and medicinal plants.
Protected areas conserve whole vegetation types and their successions, keep habitats large enough for wildlife, protect watersheds and gene pools, and support research, tourism and local livelihoods; buffer zones and community forests extend protection beyond park boundaries.

pyqs/class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding.origin: curated NEB-pattern set filling the 2021 gap for class-11 chemical bonding

questions.question: State the octet rule and give two limitations with examples. Why does $\mathrm{BF_3}$ violate it?
questions.solution:
Octet rule: atoms bond so as to have eight electrons in the valence shell (the noble-gas configuration).
Limitations: (1) Incomplete octet — $\mathrm{BF_3}$ has only 6 electrons around B, $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$ only 4; (2) Expanded octet — $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ (10), $\mathrm{SF_6}$ (12) using vacant d-orbitals; (3) odd-electron molecules like NO are stable with 7/11 electrons.
$\mathrm{BF_3}$: boron has 3 valence electrons and forms 3 single bonds (6 shared electrons). Adding a fourth bond is impossible without exceeding its available orbitals, so it stays electron-deficient — a strong Lewis acid.

questions.question: Using VSEPR theory, predict the shapes of $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$, and arrange their bond angles in decreasing order with justification.
questions.solution:
VSEPR: electron pairs repel; order lone-pair–lone-pair > lone-pair–bond-pair > bond-pair–bond-pair.
$\mathrm{CH_4}$: 4 bond pairs, no lone pair → tetrahedral, $109.5^\circ$.
$\mathrm{NH_3}$: 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → trigonal pyramidal; the lone pair squeezes the angle to $107^\circ$.
$\mathrm{H_2O}$: 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs → bent (V-shape); two lone pairs squeeze hardest, angle $104.5^\circ$.
Order: $\mathrm{CH_4}$ ($109.5^\circ$) > $\mathrm{NH_3}$ ($107^\circ$) > $\mathrm{H_2O}$ ($104.5^\circ$) — more lone pairs, smaller angle.

questions.question: Which has the strongest hydrogen bonding, and why? (a) $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (b) $\mathrm{NH_3}$ (c) $\mathrm{HF}$
questions.solution: (c) $\mathrm{HF}$. Hydrogen-bond strength follows the electronegativity of the atom holding H: F (4.0) > O (3.5) > N (3.0). The most polar H–X bond gives the most positive H, hence the strongest attraction to a neighbouring lone pair. (Water still boils higher than HF overall because each water molecule forms more H-bonds — a network effect.)

questions.prompt: State Avogadro's law. How many molecules are present in $11.2\,\mathrm{L}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ at STP, and what is its mass?
questions.solution:
Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
At STP one mole occupies $22.4\,\mathrm{L}$, so $11.2\,\mathrm{L} = 0.5\,\mathrm{mol}$. Molecules $= 0.5 \times 6.022\times10^{23} = 3.011\times10^{23}$.
Molar mass of $\mathrm{CO_2} = 44\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, so mass $= 0.5 \times 44 = 22\,\mathrm{g}$.

questions.prompt: Balance the redox reaction by the ion-electron method: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- + Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + Fe^{3+}}$ (acidic medium).
questions.solution:
Reduction half: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+}}$. Balance O with water: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$; balance H with $H^+$: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$; balance charge with electrons: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$.
Oxidation half: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + e^-}$ — multiply by 5.
Adding: $\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O}$. Atoms and charges ($+17$ each side) both balance.

questions.prompt: What is the empirical formula of a compound with 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass? (C=12, H=1, O=16)
questions.solution: Moles per 100 g: C $= 40/12 = 3.33$, H $= 6.7/1 = 6.7$, O $= 53.3/16 = 3.33$. Divide by the smallest (3.33): C:H:O $= 1:2:1$. Empirical formula $\mathrm{CH_2O}$.

questions.question: Rewrite as conditional sentences: (a) He didn't study. He failed. (third conditional) (b) It rains. The match is cancelled. (first conditional)
questions.solution:
(a) Past regret takes the third conditional — if + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If he had studied, he would not have failed.' (Both clauses step one tense back from reality.)
(b) A real future possibility takes the first conditional — if + present simple, will + verb: 'If it rains, the match will be cancelled.'

questions.question: Fill in the blanks with articles (a/an/the/×): (a) ___ Mount Everest is ___ highest peak in ___ world. (b) She plays ___ guitar and ___ football.
questions.solution:
(a) 'Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.' — no article before Mount Everest (named mountain, zero article); 'the highest' (superlative takes the); 'the world' (unique object takes the).
(b) 'She plays the guitar and × football.' — instruments take 'the' (the guitar), while games/sports take no article (football).

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag: 'You haven't seen my keys, ___?' (a) have you (b) haven't you (c) did you
questions.solution: (a) 'have you'. Tags reverse the statement's polarity: a negative statement ('haven't seen') takes a positive tag with the same auxiliary ('have you'). 'You haven't seen my keys, have you?'

questions.prompt: Change the voice: (a) 'She writes a letter.' (b) 'The teacher praised the students.'
questions.solution:
(a) Present simple passive — object becomes subject, verb becomes is/am/are + past participle: 'A letter is written by her.'

questions.prompt: Fill in the blanks with suitable prepositions: (a) He has been suffering ___ fever ___ Monday. (b) She is good ___ mathematics but weak ___ English.
questions.solution:
(a) 'He has been suffering FROM fever SINCE Monday.' — suffer takes 'from'; 'since' marks the starting point (Monday).
(b) 'She is good AT mathematics but weak IN English.' — 'good at' and 'weak in' are fixed adjective–preposition collocations.

questions.prompt: Identify the tense: 'They had finished the work before the guests arrived.'
questions.solution: 'Had finished' is the past perfect — used for the earlier of two past events. The work was completed first, then the guests arrived (simple past). So the sentence is in the past perfect tense.

questions.prompt: If $2, x, 8$ are in geometric progression, find $x$. Then find the sum of the first 6 terms of the GP $2, 2\sqrt{2}, 4, \dots$
questions.solution:
In GP the middle term squared equals the product of neighbours: $x^2 = 2\times8 = 16$, so $x = \pm 4$.
The GP $2, 2\sqrt{2}, 4, \dots$ has $a = 2$, $r = \sqrt{2}$. Sum of $n$ terms: $S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1)$.
$S_6 = 2((\sqrt{2})^6 - 1)/(\sqrt{2}-1) = 2(8-1)/(\sqrt{2}-1) = 14/(\sqrt{2}-1)$. Rationalise: $14(\sqrt{2}+1)/((2-1)) = 14(\sqrt{2}+1)$.

questions.prompt: Solve the quadratic equation $2x^2 - 7x + 3 = 0$ by factorisation, and verify the roots using the sum and product of roots.
questions.solution:
Factorise: $2x^2 - 7x + 3 = 2x^2 - 6x - x + 3 = 2x(x-3) - 1(x-3) = (2x-1)(x-3)$. Roots: $x = 1/2$ and $x = 3$.
Check: sum $= 1/2 + 3 = 7/2 = -b/a = 7/2$ ✓. Product $= (1/2)\times3 = 3/2 = c/a = 3/2$ ✓. Both relations hold, confirming the roots.

questions.prompt: If $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, what is $|A|$ (the determinant)?
questions.solution: For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, $|A| = ad - bc$. Here $|A| = 2\times3 - 1\times0 = 6$.

questions.question: Find the equation of the straight line passing through $(2, 3)$ with slope $m = -1$. Also write it in intercept form and state the intercepts.
questions.solution:
Point–slope form: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ gives $y - 3 = -1(x - 2)$, i.e. $y = -x + 5$, or $x + y = 5$.
Intercept form $x/a + y/b = 1$: divide by 5 → $x/5 + y/5 = 1$. x-intercept $a = 5$ (point $(5,0)$), y-intercept $b = 5$ (point $(0,5)$) — the line cuts equal intercepts, sloping down at $135^\circ$.

questions.question: Derive the distance formula between $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$. Use it to show that $A(1, 2)$, $B(4, 6)$ and $C(7, 2)$ form an isosceles triangle.
questions.solution:
By Pythagoras on the right triangle with legs $|x_2-x_1|$, $|y_2-y_1|$: $PQ = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$.
$AB = \sqrt{(4-1)^2 + (6-2)^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = 5$.
$BC = \sqrt{(7-4)^2 + (2-6)^2} = \sqrt{9+16} = 5$.
$AC = \sqrt{(7-1)^2 + (2-2)^2} = 6$. Since $AB = BC = 5$, the triangle is isosceles with vertex at $B$.

questions.question: What is the slope of the line $3x + 4y = 12$, and what is the slope of any line perpendicular to it?
questions.solution: Rewrite as $y = -\frac{3}{4}x + 3$, so slope $m = -3/4$. A perpendicular line has the negative-reciprocal slope $m_\perp = 4/3$ (since $m_1 m_2 = -1$).

questions.prompt: State Newton's three laws of motion. A $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass experiences a net force of $10\,\mathrm{N}$ for $3\,\mathrm{s}$ starting from rest. Find the final momentum and the distance travelled.
questions.solution:
First law: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a net external force acts (law of inertia). Second law: $F = ma$ — net force equals rate of change of momentum. Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
Acceleration $a = F/m = 10/2 = 5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Final velocity $v = u + at = 0 + 5\times3 = 15\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so momentum $p = mv = 2\times15 = 30\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$. Distance $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + 0.5\times5\times9 = 22.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

questions.prompt: Define linear momentum and state the principle of conservation of linear momentum. A $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ boy jumps off a $120\,\mathrm{kg}$ stationary boat with velocity $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the boat's recoil velocity?
questions.solution:
Linear momentum $p = mv$. Principle: if no external force acts on a system, its total momentum stays constant.
Initially both at rest, so total momentum is 0. After the jump: $m_{\text{boy}}v_{\text{boy}} + m_{\text{boat}}v_{\text{boat}} = 0$.
$60\times3 + 120\times v_{\text{boat}} = 0$, so $v_{\text{boat}} = -180/120 = -1.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ — the boat recoils at $1.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ opposite to the jump.

questions.prompt: A $0.5\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball moving at $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is stopped by a wall in $0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. What average force did the wall exert?
questions.solution: Impulse equals change in momentum: $F\Delta t = \Delta p = m(v - u) = 0.5\times(0 - 4) = -2\,\mathrm{N\,s}$. Hence $F = -2/0.1 = -20\,\mathrm{N}$ — the wall pushed back with $20\,\mathrm{N}$ on average.

pyqs/class-11/physics/gravitation/05-neb.origin: curated NEB-pattern set filling the 2020 gap for class-11 gravitation

questions.question: Define gravitational field intensity and gravitational potential. Derive the potential $V = -GM/r$ due to a point mass $M$ at distance $r$.
questions.solution:
Field intensity is the force per unit mass ($I = F/m$); potential is the work per unit mass to bring a test mass from infinity ($V = W/m$, zero at infinity).
Force on $m$ at distance $x$: $F = GMm/x^2$ toward $M$. Work bringing $m$ from infinity to $r$: $W = \int_{\infty}^{r} (-GMm/x^2)\,dx$ (negative because displacement opposes the field direction taken positive outward) $= GMm/r \cdot (-1)$… evaluating: $[-GMm/x]_{\infty}^{r} = -GMm/r$. Hence $V = W/m = -GM/r$. The negative sign means the field is attractive — work must be done by an external agent to pull a mass out.

questions.question: What is orbital velocity? Derive $v_o = \sqrt{GM/r}$ for a satellite at height $h$ above Earth (radius $R$), and find its value for a low orbit ($h \approx 0$). ($GM = gR^2$, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, $R = 6400\,\mathrm{km}$)
questions.solution:
Orbital velocity is the speed needed for a satellite's gravity to supply exactly the centripetal force: $mv_o^2/r = GMm/r^2$, giving $v_o = \sqrt{GM/r}$ with $r = R + h$.
For a low orbit $r \approx R$: $v_o = \sqrt{gR} = \sqrt{10 \times 6.4\times10^6} = \sqrt{64\times10^6} = 8000\,\mathrm{m/s} = 8\,\mathrm{km/s}$ — the first cosmic velocity.

questions.question: If Earth suddenly shrank to half its radius with the same mass, what would happen to $g$ on the surface?
questions.solution: $g = GM/R^2$. Halving $R$ divides by $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$, so $g$ becomes four times: about $40\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. (Weight would quadruple — shrinking concentrates the same mass closer to you.)

pyqs/class-12/biology/biodiversity-and-c.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Biodiversity And Conservation — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/biodiversity-and-c.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 biodiversity and conservation unit

questions.question: Define biodiversity and describe its three levels with an example of each.
questions.solution:
Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms at all levels, together with the ecological complexes they form.
Genetic diversity: variation of genes within a species, as among the many landraces of rice in Nepal.
Species diversity: the number and abundance of species in a region — the hundreds of tree species in a tropical forest against a pine plantation.
Ecosystem diversity: the variety of habitats and communities — forests, grasslands, wetlands, rivers and alpine zones in one landscape. Diversity is measured by species richness (number of species) and evenness (relative abundance), combined in indices such as Simpson's or Shannon–Wiener.

questions.question: Explain the latitudinal gradient and the species–area relationship.
questions.solution:
Latitudinal gradient: species richness is greatest near the equator and falls towards the poles. Tropical regions have a long evolutionary history without glaciation, a warm and stable climate, high and reliable rainfall, greater productivity and more complex habitats, so more niches and hence more species can coexist.
Species–area relationship: the number of species increases with the area sampled, following S = C A^z (or log S = log C + z log A), where z is about 0.1–0.2 for small areas and 0.6–1.2 for very large continents. The relationship is why small habitat fragments lose species quickly and why large protected areas conserve more diversity.

questions.question: Give the four main causes of biodiversity loss with an explanation of each.
questions.solution:
Habitat loss and fragmentation: the most important cause — forests cleared for farms, settlements and roads, wetlands drained, and remaining habitat broken into patches too small for large animals.
Over-exploitation: hunting, poaching, fishing and logging beyond the rate of replacement, as with rhino horn, tiger bone and some medicinal plants.
Invasive alien species: introduced plants and animals such as Mikania, water hyacinth, Lantana and tilapia outcompete or prey on natives.
Co-extinction and secondary effects: when a host or partner species disappears its dependants follow, and pollution plus climate change add further pressure; small populations also suffer inbreeding and loss of genetic variation.

questions.question: Describe in-situ conservation and the three zones of a biosphere reserve.
questions.solution:
In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, so the whole community and its interactions are preserved and populations keep evolving. It includes national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, conservation areas, community forests, sacred groves and Ramsar wetlands.
A biosphere reserve has three zones: a core zone, legally protected and undisturbed, where no human activity is allowed except research; a buffer zone, where research, education and limited traditional use are permitted around the core; and a transition or manipulation zone, where settlements, farming, forestry and recreation are allowed with sustainable management. The design separates strict protection from the livelihoods of local people.

questions.question: Explain ex-situ conservation with four methods and one limitation.
questions.solution:
Ex-situ conservation keeps species outside their natural habitat. Methods: botanical and zoological gardens, where living plants and animals are maintained and bred; seed and gene banks, storing seeds at low temperature and humidity for decades; cryopreservation of embryos, sperm, ova and tissue in liquid nitrogen; and tissue culture, micropropagation and DNA banks for species difficult to store as seed.
Limitation: only a small sample of individuals is kept, so genetic diversity is narrow, and behaviour, migration and ecological relationships needed for life in the wild cannot be preserved — hence it supplements but cannot replace in-situ conservation.

questions.question: What is the Red Data Book? Explain the IUCN categories with examples of Nepali species.
questions.solution:
The Red Data Book (IUCN Red List) is the global record of the conservation status of species, based on quantitative criteria of population size, decline and range.
Categories: Extinct, Extinct in the wild, Critically endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near threatened, Least concern and Data deficient; the first three of the threatened group are the highest risk.
Nepali examples: the greater one-horned rhinoceros and red panda are endangered, the snow leopard and tiger are vulnerable or endangered depending on assessment, the gharial is critically endangered, and the spiny babbler is near threatened. The list guides legal protection and conservation priority in Nepal's National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act.

questions.question: What is a biodiversity hotspot? Name the hotspot that includes Nepal and state its importance.
questions.solution:
A biodiversity hotspot is a region with exceptionally high species richness and endemism that has already lost at least 70% of its original vegetation; 36 such hotspots hold a large share of the world's threatened species in a small area.
Nepal lies within the Himalaya hotspot, which also covers Bhutan, northern India, and parts of Pakistan, China and Myanmar. Its importance lies in the steep altitudinal range that packs tropical to alpine life into short distances, many endemic and medicinal plants, and the headwaters of rivers on which hundreds of millions of people depend.

pyqs/class-12/biology/biotechnology-appl.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Biotechnology And Its Applications — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/biotechnology-appl.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 biotechnology and its applications unit

questions.question: Explain how Bt cotton is produced and why the Bt toxin does not harm the plant or human beings.
questions.solution:
Genes for the Bt toxin — cryIAc and cryIIAb for cotton bollworm — are isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis and inserted into the cotton plant with a suitable vector and promoter, so the plant makes the toxin itself.
The toxin exists in the bacterium as an inactive protoxin crystal. In the alkaline gut of the insect larva it is converted to active toxin, which binds midgut epithelial cells and perforates them, so the larva stops feeding and dies. The mammalian stomach is acidic and has no receptor for the toxin and no such crystal, so the protoxin is digested harmlessly, making Bt cotton safe for people, animals and most non-target insects.

questions.question: Explain how RNA interference was used to make nematode-resistant tobacco.
questions.solution:
The nematode Meloidogyne incognita infects tobacco roots and causes galls. A gene was introduced into the tobacco plant that produces both sense and antisense RNA of a nematode gene essential for its survival. The two RNAs base-pair into double-stranded RNA, which triggers RNA interference: the plant's Dicer cuts it into small interfering RNAs that guide degradation of the matching nematode mRNA.
The parasite's gene is therefore silenced when it feeds, the nematode cannot survive and the plant is protected. This uses no toxin and is specific to the target pest.

questions.question: Describe the production of human insulin by recombinant DNA technology.
questions.solution:
Insulin has two chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bonds. In the older method, the human genes for the A and B chains were inserted separately into E. coli plasmids, and each chain was produced and then joined chemically — the first recombinant insulin, Humulin.
The modern method inserts human proinsulin DNA with a C-peptide into a vector so that the bacteria secrete a single-chain proinsulin; the C-peptide is then removed enzymatically to give authentic human insulin. Recombinant insulin is identical to human insulin, so it avoids the allergic reactions caused by pig or cattle insulin and can be produced in unlimited quantity.

questions.question: What is gene therapy? Explain its use in ADA deficiency.
questions.solution:
Gene therapy corrects a genetic disease by introducing a normal gene into a patient's cells.
In severe combined immunodeficiency due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, the ADA gene is faulty and toxic deoxyadenosine kills lymphocytes. A normal ADA gene is inserted into a retroviral vector and used to infect the patient's own bone marrow cells or lymphocytes, which are then returned to the blood, where they make the enzyme.
Because the corrected cells are blood cells with a limited life, the treatment must be repeated; a permanent cure would need the gene in stem cells, and enzyme replacement by injection is the alternative. In 1990 this was the first approved gene therapy.

questions.question: What are transgenic animals? Describe how they are produced and give four uses.
questions.solution:
Transgenic animals carry a foreign gene that has been deliberately introduced into their genome and is passed on to offspring; the standard method is microinjection of the DNA into the pronucleus of a fertilised egg, which is then implanted into a surrogate mother.
Uses: producing biological products — goats secreting human antithrombin or sheep making alpha-1-antitrypsin in milk; studying gene function and human disease models; testing vaccine safety and drug toxicity before human trials; improving livestock for growth, milk or wool and conferring disease resistance; and producing organs or tissues as a source for transplantation, plus transgenic fish and birds for food.

questions.question: What is biopiracy? Explain with two examples, and state how patent law and the Convention on Biological Diversity address it.
questions.solution:
Biopiracy is the commercial exploitation of biological resources or traditional knowledge of a community without permission or without sharing the benefit with that community.
Examples: the US patent on basmati rice lines and the patents on the wound-healing property of turmeric and on neem were challenged by India because they claimed knowledge already public in that country; similarly, patents on certain medicinal plants and on ayurvedic formulations have been disputed.
The Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) affirms national sovereignty over biological resources and requires prior informed consent and equitable benefit sharing, while WTO's TRIPS agreement and national patent law now demand disclosure of origin and allow revocation of patents lacking novelty.

pyqs/class-12/biology/biotechnology-prin.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Biotechnology Principles And Processes — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/biotechnology-prin.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 biotechnology principles and processes unit

questions.question: What is recombinant DNA technology? List its main steps.
questions.solution:
Recombinant DNA technology is the construction of a new DNA molecule by joining DNA from two different sources and expressing it in a host organism.
Steps: (1) identify and isolate the desired gene from a donor; (2) cut the gene and a vector with the same restriction enzyme to give complementary sticky ends; (3) ligate the gene into the vector; (4) introduce the recombinant DNA into a competent host cell; (5) select and screen the cells that took it up; (6) multiply them through preferential multiplication and gene isolation; (7) grow the culture in a bioreactor; (8) extract and purify the product by downstream processing.

questions.question: What are restriction endonucleases? Explain their naming and the role of sticky ends.
questions.solution:
Restriction endonucleases are enzymes obtained from bacteria that recognise a specific palindromic sequence and cut DNA at or near it; bacteria make them as a defence against foreign DNA, protecting their own DNA by methylation. Each enzyme recognises one sequence, which is why they are called molecular scissors.
Naming uses the organism of origin: EcoRI comes from E. coli strain RY13, the fifth enzyme found; HindIII from Haemophilus influenzae serotype d.
Many cut a staggered cut, leaving short single-stranded overhangs — sticky ends — on both fragments. Because the same enzyme gives complementary overhangs on the gene and vector, the fragments can pair by base pairing and be sealed by DNA ligase.

questions.question: What is a cloning vector? Describe the features of pBR322 and explain insertional inactivation.
questions.solution:
A cloning vector is a small DNA molecule able to carry a foreign gene into a host and replicate there — plasmids, bacteriophages, cosmids, BACs or YACs.
pBR322 has an origin of replication that lets it multiply in E. coli, an ampicillin-resistance gene (bla) and a tetracycline-resistance gene as selectable markers, and several unique restriction sites including BamHI, PstI and EcoRI.
Insertional inactivation: because the restriction sites lie within a marker gene, inserting the foreign fragment destroys that gene. An insert at the BamHI site disrupts the tetracycline gene, so recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline — the failure to grow on tetracycline is what identifies them.

questions.question: Describe PCR and state why Taq polymerase is used.
questions.solution:
PCR (polymerase chain reaction) amplifies a specific DNA segment in vitro. Denaturation: the template is heated to about 94 °C so the strands separate. Annealing: two synthetic primers, complementary to the flanking sequences, bind each strand at a lower temperature. Extension: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides from the primers to copy the template. The thermal cycle is repeated, and each cycle doubles the copies, so a billion-fold amplification takes about 30 cycles.
Taq polymerase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus is used because it survives the repeated high denaturation temperature, so fresh enzyme need not be added each cycle.

questions.question: How is DNA separated by gel electrophoresis? Why is DNA treated with a stain?
questions.solution:
DNA fragments, being negatively charged because of their phosphate groups, are loaded into wells of an agarose gel placed in buffer and subjected to an electric field. The fragments migrate towards the anode, and their speed depends on size: small fragments move faster through the gel pores than large ones, so the fragment mixture separates into bands according to length, which can be visualised under UV light and compared with a standard ladder.
Ethidium bromide or SYBR Green is added because DNA itself is colourless; the dye intercalates between bases and fluoresces under ultraviolet light, so the bands become visible and can be photographed and measured.

questions.question: Describe bioreactors and downstream processing in biotechnology.
questions.solution:
A bioreactor is a vessel in which the genetically modified organism is grown at controlled pH, temperature, oxygen and mixing so that the desired product accumulates — stirred-tank reactors with impellers, airlift and sparged reactors are common, in batch, fed-batch or continuous mode, with sterile conditions to prevent contamination.
Downstream processing follows: the cells are separated by filtration or centrifugation, the product is extracted and purified by chromatography or precipitation, and it is formulated, quality-tested and packaged. It is often the most expensive step, because the product must be separated from thousands of other molecules and must meet purity and safety standards, and it decides whether a product is commercially viable.

pyqs/class-12/biology/environmental-issu.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Environmental Issues — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/environmental-issu.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 environmental issues unit

questions.question: Explain classical and photochemical smog, and give three control measures for air pollution.
questions.solution:
Classical (London-type) smog forms in cold, humid air when smoke from coal burning mixes with fog, trapping sulphur dioxide and particulates; it irritates the lungs and cuts visibility.
Photochemical (Los Angeles-type) smog forms in strong sunlight when nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons from vehicles react to produce ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate and aldehydes, which irritate eyes and damage crops and rubber.
Control: use cleaner fuel and renewable energy, fit catalytic converters and flue-gas scrubbers, expand public transport, control industrial emissions, avoid open burning and plant green belts. Air quality indices now track particulate matter, SO2, NO2, CO and ozone so that warnings and restrictions can be issued.

questions.question: What is eutrophication? Explain how sewage and fertiliser runoff cause it, and give BOD as a measure of water pollution.
questions.solution:
Eutrophication is the nutrient enrichment of a water body, mainly by nitrate and phosphate, that leads to excessive growth of algae and plants.
Sewage and fertiliser runoff add these nutrients; an algal bloom shades the water and then dies, and its decomposition by bacteria consumes dissolved oxygen, so oxygen levels fall sharply, fish die and the water turns foul, with bad odour and toxins from cyanobacteria. The lake slowly fills with organic sediment.
Biological oxygen demand (BOD) measures the oxygen used by microbes to oxidise the organic matter in a water sample over five days; clean water has a low BOD and polluted sewage-loaded water a high BOD, so BOD is a standard index of organic pollution.

questions.question: Describe solid waste management with its main methods and their problems.
questions.solution:
Solid waste — household, commercial, industrial, hospital and construction waste — is managed by the hierarchy of reduce, reuse, recycle and recover.
Methods: segregation at source into biodegradable and non-biodegradable fractions; composting and vermicomposting of organic waste; recycling of paper, glass, metal and plastic; sanitary landfill with a clay or plastic liner, leachate collection and gas venting; and incineration with energy recovery for suitable waste, with hospital waste incinerated separately.
Problems: open dumping breeds vectors and leaches leachate into groundwater, methane from landfills adds to the greenhouse effect, burning plastics releases dioxins, and recycling is limited by mixed waste and lack of markets — hence segregation and reduction are the priorities.

questions.question: Explain the hazards of nuclear radiation and the safeguards against them.
questions.solution:
Nuclear radiation comes from reactor accidents, waste from power plants and research, weapons testing and natural radon. Ionising radiation damages DNA, causing burns, radiation sickness, cancers, leukaemia, genetic defects and, at high dose, death; long-lived isotopes such as strontium-90 and caesium-137 enter the food chain and concentrate in bone and muscle, and accidents such as Chernobyl and Fukushima spread contamination over whole regions.
Safeguards: strict design with multiple containment barriers, monitoring and dosimetry for workers, shielding and remote handling, safe storage of high-level waste for long periods in stable geological sites, and international safeguards on nuclear material; medical and industrial sources must be licensed and disposed of properly.

questions.question: Explain the greenhouse effect, its causes and its consequences, and state two mitigation measures.
questions.solution:
Greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide from fossil fuels and deforestation, methane from livestock and paddy fields, nitrous oxide from fertiliser, CFCs and water vapour — are transparent to incoming sunlight but absorb outgoing infrared radiation, warming the lower atmosphere.
Consequences: rising average temperature, melting glaciers and polar ice, sea-level rise and coastal flooding, more frequent droughts, floods and heat waves, shifting crop belts, coral bleaching, spread of vector-borne disease and loss of biodiversity; Nepal sees retreating glaciers, expanding glacial lakes and more erratic monsoon.
Mitigation: cut fossil-fuel use and shift to solar, hydro and wind; plant and protect forests; improve efficiency and public transport; and adopt international commitments such as the Paris Agreement.

questions.question: Explain ozone layer depletion — its causes, effects and control measures.
questions.solution:
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. Chlorofluorocarbons released from refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays rise to the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light breaks them down and chlorine atoms catalytically destroy ozone — one chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules; halons and nitrogen oxides add to the loss, producing the Antarctic ozone hole.
Effects: more UV-B reaching the ground causes skin cancer, cataract, sunburn, weakened immunity, damage to phytoplankton, crops and materials.
Control: the Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs and halons and they were replaced by HCFCs and HFCs; recovery of the ozone layer is now being observed, though HFCs are potent greenhouse gases and are being phased down under the Kigali Amendment.

questions.question: What is rainwater harvesting? Describe its methods and its importance in Nepal.
questions.solution:
Rainwater harvesting is the collection and storage of rain from roofs or catchments for later use and for recharging groundwater.
Methods: roof catchment with gutters, first-flush diversion, storage tanks or jars; surface runoff collection in ponds, check dams, farm ponds and recharge pits; and recharge wells or trenches that send water into the aquifer.
Importance in Nepal: hill settlements and the Terai face drying springs and falling water tables in the dry season, so harvesting supplies drinking water, irrigation and livestock water, reduces flooding and soil erosion, recharges springs and reduces dependence on distant sources; traditional dhunge dhara and pokhari systems are examples of the same idea.

questions.question: What is wasteland development? Describe its causes and methods of reclamation.
questions.solution:
Wasteland is degraded land that has lost its productivity — eroded slopes, gullied and ravine land, waterlogged and saline soil, mined and industrial spoil, and overgrazed pasture. Wasteland development restores such land to productive and ecological use.
Causes: deforestation, overgrazing, unsuitable cultivation on steep slopes, faulty irrigation causing salinity and waterlogging, mining and industrial waste, and shifting cultivation.
Methods: check dams, contour bunds, terracing and gully plugging to stop erosion; planting of hardy grasses and nitrogen-fixing trees, agroforestry and social forestry; drainage and gypsum treatment of saline-sodic soil; and legal protection with community participation, so that the land returns to fuel, fodder, food and groundwater recharge.

pyqs/class-12/biology/genetics-and-evolu.origin: curated NEB-pattern set for class-12 biology genetics and evolution

questions.prompt: State Mendel's law of independent assortment. In a dihybrid cross between round-yellow (RRYY) and wrinkled-green (rryy) peas, give the phenotypic ratio of the F2 generation and explain how it arises.
questions.solution:
Law of independent assortment: when two pairs of contrasting characters are combined, the segregation of one pair is independent of the other at gamete formation.
F1 is all RrYy (round-yellow). Each F1 plant makes four gamete types — RY, Ry, rY, ry — in equal proportion. The 4×4 Punnett square gives 16 combinations: 9 R_Y_ (round-yellow), 3 R_yy (round-green), 3 rrY_ (wrinkled-yellow), 1 rryy (wrinkled-green) — the classic 9:3:3:1 ratio. It arises precisely because R/r and Y/y assort independently into gametes.

questions.prompt: A colour-blind man (X-linked recessive) marries a woman with normal vision whose father was colour-blind. What proportion of their sons will be colour-blind?
questions.solution:
Let $X^C$ = normal, $X^c$ = colour-blind. The man is $X^cY$. The woman has normal vision but her father gave her his only X ($X^c$), so she is a carrier $X^CX^c$.
Sons receive Y from the father and X from the mother: 50% get $X^C$ (normal), 50% get $X^c$ (colour-blind). So half the sons are colour-blind.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of DNA as proposed by Watson and Crick. State Chargaff's rules and explain how they are reflected in base pairing.
questions.solution:
Watson–Crick model: DNA is a right-handed double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands (one 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′). Sugar–phosphate backbones sit outside; nitrogenous bases point inward, joined by hydrogen bonds (A=T with two bonds, G≡C with three), one helix turn ≈ 3.4 nm with ~10 base pairs.
Chargaff's rules: in any DNA, $[A] = [T]$ and $[G] = [C]$ (so purines = pyrimidines). This follows directly from the pairing — every A on one strand forces a T on the other, every G forces a C — so the equalities are a structural necessity, which is exactly the clue that led to the double helix.

questions.prompt: What is natural selection? Explain Darwin's theory and show how industrial melanism in the peppered moth supports it.
questions.solution:
Natural selection: individuals with heritable traits best suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, so favourable alleles spread through the population.
Darwin's theory rests on overproduction, variation, competition, survival of the fittest and inheritance of useful variations, leading to descent with modification.
Peppered moths: before industrialisation, light moths were camouflaged on lichen-covered trees and dark (melanic) mutants were eaten by birds. Soot blackened trees in industrial areas, reversing the advantage — dark moths were hidden, light ones exposed. The melanic allele rose sharply in polluted regions and fell again after clean-air laws: a directly observed case of selection changing allele frequencies.
