pyqs/class-12/biology/heredity-and-evolu.origin: curated NEB-pattern set for class-12 heredity and evolution

questions.question: In garden pea, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). A tall plant crossed with a dwarf plant gives 50% tall and 50% dwarf offspring. What is the genotype of the tall parent? Explain with a cross.
questions.solution:
A 1:1 ratio from a tall × dwarf cross is a test cross result — the tall parent must be heterozygous Tt.
Cross: Tt × tt. Gametes: T, t from the tall parent; t, t from the dwarf. Offspring: Tt (tall) and tt (dwarf) in equal proportion — 50% tall, 50% dwarf. Had the parent been TT, all offspring would be Tt (100% tall). The 1:1 ratio therefore proves heterozygosity.

questions.question: Describe the semi-conservative mode of DNA replication (Meselson–Stahl experiment) and state why it is called semi-conservative.
questions.solution:
Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in heavy $^{15}$N medium (DNA dense), then shifted to light $^{14}$N and centrifuged samples each generation. After one generation all DNA was of intermediate density; after two, half intermediate and half light — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts.
It is called semi-conservative because each daughter double helix conserves (keeps) ONE parental strand and builds one new strand alongside it. Conservative (both old together) and dispersive (mixed fragments) models were ruled out by the density pattern.

questions.question: Which of these is a homologous structure, and what does it indicate? (a) Bird wing and insect wing (b) Human forelimb and whale flipper
questions.solution: (b) is homologous: the human arm and whale flipper share the same bone plan (humerus, radius-ulna, digits) inherited from a common mammalian ancestor, though adapted for grasping versus swimming. Homology indicates divergent evolution from common ancestry. (a) is analogous — similar function (flight) but different structural origin, indicating convergent evolution, not shared ancestry.

pyqs/class-12/biology/heredity-and-evolu.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Heredity And Evolution — 2021
NEB Class 12 Biology — Heredity And Evolution — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/heredity-and-evolu.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 heredity and evolution unit

questions.question: State Mendel's law of segregation and explain how a monohybrid cross gives a 3:1 ratio. What is the use of a test cross?
questions.solution:
The law of segregation says that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele, and they reunite at random at fertilisation.
In a cross TT × tt the F1 is all Tt (tall). Each F1 plant forms T and t gametes in equal number, so the F2 from a self-cross is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt — three tall to one dwarf — because the single tt class is the only dwarf combination.
A test cross — crossing the unknown individual with the homozygous recessive — reveals its genotype: if any dwarf offspring appear it was heterozygous, if all offspring are tall it was homozygous.

questions.question: Differentiate incomplete dominance from codominance with one example each.
questions.solution:
Incomplete dominance: neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype. In snapdragon, red (RR) crossed with white (rr) gives pink (Rr) F1, and F2 is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white — the genotypic and phenotypic ratios are the same.
Codominance: both alleles express themselves fully and independently in the heterozygote. In the human AB blood group, alleles I^A and I^B are codominant, so genotype I^A I^B gives blood group AB with both A and B antigens on the red cells, not an intermediate.

questions.question: Explain linkage and crossing over, and state how recombination frequency is used to map genes.
questions.solution:
Genes lying close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together — linkage, discovered by Morgan in Drosophila. Because they are physically joined, linked genes do not assort independently, so a dihybrid test cross gives fewer recombinant types than the expected 1:1:1:1.
During prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata — crossing over — which separates linked alleles. The proportion of recombinant offspring (recombination frequency) measures the distance between the genes: 1% recombination is defined as 1 map unit or centimorgan, so frequency is used to order genes and draw linkage maps.

questions.question: How is sex determined in human beings? Explain a cross showing the inheritance of red–green colour blindness.
questions.solution:
Human sex is determined by the XY system: females are XX and produce only X eggs; males are XY and produce X and Y sperm in equal numbers. Fertilisation by an X sperm gives a girl (XX) and by a Y sperm gives a boy (XY), so the father determines the sex, with a 1:1 chance.
Colour blindness is X-linked recessive. Let X^C be normal and X^c colour-blind: a carrier mother X^C X^c × normal father X^C Y gives daughters all normal (half carriers) and sons half normal and half colour-blind, because a son has only his mother's X. A colour-blind daughter requires a colour-blind father as well.

questions.question: State the chromosome theory of inheritance and give the evidence that supports it.
questions.solution:
Sutton and Boveri proposed that chromosomes are the carriers of Mendel's factors: chromosomes occur in pairs (homologues), behave exactly as Mendelian factors during meiosis — segregating and assorting independently — and each parent contributes one of each pair to the offspring.
Evidence: the parallel behaviour of chromosomes and genes in meiosis; sex-linked inheritance in Drosophila, where Morgan showed that the white-eye gene travels with the X chromosome; the correspondence of recombination frequency with chromosome map distance; and the later proof that DNA is the genetic material (Griffith, Avery, Hershey–Chase), identifying the chemical nature of the chromosome.

questions.question: Describe semi-conservative DNA replication and the evidence for it.
questions.solution:
Replication begins at an origin where helicase unwinds the double helix, forming a replication fork. Each strand acts as a template: DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides in the 5′→3′ direction using deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates, primase lays an RNA primer, and the leading strand is made continuously while the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments that ligase joins. Each daughter molecule therefore has one old and one new strand; topoisomerase relieves the twisting strain.
Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in heavy ¹⁵N and then transferred it to ¹⁴N medium; after one generation all DNA was of intermediate density and after two there were equal intermediate and light bands — exactly the pattern predicted by semi-conservative, not conservative or dispersive, replication.

questions.question: Explain transcription and translation briefly, and state the central dogma.
questions.solution:
Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template: RNA polymerase binds the promoter, unwinds the helix and adds complementary ribonucleotides to the growing RNA in the 5′→3′ direction, copying only one strand; in eukaryotes the transcript is processed — introns spliced out, a cap and poly-A tail added — and mRNA leaves the nucleus.
Translation makes protein on the ribosome: each mRNA codon is read and matched by the anticodon of a tRNA carrying its amino acid; initiation begins at the start codon AUG, elongation adds amino acids in order and termination stops at a stop codon, after which the chain folds into a protein.
The central dogma is DNA → RNA → protein: information flows from nucleic acid to protein, never back.

questions.question: Explain the lac operon as an example of gene regulation.
questions.solution:
The lac operon in E. coli consists of a promoter, an operator and three structural genes — lac Z (β-galactosidase), lac Y (permease) and lac A (transacetylase) — plus a regulatory gene, lac I, whose repressor protein binds the operator.
When lactose is absent the repressor blocks RNA polymerase, so the genes are switched off. When lactose is present it binds the repressor and changes its shape so that it cannot bind the operator; RNA polymerase then transcribes the three genes as one polycistronic mRNA and the cell makes the enzymes to use lactose. This is negative control that is induced by the substrate, so the cell spends energy on the enzymes only when they are needed.

questions.question: State the objectives and significance of the Human Genome Project.
questions.solution:
Objectives: determine the complete DNA sequence of the human genome, identify all genes, map them and make the data freely available, along with the genomes of model organisms and the ethical, legal and social issues arising.
Significance: it produced the reference sequence of about 3 billion base pairs and roughly 20,000–25,000 genes; it showed that most DNA is non-coding and that humans differ from each other by less than 0.1%. That gives tools for finding disease genes and designing drugs, for genetic testing and counselling, for understanding human evolution and ancestry, and for agriculture and microbiology where the same methods are used.

questions.question: State the Hardy–Weinberg principle, give its conditions and explain one use.
questions.solution:
In a large, randomly mating population with no mutation, no migration and no selection, allele frequencies do not change from generation to generation: for two alleles p + q = 1 and the genotype frequencies are p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
Conditions: very large population, random mating, no mutation, no gene flow and no natural selection; the locus must not be under differential selection.
Use: it gives the expected genotype frequencies, so a deviation reveals that selection, drift or inbreeding is acting. For example, if a recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 people, q² = 0.0001 gives q = 0.01 and the carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 2% — a result used in genetic counselling.

questions.question: What is adaptive radiation? Give one example.
questions.solution:
Adaptive radiation is the rapid evolution of many divergent species from a single common ancestor when a new habitat or an opportunity with few competitors becomes available; the descendants evolve different structures and habits to occupy different niches.
A classic example is Darwin's finches of the Galápagos, which radiated from one ancestral seed-eating bird into species with beaks specialised for seeds, nuts, insects and cactus — each adapted to a different food source.

pyqs/class-12/biology/human-health-and-d.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Human Health And Diseases — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/human-health-and-d.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 human health and diseases unit

questions.question: Name the pathogen and vector of malaria, describe its symptoms and give two control measures.
questions.solution:
Pathogen: the protozoan Plasmodium — P. vivax, P. falciparum, P. malariae or P. ovale; vector: the female Anopheles mosquito.
Symptoms: the classic cycle of chill and shivering followed by high fever and sweating every 48 or 72 hours, with headache, body ache, nausea and, in falciparum malaria, severe anaemia, jaundice, kidney failure and cerebral symptoms.
Control: destroy breeding sites (drain stagnant water, fill pools, use larvivorous fish) and prevent bites with mosquito nets, screens, repellents and indoor residual spraying; treat patients promptly with antimalarials to cut the reservoir of gametocytes.

questions.question: Describe the causative agent, vector and control of dengue and of filariasis.
questions.solution:
Dengue: the dengue virus (a flavivirus, four serotypes) carried by Aedes aegypti, which breeds in clean stagnant water in containers and bites by day. It causes high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain and rash; severe dengue brings bleeding and shock. Control: empty and cover water containers, use larvicides and nets, and search-and-destroy breeding sites.
Filariasis: Wuchereria bancrofti, transmitted by Culex mosquito, with larvae developing in the lymphatics and blocking them, so the limb swells into elephantiasis. Control: mass drug administration with DEC and albendazole, mosquito nets and vector control.

questions.question: Name the causative agents of typhoid, pneumonia, tuberculosis and the common cold, and give one preventive measure for each.
questions.solution:
Typhoid: Salmonella typhi, spread by contaminated food and water; prevention is safe water, sanitation and food hygiene, with vaccination.
Pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae (also viruses); prevention by pneumococcal and Hib vaccine, and avoiding smoking.
Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread by droplets; prevention by BCG vaccination, early case detection with DOTS treatment and ventilation.
Common cold: rhinoviruses and other respiratory viruses; prevention by hand washing, covering the mouth while coughing and avoiding close contact.

questions.question: Differentiate innate from acquired immunity, naming the components of each.
questions.solution:
Innate (non-specific) immunity is present from birth and acts the same way against any invader. Its barriers are physical (skin, mucous membranes, cilia), physiological (fever, acid in the stomach, lysozyme in tears), cellular (phagocytes such as macrophages and neutrophils, natural killer cells) and chemical (interferons, complement). It is immediate and has no memory.
Acquired (specific) immunity develops after exposure to an antigen. It is carried out by lymphocytes — B cells making antibodies (humoral) and T cells acting directly or through cytokines (cell-mediated) — and has memory, so the second exposure brings a faster, stronger response. It is the basis of vaccination.

questions.question: Define antigen and antibody and explain the primary and secondary immune responses.
questions.solution:
An antigen is any foreign molecule — usually protein or polysaccharide on a pathogen or toxin — that the immune system recognises as non-self and that provokes an immune response. An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein made by plasma cells that binds specifically to that antigen; the variable regions give specificity.
On first exposure (primary response) there is a lag of several days while the right clone of B and T cells multiplies, producing a small amount of IgM antibody and memory cells. On the second exposure (secondary response) memory cells respond at once, so antibody appears sooner, rises higher and lasts longer, mostly IgG — which is exactly how vaccines protect.

questions.question: What is vaccination? Distinguish active from passive immunisation and explain herd immunity.
questions.solution:
Vaccination is the deliberate introduction of an antigen — killed or weakened pathogen, a toxoid or a subunit — so that the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells without suffering the disease.
Active immunisation: the person's own immune system responds, giving slow but long-lasting protection — vaccines such as BCG, measles, DPT. Passive immunisation: ready-made antibodies are given, giving immediate but short-lived protection — antitetanus serum, antivenom, or maternal antibodies through breast milk.
Herd immunity is the indirect protection of unvaccinated people when a high proportion of the population is immune, which interrupts transmission; it is why coverage must stay high to protect newborns and those who cannot be vaccinated.

questions.question: Explain allergy and autoimmune disease with one example each.
questions.solution:
Allergy is an exaggerated immune response to a normally harmless antigen (allergen) such as pollen, dust mite, or a drug. IgE antibodies bind mast cells, and on re-exposure the allergen cross-links them so they release histamine, giving sneezing, itching, watery eyes, bronchospasm or, in anaphylaxis, a sudden dangerous drop in blood pressure; treatment is antihistamines, and adrenaline for anaphylaxis.
Autoimmune disease occurs when the immune system loses tolerance and attacks the body's own tissue: in type 1 diabetes the β-cells of the pancreas are destroyed, in rheumatoid arthritis the joints are attacked, and in myasthenia gravis the acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

pyqs/class-12/biology/human-health-and-d.origin: curated NEB-pattern set for class-12 biology health and diseases

questions.prompt: Name the pathogen, vector and two preventive measures for EACH of malaria and dengue.
questions.solution:
Malaria: pathogen Plasmodium (P. vivax / P. falciparum), transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Prevention — sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets; drain stagnant water / spray larvicides to destroy breeding sites.
Dengue: pathogen dengue virus (flavivirus, four serotypes), transmitted by the bite of infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which bite in daytime. Prevention — eliminate freshwater containers (tyres, pots) where Aedes breeds; wear long sleeves and use repellents during the day.

questions.prompt: Which cells produce antibodies, and which type of immunity does vaccination provide?
questions.solution: Antibodies are produced by plasma cells, the differentiated form of B-lymphocytes. Vaccination exposes the body to harmless antigen so memory B and T cells form — this is artificial active immunity: the person's own immune system makes the antibodies and remembers the pathogen.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity, giving two examples of each. What is the role of interferons?
questions.solution:
Innate immunity is present from birth, non-specific and immediate: e.g. skin/mucous barriers, phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils. Acquired immunity develops after exposure, is pathogen-specific and has memory: e.g. antibody production after infection (natural active), protection from vaccination (artificial active).
Interferons are signalling proteins released by virus-infected cells. They bind neighbouring cells and switch on antiviral defences (degrading viral RNA, blocking protein synthesis), slowing the infection while the specific response builds up — a key innate antiviral mechanism.

questions.prompt: Explain the life cycle of HIV inside a human host cell. Why is AIDS hard to cure even with antiretroviral drugs?
questions.solution:
HIV (a retrovirus) binds CD4 receptors on helper T cells. Its RNA genome enters, and reverse transcriptase builds a DNA copy, which integrates into the host chromosome as a provirus. The cell then transcribes viral RNA, translates viral proteins, and new virions bud out, killing the CD4 cell. Falling helper-T counts collapse cell-mediated immunity.
Cure is hard because: (1) the provirus hides silently in long-lived memory T cells (latent reservoirs) untouched by drugs or immunity; (2) reverse transcriptase is error-prone, so HIV mutates extremely fast and escapes drugs and antibodies; (3) the virus directly destroys the immune cells needed to fight it. Antiretrovirals suppress replication but cannot remove integrated proviral DNA.

pyqs/class-12/biology/microbes-in-human-.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Microbes In Human Welfare — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/microbes-in-human-.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 microbes in human welfare unit

questions.question: Name the microorganisms used in four household products and state what each does.
questions.solution:
Curd: Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus ferment milk sugar to lactic acid, which curdles the casein and gives curd its taste; vitamin B12 is also increased.
Bread: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast) ferments sugar, and the CO2 released makes the dough rise while alcohol evaporates during baking.
Cheese: Lactococcus and Streptococcus with Propionibacterium shermanii give the flavour and the holes of Swiss cheese; Penicillium roqueforti gives blue cheese.
Fermented batter and beverages: Leuconostoc and yeasts ferment rice and black gram batter for idli and dosa, while yeast ferments palm sap for toddy. These microbes also preserve food by producing acid that inhibits spoilage organisms.

questions.question: Describe the industrial production of an antibiotic, of alcohol and of citric acid.
questions.solution:
Antibiotic: Penicillium notatum or P. chrysogenum is grown in a stirred, aerated fermenter on a medium containing lactose and corn steep liquor; penicillin is secreted, extracted into an organic solvent at acid pH and purified as a salt. Antibiotics are also made by Streptomyces (streptomycin) and Cephalosporium.
Alcohol: Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments molasses or fruit juice anaerobically to ethanol, which is distilled to the required strength for beverages or fuel.
Citric acid: Aspergillus niger ferments a sucrose or molasses medium in aerobic submerged culture; the acid is precipitated as calcium citrate and recovered. These products are made in large bioreactors with controlled pH, temperature and aeration.

questions.question: How are microbes used as biocontrol agents and as biofertilisers?
questions.solution:
Biocontrol: Bacillus thuringiensis sprays kill caterpillars of moths and butterflies because its toxin paralyses the gut, while leaving other insects untouched; Trichoderma harzianum controls soil-borne fungal pathogens; the nuclear polyhedrosis virus attacks insect larvae; and ladybirds and Trichogramma are released to eat or parasitise pests. These agents reduce chemical pesticide load and do not leave residues.
Biofertilisers: Rhizobium in legume root nodules, free-living Azotobacter and Azospirillum, and cyanobacteria such as Anabaena and Azolla fix atmospheric nitrogen; phosphate-solubilising bacteria release bound phosphorus and mycorrhizal fungi extend the root's reach for phosphorus and water.

questions.question: Explain bioremediation and the production of biogas by microbes.
questions.solution:
Bioremediation is the use of microorganisms to remove or neutralise pollutants: Pseudomonas and other bacteria break down oil spills and petroleum hydrocarbons, some strains degrade polychlorinated compounds and pesticides, and others remove heavy metals or cyanide from effluent. Fungi such as Aspergillus help compost organic waste, and phytoremediation uses plants together with rhizosphere microbes.
Biogas: methanogens — Methanobacterium in anaerobic digestion — decompose cattle dung, sewage sludge and crop waste in a closed digester, producing biogas (about 60–70% methane and rest CO2) that is used for cooking, lighting or running engines. The spent slurry is a rich organic manure, so the process gives clean fuel and fertiliser while disposing of waste.

questions.question: Describe the stages of sewage water treatment.
questions.solution:
Primary treatment (physical): bar screens and grit chambers remove solids, and the sewage passes to a settling tank where suspended matter settles as primary sludge and grease is skimmed off; the liquid still carries dissolved organic matter.
Secondary or biological treatment: the effluent is aerated in an aeration tank where aerobic bacteria and fungi, forming flocs, digest the dissolved organic matter, and the biomass then settles in another tank — activated sludge. The clarified water has a much lower BOD and can be discharged. Anaerobic digestion of the sludge with methanogens produces biogas and digested sludge used as manure; sometimes a tertiary step of chemical treatment or filtration removes phosphorus, nitrogen or pathogens.

questions.question: Why do some cured and fermented foods keep better than fresh ones?
questions.solution: Fermenting microbes convert sugars into acids or alcohol — lactic acid in curd, pickles and sauerkraut, ethanol in wines — and so lower the pH or raise the alcohol level until most spoilage and pathogenic bacteria cannot grow. The food is therefore protected by the very process that gives it its flavour, and the useful microbes also outcompete spoilers for nutrients. This is why curd, cheese, fermented batter and pickles last much longer than raw milk, vegetables or batter.

pyqs/class-12/biology/organisms-and-envi.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Organisms And Environment — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/organisms-and-envi.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 organisms and environment unit

questions.question: Describe the adaptations of desert plants and desert animals to water scarcity.
questions.solution:
Desert plants (xerophytes): thick waxy cuticle and sunken stomata reduce transpiration, leaves reduced to spines with photosynthesis in the green stem, deep tap roots or wide shallow roots, water stored in succulent tissue, and a short life cycle completed after rain.
Desert animals: nocturnal habit and burrowing to escape heat, water from metabolic oxidation of fats (kangaroo rat), concentrated urine and dry faeces to conserve water, a thick skin or scales, and aestivation or dormancy in the hottest period; camels store fat in the hump and tolerate high body temperature, conserving water.

questions.question: Explain exponential and logistic population growth, defining r and K.
questions.solution:
Exponential growth occurs when resources are unlimited: dN/dt = rN, giving N = N₀e^{rt}, an accelerating J-shaped curve where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase (births minus deaths per individual).
Logistic growth occurs when resources are limited: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, giving a sigmoid S-shaped curve that levels off at K, the carrying capacity — the maximum population the environment can support. Growth is fastest at N = K/2. Real populations follow logistic growth: initial slow phase, rapid growth, and a plateau as competition, disease and predation increase.

questions.question: Describe five types of population interaction with one example each.
questions.solution:
Mutualism (+, +): both benefit — alga and fungus in a lichen; fig and its pollinating wasp.
Competition (−, −): both are harmed — two grass species competing for water and light, or barnacles on a rock.
Predation (+, −): the predator gains and the prey is killed — tiger and deer; the prey evolves defences such as spines or camouflage.
Parasitism (+, −): the parasite gains, the host is harmed — Cuscuta on a host plant, Plasmodium in man.
Commensalism (+, 0): one gains, the other is unaffected — an orchid growing on a mango branch, or barnacles on a whale's skin.

questions.question: Describe the structure and function of an ecosystem, and the steps of decomposition.
questions.solution:
Structure: abiotic components (light, temperature, water, soil, nutrients) and biotic components — producers, consumers of the first, second and third order, and decomposers.
Function: productivity (gross and net primary production), decomposition, energy flow through food chains and nutrient cycling, all driven by the one-way flow of energy from the sun and the cycling of matter.
Decomposition steps: fragmentation of detritus by detritivores, leaching of soluble inorganic nutrients, catabolism by bacterial and fungal enzymes, humification forming humus, and mineralisation releasing inorganic nutrients back to the soil; it is faster in warm, moist, aerobic conditions.

questions.question: What is ecological succession? Differentiate hydrarch from xerarch succession and define pioneer and climax community.
questions.solution:
Ecological succession is the gradual, directional replacement of one community by another at a site until a stable community establishes.
Hydrarch succession begins in water: phytoplankton → submerged plants → floating plants → reed swamp → marsh meadow → scrub → forest as sediment and organic matter fill the water body. Xerarch succession begins on bare rock: lichens → mosses → grasses → shrubs → trees, as the rock weathers into soil. Both are autogenic, driven by the organisms themselves changing conditions.
The pioneer community is the first to colonise (lichen on rock, phytoplankton in water); the climax community is the final stable community in equilibrium with the climate, such as a forest.

questions.question: Describe the carbon and phosphorus cycles and state how human activity disturbs them.
questions.solution:
Carbon: CO2 is fixed by photosynthesis, passed through food chains, returned by respiration and decomposition, and exchanged with the oceans and carbonate rocks; some carbon is buried as fossil fuel.
Phosphorus: it has no gaseous phase. Phosphate is released by weathering of rock, absorbed by plants, passed to animals, returned in excreta and dead matter, and deposited in sediments as calcium phosphate or guano — a sedimentary cycle.
Human disturbance: burning fossil fuels and deforestation add CO2 faster than it is fixed, driving global warming; mining rock phosphate, harvesting crops and excessive fertiliser use and runoff accelerate phosphorus loss to water, causing eutrophication.

questions.question: Explain energy flow and ecological pyramids, and state one limitation of each type of pyramid.
questions.solution:
Energy flows one way: sunlight → producers → herbivores → carnivores, and is lost as heat at every transfer. According to the ten per cent law only about 10% passes to the next level, so food chains rarely have more than four or five links.
Pyramids of number: can be inverted (many insects on one tree) and do not show energy. Pyramids of biomass: can be inverted in aquatic ecosystems where phytoplankton biomass is small but turnover is rapid. Pyramids of energy: always upright, since energy decreases at each step, and are the most reliable representation of trophic structure.

questions.question: Define population density and name three attributes used to describe a population besides density.
questions.solution:
Population density is the number of individuals of a species per unit area or volume at a given time (N/A or N/V).
Three other attributes: natality or birth rate and mortality or death rate, which decide growth; age distribution — the proportion of pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive individuals, shown as an age pyramid; and dispersion, the spatial pattern (clumped, uniform or random). Sex ratio and immigration or emigration also change population size, and density can be measured by counting, quadrat sampling or mark–recapture.

pyqs/class-12/biology/strategies-for-foo.title: NEB Class 12 Biology — Strategies For Food Production — 2025
pyqs/class-12/biology/strategies-for-foo.origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-12 strategies for enhancement in food production unit

questions.question: What is plant breeding? Describe its main steps.
questions.solution:
Plant breeding is the deliberate genetic improvement of crop plants to raise yield and quality, and to add resistance to disease, pests and stress.
Steps: (1) collection and evaluation of genetic variability — germplasm collection from wild relatives and landraces; (2) selection of parents with the desired characters; (3) hybridisation — crossing them to combine traits; (4) selection in the segregating generations, often by pedigree or bulk method, until the line is uniform; (5) testing for yield, quality and resistance in multi-location trials; (6) release and seed multiplication. Mutation breeding, polyploidy and, more recently, marker-assisted selection and genetic engineering speed up or widen the process.

questions.question: Explain the types of hybridisation used in plant breeding and give two achievements of the green revolution in India and Nepal.
questions.solution:
Hybridisation may be intraspecific (crossing two varieties of the same species), interspecific (two species of a genus) or intergeneric (two genera, used to transfer disease resistance from wild relatives). It may be a simple cross, a back-cross to recover the recurrent parent, or a three-way and double cross in self-pollinated crops.
Achievements: semi-dwarf, fertiliser-responsive Mexican wheat (Sonora-64, Lerma Rojo) and IR8 rice raised yields several-fold and made the green revolution possible; in Nepal improved rice (Radha-4, Sabitri) and wheat varieties spread widely, and hybrid maize and disease-resistant varieties raised production — though at the cost of heavier input use.

questions.question: What is single cell protein? Name two organisms used and give its advantages.
questions.solution:
Single cell protein (SCP) is protein extracted from the cells of microorganisms — algae, yeasts, fungi or bacteria — grown in bulk culture and used as a protein-rich food or feed supplement.
Organisms: the alga Spirulina and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae; also Methylophilus methylotrophus (bacterium) and the fungus Fusarium.
Advantages: fast growth gives high yield on cheap substrates including waste (molasses, whey, methanol, straw hydrolysate); it is rich in protein and B vitamins and can be produced in a small area independent of weather; it recycles waste and reduces pollution. Limits are the cost of processing, possible nucleic acid excess and consumer acceptance.

questions.question: Describe animal husbandry with reference to cattle breeds and poultry management.
questions.solution:
Animal husbandry is the scientific management of farm animals — feeding, breeding, housing, health care and record keeping — to obtain milk, meat, eggs, wool and draught power.
Cattle: indigenous breeds such as Sahiwal and Red Sindhi (disease-resistant, good for hot climates) and exotic Jersey and Holstein-Friesian (high milk yield) are crossed for combined merit; breeding is by artificial insemination, with attention to balanced feed, clean water, housing and vaccination against foot-and-mouth and haemorrhagic septicaemia.
Poultry: layers such as Leghorn and broilers such as Plymouth Rock are raised with controlled temperature, balanced feed, clean litter, vaccination against Ranikhet and culling of diseased birds.

questions.question: What are biofertilisers? Name three types and state their advantages.
questions.solution:
Biofertilisers are preparations of living microorganisms that enrich the soil with nutrients, mainly nitrogen or phosphorus, when applied to seed or soil.
Types: nitrogen-fixing bacteria — Rhizobium (symbiotic in legume root nodules) and Azotobacter and Azospirillum (free-living); cyanobacteria such as Anabaena and Azolla (used in paddy fields); phosphate-solubilising bacteria and mycorrhizal fungi, which make insoluble phosphorus available.
Advantages: they are cheap, renewable and non-polluting, reduce the need for chemical nitrogen, improve soil structure and water holding, and are suited to small farmers; they have no harmful residues and often suppress soil-borne pathogens.

questions.question: What is sustainable agriculture? Give four practices that make agriculture sustainable.
questions.solution:
Sustainable agriculture is farming that meets present food needs without damaging the soil, water, biodiversity or climate on which future production depends — it balances productivity with ecological and social costs.
Practices: crop rotation and mixed cropping with legumes to restore nitrogen; use of organic manure, compost and biofertilisers instead of only chemical fertiliser; integrated pest management with biological control and resistant varieties; conservation of soil and water by terracing, contour bunding and mulching; and agroforestry, drip irrigation and use of local seed to reduce inputs and risk.

pyqs/class-12/chemistry/chemical-kinetic.origin: curated NEB-pattern set for class-12 chemical kinetics

questions.question: Define rate of reaction, rate law, order and molecularity. For the reaction $2\mathrm{N_2O_5 \rightarrow 4NO_2 + O_2}$ with rate $= k[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]$, state the order and molecularity.
questions.solution:
Rate is the change in concentration per unit time. The rate law is the experimentally found expression rate $= k[A]^m[B]^n$. Order ($m+n$) is found by experiment; molecularity is the number of species colliding in one elementary step (a theoretical whole number).
Here the rate depends on $[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]$ to the first power, so the order is 1 (first order). The balanced equation consumes 2 molecules, but the slow (rate-determining) step is $\mathrm{N_2O_5 \rightarrow}$ products — unimolecular, so molecularity is 1. Order is experimental, molecularity is mechanistic: they need not match.

questions.question: Derive the integrated rate equation for a first-order reaction and show that its half-life is independent of initial concentration. A first-order reaction is 75% complete in $60$ minutes — find its half-life.
questions.solution:
First order: $-d[A]/dt = k[A]$. Separating and integrating from $[A]_0$ to $[A]$: $\ln([A]_0/[A]) = kt$, or $[A] = [A]_0 e^{-kt}$.
Half-life: $[A] = [A]_0/2$ gives $t_{1/2} = \ln 2/k$ — no $[A]_0$ appears, so half-life is concentration-independent.
75% complete means $[A] = 0.25[A]_0$: $k = \ln(1/0.25)/60 = \ln 4/60 = 2\ln 2/60$. Then $t_{1/2} = \ln 2/k = 60/2 = 30$ minutes.

questions.question: The activation energy of a reaction is $E_a$. A catalyst provides an alternative path with lower $E_a$. What happens to the rate constant $k$, and does the catalyst change the equilibrium constant?
questions.solution: By Arrhenius $k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, lowering $E_a$ increases the fraction of successful collisions, so $k$ increases (reaction speeds up). The catalyst lowers the barrier for forward AND reverse reactions equally, so it reaches equilibrium faster but the equilibrium constant $K$ — fixed by thermodynamics ($\Delta G^\circ$) — is unchanged.

questions.prompt: State the first law of thermodynamics. Derive the expression for pressure–volume work in a reversible isothermal expansion of $n$ moles of an ideal gas from $V_1$ to $V_2$, and give the heat absorbed.
questions.solution:
First law: energy is conserved — $\Delta U = q + w$ (heat added to the system plus work done on it equals the change in internal energy).
For a reversible change $w = -\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P_{\text{ext}}\,dV = -\int P\,dV$. For an ideal gas $P = nRT/V$, so $w_{\text{rev}} = -nRT\int_{V_1}^{V_2} dV/V = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$.
Isothermal means $T$ constant, and for an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$, so $\Delta U = 0$. Then $q = -w = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$ — all the heat absorbed is converted into expansion work.

questions.prompt: For the reaction $\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}$, with $\Delta H = -92.4\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, what are the signs of $\Delta S$ and $\Delta G$ at low temperature, and is the reaction spontaneous?
questions.solution: Moles of gas fall from 4 to 2, so disorder decreases: $\Delta S < 0$. $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$; at low $T$ the negative $\Delta H$ dominates, so $\Delta G < 0$ and the reaction is spontaneous. (At high temperature the $-T\Delta S > 0$ term wins and it becomes non-spontaneous — why ammonia is made at moderate temperatures.)

questions.prompt: Define entropy. State the second law of thermodynamics and use it to explain why heat flows spontaneously from a hot body to a cold body but never the reverse.
questions.solution:
Entropy $S$ measures the number of microscopic arrangements of a system — the degree of disorder; $\Delta S = q_{\text{rev}}/T$.
Second law: the entropy of an isolated system (the universe) never decreases; every spontaneous process increases total entropy.
If heat $q$ flows from hot ($T_h$) to cold ($T_c$), $\Delta S = -q/T_h + q/T_c = q(1/T_c - 1/T_h) > 0$ since $T_c < T_h$ — allowed. Reverse flow would give $\Delta S < 0$, forbidden in an isolated system. Refrigerators achieve it only by doing external work, increasing entropy elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Standard enthalpies of formation: $\Delta H_f^\circ[\mathrm{CO_2(g)}] = -393.5$, $\Delta H_f^\circ[\mathrm{H_2O(l)}] = -285.8$, $\Delta H_f^\circ[\mathrm{C_2H_5OH(l)}] = -277.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ (all in kJ/mol). Calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion of ethanol, and the heat released by burning $9.2\,\mathrm{g}$ of ethanol.
questions.solution:
Combustion: $\mathrm{C_2H_5OH(l) + 3O_2(g) \rightarrow 2CO_2(g) + 3H_2O(l)}$.
$\Delta H_c^\circ = \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{reactants}) = [2(-393.5) + 3(-285.8)] - [(-277.7) + 0]$.
$= (-787.0 - 857.4) + 277.7 = -1644.4 + 277.7 = -1366.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.
Molar mass of ethanol $= 46\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, so $9.2\,\mathrm{g} = 0.2\,\mathrm{mol}$. Heat released $= 0.2 \times 1366.7 = 273.3\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

questions.prompt: State Faraday's first and second laws of electrolysis. A current of $2\,\mathrm{A}$ passed for $30$ minutes deposits $2.22\,\mathrm{g}$ of a metal (valency 2). Calculate the metal's atomic mass. ($F = 96500\,\mathrm{C/mol}$)
questions.solution:
First law: mass deposited is proportional to charge passed, $w = ZQ$. Second law: masses deposited by the same charge are proportional to chemical equivalents $E = A/valency$.
Charge $Q = It = 2 \times 1800 = 3600\,\mathrm{C}$. Moles of electrons $= Q/F = 3600/96500 = 0.0373\,\mathrm{mol}$.
$M^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow M$, so moles of metal $= 0.0373/2 = 0.01865\,\mathrm{mol}$.
Atomic mass $= 2.22/0.01865 \approx 119\,\mathrm{g/mol}$ (tin).

questions.prompt: The standard reduction potentials are $E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}) = +0.34\,\mathrm{V}$ and $E^\circ(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}) = -0.76\,\mathrm{V}$. What is the standard emf of the Daniell cell $\mathrm{Zn|Zn^{2+}||Cu^{2+}|Cu}$, and which electrode is the anode?
questions.solution:
The more negative electrode oxidises: Zn is the anode, Cu the cathode.
$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\,\mathrm{V}$. A positive emf means the cell reaction $\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}$ is spontaneous.

questions.prompt: Write the Nernst equation for a general reduction $M^{n+} + ne^- \rightarrow M$. Use it to calculate the electrode potential of a $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}$ electrode dipped in $0.01\,\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{ZnSO_4}$ at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$. ($E^\circ = -0.76\,\mathrm{V}$)
questions.solution:
Nernst equation: $E = E^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{n}\log_{10}\frac{[\text{reduced}]}{[\text{oxidised}]}$ at $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
For $\mathrm{Zn^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Zn(s)}$: $E = E^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{2}\log\frac{1}{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}$.
With $[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}] = 0.01$: $E = -0.76 - 0.0295 \times \log(100) = -0.76 - 0.0295 \times 2 = -0.76 - 0.059 = -0.819\,\mathrm{V}$. Dilution makes the reduction potential more negative, as expected.

questions.prompt: Explain rusting of iron in terms of electrochemistry (anodic and cathodic regions). Give two methods of preventing corrosion with the principle behind each.
questions.solution:
Rusting is an electrochemical cell on the iron surface. At anodic spots iron oxidises: $\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}$. Electrons flow through the metal to cathodic spots where oxygen is reduced: $\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}$. $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ diffuse together and precipitate as $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_2}$, which oxidises further to hydrated ferric oxide $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3\cdot xH_2O}$ (rust). Water with dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$/salts acts as the electrolyte.
Prevention: (1) Barrier methods — painting, oiling or galvanising (zinc coating) keep water and oxygen away from iron. (2) Sacrificial protection — connecting iron to a more reactive metal (Mg/Zn) makes iron the cathode of the cell so it cannot oxidise; the sacrificial metal corrodes instead.

questions.question: Rewrite using the connector in brackets without changing the meaning: (a) He is rich. He is not happy. (although) (b) You must work hard. You will fail. (unless)
questions.solution:
(a) Concession with 'although' — the unexpected result goes in the main clause: Although he is rich, he is not happy. (Equivalently: He is not happy although he is rich.)
(b) 'Unless' means 'if … not', replacing the negative condition: You will fail unless you work hard. (The original 'must work hard' condition becomes the unless-clause; the consequence stays.)

questions.question: Put the verbs in the correct tense: (a) By this time tomorrow, I ___ (finish) my exams. (b) She ___ (work) here since 2015.
questions.solution:
(a) An action completed before a future point needs the future perfect: 'By this time tomorrow, I will have finished my exams.'
(b) An action starting in the past and continuing now needs the present perfect continuous: 'She has been working here since 2015.' ('Since' + starting point; 'for' would mark a duration.)

questions.question: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence: (a) Its a beautiful day, isn't it. (b) It's a beautiful day, isn't it?
questions.solution: (b) is correct. 'It's' = 'it is' (the apostrophe marks the missing letter), while 'its' without an apostrophe is the possessive ('its colour'). The tag question 'isn't it?' needs its own comma and question mark.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the following in reported speech: (a) She said, "I am visiting my grandmother tomorrow." (b) He asked, "Did you finish the assignment?"
questions.solution:
(a) Direct speech in the present continuous with 'tomorrow' shifts one step back: She said (that) she was visiting her grandmother the next day. Pronoun I→she, my→her, tomorrow→the next day.
(b) A yes/no question becomes an if/whether clause with statement word order: He asked (me) if/whether I had finished the assignment. The past simple 'did finish' backshifts to past perfect 'had finished'.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: "The committee ___ the report by Friday." (a) will submit (b) will have submitted (c) will have been submitted by — the report ___ by Friday.
questions.solution: The report receives the action, so the passive is needed: 'The report will have been submitted by the committee by Friday.' The correct choice is the future-perfect passive: will + have + been + past participle.

questions.prompt: Combine each pair into one sentence using the connector in brackets: (a) The road was icy. The bus skidded off it. (because) (b) Study hard. You will fail. (otherwise)
questions.solution:
(a) Cause goes with 'because' in the subordinate clause: The bus skidded off the road because it was icy. (Equivalently: Because the road was icy, the bus skidded off it.)
(b) 'Otherwise' warns of the consequence of not obeying the first clause: Study hard; otherwise, you will fail. (Note the semicolon or full stop before 'otherwise', which is a conjunctive adverb, not a plain conjunction.)

questions.prompt: Correct the errors in this paragraph (one per sentence): 'Neither of the answers are correct. She is senior than me. I have been living here since five years. He gave a speech full with wisdom.'
questions.solution:
1. 'Neither of the answers are correct' → 'Neither of the answers IS correct' (neither is singular).
2. 'She is senior than me' → 'She is senior TO me' (senior/junior take 'to', not 'than').
3. 'since five years' → 'FOR five years' (for + duration; since + starting point).
4. 'full with wisdom' → 'full OF wisdom' (the adjective 'full' collocates with 'of').

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph of about 150 words on 'The Importance of Reading Books', with a clear topic sentence, supporting details and a concluding sentence.
questions.solution: Model answer: 'Reading books is one of the most rewarding habits a student can develop. First, books expand vocabulary and strengthen language skills far better than short social-media posts, because they expose readers to varied sentence structures. Second, reading improves concentration and critical thinking: following a long argument trains the mind to analyse rather than merely react. Finally, books build empathy by letting readers live lives very different from their own. In short, regular reading sharpens the mind, enriches expression and widens one's view of the world — benefits no shortcut can replace.' Check: topic sentence opens, three supports follow, conclusion closes.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the correct format for the salutation and closing of a FORMAL letter? (a) 'Hi Sita,' … 'Bye' (b) 'Dear Sir/Madam,' … 'Yours faithfully,' (c) 'Hey there,' … 'Cheers'
questions.solution: Formal letters to unknown recipients open with 'Dear Sir/Madam,' and close with 'Yours faithfully,' (or 'Yours sincerely,' when the name is known). Options (a) and (c) are informal and only suit personal letters or messages.

questions.prompt: Draft a formal letter to the principal of your college requesting a character certificate, giving your name, class, roll number and the reason for the request.
questions.solution: Layout: sender's address and date at the top; receiver's designation and address; subject line ('Subject: Request for a character certificate'); salutation ('Dear Sir/Madam,'); body in 2–3 short paragraphs — (1) self-introduction: name, class 12, roll no.; (2) reason: applying for a scholarship/job requiring the certificate; (3) polite request and thanks; closing ('Yours obediently,') with signature, name and roll number. Keep language respectful and factual — no slang, no contractions.

questions.prompt: Write an essay outline (thesis + three main points with one supporting detail each) on 'Social Media: Boon or Bane?'
questions.solution:
Thesis: Social media is a powerful tool whose value depends on disciplined use — a boon for connection and learning, a bane when it controls attention.
Point 1 — Connection: reunites distant families and enables study groups across cities (e.g. exam-preparation communities).
Point 2 — Knowledge: free tutorials and news reach villages that lack libraries.
Point 3 — Harm: addictive design and comparison culture damage focus and self-esteem (e.g. falling grades linked to late-night scrolling).
Conclusion: regulate use — fixed hours, purposeful follows — and the boon outweighs the bane.

questions.question: Differentiate with respect to $x$: (a) $y = x^3 \sin x$, (b) $y = \frac{e^x}{x^2 + 1}$.
questions.solution:
(a) Product rule $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$ with $u = x^3$, $v = \sin x$: $dy/dx = 3x^2\sin x + x^3\cos x = x^2(3\sin x + x\cos x)$.
(b) Quotient rule $(u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2$ with $u = e^x$, $v = x^2+1$: $dy/dx = \frac{e^x(x^2+1) - e^x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2} = \frac{e^x(x^2 - 2x + 1)}{(x^2+1)^2} = \frac{e^x(x-1)^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$.

questions.question: If $x = at^2$ and $y = 2at$, find $dy/dx$. Then find the second derivative $d^2y/dx^2$.
questions.solution:
Parametric differentiation: $dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)$. $dy/dt = 2a$, $dx/dt = 2at$, so $dy/dx = 2a/(2at) = 1/t$.
For the second derivative, differentiate with respect to $x$: $d^2y/dx^2 = \frac{d}{dx}(1/t) = \frac{d}{dt}(1/t)\cdot\frac{dt}{dx} = (-1/t^2)\cdot\frac{1}{2at} = -\frac{1}{2at^3}$. (This is the tangent slope behaviour of the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$.)

questions.prompt: Evaluate $\int x e^{2x}\,dx$ using integration by parts.
questions.solution:
Take $u = x$, $dv = e^{2x}dx$, so $du = dx$, $v = e^{2x}/2$.
$\int x e^{2x}dx = u v - \int v\,du = x\cdot e^{2x}/2 - \int (e^{2x}/2)dx = \frac{xe^{2x}}{2} - \frac{e^{2x}}{4} + C = \frac{e^{2x}(2x - 1)}{4} + C$.

questions.prompt: What is $\int_0^{\pi} \sin x\,dx$?
questions.solution: $\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x$, so $\int_0^{\pi}\sin x\,dx = [-\cos x]_0^{\pi} = (-\cos\pi) - (-\cos 0) = 1 + 1 = 2$.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the definite integral $\int_1^3 \frac{dx}{x^2 - 2x + 5}$ by completing the square.
questions.solution:
Complete the square: $x^2 - 2x + 5 = (x-1)^2 + 4$. Substitute $u = x - 1$ ($du = dx$); limits become $u = 0$ to $2$.
$\int_0^2 \frac{du}{u^2 + 4} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\tan^{-1}\frac{u}{2}\right]_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}(\tan^{-1}1 - 0) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi}{8}$.

questions.prompt: Find the area enclosed between the parabola $y = x^2$ and the line $y = 4$.
questions.solution:
They meet where $x^2 = 4$, i.e. $x = \pm 2$. Between $x = -2$ and $2$ the line $y = 4$ lies above the parabola.
Area $= \int_{-2}^{2} (4 - x^2)\,dx = \left[4x - x^3/3\right]_{-2}^{2} = (8 - 8/3) - (-8 + 8/3) = 16/3 + 16/3 = 32/3$ square units.

pyqs/class-12/mathematics/limits-and-con.origin: curated NEB-pattern set for class-12 mathematics limits and continuity

questions.prompt: Evaluate: (a) $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 5x}{x}$, (b) $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{3x} - 1}{x}$, (c) $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$.
questions.solution:
(a) Standard limit $\lim_{t\to 0}\sin t/t = 1$. Write $\sin 5x/x = 5\cdot\sin 5x/(5x) \to 5 \times 1 = 5$.
(b) Standard limit $\lim_{t\to 0}(e^t - 1)/t = 1$. Write $(e^{3x}-1)/x = 3\cdot(e^{3x}-1)/(3x) \to 3 \times 1 = 3$.
(c) Factor: $(x^2-4)/(x-2) = (x-2)(x+2)/(x-2) = x + 2$ for $x \ne 2$, so the limit is $2 + 2 = 4$.

questions.prompt: If $f(x) = \frac{|x|}{x}$ for $x \ne 0$, what are the left-hand and right-hand limits at $x = 0$? Does $\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)$ exist?
questions.solution: For $x > 0$, $|x| = x$ so $f(x) = 1$ and the right-hand limit is 1. For $x < 0$, $|x| = -x$ so $f(x) = -1$ and the left-hand limit is $-1$. Since the one-sided limits differ, the two-sided limit at $x = 0$ does not exist.

questions.prompt: Discuss the continuity of $f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 1, & x < 1 \\ x^2 + 1, & x \ge 1 \end{cases}$ at $x = 1$.
questions.solution: Left-hand limit: $\lim_{x\to 1^-} f(x) = 2(1) + 1 = 3$. Right-hand value/limit: $f(1) = 1^2 + 1 = 2$, and $\lim_{x\to 1^+} f(x) = 2$. Since LHL $= 3 \ne 2 =$ RHL $= f(1)$, the limit does not exist and $f$ has a jump discontinuity at $x = 1$ — it is not continuous there.

questions.prompt: Using L'Hôpital's rule where valid, evaluate (a) $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1 + x)}{x}$, (b) $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^2}{e^x}$. State the condition that allows L'Hôpital's rule in each case.
questions.solution:
L'Hôpital's rule applies to $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$ forms (with differentiable numerator/denominator near the point, denominator derivative non-zero).
(a) $0/0$ form. Differentiate top and bottom: $\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{1/(1+x)}{1} = 1$.
(b) $\infty/\infty$ form. First application: $\lim 2x/e^x$ (still $\infty/\infty$). Second application: $\lim 2/e^x = 0$. Exponentials dominate polynomials, so the limit is 0.

questions.question: समास भनेको के हो? तत्पुरुष र बहुव्रीहि समासको एक-एक उदाहरणसहित भिन्नता देखाउनुहोस्।
questions.solution:
दुई वा बढी शब्द मिलेर एउटा स्वतन्त्र शब्द बन्दा त्यसलाई समास भनिन्छ।
तत्पुरुष समास — पहिलो पद गौण, दोस्रो पद प्रधान हुन्छ (विग्रहमा कारकचिह्न आउँछ): जस्तै 'राजपुत्र' = राजाका पुत्र (यहाँ 'पुत्र' प्रधान)।
बहुव्रीहि समास — दुवै पद गौण भई तेस्रो अर्थ प्रधान हुन्छ: जस्तै 'चक्रपाणि' = चक्र छ पाणिमा जसको (अर्थात् विष्णु — यहाँ विष्णु प्रधान)।
भिन्नता: तत्पुरुषमा मूल शब्दकै अर्थ बलियो हुन्छ, बहुव्रीहिमा भने अर्कै (तेस्रो) वस्तु बुझिन्छ।

questions.question: तलका वाक्यलाई कर्तृवाच्यबाट कर्मवाच्यमा बदल्नुहोस्: (क) रामले पत्र लेख्यो। (ख) उसले गीत गाउँछ।
questions.solution:
कर्मवाच्यमा कर्तामा 'बाट/द्वारा' लाग्छ र क्रिया कर्मअनुसार बदलिन्छ।
(क) 'रामबाट पत्र लेखियो।' — कर्ता 'रामले' → 'रामबाट', क्रिया 'लेख्यो' → 'लेखियो' (पत्र नपुंसक/तटस्थ)।
(ख) 'उसबाट गीत गाइन्छ।' — कर्ता 'उसले' → 'उसबाट', क्रिया 'गाउँछ' → 'गाइन्छ'।

questions.question: 'सूर्योदय' शब्दको सही सन्धि-विच्छेद कुन हो? (क) सूर्य + उदय (ख) सूर्या + उदय (ग) सूर्यो + दय
questions.solution: सही उत्तर: (क) सूर्य + उदय। 'अ/आ + उ/ऊ = ओ' गुण सन्धि नियमले 'सूर्य + उदय = सूर्योदय' बन्छ। (ख) मा 'सूर्या' गलत ह्रस्व-दीर्घ हो, (ग) मा विभाजन नै अशुद्ध छ।

questions.prompt: तलका वाक्यलाई शुद्ध पार्नुहोस्: (क) म बजार गएर आएँ। (ख) उनीहरू सबैजना आ-आफ्नो घर गए। (ग) यो किताप राम्रोसँग लेखिएको छन्। (घ) हामी भोलि घुम्न जानेछौँ।
questions.solution:
(क) शुद्ध: 'म बजार गएर आएँ।' — यो वाक्य ठीक छ; संयुक्त क्रिया 'गएर आएँ' सही प्रयोग हो।
(ख) शुद्ध: 'उनीहरू सबै आ-आफ्नो घर गए।' — 'सबैजना' र 'उनीहरू' दोहोरो बहुवचन भएकाले 'सबैजना' हट्छ।
(ग) शुद्ध: 'यो किताब राम्रोसँग लेखिएको छ।' — 'किताब' पुलिङ्ग एकवचन भएकाले क्रिया 'छ' हुन्छ, 'छन्' होइन।
(घ) शुद्ध: 'हामी भोलि घुम्न जानेछौँ।' — भविष्यत् बहुवचन क्रिया 'जानेछौँ' सही छ।

questions.prompt: 'ऊ बिरामी भएकाले आज विद्यालय आएन।' — यो कस्तो वाक्य हो? (क) सरल (ख) संयुक्त (ग) मिश्र (घ) आज्ञार्थक
questions.solution: सही उत्तर: (ग) मिश्र वाक्य। 'भएकाले' भन्ने कारणबोधक योजकले आश्रित उपवाक्य ('ऊ बिरामी भएकाले') र प्रधान उपवाक्य ('आज विद्यालय आएन') जोडेको छ, त्यसैले यो मिश्र वाक्य हो।

questions.prompt: सन्धि भनेको के हो? स्वरसन्धिका कुनै दुई नियम उदाहरणसहित लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
दुई वर्ण आपसमा मिल्दा हुने स्वाभाविक ध्वनि परिवर्तनलाई सन्धि भनिन्छ।
नियम १ — अ/आ + इ/ई = ए: जस्तै 'रमा + ईश = रमेश', 'गण + ईश = गणेश'।
नियम २ — अ/आ + उ/ऊ = ओ: जस्तै 'सूर्य + उदय = सूर्योदय', 'महा + उत्सव = महोत्सव'।
यसरी पहिलो स्वर र दोस्रो स्वर मिलेर नयाँ संयुक्त स्वर बन्छ।

questions.prompt: प्रत्यक्ष कथनलाई अप्रत्यक्ष कथनमा बदल्नुहोस्: (क) उसले भन्यो, 'म भोलि काठमाडौँ जान्छु।' (ख) शिक्षकले सोध्नुभयो, 'तिमीहरूले गृहकार्य गर्यौ?'
questions.solution:
(क) अप्रत्यक्ष: 'उसले आफू भोलिपल्ट काठमाडौँ जाने कुरा बतायो।' — 'म' → 'आफू', वर्तमान 'जान्छु' → सामान्य भूत/अपूर्ण 'जाने', 'भोलि' → 'भोलिपल्ट'।
(ख) अप्रत्यक्ष: 'शिक्षकले विद्यार्थीहरूले गृहकार्य गरे-नगरेको सोध्नुभयो।' — प्रश्नवाचक वाक्य 'कि/भनेर' संरचनामा बदलिन्छ, 'तिमीहरू' → 'विद्यार्थीहरू', क्रिया भूतकालमा सर्छ।

questions.prompt: 'पुस्तकालयको महत्त्व' विषयमा करिब १५० शब्दको अनुच्छेद लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution: नमुना उत्तर: 'पुस्तकालय ज्ञानको भण्डार हो। यसले विद्यार्थीलाई पाठ्यपुस्तकबाहेकका विविध पुस्तक पढ्ने अवसर दिन्छ, जसले शब्दभण्डार र चिन्तनशक्ति बढाउँछ। पुस्तकालयको शान्त वातावरणले एकाग्र भएर अध्ययन गर्ने बानी बसाउँछ। साथै, इन्टरनेट नभएका ठाउँमा पनि पुस्तकालयले निःशुल्क ज्ञान पुर्‍याउँछ। त्यसैले हरेक विद्यालयमा समृद्ध पुस्तकालय हुनु आवश्यक छ।' जाँच: विषयवाक्य सुरुमा, तीन-चार सहयोगी वाक्य बीचमा, निष्कर्ष अन्त्यमा।

questions.prompt: औपचारिक निवेदनमा तलको कुन संयोजन सही हो? (क) 'नमस्ते' … 'बाइ' (ख) 'श्रीमान्' … 'भवदीय' (ग) 'ए साथी' … 'चियर्स'
questions.solution: सही उत्तर: (ख)। औपचारिक निवेदन 'श्रीमान्' (वा 'महोदय') सम्बोधनबाट सुरु हुन्छ र 'भवदीय' वा 'निवेदक' बन्दनले सकिन्छ। (क) र (ग) अनौपचारिक शैली हुन्।

questions.prompt: आफ्नो विद्यालयका प्रधानाध्यापकलाई चरित्र प्रमाणपत्र माग गर्दै निवेदन लेख्नुहोस् (नाम, कक्षा, रोल नम्बर र कारणसहित)।
questions.solution: संरचना: माथि निवेदकको ठेगाना र मिति; त्यसपछि प्राप्तकर्ता (प्रधानाध्यापक, विद्यालयको नाम-ठेगाना); विषय ('विषय: चरित्र प्रमाणपत्र उपलब्ध गराइपाऊँ।'); सम्बोधन ('श्रीमान्,'); शरीर — (१) परिचय: नाम, कक्षा १२, रोल नं.; (२) कारण: छात्रवृत्ति/रोजगारीका लागि आवश्यक; (३) विनम्र अनुरोध र धन्यवाद; अन्त्यमा 'भवदीय' सहीछाप-नाम-रोल नम्बर। भाषा शिष्ट र तथ्यपरक हुनुपर्छ।

questions.prompt: 'सामाजिक सञ्जाल: वरदान कि अभिशाप?' विषयमा निबन्धको रूपरेखा (थेसिस + तीन मुख्य बुँदा, प्रत्येकसँग एक सहयोगी विवरण) लेख्नुहोस्।
questions.solution:
थेसिस: सामाजिक सञ्जाल शक्तिशाली साधन हो — अनुशासित प्रयोगमा वरदान, नियन्त्रणबाहिर अभिशाप।
बुँदा १ — सम्पर्क: टाढिएका परिवार जोड्छ, परीक्षा तयारी समूह सम्भव बनाउँछ।
बुँदा २ — ज्ञान: गाउँसम्म निःशुल्क ट्युटोरियल र समाचार पुर्‍याउँछ।
बुँदा ३ — हानि: लत लाग्ने डिजाइन र तुलना संस्कृतिले ध्यान र आत्मविश्वास घटाउँछ।
निष्कर्ष: समयसीमा र उद्देश्यपूर्ण प्रयोगले वरदानलाई अभिशापमाथि जिताउँछ।

questions.question: In a series LCR circuit at resonance: (A) $X_L > X_C$ (B) $X_L = X_C$ and the power factor is unity (C) impedance is maximum (D) current is minimum
questions.solution:
At resonance $X_L = X_C$, so they cancel: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = R$, which is the minimum possible impedance.

Current is then maximum, $I = V/R$, and the phase angle is zero, so $\cos\phi = 1$. Answer (B).

questions.question: The peak value of the $220\,\mathrm{V}$ mains supply (rms) is about: (A) $110\,\mathrm{V}$ (B) $220\,\mathrm{V}$ (C) $311\,\mathrm{V}$ (D) $440\,\mathrm{V}$
questions.solution:
$V_0 = \sqrt2\,V_{\mathrm{rms}} = 1.414 \times 220 \approx 311\,\mathrm{V}$. Answer (C).

The insulation of appliances must withstand this peak, not just the quoted rms value.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the average power dissipated in a series AC circuit, $P = V_{\mathrm{rms}} I_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\phi$, and explain what is meant by wattless current.
questions.solution:
With $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, the instantaneous power is $p = vi = V_0I_0\sin\omega t\,\sin(\omega t-\phi)$.

Using $\sin A\sin B = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(A-B) - \cos(A+B)]$: $p = \frac{V_0I_0}{2}[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)]$.

The cosine term averages to zero over a cycle, so $\bar{P} = \frac{V_0I_0}{2}\cos\phi = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{I_0}{\sqrt2}\cos\phi = V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}\cos\phi$.

$\cos\phi$ is the power factor. If $\phi = 90^\circ$ (pure inductor or capacitor) the average power is zero even though a large current flows; such a current is called wattless current — it only shuttles energy back and forth between source and reactive element.

questions.question: A series circuit has $L = 1\,\mathrm{H}$ and $C = 1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. Find the resonant frequency. What happens to the current at resonance if the resistance is small?
questions.solution:
At resonance $X_L = X_C$: $\omega L = \frac{1}{\omega C}$, so $\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ and $f = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.

$LC = 1 \times 1\times10^{-6} = 1\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^2}$, so $\sqrt{LC} = 1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}$ and $f = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 10^{-3}} \approx 159\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

At resonance $Z = R$, so the current peaks at $V/R$. With small $R$ the peak is very sharp and large — the circuit is highly selective, which is how a radio tuner picks out one station.

questions.question: Why is a choke coil preferred over a resistor for reducing current in an AC circuit?
questions.solution:
A choke is an inductor of large self-inductance and negligible resistance. Its reactance $X_L = \omega L$ limits the current without dissipating power, because in a pure inductance the current lags the voltage by $90^\circ$ and the average power is $V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}\cos 90^\circ = 0$.

A resistor would reduce the current equally well but would dissipate $I^2R$ as heat, wasting energy and heating the appliance.

A real choke has small resistance, so only a little power is lost; that is why chokes are used in tube lights and fans rather than series resistors.

questions.question: (a) Draw the phasor diagram for a series LCR circuit and derive the expression for impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$. (b) A series circuit with $R = 30\,\Omega$, $X_L = 70\,\Omega$ and $X_C = 30\,\Omega$ is connected to a $220\,\mathrm{V}$, $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ supply. Find $Z$, the current, the phase angle and the power consumed.
questions.solution:
(a) Take current as the reference phasor. $V_R$ is in phase with $I$; $V_L$ leads by $90^\circ$; $V_C$ lags by $90^\circ$. Since $V_L$ and $V_C$ are opposite, the resultant reactive voltage is $(V_L - V_C)$ perpendicular to $V_R$.

So $V^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2 = I^2R^2 + I^2(X_L - X_C)^2$, giving $V = I\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L-X_C)^2}$ and hence $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L-X_C)^2}$ with $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$.

(b) $X_L - X_C = 70 - 30 = 40\,\Omega$, so $Z = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\,\Omega$.

Current: $I = V/Z = 220/50 = 4.4\,\mathrm{A}$.

Phase angle: $\tan\phi = 40/30 = 1.333$, so $\phi \approx 53^\circ$ — the current lags the voltage (inductive circuit).

Power: $P = I^2R = (4.4)^2 \times 30 = 581\,\mathrm{W}$ (equivalently $VI\cos\phi = 220 \times 4.4 \times 0.6 = 581\,\mathrm{W}$).

questions.question: The bandwidth required for an amplitude-modulated wave with modulating frequency $f_m$ is: (A) $f_m$ (B) $2f_m$ (C) $f_m/2$ (D) zero
questions.solution:
An AM wave carries the carrier plus two sidebands at $f_c + f_m$ and $f_c - f_m$.

Bandwidth $= (f_c + f_m) - (f_c - f_m) = 2f_m$. Answer (B).

questions.question: Ground wave propagation is best suited for: (A) very high frequency signals (B) low frequency signals (C) satellite communication (D) line-of-sight links
questions.solution:
Ground waves travel along the surface and are attenuated strongly as frequency rises, so they serve long-distance low-frequency and medium-wave broadcast (up to a few MHz).

Higher frequencies do not diffract around the curvature of the Earth and need line of sight. Answer (B).

questions.question: Why is modulation necessary in communication? A carrier of $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ is used; find the minimum height of a transmitting antenna.
questions.solution:
Two reasons. (i) Radiation: an antenna must be comparable with $\lambda/4$ to radiate efficiently, and a baseband audio signal (kHz) would need an antenna kilometres long; adding a high-frequency carrier reduces the required height. (ii) Multiplexing and noise: different stations can share the medium by using different carriers, and a high-frequency carrier can carry the information over long distances.

Wavelength: $\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3\times10^{8}}{1\times10^{6}} = 300\,\mathrm{m}$.

Minimum antenna height $\approx \frac{\lambda}{4} = 75\,\mathrm{m}$ — practical for a mast, unlike the tens of kilometres a $1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ baseband signal would need.

questions.question: Distinguish between sky wave and space wave propagation. Why is satellite communication limited to frequencies above about $30\,\mathrm{MHz}$?
questions.solution:
Sky waves are reflected by the ionosphere and can travel beyond the horizon by successive hops; this works only below about $30\,\mathrm{MHz}$, because higher frequencies pass straight through the ionosphere.

Space waves travel in a straight line from transmitter to receiver, are not reflected by the ionosphere, and require line of sight — used for VHF/UHF television, microwave links and satellites.

Below $30\,\mathrm{MHz}$ the ionosphere reflects the signal back to Earth rather than letting it reach the satellite, and the ionosphere also introduces severe distortion; hence satellite links use microwaves and above.

questions.question: Explain how an optical fibre carries a signal, and give two advantages over a coaxial cable.
questions.solution:
Light from a laser or LED enters the core (higher refractive index) surrounded by cladding of lower index. Striking the core–cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, the ray suffers total internal reflection repeatedly and is guided along the fibre with very little loss.

Advantages: enormous bandwidth (a single fibre carries thousands of telephone channels) and very low attenuation, so repeaters can be far apart; also immunity to electromagnetic interference and no cross-talk, since the signal is light rather than current.

questions.question: (a) Draw the block diagram of a communication system and explain the function of each block. (b) A message signal of $5\,\mathrm{kHz}$ is amplitude-modulated on a $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ carrier. State the frequencies present in the modulated wave and the bandwidth used.

questions.diagramCaption: Figure: block diagram of a communication system — information source, modulator, transmitter, channel, receiver with demodulator, and destination.
questions.solution:
(a) Information source produces the message (speech, data, picture). The modulator superimposes it on a high-frequency carrier, changing the carrier's amplitude (AM), frequency (FM) or phase (PM). The transmitter amplifies the modulated wave and feeds the antenna.

The channel is the physical medium — free space, coaxial cable, optical fibre — and is where noise enters. The receiver picks up the wave, amplifies it and the demodulator recovers the original message, which the destination (loudspeaker, screen, computer) presents.

(b) AM produces three components: the carrier at $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$, the upper sideband at $1\,\mathrm{MHz} + 5\,\mathrm{kHz} = 1.005\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and the lower sideband at $0.995\,\mathrm{MHz}$.

Bandwidth $= 2f_m = 2 \times 5\,\mathrm{kHz} = 10\,\mathrm{kHz}$. Suppressing the carrier and one sideband (SSB) would cut this to $5\,\mathrm{kHz}$ and save transmitter power.

questions.prompt: State Kirchhoff's laws. Use Kirchhoff's voltage law to derive the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge with resistances $P, Q, R, S$ (galvanometer between the junctions carries no current at balance).
questions.solution:
Kirchhoff's current law: the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero ($\sum I = 0$, charge conservation). Kirchhoff's voltage law: the algebraic sum of voltages round any closed loop is zero ($\sum V = 0$, energy conservation).
Label the bridge ABCD with battery across A–C and galvanometer across B–D. At balance $I_g = 0$, so the current $I_1$ through P also flows through Q, and $I_2$ through R also flows through S.
Loop ABD: $-I_1 P + I_2 R = 0$, so $I_1 P = I_2 R$. Loop BCD: $-I_1 Q + I_2 S = 0$, so $I_1 Q = I_2 S$. Dividing gives $P/Q = R/S$ — the balance condition. Equivalently $P/Q = R/S$ lets the unknown resistance be found from three known ones.

questions.prompt: A wire of resistance $12\,\Omega$ is bent into a circle. What is the effective resistance between the ends of any diameter?
questions.solution: Bending into a circle splits the wire into two semicircular halves, each of resistance $12/2 = 6\,\Omega$. The ends of a diameter connect these two halves in parallel, so $1/R_{\text{eq}} = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3$, giving $R_{\text{eq}} = 3\,\Omega$.

questions.prompt: Define drift velocity. Derive the relation $I = neAv_d$ between current and drift velocity, and explain why the drift speed is small even though electric signals travel fast.
questions.solution:
Drift velocity $v_d$ is the slow average velocity superimposed on electrons' random thermal motion by an applied electric field.
In time $t$, electrons within length $v_d t$ of a cross-section $A$ pass through it: volume $Av_d t$, number $nAv_d t$ (with $n$ = free electrons per unit volume), charge $neAv_d t$. Hence $I = Q/t = neAv_d$.
$v_d$ is of order $10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ because electrons collide constantly with lattice ions. Signals travel near light speed because the electric field propagates through the wire almost instantly and pushes every free electron simultaneously — individual electrons still drift slowly.

questions.prompt: A cell of emf $E = 6\,\mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $r = 1\,\Omega$ drives current through an external resistor $R$. (a) Find $R$ for maximum power delivered to it and the value of that power. (b) Show the efficiency at maximum power transfer is 50%.
questions.solution:
(a) Current $I = E/(R + r)$. Power in $R$: $P = I^2 R = E^2 R/(R+r)^2$. Maximising over $R$: $dP/dR = E^2[(R+r)^2 - 2R(R+r)]/(R+r)^4 = 0$ gives $R + r - 2R = 0$, i.e. $R = r = 1\,\Omega$ (maximum power transfer theorem).
$P_{\max} = E^2 r/(2r)^2 = E^2/4r = 36/4 = 9\,\mathrm{W}$.
(b) Power supplied by the cell: $P_{\text{total}} = EI = E^2/(R+r) = 36/2 = 18\,\mathrm{W}$. Efficiency $\eta = P/P_{\text{total}} = 9/18 = 0.5$, i.e. 50% — half the power is wasted heating the internal resistance.

questions.question: A wire of resistance $R$ is stretched to double its length at constant volume. Its new resistance is: (A) $R/2$ (B) $2R$ (C) $4R$ (D) $R$
questions.solution:
Volume is constant, so $A' = A/2$ when $l' = 2l$.

$R' = \rho\frac{l'}{A'} = \rho\frac{2l}{A/2} = 4\rho\frac{l}{A} = 4R$. Resistivity $\rho$ is unchanged — it is a property of the material, not the shape. Answer (C).

questions.question: A cell of emf $12\,\mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $1\,\Omega$ delivers a current of $2\,\mathrm{A}$. The terminal potential difference is: (A) $12\,\mathrm{V}$ (B) $10\,\mathrm{V}$ (C) $14\,\mathrm{V}$ (D) $6\,\mathrm{V}$
questions.solution:
$V = \varepsilon - Ir = 12 - (2)(1) = 10\,\mathrm{V}$. Answer (B).

The $2\,\mathrm{V}$ "lost" is the drop across the internal resistance; it appears as heat inside the cell.

questions.question: Define drift velocity and derive the relation $I = neAv_d$. A copper wire of cross-section $1.0\,\mathrm{mm^2}$ carries $1.0\,\mathrm{A}$; if $n = 8.5\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, find the drift speed and explain why it is so small.
questions.solution:
Drift velocity is the average velocity with which free electrons move along the wire under an applied field, opposite to the field.

In time $t$ every electron in a length $v_d t$ crosses a section, so the charge crossing is $q = neA v_d t$, giving $I = q/t = neAv_d$.

$v_d = \frac{I}{neA} = \frac{1.0}{(8.5\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})(1.0\times10^{-6})} = \frac{1.0}{1.36\times10^{4}} \approx 7.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The drift speed is tiny because electrons collide constantly with the lattice (mean free path ~$10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m}$) and their motion is a slow random walk with a small superimposed drift. The lamp still lights instantly because the electric field — and hence the push on every electron — is set up along the wire at nearly the speed of light.

questions.question: State the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge and derive it. Why is the bridge unsuitable for measuring very low resistances?
questions.solution:
Four resistances $P, Q, R, S$ form a quadrilateral; a cell is connected across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection, and then $\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$.

At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so $B$ and $D$ are at the same potential: $V_A - V_B = V_A - V_D$ and $V_B - V_C = V_D - V_C$. With current $I_1$ through $P$ and $Q$, and $I_2$ through $R$ and $S$: $I_1P = I_2R$ and $I_1Q = I_2S$. Dividing, $\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$; the unknown arm is found from the three known ones.

For very low resistances the resistance of the connecting wires and contact resistance become comparable with the unknown, so the ratio is no longer reliable. A metre bridge or a Kelvin double bridge is used instead.

questions.question: A potentiometer wire of length $10\,\mathrm{m}$ has a resistance of $20\,\Omega$ and carries $0.1\,\mathrm{A}$. A cell balances against $60\,\mathrm{cm}$ of the wire. Find the emf of the cell, and state one advantage of a potentiometer over a voltmeter.
questions.solution:
Potential gradient: $k = \frac{I R}{L} = \frac{0.1 \times 20}{10} = 0.2\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$.

Balancing length $l = 0.60\,\mathrm{m}$, so $\varepsilon = k l = 0.2 \times 0.60 = 0.12\,\mathrm{V}$.

Advantage: at balance the cell draws no current, so the potentiometer measures the true emf; a voltmeter always draws some current and reads the terminal voltage $\varepsilon - Ir$, which is less than the emf.

questions.question: (a) State Kirchhoff's laws for an electrical network. (b) Two cells of emf $12\,\mathrm{V}$ (internal resistance $1\,\Omega$) and $6\,\mathrm{V}$ ($0.5\,\Omega$) are connected in parallel across a $4\,\Omega$ resistor. Find the current through the resistor and through each cell.
questions.solution:
(a) Junction rule: the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero (conservation of charge). Loop rule: around any closed loop the algebraic sum of potential differences is zero (conservation of energy).

(b) Let $I_1$ flow from the $12\,\mathrm{V}$ cell and $I_2$ from the $6\,\mathrm{V}$ cell into the resistor, so the resistor current is $I = I_1 + I_2$.

Loop with $12\,\mathrm{V}$ cell and the resistor: $12 - 1I_1 - 4(I_1 + I_2) = 0 \Rightarrow 5I_1 + 4I_2 = 12$.

Loop with $6\,\mathrm{V}$ cell: $6 - 0.5I_2 - 4(I_1 + I_2) = 0 \Rightarrow 4I_1 + 4.5I_2 = 6$.

Solving: from the first, $I_1 = (12 - 4I_2)/5$. Substituting, $4(12-4I_2)/5 + 4.5I_2 = 6 \Rightarrow 48 - 16I_2 + 22.5I_2 = 30 \Rightarrow 6.5I_2 = -18$, so $I_2 = -2.77\,\mathrm{A}$ (the $6\,\mathrm{V}$ cell is being charged, current driven into it). Then $I_1 = (12 + 11.08)/5 = 4.62\,\mathrm{A}$ and $I = I_1 + I_2 = 1.85\,\mathrm{A}$.

Check with the terminal voltage: $V = 4 \times 1.85 = 7.4\,\mathrm{V}$; the $12\,\mathrm{V}$ cell gives $12 - 4.62 = 7.4\,\mathrm{V}$ and the $6\,\mathrm{V}$ cell gives $6 + 2.77\times0.5 = 7.4\,\mathrm{V}$, confirming the result.
